title: $1.6M DOD Grant Enables Researchers to Expand Digital Mental Health Support for Dementia Caregivers
summary: For more than 11 million Americans who provide unpaid care for a loved one living with dementia, the daily emotional, mental, and physical demands can feel overwhelming. Among them are hundreds of thousands of active-duty service members, military spouses, and veterans who carry the heavy responsibility of dementia caregiving. To help meet this critical need, an interdisciplinary team of researchers across the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences has secured a $1.6M grant from the U.S. Department of Defense to expand accessible digital mental health interventions tailored specifically for family members caring for a loved one with dementia. Individuals supported by this program may include veterans and military families, but the program also supports civilian family caregivers who feel some kind of distress from their caregiving role. The project also provides brief online mental health training for the person living with dementia. Led by Beth Fauth, professor and director of the state-funded Alzheimer’s Disease and Dementia Research Center, the DOD-funded project builds on years of clinical research that adapts Acceptance and Commitment Therapy to support dementia caregivers. ACT is a form of psychotherapy that uses acceptance, mindfulness, and values-based strategies to promote mental health and psychological flexibility. The initiative aims to make evidence-based mental health support accessible to families across the country. “Traditional caregiver interventions do a wonderful job of teaching skills and disease management, and support groups are very valuable, but a lot of caregiver programs cannot actively build skills to teach caregivers how to cope with the emotional and psychological toll more effectively,” Fauth said. “By supporting this project, the DOD is helping us evaluate whether an online, self-guided therapeutic tool can help dementia caregivers with their emotional health as well as their physical health behaviors and relationships. We also use a brief version of the tool to help the person living with dementia manage their own stress, if they are able to participate.” ACT for Caregivers directly addresses the emotional burden on caregivers. Rather than trying to eliminate stress — which is often impossible — the intervention teaches caregivers how to live alongside it. Participants learn skills to notice and accept difficult thoughts and emotions, clarify their personal values, and take meaningful action even in the presence of ongoing hardship. “It’s not about making the stress go away, because for someone providing love and care to someone with dementia, it is a difficult role to be in even with support and resources,” Fauth said. “Our program is designed to teach skills to help caregivers live with their stressful situation more comfortably.” Delivering the program as a self-guided digital mental health intervention removes barriers for caregivers who cannot easily leave home, afford traditional therapy, or find time for clinic visits. The newly funded initiative brings together expertise across several departments and centers within the college. Fauth oversees the project’s caregiving application and serves as the intervention lead. Michael Levin from the Department of Psychology helped repackage the traditional therapist-delivered ACT into a self-guided digital format. Community engagement is directed by Ty Aller and Heather Kelley, both researchers for the Center for Mental Health Promotion within the Institute for Disability Research, Policy & Practice. A key aspect of this proposal is including people with lived experience in dementia, caregiving, the military, or rural contexts, and the IDRPP’s expertise in working with people living with chronic conditions and caregiving for someone are critical to the success of this project. Senior researcher Alyson Ward and the Tailored Research, Evaluation, and Continuous Improvement team at the IDRPP will evaluate program outcomes. To ensure the self-guided intervention resonates with caregivers, including military and veteran families, the Center for Mental Health Promotion is embedding teams of caregivers and community stakeholders directly into the project to guide how the intervention is shaped and delivered. “We need people from those communities informing us on what works best,” Aller said. Community partners include the University of Massachusetts Boston and the University of Alaska Anchorage because each group has military family networks. Also, a Utah-based active-duty veteran, Mike Spencer, is contributing his military and dementia-support experiences to lead the community stakeholder panel, building an essential connection between research projects and people with lived experience. As the study moves forward, the team’s goal is to establish a resource that clinics, veterans’ service organizations, and family networks can rely on long after the grant concludes. “It’s amazing what this program can do for both caregivers and individuals with dementia,” Kelley said. “In our pilot work, I’ve interviewed folks who have called the program ‘life-changing’ and reported real improvements in their quality of life. This grant will allow us to get this program to more individuals and families who need the support.” Aller added: “We hope families and community partners come away knowing that real, effective supports exist for veterans and for all dementia caregivers. They are cost-effective and they can reach people in diverse locations.”

title: A Wider Lens: Winners announced for 2026 Field Season Photo Contest
summary: For the last five years, the Quinney Field Season Photo Contest has showcased research, fieldwork, travel, and hands-on learning from students, faculty, and staff taken during the summer field season. This year’s entries captured a wide range of experiences, including starry landscapes, hungry wildlife, flipped perspectives, and Aggie adventures around the world. Winners this year were recognized in five categories — landscapes, animals, people, closeups, and “Awesome, Awkward, and Amazing” — along with a Dean’s Choice Award selected by the dean of the Quinney College, Derek McLean. This year's Dean's Choice goes to Sam Thompson for a striking image of a horseback rider trailing a herd of cattle across a dusty sagebrush range. The photograph captures the energy of people working in the West, along with the dramatic light and natural colors of the landscape. Other winners include: Landscape : Landon Huter for his transcendent image of cowboy camping under a stellar summer night sky and the Milky Way. Animals : Adam Hess for his serendipitous timing, a Western kingbird poised to ingest an unlucky insect. People : Adrian Bastidas for an image of a determined hiker heading away into a green wild. Closeup : Madaline Buttars for an upward perspective of some tenacious and elegant mushrooms sharing space with a carpet of moss. Awesome, Awkward and Amazing : Chase Bonnett for a cleverly framed and flipped view of a geometrical world. See the complete gallery of photo entries from this year’s contest. “I love seeing the huge variety of experiences our students, staff, and faculty find in their own communities and around the world,” said Stacie Denetsosie, contest coordinator and one of five judges on the panel. “Every year I’m impressed that so many students are seeking experiences that build their skills and push them out of their comfort zones.” The stories behind the photos are often as impressive as the images themselves. Huter, an undergraduate student from the Department of Wildland Resources, captured his photo when he and a friend found their way to the top of a ridge in the White Cloud mountains in the middle of the night, after a long drive from Nampa, Idaho. “We were planning to hike to the top of a nearby peak in the morning,” Huter said. “We arrived at the top of the ridge in complete darkness — or at least it seemed so. Once we got out of the car and our eyes adjusted, the stunning scene of the milky way over the 11,000-foot peaks appeared. We set up a cowboy camp behind the 4-runner, and I used my new camera to take the image.” A thunderstorm rolled into the area at 4 a.m., forcing the two to descend for fear of being struck by lightning. “Since we arrived after dark, and left before sunup, we never got to see the peaks with our own eyes. That photo is all I have from the trip.” Huter has won a category in the contest for two consecutive years. This college-wide contest has drawn a remarkable range of submissions since it began in 2022 — from stunning landscapes, to world travel adventures, to close-up views of the natural world at work, letting Aggies from across the university showcase their diversity and skills with the camera. The winning photos and some runners-up will be showcased on social media and added to the gallery wall located in the Natural Resource building atrium on USU’s Logan Campus. Next year’s contest will launch at the start of the fall semester.

title: Alder Family Makes $2.5 Million Gift to Support Utah State Athletics
summary: LOGAN, Utah — From the generosity of two lifelong Aggies, Kent and Donna Alder, Utah State University Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker announced a transformative $2.5 million investment in Aggie athletics on Wednesday. In recognition of their impact on the athletics department, the club space in the West Stadium Center at Maverik Stadium will be named the Alder Champions Club. The Alders' gift marks the second major commitment the athletics department has received in the past month, bringing $5 million in major commitments since the announcement of the Show Me initiative. "Kent and Donna Alder are among the most passionate supporters of Utah State University, Aggie Athletics, and the Cache Valley community," Walker said. "The Alders' gift reflects their belief in what we are building as a department and a commitment to help us reach new heights as we move into the new Pac-12. It will be commitments like this and others that help us continue our pursuit of excellence." Read more at UtahStateAggies.com .

title: An Olympic Legacy: USU Researchers Outline Opportunities for Cleaner Air Ahead of 2034 Games
summary: As Utah prepares to welcome the world for the 2034 Winter Olympics, three Utah State University researchers say the games could provide an opportunity to create lasting improvements to Utah’s air quality. In a new article published in Sustainability and Climate Change, USU researchers Edwin Stafford, Roslynn Brain, and Randy Martin outline eight opportunities Utah could pursue to reduce the risk of poor air quality during the 2034 Games and build a lasting clean-air legacy. “My research has found that the Olympics gives you a political lever with which to get things done,” Stafford said. “That’s what makes the Olympics an innovative opportunity for lasting change.” Their recommendations include: Electrifying transportation and buildings. Expanding electric vehicle charging infrastructure. Increasing renewable electricity generation. Investing in clean-air education. Expanding air-quality monitoring. Restoring the Great Salt Lake. Enhancing green infrastructure. “The Olympics puts Salt Lake and the Wasatch Front on a global stage that will hopefully motivate people to take some steps that we probably should be taking anyway,” said Martin, a professor in USU’s Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “We’ve got to get into the mindset of thinking about these alternatives, and maybe the Olympics can help move us in that direction.” Utah’s winter inversions can trap pollutants in the valleys for days at a time. Martin compares an inversion to a sealed bathtub, where pollutants accumulate until a storm or other weather system clears them. “There’s not much we can do about the actual setup of the inversion or its strength, but we can certainly modify what we put into it,” Martin said. The researchers suggest that the eight years leading up to the games provide time to begin making those changes. Martin said he would particularly like to see Utah expand its air-quality monitoring network around Olympic venues well before 2034, allowing researchers to track pollution levels and measure changes before, during, and after the games. Education is another piece of the researchers’ approach. Stafford, a professor of marketing in the USU Huntsman School of Business, and Brain, a sustainable communities professor and USU Extension specialist, lead the Utah High School Clean Air Marketing Contest, which has educated Utah high school students and their families about air pollution since 2015. This year, they are adding an Olympics edition to the contest, giving students a chance to create public service announcements that connect clean air with the 2034 Games. “We’re hoping the kids will come up with even better ways to tie Olympic themes with some of the big initiatives that are necessary for us to get our air cleaned up by 2034,” Stafford said. Stafford said involving young people now is particularly meaningful because today's high school students will be adults by the time Utah hosts the Olympics and could be among the volunteers and community members participating in the games. The eight recommendations are intended as a starting point for conversation and action. The researchers hope the Olympics can provide momentum for changes that benefit Utah long after the competition ends. “Pursuing the air quality opportunities outlined here will demonstrate to the world that Utahns took bold stewardship of their air, not just for the games, but as an Olympic legacy as well,” the researchers wrote. The article, “The Utah 2034 Winter Olympics: Leaving a Lasting Clean Air Legacy,” was published in Sustainability and Climate Change by Stafford, Brain, and Martin in August 2026.

title: Ask an Expert — 2026 Fall Yard and Garden Tips
summary: Autumn is officially here, and there is much to look forward to — pumpkins on the porch, apple cider, cooler temperatures, and walks through crunchy leaves. But before you get too comfortable, don’t forget there are yard and garden end-of-season tasks to complete. Here are tips from the Utah State University Extension Gardeners Almanac to help. Included are links to fact sheets and videos for more information. Learn about average first and last frost dates around the state. Consider adding a smaller structure, such as a low tunnel , or a larger high tunnel to extend your growing season. Learn how and when to harvest winter squash and store it in a cool (50-55 degrees F), dry location. Plant garlic cloves from mid-October through early November. Refer to this list of fall cleanup chores and good landscape practices to get your yard ready for winter. Remove vegetable plants from the garden once harvest is complete to reduce overwintering sites for insect pests. Protect tomatoes from early frost by covering the plants with a blanket or tarp. Place mulch over carrots , beets , and parsnips to prevent the ground around them from freezing. Rototill leaves, compost , or manure into the vegetable garden to enhance soil microbe activity. Prune roses by heading back excessively long canes to prevent damage from heavy snow loads. Cut back ornamental grasses in snow-prone areas once the foliage has died down. Otherwise, leave them until spring and enjoy the vertical accent during the winter. Plant spring-blooming bulbs through early November. Plant trees and shrubs in the fall to enhance root establishment. Dig tender perennials such as gladiolas, dahlias, begonias, and canna lilies after the foliage has died down, and store them in a cool (45-50 degrees F), dry place. Protect trunks of young trees from winter cracking by wrapping them with a white reflective tree wrap. Dig and remove annual flowers. Plant cold-hardy annuals, including pansies, primrose, kale , and ornamental cabbage. Prune raspberry canes to the ground after they have fruited. Control tough perennial weeds such as field bindweed (a.k.a. morning glory). Refer to this list of weed control options . Mow grass to a height of 1 to 1½ inches at the end of the season to minimize disease problems. Apply a quick-release nitrogen fertilizer after the last mowing (late October to early November) for early greening next spring. Pests and Problems Send diseased vegetable plants and leaves to the local landfill. Use burlap or other soft materials to wrap evergreens to prevent snow breakage. Treat stone fruits (cherries, peaches, nectarines, apricots, and plums) for coryneum blight at 50% leaf drop. Clean up and discard all fallen fruit to reduce overwintering sites for disease and insect pests. To see a video of the October Gardener’s Almanac tips, click here . Consider taking a USU Extension online gardening course . Courses cover topics such as container vegetable gardening, creating the perfect soil, planting trees, and controlling pests. Courses are geared toward both beginning and professional gardeners. Explore more gardening tips on Extension’s yard and garden website .

title: Ask an Expert — Be Ready: What to Do If You Need to Evacuate
summary: With wildfires threatening communities across the state, evacuation orders can happen with little warning. Preparing your household now can help you evacuate quickly and safely if it becomes necessary. Assemble grab-and-go kits. The Ready.Gov website offers printable instructions for building a basic disaster supply kit, including: Water : one gallon per person per day for three days for drinking and sanitation. Food : at least a three-day supply of non-perishable food per person. Sleeping bag or warm blanket. Change of clothes. Cash (small bills). Battery, solar or hand-cranked radio. Flashlight, extra batteries. First-aid kit. Portable power bank or solar charger. Whistle (to signal for help). Dust mask (to help filter contaminated air). Plastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape for sheltering in place . Moist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties as well as soap, hand sanitizer and disinfecting wipes. Personal hygiene items. Cell phone with chargers and a backup battery or solar charger. Prescriptions and other medications. Pet food, water and supplies. Infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and other supplies. A complete change of clothing for each person, including underwear and sturdy shoes. Mess kits, paper cups, plates, paper towels and plastic utensils. Paper and pencil plus books, games, puzzles and activities for children. Ensure that a copy of your important documents, such as birth certificates, insurance policies and financial records, is easily accessible. Identify emergency meeting spots and practice going there regularly. Make sure at least one family member knows first aid and CPR. Write down or memorize all family members’ contact information, including phone numbers and birthdates. Have a family communication plan. Review and practice the plan regularly. Be sure to involve children and youth in preparedness efforts. Research shows that youth who are involved experience less stress and anxiety during and after an emergency. Visit USU Extension’s preparedness website for additional emergency preparedness information.

title: Ask an Expert — Family Meals Matter: Strengthening Connections One Meal at a Time
summary: September marks National Family Meals Month, providing an excellent opportunity to establish the tradition of consistent family meals at home. Regular family mealtimes can benefit the entire family. Utah State University Extension experts note that the more meals a family shares each week, the greater the benefit. In addition, children who participate in family mealtimes five or more times a week, compared with those whose families eat together two or fewer times each week, may experience improved: Nutrition and physical development — Children who participate in family mealtimes tend to be more open to trying a variety of healthy foods and develop healthy eating habits that last into adulthood. Family mealtime is an excellent opportunity to provide nutrient-rich foods such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and calcium-rich foods. The variety of nutrients consumed at these mealtimes has been shown to lower rates of childhood obesity, reduce the risk of chronic diseases, and increase the likelihood that youth will make healthier food choices when away from home. Emotional development — Children and adolescents who participate in routine family mealtime can better navigate emotions and mental wellness, are less likely to develop eating disorders, and have more positive interactions with food and others. This can also be a protective factor for adolescents, reducing the severity of depression and suicidal ideation and improving overall well-being. Social development — Children and youth can learn important social skills, such as taking turns and sharing thoughts, feelings, and opinions appropriately. They can also learn to connect more effectively and often discover a deeper sense of belonging. Academics — Children and adolescents who participate in and listen to family mealtime conversations are more likely to earn good grades in school and develop larger vocabularies — even more than those who read together with their parents. Behavior — Although many factors influence adolescent risky behavior, there is evidence that routine family meals may serve as a protective factor against certain risky behaviors such as substance use, sexual activity, and violence. If eating meals together regularly is new to your family and feels overwhelming, start slowly. You could start with one or two meals a week. If dinner doesn’t fit your family's schedule, try having breakfast, lunch, or even snack time together. Remember that each opportunity to sit around the table together provides many benefits. Here are tips for making family mealtime a positive experience: Make weekly meal plans. Schedule a set time for meals. Involve all family members in meal preparation and cleanup. Set boundaries to create more connections, such as not having electronic devices at the table or encouraging everyone to sit together until the last person has finished. Keep conversations upbeat and leave discipline and negative emotions for another time. Share responsibilities with young children. The parent or caretaker’s responsibility is to decide when the meal is served and what food is provided, while the child’s responsibility is to decide how much food they want. Get creative. Have mealtime themes (i.e., taco Tuesday), try new recipes, create a conversation jar, play word games, share stories, etc. A healthy goal for family mealtime is to connect and nourish. That will look different at each table, so have fun this month and find new family traditions that make mealtimes positive. Download the Create Better Health Family Mealtime Cookbook , which includes recipes, conversation starters, meal-planning tips and ideas, and additional information on the benefits of regular family mealtimes.

title: Ask an Expert — Five Ways to Help Someone Struggling With Mental Health
summary: Observant family members can be the first responders to mental health or substance use concerns. Recognizing changes, listening without judgment, and simply being available can make a meaningful difference. In recognition of World Mental Health Day on Oct. 10, Utah State University Extension’s Health Extension: Advocacy, Research and Teaching (HEART) Initiative is offering five strategies families can use to support loved ones facing mental health challenges. 1. Recognize the Power of Family Support Family members are often among the first to notice changes in behavior, routines, or emotional well-being. Because of these close relationships, families can provide an important support network and help people connect with treatment and other resources. Families can also help reduce the stigma surrounding mental health treatment. In some situations, family therapy can help family members better understand how to support a loved one while strengthening relationships within the family. 2. Avoid Stigmatizing Language and Beliefs Words matter. Stigma can occur when differences or mental health conditions are labeled negatively, creating an “us vs. them” attitude. People who experience stigma may feel isolated or discriminated against and may become less likely to seek help. Family members can create a safer environment by avoiding judgmental language and treating mental health and substance use disorders as health concerns that deserve understanding and appropriate care. 3. Be Available, Listen, and Be Patient Social support can help people cope with stress, and feeling connected to others can benefit overall health. Families can provide that connection through face-to-face conversations, phone calls, texts, or video chats. When talking with someone who is struggling, ask open-ended questions that let them explain what they are experiencing. Families may also benefit from discussing their history of mental health concerns. Understanding possible genetic predispositions can help people better understand their experiences and realize they are not alone. Above all, be patient. Finding appropriate resources and treatment can take time. 4. Offer Realistic Hope Hope is more than simply wishing things will improve. It can build resilience by acknowledging past difficulties while maintaining confidence in the future. Family members can offer hope by being genuine and drawing from shared experiences. A simple message such as, “We have been through difficult things before, and we can get through this together,” can reassure them without minimizing what they're experiencing. 5. Take Care of Yourself Supporting someone experiencing mental health or substance use concerns can be stressful. Family members and caregivers need to protect their own physical and emotional well-being and take appropriate steps for self-care. Families should educate themselves about their loved one’s treatment, ask appropriate questions, and communicate with those involved in their care when possible. Family or marriage therapy may also help rebalance relationships and promote healing. For additional mental health resources and information, visit the Utah State University Extension HEART Initiative website, or call 988 for help.

title: Ask an Expert — Gardening Counts as Exercise: Protect Your Body While You Work
summary: Gardening can be a full-body workout, so it’s important to treat it like any other physical activity. Hydrate and stretch throughout the day and use correct techniques and tools to help you avoid injuries and minimize pain and soreness. Helpful Techniques Three techniques can help with most gardening tasks. These distribute the work to larger muscles or improve your body’s natural movement to help you avoid repetitive strain injuries. These occur in muscles, tendons and nerves from repetitive movements or overuse. They mostly happen in hands, wrists, shoulders, elbows, knees and lower back. Squat — This exercise works well for picking up and putting items down. It engages the quads, hamstrings, hips, glutes and abdominals and helps avoid strain to the back, knees, ankles, neck and shoulders. Pivot technique — This technique allows you to change directions without twisting. It works well for shoveling and dumping dirt or moving bags and other materials from one side to another. It also helps avoid strain to the back, knees and ankles. Back-and-forth weight transfer — This technique helps when moving items back and forth with a long-handled tool, such as a rake. This helps avoid hunching over, pulling and twisting. It uses larger leg muscles that prevent straining the back, shoulders and arms. Your garden layout as well as soil type can also determine the amount of work, materials and equipment you need to make tasks easier and less stressful on the body. Safety for Various Soil Types Heavy Soils Heavy soil types, such as clay or loam, hold nutrients, don’t drain well and are dense, making them a challenge to work with. That resistance can make working with tools harder, which in turn can cause injuries to the wrists, lower back and shoulders. Tips for working with heavy soils: Work with smaller loads when shoveling, hoeing or digging. Amend the soil when planting to make it less dense and easier to work with. Take breaks more often to avoid over-exerting yourself. Wear proper footwear with ankle support and grip. Sandy Soils Sandy soil drains quickly, lacks cohesion and is unstable, increasing the risk for ankle injuries, falls and repetitive strain injuries from working with loose soil. Amend the soil to retain nutrients and moisture, Use tools with wider scoops to help capture more soil at a time, Wear proper footwear that provides ankle support and full foot coverage. Consider making walking areas and working areas more stable by laying wood chips, flagstone or pavers. Rocky Soils Rocky soils have features of both heavy and sandy soils, with rocks of all shapes and sizes added to the mix. To maintain safety: Work with smaller loads. Take breaks more often. Wear proper footwear. Work carefully with equipment to prevent injury. Click here to see a video on the three techniques of movement in the yard and garden.

title: Ask an Expert — Tips for Preserving the Harvest Safely
summary: It’s peak canning season, and preserving bottled food is a long-held tradition for many Utahns. Whether you’re a longtime canner or a first-time food preserver, it’s important to stay up to date on best canning practices. There is always something new, and possibly safer, to learn and apply to your own kitchen/canning laboratory. But before you get started, be aware that there isn’t room for creativity in canning. Food preservation is a science- and research-based practice. Even though Grandma or Uncle Don may have “always done it this way,” using researched and tested recipes with proper procedures will bring you the safest results. Few things are more discouraging than investing time, money and effort into growing, harvesting and preserving food, only to have it spoil or cause illness. In addition, deviating from a tested recipe can alter the storability and flavor of your food. Once your food is processed, then you can get creative. For example, make tomato sauce as the tested recipe states, store it properly and then when you open it, season it to your desired taste to make a marinara sauce, enchilada sauce or tomato soup. As always, the USU Extension Food Preservation website has free, tested recipes, how-to guides and best practices, as well as the answers to questions like: Can I use sugar substitutes in jam recipes? Can I leave the salt out of a recipe? Do I have to have a pressure canner? How long will my canned foods last? Are there foods that are not safe to can or bottle? If you have other canning questions, the best option for finding safe, scientifically based answers for proper food preservation is to contact your local USU Extension office. Click here for office locations and contact information. You can also check out Extension’s Preserve the Harvest online course .

title: Ask an Expert — Utah's 2026 Wildfire Season by the Numbers
summary: Utah entered 2026 with heightened concerns about the wildfire season, given the record-low snowpack. Those concerns materialized as wildfires burned across Utah, affecting nearly every corner of the state. The 2026 wildfire season might be better described as a wildfire year. For example, on Jan. 22, the Beaver Canyon Fire started near Strawberry Reservoir in Wasatch County. At that time of year, the area should have been under several feet of snow. This is how 2026 stacked up against recent fire history in Utah: More than half a million acres have burned in Utah in 2026, making it the state's most severe fire season since 2007, when over 600,000 acres burned. The next-highest total in recent history was more than 400,000 acres in 2018 (see Utah Wildfires by Acres 2012-2026 chart below). This summer, Utah experienced several megafires, three of which made the list of the top 10 Utah wildfires since 2002 (see Largest Wildfires in Utah from 2002-2026 table below). These include: No. 3: Widemouth 2 Fire — Nearly 130,000 acres burned on the Fishlake National Forest. No. 5 Babylon Fire — Less than 110,000 acres burned on the Manti-La Sal National Forest. No. 7 Cottonwood Fire — Less than 100,000 acres burned on the Fishlake National Forest. This year’s fire season saw a shift toward larger fires at mid-to-higher elevations, particularly in timbered areas, rather than in lower-elevation rangelands where larger fires historically were more common. In Utah, 2005-2007 were major fire seasons, but these larger fires generally occurred on rangelands and Bureau of Land Management lands. Since the Brianhead Fire in 2017, most large fires have occurred in timber fuels on U.S. Forest Service lands. Over the past 10 years, 41% of Utah wildfires were caused by lightning. Although the fire season is not over, 54% of our fires were lightning-caused, according to data from the Great Basin Coordination Center. As the monsoonal season slows and we transition into autumn, lightning generally decreases but human-caused ignitions can increase. Several tragic incidents occurred during the 2026 fire season. On June 27, five wildland firefighters from the Rifle Helitack crew were attacking the Knowles and Gore fires near the Utah-Colorado border when they were overtaken by extreme fire behavior linked to the Snyder and Jones fires, which had started 8 miles away in Utah. Four firefighters died in the burnover. The last wildland firefighter fatality in Utah occurred in 2006, when Spencer Koyle was overrun by fire on the Devil's Den Fire in Millard County. On Aug.7, two pilots were killed on the Widemouth 2 Fire when their Skycrane helicopter crashed. Prior to this fire season, the last pilot fatalities on a Utah wildfire occurred in 2012, when air tanker pilots Todd Tompkins and Ron Chambless died fighting the White Rock Fire. Beyond these tragic fatalities, wildfires also caused extensive structural damage. Two-hundred and six structures have been documented as destroyed across six wildfires, including homes, cabins, and a major ski resort. In the Cottonwood Fire alone, 185 structures were destroyed, and the Eagle Point Ski Resort sustained significant structural damage. In 2018, the Dollar Ridge Fire destroyed or damaged 80 homes and nearly 400 trailers, sheds, and vehicles. The impacts of a wildfire often extend well beyond the flames. Post-fire flooding occurred in areas affected by the Cottonwood Fire near Beaver, and Pine Valley continued to flood after last year's Forsyth Fire. In some burned areas, high-severity wildfires can damage soils, and recovery can take several years. Grazing impacts are also expected to be significant for the ranching community, with an estimated less than 12,000 cattle and about 11,000 sheep affected over the next two years, as burned grazing allotments must be rested to allow vegetation to recover. With monsoonal moisture arriving from late August through early September, fire activity is expected to decline before winter snow arrives. Although wildfire activity and human-caused ignitions typically increase during hunting season, additional large fires are not anticipated this fall. The Great Basin Coordination Center's Predictive Services Significant Wildland Fire Potential Outlook forecasts normal fire potential for the rest of the year. However, weather conditions can still influence late-season wildfire activity. A few Red Flag Warning days could elevate fire risk, while early snowfall could further reduce fire potential heading into winter. Several factors contributed to increased wildfire activity this summer, including climate-related reductions in snowpack, ongoing drought, the exclusion of wildland fire (which has allowed fuels to accumulate), and continued population growth in the wildland-urban interface. Together, these factors increased wildfire impacts on ecosystems that evolved with fire. Looking ahead, a strengthening El Niño pattern — described by some forecasters as a "Super El Niño" — is expected to increase snowpack in southern Utah and potentially statewide, helping reduce drought conditions. While improved moisture may reduce some wildfire risk, accumulated fuels, such as dead and downed trees and branches, and continued development in and near wildlands will remain significant factors shaping future fire seasons. Our recent fire season underscores the need to build resilient landscapes, develop fire-adapted communities, and support safe, effective wildfire response. This fall, USU Extension and the Gateway & Natural Amenity Region Initiative will host an online learning series, “Wildfire Ready Utah.” USU Extension experts developed the five-part webinar series, focused on community resiliency, for property owners in the wildland/urban interface, local elected officials and staff, and fire and emergency response personnel. For further information, contact Brad Washa, USU Extension assistant professor of wildland fire science, Brad.Washa@usu.edu . title: Ask an Expert — Why Pumpkin Deserves a Place on Your Plate
summary: Many people buy pumpkins for fall décor and carving. But the next time you buy pumpkins, consider buying extras for cooking. Pumpkins are low in calories and packed with key nutrients that help keep our bodies healthy, especially during cold and flu season. The Cleveland Clinic notes five benefits of pumpkin: Good for eye health. Pumpkins are a great source of vitamin A and other nutrients that help protect our eyes from age-related degeneration and cataracts. Good for heart health. Heart disease is a prevalent chronic disease in America. Eating foods that are good sources of heart-healthy nutrients can decrease the risk of heart disease. Pumpkins are rich in potassium, fiber, and antioxidants, all of which are beneficial for heart health. Boosts the immune system. Vitamin C is usually the first nutrient we think of when it comes to preventing colds or flu. Pumpkins are a great source of vitamin C and other immune-boosting nutrients, including vitamins A and E and iron. Contains carotenoids. Carotenoids are the pigments produced by yellow, orange, and red plants. Carotenoids may help protect against certain types of cancer. Great for snacking. If you don’t want to cook your pumpkin, save the seeds when you scoop them out for carving. Clean the seeds, season them lightly, and roast them in the oven for the perfect fall snack. Roasted seeds also offer great health benefits. Pumpkins can be a healthy addition to a balanced eating pattern. Consider incorporating them into your cooking this fall. When buying pumpkins for cooking, make sure they are labeled as “cooking” pumpkins, which are more tender and thinner, making them better suited for cooking than regular carving pumpkins. Try these recipes to get started. Homemade pumpkin puree: https://www.thepioneerwoman.com/food-cooking/recipes/a11184/make-your-own-pumpkin-puree/ . How to freeze homemade pumpkin puree: https://www.thepioneerwoman.com/food-cooking/cooking-tips-tutorials/a45686740/can-you-freeze-pumpkin-puree/ . Pumpkin soup: https://cookieandkate.com/creamy-vegan-pumpkin-soup/ . Fall salad with roasted pumpkin: https://themodernproper.com/roasted-sweet-potato-salad-with-orange-vinaigrette . (Substitute roasted pumpkin for roasted sweet potato in the recipe.)

title: Ask an Expert: September Is National Preparedness Month: 'Americans Stand Ready'
summary: September is National Preparedness Month, a time to reflect on how ready we are when life takes an unexpected turn. This year's Federal Emergency Management Agency theme, "Americans Stand Ready," highlights the key role individuals and families play in preparing for emergencies before they happen. For many Utahns, emergency preparedness has become a hard reality. This year alone, communities across the state have experienced devastating wildfires, flash floods, damaging hailstorms, extended power outages, and evacuations that have affected families, communities, first responders, farmers, and ranchers. These events remind us that emergencies can happen anywhere, often with little warning. During one of the most difficult periods in our nation's history, as Americans faced the hardships of the Great Depression, President Franklin D. Roosevelt reminded the country that fear itself can become an obstacle to progress and action. In his first inaugural address in March 1933, he said, “The only thing we have to fear is fear itself,” encouraging Americans to move forward with courage and determination. Roosevelt's message reminds us that preparation begins with action. Most of us cannot control wildfires, floods, or power outages, but we can take steps to be ready. A little stored water, a family communication plan, an emergency kit, or even better health habits can go a long way when challenges arise . Preparedness is not about living in fear of what might happen. It is about replacing uncertainty with action. As we commemorate 250 years of American independence, preparedness helps us build community resilience, making families and neighborhoods stronger and more connected for the future. When people hear the term emergency preparedness, they often think of flashlights, generators, emergency kits, or food storage. These supplies are important, especially in rural communities where wildfires, severe weather, and other emergencies can disrupt normal services. FEMA recommends that households plan, stay informed about local hazards, and build emergency supply kits with water, food, medications, and important documents. However, one critical aspect of preparedness that can significantly affect response and recovery is our health. Healthy living plays a vital role in emergency preparedness, and taking proactive steps can improve our ability to respond during disasters and recover more quickly afterward. Simple health habits can help individuals feel confident in their preparedness. Eating nutritious foods, staying physically active, maintaining hydration, prioritizing sleep, and managing stress can improve overall health and increase our ability to cope with challenging situations. Preparedness also includes managing personal health needs. Keep an updated list of medications, maintain adequate supplies of prescription medications when possible, and store copies of important medical information in a secure location. Many of us know where our flashlights and extra batteries are stored, but would we have enough medication if roads were closed, evacuations were ordered, or local services were interrupted for several days? Individuals who rely on medical equipment, specialty supplies, or routine treatments should also include those needs in their emergency plans. Families should also develop an emergency communication plan. Determine how family members will contact one another, where you will meet if separated, and how you will receive emergency alerts. FEMA recommends including pets and individuals with specific medical or mobility needs in emergency planning efforts. USU Extension offers this Emergency Action Plan for free download that walks you through every step. This September, take one small step toward readiness: Check your emergency supplies. Store extra water. Review your family communication plan. Schedule a preventive healthcare appointment. Go for a walk or lift something heavy. Prepare a healthy meal. These simple actions may seem small, but they build self-reliance and resilient habits that will help your family during tough times. For 250 years, Americans have faced challenges by preparing, adapting, and helping one another. Americans stand ready when we prepare before disaster strikes. We stand ready when we invest in our health. We stand ready when we support our neighbors, and we stand ready when we take responsibility for our own preparedness. For a list of references, visit Extension.usu.edu .

title: Barnes Family Legacy Runs Through Olympus & Utah State
summary: Editor's note: This story was originally published on Jan. 22, 2026, by the Utah Statesman When Jordy Barnes steps onto the court for Utah State, he brings with him a lifetime of basketball experience that began long before college — rooted in one of Utah’s most consistent and successful high school programs. Barnes, a sophomore guard for the Aggies, grew up immersed in the game. Though his family lived in South Jordan, he identifies with Holladay, the community surrounding Olympus High School, where he attended and where his father Matt Barnes has been the boys’ basketball head coach for nearly three decades. Barnes’ earliest memories revolve around Olympus gym floors. He spent hours at practices and games, not as a player at first, but as part of the fabric of a program led by his father. “My dad is the reason I love basketball,” Barnes said. “I grew up going to practice, his games, coaches, dinners, shootaround.” Despite that environment, Barnes said his father never pushed him to play, instead allowing him to decide his own path. “He always was the chillest coach dad,” Barnes said. “Once I got to sixth grade, seventh grade, I decided this is all I want to do and quit playing my other sports — and then we really took it serious and spent more time in the gym and really focused on becoming a good basketball player because I had dreams and goals to get to the DI level. He was a huge part of that.” At Olympus, Barnes became a four-year varsity starter and helped sustain one of the state’s top programs. Under his father’s coaching, Olympus won multiple Class 5A state championships, including the 2023-24 title, marking the school’s fourth championship in nine seasons. Barnes’ senior year performance reflected his all-around game. He averaged 14.3 points, 7.5 rebounds, 10.5 assists and 3.6 steals per game. He also set the Utah high school record with 934 career assists. His high school experience carried more than wins — it carried atmosphere. Barnes recalls student sections packed into gyms and local rivalries that gave every game energy beyond the scoreboard. “All our games were mostly packed and sold out,” Barnes said. “Every night, you’re just playing in front of your best friends, and that stuff was really what made it a lot of fun.” Basketball runs deep in the Barnes family. Matt, who recently had the basketball court at Olympus named after him in recognition of his long tenure, played there as a student and later at Utah State from 1989-91 . He began coaching at Olympus in 1997 after assistant stints at Sky View and his alma mater. In nearly 30 years leading the Titans, he built a program with sustained success and national-level competitiveness, including multiple undefeated region seasons and state titles. Administrators once surprised him on midcourt to celebrate 25 years as head coach, a testament to his standing in the community and consistency with the program. “My career has been right here,” Matt said. “I love teaching and coaching, and this community has been great. That’s why I’ve stayed.” Utah State was on Jordy Barnes ’s radar early. He committed to the Aggies as a sophomore in high school — a decision informed by family ties and his belief that Logan would be the right place to play and grow. “When I committed, it was because of the fans and the culture,” Barnes said. “I wanted to stay home, and I knew it was a special place.” His commitment weathered multiple coaching changes, including the departures of head coaches Ryan Odom and Danny Sprinkle. When current coach Jerrod Calhoun arrived, Barnes had already signaled his intent to join Utah State. After earning a scholarship and minutes as a freshman, he said the process is affirmation of his work ethic and the coaching staff’s confidence in him. “Earning a scholarship from [Calhoun] is just all that I dreamed of, and I’m really appreciative of him and his staff and how they developed me to earn that,” Barnes said. “The confidence they had in me as a freshman to go from a walk on to a scholarship player to playing big minutes in some of our big wins — I couldn’t have done that without Calhoun and all his staff.” In his first year, Barnes appeared in 33 games, contributing primarily off the bench with his playmaking and floor management. He entered his sophomore season as one of several returning guards, bringing experience and a willingness to help younger teammates learn the system. A foot injury early in the season slowed his start, but Barnes said his comfort level and strength have improved. “It’s a different game at this level,” Barnes said. “But having a year of experience makes a big difference.” Teammates and coaches appreciate Barnes’ understanding of the game. His father, while speaking broadly about his son’s development, emphasized his adaptability and team-first attitude. “He understands it’s a big boys’ game now,” Matt said. “He works every day to make the team better, whether that’s on the court in games or in practice.” With Utah State poised for its transition into the Pac-12, Barnes’ role could grow in significance. He said his goal is to help the Aggies compete at a high level in both the remaining Mountain West schedule and as part of a Power Five conference in the future. “I love Aggie basketball,” Barnes said. “I love the fans and what it means to play here. I want to help this team win.” For a guard shaped by years of preparation and a family deeply connected to the game, his focus is consistent: contribute where needed and let winning define success.

title: Ben Jacobson Hired as Utah State Head Men's Basketball Coach
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Utah State tapped one of the most successful head coaches of the past two decades, Ben Jacobson, as its 23rd men's basketball head coach in program history on Monday, as announced by Utah State Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker. Jacobson is one of the most respected and consistent winners in college basketball, bringing a track record of sustained success, player development and championship culture to Utah State. He comes to Logan after a successful 20-year tenure at the University of Northern Iowa, where he built a dominant program. His teams earned multiple top-25 rankings, posted NCAA Tournament wins over top-seeded opponents and achieved strong academic and on-court success. "Utah State is one of the country's premier men's basketball programs, and we needed a leader who embodies that tradition and is committed to building on our rich history," Walker said. Read more at UtahStateAggies.com .

title: Beyond the Buzzer: Barbara Troisi's Impact on Aggie Athletics
summary: The rhythm of a bouncing ball, the squeak of sneakers on hardwood, the energy of a packed arena — for Barbara Troisi, basketball has always been more than a game. It’s a lifelong passion that has grown into something even more meaningful: a way to connect, to uplift and to invest in the lives of students she has come to know and love. That connection has deep roots. Growing up in a small town, Barbara often found herself playing basketball with the boys and loving every minute of it. In high school, when girls were restricted to half-court, she was assigned to defense, though she always wanted the chance to shoot. That passion for the game stayed with her as she supported her late husband, Guy, throughout his playing career, and it continues today as she cheers on Aggie basketball. “I’ve just always loved it,” Barbara said. “When I hear the squeak of the shoes on the court, I know it’s basketball season, and I can hardly wait.” Barbara is a familiar and beloved presence at the Dee Glen Smith Spectrum. She doesn’t just attend games, she builds relationships. She learns players’ stories, celebrates their milestones, and finds small but meaningful ways to make them feel at home, like bringing them homemade cookies. “One of the reasons I do cookies is so the players have a taste of home,” she said. “I make them for their away games when they travel. It’s something small, but I’ve always remembered how much it can mean.” It’s a simple gesture, but for Barbara, it speaks to something deeper: helping students feel grounded, cared for and connected. “Most of these students are away from home, in a new environment,” Barbara said. “They need encouragement. I just want to be there for them, for whatever they need.” That same spirit guides her philanthropy. Barbara has made significant investments in Utah State Athletics , supporting both men’s and women’s basketball recruitment and retention and establishing a scholarship endowment . She has also contributed to programs across the university, including the College of Veterinary Medicine. Her giving is rooted in a deep belief that students, whether athletes or not, deserve every opportunity to succeed. “My husband had to work for everything when he was in school,” Barbara said. “He earned his scholarship through a job on campus and still had to work very hard. I’ve always felt like I wanted to make things better for students — to give them a little more support so they can focus on what they’re here to do.” That belief extends beyond athletics. Through her involvement with veterinary students and other programs, Barbara has built lasting relationships across campus, often staying in touch with students long after they graduate. “I’m really proud that I taught for 40 years,” Barbara said. “I taught first grade my entire career, and that’s where I found my desire to make a difference for students. You care about them. You want to see them succeed. And when you stay connected and watch what they go on to do, that’s the joy.” Her journey to Utah State was, in many ways, serendipitous. Years ago, while visiting Logan for a game, Barbara stepped outside into a snowfall after watching McFarland, USA , a story about a cross-country team in California not far from where she once lived. The film’s themes of hard work, family and opportunity resonated deeply, and in that quiet moment in the snow, she felt an unexpected sense of belonging. As a cross-country skier, she could also picture herself in Logan, with easy access to the mountains and the sport she loved. “I walked back to the hotel in the snow and thought, ‘This is where I want to be,’” Barbara said. “It just felt right.” Today, that feeling has only deepened. From traveling to tournaments to volunteering alongside student-athletes in the community, Barbara has embraced every opportunity to be part of the Aggie experience. “They dedicate so much time and effort to what they do,” Barbara said. “I love their desire to be their best, not just for themselves but for their team.” For Barbara, giving is simply another way of showing up. “I wish I could provide a scholarship for every one of them,” Barbara said. “I just want to promote their chances of success.” Her impact is felt in countless ways: in the encouragement she offers, the traditions she carries forward, and the investments she makes in students’ futures. But perhaps most importantly, it’s felt in the relationships she builds. “It’s a joy,” Barbara said. “To see them succeed, to be part of their lives — that’s what it’s all about.” Create Your Aggie Impact Student access and success are at the heart of Utah State University’s mission. Through scholarships, programs, and experiences that support students both in and out of the classroom, donors like Barbara Troisi help open doors and create lasting opportunity. You can Create Your Aggie Impact by supporting the student-focused area that inspires you most and making a difference for Aggies today and tomorrow.

title: BLM Director, Utah Lt. Gov. to Keynote USU Conference on 50 Years of Federal Public Lands Law
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Bureau of Land Management Director Steve Pearce and Utah Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson will deliver keynote remarks Oct. 21 at Utah State University, where the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air is hosting a one-day conference marking the 50th anniversary of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. ILWA is presenting the conference in partnership with the BLM and the Foundation for America’s Public Lands. Signed into law on Oct. 21, 1976, FLPMA gave the BLM its modern mission and directed the agency to manage the nation’s public lands for multiple use and sustained yield. The BLM now manages about 245 million acres, more than any other federal agency, including roughly 22.9 million acres in Utah, about 42 percent of the state. The conference will be held on the USU campus in Logan and is open to the public. Registration is $20 and includes lunch, and students can attend for free. “This conference is a chance for Utah State to help shape the national conversation about public lands,” said Anna McEntire, executive director of ILWA. “National leaders are coming to our campus, and they’ll hear directly from USU researchers and community members about the work happening here.” The morning session will look back at the law’s first half-century. Following opening remarks by USU President Brad Mortensen and keynote addresses from Pearce and Henderson, Brian Steed, USU vice president for government and external relations and former acting director of the BLM, will moderate a panel that includes former BLM Director Jim Caswell and present and former BLM state directors Jamie Connell (Colorado), Jon Raby (Nevada), Greg Sheehan (Utah), and Mitch Leverette (Eastern States). “The BLM’s decisions shape daily life in Utah and across the West,” Steed said. “We’re excited to bring this conversation to Utah State and to the people who live and work on these lands.” Over lunch, the program will turn to USU’s own work on public lands. Researchers Jordan Smith (recreation), David Stoner (wildlife), Eric Thacker (grazing), Reagan Wytsalucy (Indigenous food systems), and Larissa Yocom (forestry) will share their research in an interactive session that also features art curated by Danielle Stewart, curator and head of academic initiatives at USU’s Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art. The afternoon will focus on the next 50 years. I Ling Thompson, CEO of the Foundation for America’s Public Lands, will moderate a panel representing the many uses of public lands, with national perspectives from energy (Robin Rorick, American Petroleum Institute), ranching (Eamon O’Toole, Ladder Ranch), outdoor recreation (Jess Rogers, Polaris), and wild horse management (Cindy Day, Piceance Mustangs). Attendees will then work in small groups to discuss current challenges and areas for opportunity that could be addressed by testing new innovations and/or forging unlikely partnerships. Report outs will be synthesized and later shared with attendees and decision makers. “The BLM manages some of the hardest working lands in America. They support local economies, power our homes, put food on our tables, are home to iconic wildlife, and offer some of the most unique recreation opportunities around. FLPMA is the reason all of those uses have a place,” Thompson said. “The future depends on the people who know these lands best, the ranchers, scientists, Tribal nations, and volunteers who already care for them. Getting those voices in one room is how planning for what comes next begins.” A free research poster session will run throughout the day during breaks and the lunch hour. Proposals for scientific research posters on topics related to federal lands, including geology, paleontology, wildlife, forestry, wildfire, aquatic species, rangeland, ecology, recreation, policy and multiple-use management, are being accepted through an extended deadline of Oct. 7. Those interested in presenting should indicate so when registering; a poster proposal form will open after registration is complete. "We're grateful to Utah State University and the institute for hosting this event," said Jeff Krauss, acting deputy director of administration and programs for the BLM. "FLPMA has guided the BLM's work for decades, and this anniversary belongs to everyone who cares about our public lands. This is a moment to celebrate them." About the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air The Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air at Utah State University connects decision-makers with high-quality research to support informed land, water, and air policy in Utah. Through applied research, public convening, and cross-sector collaboration, ILWA helps the state address complex natural resource challenges. Learn more at usu.edu/ilwa. About the Foundation for America’s Public Lands As the official charitable partner of the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), the Foundation for America’s Public Lands serves as a convener, partner, and fundraising catalyst to help ensure the health and stewardship of America’s public lands and waters today, and for the future. To learn more, visit americaslands.org .

title: Breaking Ground at ASPIRE: ASPIRE Studies Pavement Integrity With University of Texas at El Paso
summary: Researchers at ASPIRE are not only looking at ways to build electrification up but also studying the ways it breaks down. The Utah Department of Transportation sent a truck equipped with a falling weight deflectometer to the research center on Sept. 23. In this effort with ASPIRE’s team at the University of Texas at El Paso, researchers sought to test different pavement materials and whether they can withstand the same wear and tear as traditional roads. One of the goals of ASPIRE’s dynamic wireless power transfer, or DWPT, project is building confidence in electrified roadways. Because these roads need wireless charging pads embedded in the pavement, it’s important to know how well they hold up under real traffic. “The question we wanted to answer is whether having that pad in the road changes how the pavement carries traffic loads,” said Pedram Balooch Sirgani, a civil engineering doctoral candidate with ASPIRE at University of Texas at El Paso. “In the lab we control almost everything. At the EVR we got to see how the same ideas hold up at full scale with a real truck and real pavement layers.” Sirgani has been with ASPIRE since 2023. His doctoral research focuses on wireless charging systems embedded in asphalt pavements, a direct connection to the project at ASPIRE’s headquarters, the Electric Vehicle & Roadway research facility. At the USU site, Sirgani was in the field during the drop tests and has since been working on processing the fiber optic and deflection data. “That includes turning millions of strain readings into profiles and animations that show how the pavement responds as the truck tire moves over the pad,” he said. A Look Inside the Pavement Fiber optic sensors were embedded through the pads sitting beneath concrete, asphalt, and interlocking pavers. The team used distributed strain sensing fiber optics that measure the response of the pavement sections as a loaded electric truck drives over them. At the same time, the falling weight deflectometer truck applied controlled impulse loads to the pavement surface, which measured the resulting surface deflections. “As the truck moves across the pavement, these sensors capture the strain response continuously along the section,” said Cesar Tirado, University of Texas at El Paso associate professor. “That allows us to see whether the embedded DWPT components and their interfaces affect how the pavement responds to traffic loads, which is directly tied to its long-term structural performance and service life.” Tirado became involved with the project through University of Texas at El Paso and the Center for Transportation Infrastructure Systems. Through collaboration with ASPIRE on pavement systems and dynamic wireless power transfer research, Tirado helps with the coordination of UTEP’s pavement and instrumentation research and mentors the students who carry out much of that research. “At UTEP, we usually study pavement performance in controlled settings. The EVR takes that work to full scale,” Tirado said. “It is not separate from our work at UTEP. It is an extension of it, and it gives our students the opportunity to connect modeling and laboratory research with a real-world application.” From Prediction to Real-World Application Finding out the strain is instrumental in determining the life of the pavement and estimating how long it’s going to last. It’s better to determine these figures before being laid under real traffic by designing models here at ASPIRE. “For transportation agencies, a central question is whether embedded charging systems will compromise pavement performance or shorten service life,” Tirado said. “The field data will help ASPIRE evaluate DWPT designs that provide charging capability while preserving the structural performance expected of a roadway.” Tyler Munk, ASPIRE’s engineering and infrastructure project manager, has operated as the project lead and liaison between ASPIRE and the Concrete Masonry & Hardscapes Association — who supported the paving stone installations that were among the pavements tested. He believes that this research will strengthen ASPIRE’s capacity to seamlessly integrate wireless power transfer systems into various scenarios. “Each pavement type has its own pros and cons to installation, cost, durability, longevity,” Munk said. “We’d really like to understand what strain our electrical system is seeing underneath each of those pavement types so we can identify the rights times and the right cases to use each pavement type.” While the field testing might be over, the research surrounding pavement integrity is far from complete. ASPIRE researchers at UTEP are still interpreting the data gathered from the FWD and fiber optic cables in hopes of furthering real-world electrified roadway deployment. “We are still analyzing the data so I would not draw conclusions yet,” Tirado said. “But seeing that level of detail in a full-scale electrified pavement was exciting. It is one thing to predict the pavement response in a model; it is another to measure that response directly in the field under a real vehicle load.” For the latest news, publications, and research highlights from ASPIRE, visit aspire.usu.edu .

title: BTECH Now, USU Next: New Partnership Creates a Seamless Pathway
summary: Students can now begin their education at Bridgerland Technical College knowing a seamless pathway to a bachelor's degree at Utah State University is available, thanks to a new partnership. BTECH Now, USU Next is designed to help students build a strong foundation through BTECH’s hands-on, career-focused education at Bridgerland Technical College while planning their future at Utah State from day one. The program removes barriers to transfer by providing direct admission to USU, personalized academic advising, established transfer pathways, automatic scholarship consideration, and dedicated support throughout the student's educational journey. Students enrolled in the program will also become part of the Aggie community before officially enrolling at USU. Participants are eligible to engage in campus life through student activities, recreation opportunities at the ARC, housing, athletics, and other campus events, helping them build connections and experience university life while completing their technical education. At the same time, students continue to benefit from Bridgerland's accelerated, hands-on training, industry partnerships, and career-focused learning environment that prepares them for immediate employment. "Our responsibility is to make it easier for students to reach their goals," said USU President Brad Mortensen. "Bridgerland Now, USU Next gives students the flexibility to start with the education that best fits their needs today while creating a straightforward path to a Utah State degree tomorrow. It's a great example of how Utah's public institutions can work together to expand opportunity, strengthen our workforce, and better serve students across the state." The partnership builds on the long-standing relationship between the two institutions and recognizes that today's students benefit from flexible educational options that combine hands-on technical training with the opportunity to earn a bachelor's degree. “BTECH students come to us to gain industry-valued credentials and prepare for rewarding careers,” said Lisa Moon, interim president of Bridgerland Technical College. “BTECH Now, USU Next strengthens that experience by connecting students to Aggie campus life and providing a seamless next step for those who later decide to pursue a degree.” Rather than navigating the transfer process on their own, students in USU Next receive coordinated support from both institutions. They can confidently plan their coursework, understand how credits apply toward a bachelor's degree, and remain focused on achieving their academic and career goals. Bridgerland Now, USU Next demonstrates the shared commitment of Utah State University and Bridgerland Technical College to increasing educational access, strengthening Utah's workforce, and helping students earn valuable credentials every step of the way. For students considering their future, the message is simple: Start at Bridgerland. Build your skills. Continue with confidence. Become an Aggie through USU Next.

title: Bringing War Home: Exhibits at USU Eastern Share Personal Stories Behind Military Service
summary: The Utah State University Eastern Library & Learning Commons is hosting two exhibits sharing the stories, memories, and objects of those whose lives have been shaped by war. Through Sept. 30, the Library & Learning Commons is hosting the traveling exhibit “Bringing War Home: Object Stories, Memory, and Modern War,” alongside USU graduate student A.J. Arriola’s companion exhibit, “Paint in the Desert: Memory, Identity, and Commemoration on the T-Walls of the Global War on Terror.” Rather than focusing solely on battles and dates, the exhibits explore the human side of military service and its lasting impact on service members, families, and communities. “Bringing War Home” was developed through a National Endowment for the Humanities-sponsored program led by USU faculty members Susan R. Grayzel and Molly Boeka Cannon. The exhibit includes meaningful objects and the personal stories surrounding them. “The ‘Bringing War Home’ project invites the community, military and civilian alike, to connect with the history of war,” said Aimee Lauritsen of the Library & Learning Commons. Arriola’s exhibit continues that personal approach through photographs, uniforms, and memorabilia from several wars. A replica T-Wall, modeled after concrete barriers used at military installations during the Global War on Terror, serves as a backdrop for photographs showing how soldiers transformed these barriers with artwork, messages, and personal expression. Visitors can add their own names to the replica. “The T-Wall display stood out to me personally,” Lauritsen said. “I feel it is hard to truly understand what our soldiers go through personally on a daily basis.” Visitors are also encouraged to view the Carbon College WWII Memorial Roll in LLC Room 108. Dedicated in April 1946, the memorial honors 39 young men associated with Carbon High School and Carbon College who lost their lives during World War II. The Library & Learning Commons continues searching for information about those named to help preserve their individual stories. Together, the exhibits and memorial remind visitors that behind every uniform, photograph, object, and name is an individual story worth preserving. The exhibits will remain on display through Sept. 30. LLC hours are: 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday-Thursday. 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Friday. 4-9 p.m. Sunday.

title: Caffe Ibis Coffee Director to Speak at USU Libraries Lecture
summary: LOGAN — Tom Wilson, director of coffee at Caffe Ibis, will discuss the growth of specialty coffee at the next Friends of Merrill-Cazier Libraries Lecture Series event from 7-9 p.m. Oct. 21 in Room 154 of Utah State University’s Merrill-Cazier Library. The lecture, “Specialty Coffee Growth and Expansion,” will explore coffee’s history and its role in society. It connects to “Eating the Past: Cookbooks in the Archives,” the exhibit now on display in the library atrium. The talk also comes as Caffe Ibis prepares to celebrate its 50th anniversary in December. Wilson will look at how the modern specialty coffee movement has developed. Wilson has spent 16 years at Caffe Ibis, where he now serves as general manager and as director of coffee at the company’s nearby roasting facility. He earned his Q Grader certification in 2025, and his work spans green coffee sourcing, roasting, and café service. For more information, contact Traci Hillyard, senior administrative assistant, at traci.hillyard@usu.edu .

title: Camp Sage: USU Libraries Invites Connections Students to Library After Hours
summary: LOGAN — USU Libraries will host Library After Hours from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. Aug. 28 at the Merrill-Cazier Library, exclusively for incoming Connections students. Library After Hours gives new students a relaxed, no-pressure way to familiarize themselves with the library outside its regular hours, helping them build confidence in the spaces and services they will rely on throughout their academic careers. This year’s Library After Hours is Summer Camp-themed, which will feature campfire storytelling, stargazing and more. Students will also be free to explore the library's spaces while enjoying games, pizza, karaoke, hobby horsing, quiet spaces and prizes throughout the evening. Participants are encouraged to bring their curiosity, appetite and sense of adventure. This event is designed to help first-year Connections students feel at home in the Merrill-Cazier Library. By experiencing the library outside of traditional hours, students can learn about its resources and services in a relaxed environment, fostering a sense of belonging that will support their academic journey.

title: Community Invited to Explore 'The Odyssey' Through Book Club, Film Discussion
summary: LOGAN — After Christopher Nolan's film adaptation introduced new audiences to "The Odyssey" this summer, Utah State University is inviting students, faculty, staff, and community members to take a deeper dive into the ancient epic through a semester-long book club and discussion series . Hosted by the Department of History, Cultures, and Ideas , the program will explore the themes, characters, and cultural legacy that have kept Homer's story relevant for thousands of years. The book club will meet throughout the fall semester and culminate with a community screening and discussion of Nolan's film adaptation Dec. 11 in the Russell/Wanlass Performance Hall. "We started this book club because of the excitement around Christopher Nolan's new adaptation," said C. Jacob Butera, assistant professor of classics at USU. "The new film has garnered a lot of conversation and controversy, and we hope that by reading the book and then watching the film, the audience can engage more deeply in the changes that Nolan made and why." Open to all, the book club will meet from 5:30 to 7 p.m. Oct. 1, Nov. 5, and Dec. 3 in Room 201 of the Mehdi Heravi Global Teaching and Learning Center on USU's Logan campus. Organizers are also developing virtual participation options for statewide audiences. The first 52 registrants will receive complimentary copies of the book courtesy of Penguin Publishing. The program arrives at a moment of renewed public interest in the ancient epic, demonstrating how the humanities can help audiences engage more deeply with contemporary culture through enduring stories and ideas. "All of the excitement around ‘The Odyssey’ right now is a great opportunity for the classics and for the humanities more broadly," Butera said. "There is still clearly a lot of interest in the ancient world and its stories." Those wishing to learn more can listen to Butera's recent appearance on Utah Public Radio's Access Utah, where he discussed "The Odyssey," the field of classics, and the continued study of ancient literature. Written nearly 3,000 years ago, the epic poem follows the hero Odysseus as he journeys home after the Trojan War, facing monsters, temptations, and personal trials along the way. Its themes of perseverance, family, identity, and belonging continue to resonate across cultures and generations. "We have a classic hero's tale as Odysseus overcomes numerous challenges so that he can get back home to his wife and son," Butera said. "These are human themes that are relatable as much to the modern world as they were to the ancient." Butera believes studying the ancient world can provide valuable tools for understanding contemporary society. "For students and lifelong learners alike, the ancient world provides us a lens through which to better understand ourselves and our own times," he said. "And, perhaps even more importantly, these stories can provide us the vocabulary we need to discuss difficult subjects and ideas with those around us. It's a great way to build community and tear down barriers." The series also introduces students, faculty, and community members to USU's newest classics faculty member. Butera joined the university this year after teaching at several institutions across the country and completing graduate studies at Duke University. "I came to the classics a bit by accident," he said. "As is so often the case, one professor made all the difference." Inspired by a series of mentors who encouraged his interest in the ancient world, Butera went on to study classical languages and cultures, travel extensively to archaeological and historical sites across the Mediterranean, and build a career dedicated to teaching and scholarship. "I really hope that I can share with my students the same sorts of experiences that led me here," he said, "whether they want to pursue a career in the field or are just interested in learning more." Registration for the “A Semester of The Odyssey” book club and the Dec. 11 film screening is available at artsci.usu.edu/events/semester-of-the-odyssey .

title: Countdown to Aggie Spirit: Celebrate USU's 2026 Homecoming
summary: Utah State University’s 2026 Homecoming is just around the corner — Sept. 21-26 — and it’s shaping up to be a week packed with Aggie pride, tradition, and celebration. On Thursday, Sept. 24, the university will host A Day of Giving , a 24-hour, university-wide fundraising event for Aggies everywhere to make a gift in support of student scholarships and programs. On Friday, Sept. 25, Utah State Athletics will induct its 2026 Hall of Fame Class at 7 p.m. in the Russell/Wanlass Performance Hall, honoring three outstanding individuals and two teams. Later that night, students and alumni can take part in one of USU’s most cherished traditions during True Aggie Night at 11:59 p.m. at the Block A. Saturday, Sept. 26, keeps the energy high. The Running with the Bulls 5K sign in begins at 7:30 a.m. with an 8:30 a.m. start at the USU Welcome Center. Those who register early will get the best discounts . The Homecoming Parade will follow at 10 a.m. along Main Street from Center Street to 800 North. From 2-5 p.m., the Utah Agricultural Products BBQ will bring another favorite fall tradition to Craig Aston Park , located north of Maverik Stadium.
