The barbecue will feature Utah-grown beef, dairy products, pork, lamb, corn, apples, onion rings, salad, Creamies, and more, bringing together members of the agricultural community, alumni, donors, and friends. Homecoming festivities culminate Saturday evening when the Aggies take on Troy at 5:30 p.m. in Maverik Stadium. As part of the celebration, USU will recognize four outstanding Aggies for their contributions to the university and beyond. Leading the parade as grand marshals will be Craig and Lorraine Earl, joined by 2026 Alumni of the Year Randy B. Elliott and Chad R. Warnick. Together, they embody the service, leadership, and pride that define the Aggie family. Craig ’75 and Lorraine Earl Grand Marshals Craig and Lorraine Earl’s roots in Cache Valley run deep. Born the same year at Logan Hospital, Craig grew up in River Heights and Lorraine on a dairy farm in Smithfield. Today, they live in North Logan, where they can see the press box of Utah State’s football stadium from their front lawn — a fitting view for two lifelong Aggies. Their story together began at Sky View High School, where they met in sophomore health class. Craig played three sports, while Lorraine was a member of the Vistaun drill team. They graduated in 1970, married in 1972 and recently celebrated 54 years together. Craig’s connection to Utah State began long before he became a student. Some of his earliest Aggie memories are of buying a Huddle Club season football pass for $1 and watching games in the old Romney Stadium. He remembers the great football teams of the early 1960s and the excitement surrounding Aggie basketball during the Wayne Estes era. Craig enrolled at Utah State and earned a degree in food science in 1975, while Lorraine worked for the City of Logan to help support their family. After graduation, his career in milk processing took the couple to four different locations, but Cache Valley remained home. They returned to Logan in 1979, and Craig began producing an ice cream bar in the back of a small factory on Main Street. Originally called a “fudgie,” the treat was renamed the Creamie in 1983. What began as a small northern Utah product grew into a regional favorite sold throughout the West. Although Craig sold the Creamie factory in 2021, it continues to produce and distribute more than 30 million Creamies annually. In 1990, Craig and Lorraine opened Charlie’s Ice Cream in Logan. Named for generations of family members, Charlie’s has served the community for more than three decades. Along the way, countless USU students have worked at Charlie’s and in Creamie production before graduating and beginning careers of their own — something Craig and Lorraine consider especially rewarding. Their commitment to community extends well beyond their businesses. They have supported Utah State endowments and numerous charitable organizations, reflecting their belief in giving back and helping others. Family remains at the center of their lives. Craig and Lorraine have two children, Kirk and Angela, six grandchildren, and a great-grandson. Their son, Kirk, and his wife, Rebecca, are USU graduates, continuing a family tradition that includes several generations of Aggies. Craig’s mother, Gloria, began her own Utah State journey as a freshman at age 50 and graduated in 1985. From Friday nights in high school at the old Romney Stadium to building businesses that have become part of Cache Valley life, Craig and Lorraine have spent a lifetime rooted in the community and connected to Utah State. Their generosity, entrepreneurial spirit, and unmistakable Aggie pride embody the enduring spirit of Homecoming. Randy B. Elliott ’08 Alumnus of the Year Randy B. Elliott’s connection to Utah runs deep. Raised in Farmington as part of a family that has farmed in Davis County for generations, he learned early the values of hard work, persistence and service — principles he carried with him to Utah State University and throughout his career. Elliott earned a bachelor’s degree in political science from USU in 2008. While a student, he developed his leadership skills and gained firsthand experience in public service, including an internship in Washington, D.C., with U.S. Sen. Mike Crapo. After graduation, Elliott returned home determined to invest his time and talents in the community that shaped him. An entrepreneur and business leader, Elliott has built his career developing businesses, cultivating relationships, and creating strategic partnerships. He also spent eight years serving as a Davis County commissioner from 2017 to 2024, helping guide one of Utah’s fastest-growing counties through significant growth and investment. During his tenure, he supported efforts to strengthen communities, preserve the county’s agricultural heritage, and expand opportunities for residents. Among those efforts was a partnership with Utah State University to establish the Davis County Agricultural Heritage Center, creating a resource that celebrates the region’s agricultural legacy while supporting education for future generations. Elliott’s commitment to his alma mater extends well beyond that partnership. He serves as chair of the S.J. & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture and Natural Resources Advancement Board, working with university leaders, alumni, and industry partners to strengthen programs and philanthropic support. In 2020, he received Utah State Extension’s Friend of Extension Award for his advocacy and service. Elliott and his wife, Julia, are the parents of four daughters, and he considers his family his greatest accomplishment. Through business, public service and steadfast support of Utah State, Elliott has demonstrated what it means to put leadership into action. Chad R. Warnick ’06, ’09 MS Alumnus of the Year For Chad R. Warnick, becoming an Aggie was never really a question. Growing up in Delta, Utah, as a third-generation Aggie, Utah State University was the only university he applied to — and the place that helped him turn his passion for agriculture, leadership and service into a career devoted to helping young people succeed. Warnick earned a bachelor’s degree in agricultural education in 2006 and a master’s degree in agricultural systems technology in 2009. As a student, he served as a College of Agriculture senator and an Agriculture Ambassador. He was also active in 4-H and Collegiate Future Farmers of America. Since 2006, Warnick has served as an agricultural educator and FFA advisor at the Delta Technical Center. His belief that students learn best by doing has shaped his career. He has helped develop a school livestock facility, operated a greenhouse that combines education with commercial production, and partnered with more than 35 local businesses to provide students with hands-on learning opportunities. Under his leadership, Delta FFA students have earned 36 state team championships, with more than 90 students competing at 17 National FFA Conventions. Warnick’s influence extends beyond his classroom to agricultural education at the local, state, and national levels through mentoring, teacher training, and service. In 2023, he was named Utah Teacher of the Year, following in the footsteps of his father, Waldo Warnick, who received the same honor 32 years earlier. Warnick has also received the Utah FFA Golden Owl Award. Warnick and his wife, Traci ’05, are both Aggies and agricultural education graduates of Utah State. Together, they are raising four future Aggies: Campbell, Kinley, Pyper, and Paxton. Through two decades of teaching and service, Warnick has exemplified the Aggie values of hard work, leadership and commitment to others. For more information on Homecoming week 2026, visit the Homecoming website: usu.edu/homecoming .

title: Country Star Cole Swindell Adds Tour Stop in Logan
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Multi-platinum country superstar Cole Swindell will bring his chart-topping hits to Maverik Stadium at 7 p.m. July 23. The concert at Maverik Stadium will be followed by post-show fireworks presented by Fox Pest Control. An opener will be announced at a later date. Swindell, a hit songwriter, recording artist and headlining performer for more than 12 years, has earned multiple No. 1 singles and industry honors. His most recent hit, "Make Heaven Crowded," reached No. 1 on the iTunes country chart and No. 2 on the all-genre iTunes chart. From his fifth studio album, Spanish Moss, "Forever To Me" became his 13th No. 1 single as an artist and his 14th as a songwriter. Twelve of Swindell's 13 No. 1 singles have been certified platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA), with three reaching triple-platinum status, including "Chillin' It," "You Should Be Here" and "She Had Me at Heads Carolina." Read more at UtahStateAggies.com .

title: David Fukuda Named as New Department Head of Kinesiology and Health Science
summary: The Emma Eccles Jones College of Education and Human Services has named David Fukuda as department head of Kinesiology and Health Science at Utah State. "I am excited for Dr. Fukuda to lead our popular and successful KHS department into its next chapter of growth and impact," said Emma Eccles Jones Endowed Dean Al Smith. "His scholarly background and leadership experience set him apart during our search process and prepare him to be highly effective at USU." Fukuda says USU's land-grant mission, extension services and commitment to community engagement were among the strongest factors that attracted him to the university. "Growing up in Idaho, I participated in 4-H and a variety of community activities, and those experiences had a lasting impact on me," Fukuda said. "I'm eager to join a team that values many of those same principles and invests in the community in meaningful ways." Fukuda was also impressed with the breadth of programs within the KHS department, including kinesiology, health science, recreation administration, sport management, and lifetime activity. He aims to build upon these programs as part of a broader initiative focused on promoting healthy lives. "The combination of programs creates opportunities to address health and human performance from multiple perspectives, while also preparing students to make meaningful contributions in a rapidly changing world," Fukuda said. In his new role, Fukuda hopes to create stronger pathways for student success and help them discover opportunities they may not initially recognize. "We need to develop the best prepared students in the state for health, recreation, sport and human performance," Fukuda said. "We want them to be leaders in their field and see all the possibilities they can pursue." Another key priority for Fukuda is increasing the visibility of the KHS department. "There's already great work going on here," he said. "We have talented faculty, strong programs and meaningful research taking place every day. We just need to be more visible, and that visibility extends beyond Utah." Prior to USU, Fukuda spent 13 years at the University of Central Florida, where he was a professor of kinesiology and division chair. His research focuses on sports science, body composition and exercise and nutritional interventions across the lifespan. While at UCF, Fukuda was also involved in the institution's growth and development. He played a role in the transition of the sport and exercise science program into kinesiology and contributed to the creation of the School of Kinesiology and Rehabilitation Sciences and the College of Health Professions and Sciences as part of an Academic Health Sciences Center that brought together medicine, nursing and other health disciplines. Additionally, Fukuda was the recipient of Educator of the Year in 2022 from the National Strength and Conditioning Association and serves as a Fellow of the NSCA and the American College of Sports Medicine. He has a black belt in judo, which has influenced his research in combat sports and martial arts participation. "All of these experiences helped prepare me for this role," Fukuda said. "Throughout my career, I have recognized the importance of the connection between health and education — those things can't be separated. I'm grateful for the journey I've had this far, and I'm excited to see what the future brings."

title: Diné Experience, New Data: Weather Stations Enrich Navajo Nation Record With Real-Time Monitoring
summary: Across more than 16 million acres of the southwestern U.S. is the Navajo Nation, a dramatic and varied landscape of sandstone, communities, and desert, roughly the size of Ireland. The people who live and work here have a thousand-year history of stewardship and traditional ecological knowledge, tracking conditions that their livelihoods depend on. In the last few decades things have begun to shift. Across the narrow canyons, rangelands, and arroyos rainfall has decreased. When it comes, the soil doesn’t hold it. Groundcover is disappearing, temperatures are climbing, and there isn’t enough livestock forage to go around. Reagan Wytsalucy is determined to find ways for these communities to adapt. She is Utah State University’s Extension associate professor of agriculture and natural resources and San Juan County Extension director. Her efforts have started at ground level this month, with the installation of the first of six new real-time weather stations at key locations within the Navajo Nation that will fill vital gaps in the regional climate record. Most people in the U.S. take for granted that real-time, hyperlocal weather information will be conveniently, constantly at their fingertips. The weather information on your phone comes from data collected by weather stations, often at airports managed by the National Weather Service, and thousands of other sites managed by various groups that collect and share it in larger networks. But on the Navajo Nation gaps in weather data from the topographically diverse region have made forecasts less accurate and good information harder to get. “Satellites might say there’s a storm overhead, but there’s no rain reaching the ground,” Wytsalucy said. “Forecasts say to prepare for rain, but the clouds just move around the area. We need on-the-ground information about what’s contributing to these patterns, to know accurately when precipitation is falling.” Wytsalucy saw an open opportunity to monitor and track the area, as well as begin to ask questions and pursue research that can help communities adapt to change. Accurate information about weather can empower ranchers, land managers, emergency crews, and water managers to make important safety and planning decisions. It is essential for long-term planning, especially important because Navajo rangelands are already under severe strain from ongoing drought. But the data currently used for long-range planning and on-the-ground decisions about things like grazing permits is more than a century old. “The rules we are trying to use were written for another time,” Wytsalucy said. Active grazing permits determine how many animals can forage a given piece of land. The outdated data means that current grazing exceeds ecological carrying capacities, with overgrazing removing ground cover plants and leaving soils dry and even hydrophobic. “We really can’t address these problems without starting with accurate information. Communities have been asked to develop conservation management plans without the basic knowledge they need to make the best decisions for the current situation,” Wytsalucy said. With the help of USU’s Utah Climate Center and regional partners, six new weather stations are planned to capture storm movements and microclimates at strategic locations including Oljato-Monument Valley, Mexican Water, Montezuma Creek, the U.S. Highway 191 corridor near Aneth, and two sites along Navajo Mountain. Environmental data collected by the network will feed directly into national databases, including USU's Mesonet system and further, to agencies of the State of Utah and the federal agency, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, ensuring Navajo Utah communities are represented in state and federal climate reporting. The Utah Climate Center operates a Mesonet network of around 140 stations. The network enhances the accuracy of local weather forecasts, severe storm warnings, agricultural planning, and regional climate reporting for historically underrepresented areas. “By establishing Utah’s Mesonet and building it out with these weather stations, the Utah Climate Center is furthering its mission to offer access to climate data and information and to use expertise in atmospheric science to interpret climate information in accurate ways,” said Robert Gillies, director of the Utah Climate Center. The data will also be valuable for local management and education, Wytsalucy said. Tribal leaders want to create ways that this new data becomes connected to traditional ecological knowledge — the skills of observation of patterns, seasonal cycles, and direct awareness, Wytsalucy said. She plans to work with students and partners to gather, record, and document these skills and incorporate them into educational materials that can be shared in Extension work and school programs. “We get to use this data to acknowledge and to retain a traditional connection,” she said. And to consolidate what they know — through weather data, observation, tradition, and community — to adapt important practices like grazing, improve soil health, manage feral livestock, support healthy rangelands, and protect traditional crops and native plants used for ceremonial and medicinal purposes, she said. “You have to be able to look at all of these systems as a whole,” she said. “We can’t think of any one action as independent anymore. When you honor and incorporate good practices, you see recovery in ecosystems. Life gives back.” With the new weather stations, she wants not only to document problems but to create a path to solutions. All these strategies start with good data, she said.

title: ETE Champions Recognized for Commitment to Teaching & Professional Development
summary: Utah State University’s Center for Empowering Teaching Excellence has named Shalyn Drake and Sarah O’Neill its ETE champions for the 2026-27 academic year. Drake, a lecturer in aviation technology and Unmanned Aircraft System program lead at USU Eastern in Price, earned the ETE World Championship after earning the most badges through ETE’s Professional Development Pathways program. In doing so, Drake took the title from fellow aviation technology faculty member and mentor Baron Wesemann, the first person to receive the ETE World Championship belt. Drake said winning the belt wasn’t originally her goal. Her focus was on improving her teaching. “I honestly did not intend initially to steal the belt,” Drake said. “I was focused on learning and that led to realizing I could steal the belt from my mentor. Then I kicked it into another gear.” Her work through ETE has focused on peer reviews, developing her teaching philosophy, and community-engaged learning. Drake has sought feedback from faculty both inside and outside her department, as well as from students. “I think [student peer reviews are] a little different, but it gives me a good perspective, plus gives the students a good experience,” Drake said. Drake said these teaching practices have contributed to an 80% employment placement rate for students in the drone program. She also encourages other faculty members to recognize that professional development does not necessarily mean adding something completely new to their workload. “These practices are things we all already do,” Drake said. “Just jump in and document it.” For Drake, ETE also provided support during what she described as an extremely difficult year. Her advice to other faculty is to find what motivates them and connect professional development to what matters to them as educators. O’Neill, from the Department of World Languages and Cultures in the College of Arts and Sciences at the Logan campus, received the ETE Intercontinental Championship. O’Neill earned the most badges during the previous academic year and received her championship belt at the ETE conference on Aug. 19. Although O’Neill had attended ETE events since joining USU six years ago, the 2025-26 academic year was her first year submitting badges through the Professional Development Pathways program. It was also her first year directing and coordinating the Master of Second Language Teaching program as it transitioned to a fully online, asynchronous format. “ETE was an essential part of that growth,” O’Neill said. Before offering her first online asynchronous course, O’Neill worked with CIDI instructional designer Amy Carpenter to develop her Canvas course. She attended an ETE workshop on active learning in online courses led by Chris Babits and worked with Student Collaborator on Teaching Kinsley Sorensen, who reviewed her courses during the fall and spring semesters and helped her identify areas for improvement. O’Neill said ETE has also become a useful resource for students in the Master of Second Language Teaching program, many of whom are preparing to become teachers themselves. “Though the experience of earning an online degree can be isolating, ETE helped connect these students not only with professional development but with the community of educators at USU,” O’Neill said. O’Neill also participated in a spring 2026 Learning Circle on “playful pedagogies” facilitated by Tamryn McDermott. The experience built upon her interest in using collaborative storytelling games in second-language classrooms and gave her ideas she could bring into her graduate courses. The Learning Circle brought together instructors from several disciplines, including art, accounting, English, nursing, and world languages. O’Neill and other members later shared their approaches to playful pedagogy at the ETE Conference in August. “One of the most incredible aspects of that Learning Circle was that we were such a diverse group of teachers,” O’Neill said. ETE has also helped O’Neill connect with colleagues within her own department. Through ETE’s peer evaluation program, she had a class observed by the colleague in the office directly next to hers and served as a peer evaluator for a longtime Spanish faculty member. “ETE has been a vital tool for connecting me to teachers from other disciplines, but it’s helped me strengthen ties to members of my own department, too,” O’Neill said. ETE created the championship belts to recognize faculty and instructors who demonstrate an ongoing commitment to professional development. The belts are meant to make those accomplishments more visible while adding some fun and friendly competition to work that can often go unrecognized. Designed to be displayed and shared, the belts give recipients a way to celebrate their accomplishments with colleagues and students while highlighting the value of continued learning and growth in teaching. For Drake, the competition may have helped push her toward the championship, but the experience ultimately came back to professional growth. “Find your reason,” Drake said, “and use your values to keep moving forward.” To learn more about Empowering Teaching Excellence and its professional development opportunities, visit usu.edu/empowerteaching .

title: Events Welcome USU Eastern Students Back
summary: Students are back at Utah State University Eastern, and the start of the new academic year has been about more than returning to classrooms. Through Town Ties, the Luminary Ceremony and the Blue Blast Block Party, USU Eastern welcomed students with opportunities to connect with campus programs, local businesses, community resources, and the people who will support them throughout their time at Eastern. On Friday evening, hundreds of students gathered at the Jennifer Leavitt Student Center for Town Ties, an annual event designed to introduce students to local businesses and services. “The idea behind Town Ties is to introduce students who are new to the area to businesses that they might not know,” said Barbie Haeck, director of the Carbon County Chamber of Commerce. Healthcare, banking, recreation, shopping, and other services were represented, with participating businesses bringing carnival-style activities for students. Dinner was provided free of charge, and students who visited the businesses could win a variety of prizes. For Samantha Madrid, nurse practitioner with Castleview Urgent Care, Town Ties made students aware of healthcare resources available to them. “I thought it was awesome to interact with the students and make sure they were aware of the free visits they are offered,” Madrid said. “The students seemed to enjoy it and so did we.” Friday concluded with USU Eastern’s Luminary Ceremony, where Kevin Hurst, Kristian Olsen and Price City Mayor Terry Willis helped light the way into a new school year. “We need USUE students to feel they are part of our community from the minute they arrive until the day they graduate,” Willis said. “I feel Town Ties and Luminary is an amazing way to start letting the students understand that we truly want that to happen.” The celebration continued Monday with the Blue Blast Block Party, bringing students, USU Eastern departments, local businesses and the general public together to showcase programs, services and opportunities. For campus departments, Blue Blast connects students with resources they may need during their college experience. “This event is awesome for us so we can get our names out as the therapists on campus and let them know of the services available to those in need,” said Eric Hansen with the Social Work Program and Counseling Services. “Then it's a great way to recruit new students into our program and educate the community.” Community partners also highlighted opportunities beyond the classroom, including businesses such as Intermountain Electronics that work closely with the university to connect students with internships and career opportunities. Through its growing internship partnership with USU Eastern, Intermountain Electronics is able to educate students about available career paths while also recruiting future interns. Despite Blue Blast being moved indoors at the last minute due to weather, Student Life Coordinator Allie Chamberlain said the campus and community quickly adapted. “Everyone was so flexible and willing to jump in and make the best of it,” Chamberlain said. “It was great to see our students, campus and community all come together to kick off the year.” Now in her ninth year organizing Blue Blast, Chamberlain said the event continues to be made possible by the many people who show up each year to support Eastern and its students. She expressed her appreciation for the local businesses, sponsors, university employees, volunteers, and community members whose continued support helps bring the event together and makes it a successful start to the school year. Together, the three events reinforced an important message as another academic year begins at USU Eastern: Students are not only part of a campus, but part of a community invested in helping them feel welcome, supported, and successful.

title: First Utah Navajo Weather Station to Bring Local Data to Monument Valley
summary: Monument Valley is getting a new source of local weather data. The first Utah Navajo weather monitoring station will provide locally collected information to help ranchers, community leaders, emergency responders, and others navigate drought, changing weather patterns, and other challenges in the region. The installation will be celebrated from 10:30 a.m. to noon Oct. 15 at Goulding’s Air Hangar Building in Oljato/Monument Valley, Utah. The station is part of a collaborative effort involving Utah State University and several regional and national partners to improve access to local weather information and support long-term planning for Navajo communities. “For generations, families in the region have relied on the land for grazing and agriculture,” said Reagan Wytsalucy, USU Extension associate professor and event organizer. “Today, ranchers face recurring drought and shifting weather, and some grazing guidelines still rely on climate data collected nearly a century ago.” The new station will help address that gap by collecting weather data directly in Monument Valley, providing information that better reflects local conditions. “Leading up to this moment, I realized the Navajo communities would continue to struggle to reclaim their rangelands unless we begin improving the existing methods for data collection across their rangelands,” Wytsalucy said. “Installing a weather station as the initial step toward more accurate climate data will support ongoing rangeland improvement planning and lead to educational programming that supports the next generation of agricultural producers in Utah Navajo communities.” Wytsalucy said the data could help emergency responders and transportation crews prepare for hazardous weather. It could also help tribal leaders make decisions about water resources and provide new educational opportunities for local youth. Beyond collecting weather data, project partners hope to develop programming that combines modern climate monitoring technology and traditional ecological knowledge passed down through generations, she said. The project brings together the Upper Colorado River Commission, Utah Colorado River Authority, Campbell Scientific Inc., Walton Family Foundation, Conscience Bay Research, Apogee Instruments, USU Climate Center, USU Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air, and USU Extension. The Oct. 15 celebration will include brief remarks from project partners and opportunities for community members to discuss future climate data programming.

title: Five Utah State Faculty, Staff Selected for Fulbright Awards
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Five Utah State University faculty and staff members have been selected for 2026-27 Fulbright awards, earning opportunities to conduct research, teach, and further international partnerships around the world. Sponsored by the U.S. Department of State, the Fulbright Program is the U.S. government's flagship international academic exchange program. Fulbright awards support scholars, educators, students, and professionals as they collaborate with institutions around the world, advance research and teaching, and foster mutual understanding between nations. This year's recipients of the Fulbright U.S. Scholar Program represent colleges and departments across Utah State University and will pursue projects in Hungary, Iceland, Japan, Norway, and Morocco. Their work spans music, Arctic ecology, international education, psychology, and landscape architecture, highlighting Utah State's commitment to global engagement and international collaboration. "Fulbright awards represent the very best of international scholarship, collaboration, and cultural exchange," said Janis Boettinger, senior vice provost for global engagement at Utah State University. "We are incredibly proud of this year's recipients and the meaningful work they will undertake, and have already undertaken, around the world. Their projects strengthen Utah State's global partnerships, advance knowledge across a wide range of disciplines, and create opportunities that will benefit our students, our university, and the communities they serve." Sara Bakker | Fulbright U.S. Scholar — Hungary Sara Bakker, associate professor in Utah State University's Department of Music in the College of Arts and Sciences, has been selected as a 2026-27 Fulbright U.S. Scholar and will spend the fall semester in Budapest, Hungary, researching the early works and writings of composer György Ligeti. For Bakker, pursuing a Fulbright has been a long-term goal. She said she first became interested in the program after becoming a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2016. Support from Utah State's Office of Research included grant-writing workshops and seed funding that helped her build relationships with scholars in Hungary, which ultimately laid the foundation for her successful application. "I chose Hungary because I believe it was a formative place in the life of the composer I study, György Ligeti," Bakker said. "My project aims to gather contemporary sources from 1945 to 1956, including compositions, letters, and publications, and compare what he was composing with what he was teaching his students." Bakker's research focuses on evidence-based pedagogy, music theory, and the connections between music and language. At Utah State, she teaches undergraduate and graduate courses in music theory and aural skills and serves as assistant department head and departmental honors advisor. She was named the College of Arts and Sciences' Teacher of the Year in 2020-21. She hopes her time in Hungary will lead to new scholarship while also enriching the classroom experience for her students when she returns to Utah State. "I hope to publish my findings in a journal article and share my experience with students after I get back to campus," she said. Karen Beard | Fulbright-National Science Foundation Arctic Research Grant — Iceland Karen Beard, professor in the Department of Wildland Resources in the S.J. & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture & Natural Resources, has received a Fulbright-National Science Foundation Arctic Research grant. She will conduct collaborative research at the Agricultural University of Iceland from September through December 2026. Her research will investigate how herbivores influence Arctic ecosystems by expanding international research databases and participating in long-term ecological experiments examining the impacts of grazing animals on vegetation, carbon cycling, and climate change. "Iceland is the ideal location for my Fulbright research because it is home to world-renowned leaders in Arctic herbivory research," Beard said. "Working there will allow me to actively collaborate with international research networks while contributing my expertise in goose herbivory and carbon cycling." Beard brings more than 15 years of Arctic research experience to the project and hopes the collaboration will strengthen global research partnerships while creating new opportunities for future research and student engagement. Katie Davidson | Fulbright International Education Administrators Award — Japan Katie Davidson, assistant director for exchanges in Utah State University's Office of Global Engagement, recently completed the Fulbright International Education Administrators program in Japan. "I specifically chose to apply for Fulbright Japan because we have a very popular and healthy exchange program with seven partner institutions there. I have advised many students going to and coming from Japan through those partnerships over the years, though I had never been there before this experience," Davidson said. "I wanted to learn more about the culture to better advise both our incoming and outgoing students." During her time in Japan, Davidson visited 14 universities, including all seven partners, explored Japan's higher education system and job search process, participated in homestays with local families, hiked in the mountains, and toured the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency. She also described visiting the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and Peace Memorial Park as one of the most meaningful experiences of the program. "I came away from my time in Japan feeling calmer, with the desire to slow down more," Davidson said. "I think there's much to be learned from Japanese culture — the welcoming nature and kindness of strangers, the courteous respect people show one another, the efficiency, and the ‘kawaii’ culture. I am forever grateful for this adventure." Davidson said the experience has already strengthened the way she advises students preparing to study abroad by giving her firsthand knowledge of Japan's academic system, culture, and everyday life. Renee Galliher | Fulbright Distinguished Arctic Scholar — Norway Renee Galliher, professor and director of clinical training for the combined clinical/counseling specialization in Utah State University's Department of Psychology in the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences, has been selected as a 2026-27 Fulbright Distinguished Arctic Scholar. Galliher will spend spring 2027 at UiT, The Arctic University of Norway in Tromsø, where she will work with faculty and students on research focused on identity development and its connections to mental health, education, and overall well-being in rural and High North communities. The project has a personal connection for Galliher, who grew up on a small ranch in rural northern Wyoming and attended a one-room elementary school. Those experiences have shaped much of her career as a psychologist, particularly her interest in supporting people from rural and underserved communities. During her time in Norway, Galliher will work with students and faculty to explore how different aspects of identity, including educational, cultural, and social identities, intersect and influence well-being. She also plans to mentor student research projects and serve as a guest lecturer in a graduate cultural and community psychology course. The collaboration will allow Galliher to compare experiences across different rural and underserved settings while building relationships between researchers and students in Norway and Utah. She hopes the work will lead to new research projects and publications, as well as ideas she can bring back to her students and colleagues at Utah State. Caroline Lavoie | Fulbright U.S. Scholar — Morocco Caroline Lavoie, professor in the Landscape Architecture and Environmental Planning Department in the S.J. & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture & Natural Resources, has been named a 2026-27 Fulbright U.S. Scholar and will spend the fall semester at the École Nationale d'Architecture in Rabat, Morocco. Her project, Contours of Change: Collaborative Studio Pedagogy and Drawing-Based Research in Rabat, Morocco , explores how drawing can serve as a research method to better understand the relationships among water, public space, movement, and urban form. "I chose Morocco because Rabat offers a rich setting where historic urban fabrics, modern planning, river landscapes, and every day public spaces overlap," Lavoie said. "I was also drawn to the opportunity to work in a Francophone academic setting, which connects to my background as a French Canadian and native French speaker." Through collaborations with faculty and students in Morocco, Lavoie hopes to deepen her drawing-based research while developing future teaching, writing, and exhibition projects. To learn more about Fulbright programs and other international opportunities for faculty, staff, and students at Utah State University, visit the Office of Global Engagement website at usu.edu/global-engagement .

title: Former Utah State Football Great Dave Kuresa Passes Away
summary: LOGAN, Utah – Former Utah State football great Dave Kuresa passed away on Monday, May 11. He was 63 years old. Kuresa was a four-year letterwinner at offensive guard for Utah State from 1981-84 and was named an Associated Press Honorable Mention All-American three years in a row from 1982 to 1984. Kuresa earned first-team All-Pacific Coast Athletic Association accolades during his sophomore, junior and senior campaigns. He is one of just 10 Aggies all-time, including one of just two offensive linemen, to be a three-time first-team all-conference selection. Following his collegiate career, Kuresa was a long-time assistant coach and offensive coordinator at Mountain Crest High School in Hyrum, Utah. For the last four years, he was an assistant coach at Ridgeline High School in Millville, Utah. In 1993, Kuresa was named to the Utah State Football All-Century Team.

title: Grand County 4-H Youth Earn Recognition Through Leadership, Higher Education Opportunities
summary: MOAB — Youths from Grand County recently participated in leadership and educational experiences through Utah State University Extension Home and Community, including the Saturday Academy at the University of Utah, the national IGNITE by 4-H Conference in Washington, D.C., and the annual Pathways to Higher Education program. Ten youths attended the Saturday Academy through a partnership between the BEACON Program and USU Extension. Students explored careers in medicine, nursing, dentistry, pharmacy and health sciences through hands-on activities, campus tours and mentoring opportunities. Before the academy, participants also visited Clark Planetarium to explore interactive science and technology exhibits. Grand County youth from the Uniting Cultures Club also traveled to Washington, D.C., for the third consecutive year to attend IGNITE by 4-H, where they presented the CUBE Challenge workshop to more than 60 youths from across the country. Their workshop focused on collaboration, listening to diverse perspectives and teamwork. Following the conference, participants were invited by the University of Utah School of Nutrition and Dietetics to tour campus and learn about careers in nutrition and wellness. The first week of June, 17 youths from Grand and San Juan counties participated in the third annual Pathways to Higher Education event. Students visited Utah State University campuses in Moab, Price and Logan while attending workshops on career preparation, scholarships, concurrent enrollment opportunities and college planning. The event is made possible through partnerships across the state and continues to expand opportunities for rural youth to explore higher education. In recognition of these efforts, the program received the Utah 4-H Expanding the 4-H Audience: Creating Opportunities 4 All Award for increasing access to educational opportunities, strengthening community engagement and expanding participation among youth and families from underserved and rural communities. Building on this achievement, the program was also selected as the 2026 Western Regional winner of the same award by the NAE4-HYDP Member Recognition Committee and will be recognized at the 2026 NAE4-HYDP Conference in Kansas City, Missouri.

title: How Far They've Come: USU Moab Celebrates Latest ESL Grads
summary: Utah State University Moab hosted a graduation ceremony July 14 for 19 students who successfully completed the campus’s six-week course for English as a second language. During the ceremony, the students each shared a personal story about their journey. The stories were full of overcoming adversity, finding confidence, and bettering their circumstances. Leticia Bentley, one of the course’s instructors, said that watching the students realize how far they have come was inspiring. “One student explained that for the first time he had enough confidence and vocabulary to pay his utility bills without asking for help,” she said. “Another shared how speaking more English at work allowed her to communicate with restaurant customers, resulting in better service and bigger tips. Several students talked about feeling confident enough to apply for better jobs and pursue new opportunities.” This particular cohort was unique because it included students with a wide range of English proficiency. While the course was split into two levels — beginning and advanced — it was still a challenge to tailor the courses so that all could learn at their own level and pace. “Our goal was to make every student feel included and continue growing, regardless of their starting point,” Bentley said. “It required creativity, flexibility, and a great deal of teamwork from our volunteer tutors.” The ESL course at USU Moab is an intensive six-week course held two days a week. The course is aided by volunteer tutors who work with students every week on their homework and to provide extra help when conflicts have prevented them from attending class. The next ESL course will begin at the end of October. “We hope to welcome both returning students and new learners who are ready to improve their English, expand their opportunities, and become even more connected to the Moab community,” Bentley said. Those interested in learning more about the course are encouraged to reach out to Samantha Campbell at samantha.campbell@usu.edu for more information. Located in the outdoor recreation paradise of Moab and boasting one of the greenest buildings on any USU campus, Utah State University Moab offers students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university. With programs such as Nursing, Elementary Education, Recreation Resource Management and Social Work, technical education in Health Professions, Automotive and Business, and degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees, USU Moab offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at moab.usu.edu .

title: How to Reduce Your Dog's Risk of Tick-Borne Diseases
summary: Tick populations continue to change across the climates of the Western states. Short of keeping your dog inside all the time, there is no tick-free lifestyle for dogs. You can, however, mitigate the risk of tick bites and tick-borne diseases. According to Chloe Stenkamp-Strahm, Utah State University Extension veterinarian, the simple answer is to be aware of your surroundings and use tick preventatives for your dog. She said there are topical products, monthly oral chew options and injectable medications that can last for several months to mitigate the risk of tick bites and tick-borne disease. These options can be discussed with your veterinarian. “Though tick populations vary seasonally, most experts recommend year-round treatment for peace of mind,” she said. “If you are already giving your dog heartworm preventatives, some also offer combination coverage for ticks and other ectoparasites, as well.” She said there are two ticks in Utah that are of the highest concern for dogs: the Rocky Mountain wood tick and the brown dog tick. Both can carry diseases such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia, which can be transmitted to dogs through tick bites. “There is also a risk of dogs developing tick paralysis from these ticks,” Stenkamp-Strahm said. “However, just because a tick can cause tick paralysis does not mean every dog bitten by one will develop the condition. More than 70 tick species have been associated with tick paralysis, making it another health concern dog owners should be aware of.” She said ticks are most active in spring and early summer when moisture levels are higher. As it gets hotter and drier, ticks may be less active, but they can become active again later in the year. “In general, be vigilant and aware of ticks in your surroundings,” she said. “Ideally, don't take your dog into areas where ticks are active if you are not using tick products or preventatives. If you do, inspect your dog thoroughly afterward. Some ticks feed on dogs in their nymph or non-adult stages, when they are only the size of a poppy seed or pinhead, so they are difficult to see, especially on dogs with long fur.” Stenkamp-Strahm said pet owners should inspect their dog's entire body after spending time outdoors. Pay particular attention to the areas around the ears, eyes, mouth, nose, and between the toes. Since dogs often sit on the ground, the area under their tail near the anus may be exposed to ticks and should be inspected as well. A bath may help after tick exposure, but only shampoos formulated to kill ectoparasites will effectively eliminate ticks. “If you do find a tick on your dog, the most effective way to remove it is with fine-tipped tweezers,” she said. “Grab the tick as close to its head as possible and pull it out using steady, gentle pressure without twisting. Folk remedies such as nail polish or lit matches are not recommended.”

title: Huntsman School Names Finance Trading Room in Honor of Marriner S. Eccles
summary: LOGAN, Utah — The Jon M. Huntsman School of Business at Utah State University officially named the Marriner S. Eccles Finance Trading Room during a ribbon-cutting ceremony on Sept. 14, honoring the legacy of one of Utah’s most influential business and economic leaders while creating a dedicated space for students to gain hands-on experience in finance. Located on the main floor of the George S. Eccles Business Building, the new trading room serves as a hub for experiential learning within the Huntsman School’s Department of Economics and Finance. The space houses nine Bloomberg terminals, providing students access to industry-leading investment and trading platforms, and will support student investment and trading practicums, case competitions, research, and other applied learning opportunities. Hope Eccles, trustee of the Marriner S. Eccles Foundation and great-niece of Marriner S. Eccles, joined Huntsman School students, faculty, and leaders for the ribbon cutting. The Marriner S. Eccles Foundation continues Eccles’ legacy of philanthropy through support of organizations and causes throughout Utah, including higher education, health, arts and culture, and social services. “This trading floor is about far more than screens, numbers, and moving prices. It offers students an extraordinary opportunity to apply what they learn in the classroom to real-world situations,” Hope Eccles said. “Here, students will learn not only how markets work, but also how to think under pressure, weigh risk against reward, respond to changing conditions, and make responsible decisions when the answers are not obvious. “Those lessons will serve them not only as investors and business leaders, but also as thoughtful and engaged citizens.” The trading room carries forward a connection between the Eccles family and business leadership in Utah that spans generations. Marriner S. Eccles and his brother, George S. Eccles, were sons of Utah industrialist David Eccles and Ellen Stoddard Eccles and native sons of Logan. Marriner S. Eccles went on to become a prominent banker and business leader before guiding the nation’s economic policy during the Great Depression and World War II as Chairman of the Federal Reserve. “We are extremely grateful to have a finance trading room named after Marriner Eccles,” said Ben Blau, head of the Department of Economics and Finance. “His role during the Great Depression, both in the state and the country, is a prime example to our students of outstanding leadership and economic thinking.” The room will provide a dedicated home for the department’s growing experiential learning programs, including state and national case competitions and hands-on experiences in investment, venture capital, real estate, and trading. “This trading room will be home to the experiential learning programs in the Department of Economics and Finance,” Blau said. “These programs, which include state and national case competitions, hands-on experience in both venture capital and real estate, and various practicum courses, will continue to grow and develop as students prepare for an ever-changing labor market. We are delighted that this trading room will serve as a home to these programs.” Students in the department have established a strong record in experiential competitions. In 2025, Huntsman teams earned first place at the Rocky Mountain Stock Pitch Competition, Utah Real Estate Challenge, and Bellwether Real Estate Case Competition. Huntsman students have also won the statewide CFA Institute Research Challenge seven of the past eight years and the nationwide Women’s Stock Pitch Competition hosted by William & Mary University three consecutive years. The department also offers investment, real estate and trading practicums in which student teams manage real portfolios under faculty mentorship. The new trading room brings those experiences together with the technology, collaborative space, and faculty support students need to put financial theory into practice. The Marriner S. Eccles Finance Trading Room represents the Huntsman School’s continued investment in learning by doing, providing students opportunities to develop real-world skills, make complex decisions, and prepare for careers in a changing financial landscape.

title: Investiture Celebrates Inaugural Endowed Dean Derek McLean and Supporting Foundations
summary: Leading a college with the breadth and impact of the S.J. and Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture and Natural Resources takes remarkable leadership — someone who can see connections and build on them, who can help students to build judgment and discover how their strengths complement the world around them, according to Provost Chris Corcoran during the investiture of the Janet Q. Lawson Endowed Deanship on Oct. 2. It’s a unique skill set, and one that Dean Derek McLean brings to the job, Corcoran said. The event marks the college’s first endowed deanship, with speakers recognizing the positive trajectory that the support has already created during significant structural shifts, as well as the unique role the college plays in a time of social, environmental, and political change. “This is a college that believes in showing up — for one another, for communities, landscapes, and agriculture. That combination of serious purpose and genuine community is what makes the college such a unique place,” McLean said. The Janet Q. Lawson and S.J. and Jessie E. Quinney foundations have a remarkable history of support for environmental research and science at Utah State University, noted The Very Rev. Frederick Quinney Lawson, representing the donors. The two foundations collaborated to create the endowed deanship for the college. “It’s a new chapter, a culmination and a beginning,” Lawson said. McLean joined USU in July 2026 from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, where he served as dean of the Agricultural Research Division. He now leads 12 departments spanning a range of disciplines, including nutrition, geology, engineering technology, aviation, and a suite of associate degrees and technical certificates at statewide campuses. McLean’s leadership background includes serving as a senior science adviser at the National Institutes of Health, senior director of collaborative research for Phibro Animal Health Corporation, and a decade as a faculty member at Washington State University. He has a Ph.D. in animal sciences from Oregon State University, along with a master’s in animal physiology and a bachelor’s in mathematical sciences from Clemson University. “What makes this even more meaningful is that it builds on a tradition that stretches back generations,” said Matt White, vice president for advancement and president of the USU Foundation. The Quinney and Lawson families helped shape USU through their commitment to education, agriculture, natural resources, and the landscapes that define our state, said White. S.J. “Joe” Quinney and Jessie Eccles Quinney were both graduates of the Agricultural College of Utah, and the legacy they began has continued through their children and grandchildren — particularly their daughter, Janet Quinney Lawson. In 1982, Joe and Jessie established the S.J. and Jessie E. Quinney Foundation, and Janet followed their example by establishing the Janet Q. Lawson Foundation in 1990. Through the decades, their combined generosity has advanced research, funded more than 200 Quinney Scholarships, and created countless opportunities for students and faculty.

title: ITLS Looks Back at Decade of Growth as Dept. Head Prepares to Step Down
summary: Andrew Walker has announced he will step down as department head of the Instructional Technology and Learning Sciences Department within the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education and Human Services after 10 years of service. Walker credits his faculty, staff and student colleagues for the department’s past decade of successes as it has expanded its degree offerings, increased enrollment and created a lasting culture of student support. “I have been so impressed with how Andy has fulfilled his responsibilities with thoughtfulness and a long-term perspective. He is willing to challenge assumptions, ask insightful questions, and offer helpful perspectives,” said CEHS Endowed Dean Al Smith. “I have enjoyed the opportunity to work closely with him and look forward to the many scholarly and other contributions he will make as he resumes his faculty work.” Walker earned a bachelor’s degree in English from Washington State University then came to Utah State in 1998 for a master’s degree in instructional technology. Two years later, at the invitation of his colleague Mimi Recker (who preceded him as ITLS department head), he decided to stay on to complete a doctorate with Recker as his mentor. When Walker stepped into the department head role in 2016 (after assuming the role of interim department head the year before), he navigated the job using guiding principles. “As a department head, I identified mostly as a cheerleader,” he said. “I helped all of us to see and celebrate each other’s work, whether we are going after large federal grants, growing programs or mentoring and advising students. I tried to acknowledge that I rarely had the best idea in the room. I had an internal motto of trying anything once. I also tried to acknowledge that even — and especially — when things are going well in general, there is always at least one person who is struggling.” At the time he started as department head, one of the greatest concerns within ITLS was enrollment. The department had been a pioneer in online education, launching one of the nation’s first online master’s degree programs in its field in 2007, but its success led to increased competition. “At peak popularity we had over 300 directly competing online master’s programs,” Walker said. College leadership challenged the ITLS department to develop a plan for growth, so the faculty began a redesign of the master’s program by gathering feedback from employers, alumni and current students to better understand what graduates face in the workforce. They then revised coursework and curriculum to address industry needs. In addition to improving the master’s program, department faculty also recognized the need for expansion. They began to develop an undergraduate degree: Human Experience Design and Interaction. Until that time, ITLS only offered a minor for undergraduates. “What makes HEDI special is that it has to keep reinventing itself to stay current with fast-evolving technology and the needs of the market our students enter — and Andy is the person who made that constant evolution possible,” said Ramy Shaaban, HEDI program director. “He embraced change, encouraged continuous improvement and moved quickly to turn new ideas into reality, from championing an AI course to bringing new tools like Roblox into our classrooms.” “During Andy Walker’s tenure, he championed the new bachelor’s program that has proven tremendously successful,” said Kristy Bloxham, professional practice faculty member. “He is leaving behind a legacy of thoughtful leadership and meaningful growth.” Student response to the new major, which was finalized in 2020, has been enthusiastic. Walker credits his colleagues for shaping the new program. “The faculty did the heavy lift of designing and eventually teaching classes in the new undergraduate degree,” Walker said. “We wanted to start with 40 in the program each year and we increased significantly after our first year.” Since then, enrollment has grown across the degree programs in ITLS. Student credit hours continue to increase, according to Walker, with a 57 percent increase over the past decade. The master’s degree has regained momentum and was recognized in 2025 as the fastest growing online graduate program at Utah State. The job outlook is remarkable, with 97 percent of undergraduate and graduate students finding employment in the field within three months of graduation. Beyond enrollment breakthroughs, Walker sees the department’s culture as one of its greatest strengths. Faculty members focus on supporting their students, many of whom are non-traditional students balancing coursework with full-time jobs, family responsibilities and other life demands. “Andy has been a caring and steady presence for every faculty member, guiding us through the challenges facing higher education with empathy and understanding,” Bloxham said. “He has taught me invaluable life lessons about understanding others and checking my biases at the door. His desire to be kind to everyone will be his legacy, something that we can all hope to emulate.” Walker recalled that a student-centered culture became especially important during the COVID-19 pandemic. As USU scrambled to move its courses online, ITLS faculty, students and alumni volunteered their expertise to help instructors begin teaching remotely, even donating their time before emergency funding became available. Walker said those days were some of the most meaningful of his tenure. Students and alumni were motivated simply by the desire to serve the university community during a crisis. After the pandemic, Walker supported ITLS faculty and student instincts to find ways to build a stronger sense of community within the department. They launched cultural celebrations that brought together students and faculty who come from around the world. Celebrating holidays and student cultures have now become annual traditions. Walker consistently emphasizes that the department’s successes are the result of the ITLS community. “My colleagues rise to the occasion every time,” he said about the major accomplishments he’s seen in the past decade. Looking ahead, Walker described a new pathway under development that will allow students to earn both a bachelor’s and master’s degree in five years. ITLS also remains committed to adapting to technology, including the influence of artificial intelligence. In July, Walker will take a sabbatical and return to campus to resume his research faculty role in 2027.

title: Jake Powell Announced as Associate Director of USU's Institute for Land, Water, & Air
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Jake Powell will join the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air at Utah State University as associate director on Oct. 1, where he will lead the institute’s research and programs. Powell comes to the institute from the Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning in the S.J & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture & Natural Resources, where he is an associate professor and Extension specialist. Powell's appointment strengthens the institute's leadership team. Brian Steed, the institute's founding executive director, was named USU vice president for government and external relations earlier this year and continues as the institute's principal advisor. The institute now reports to his office, which keeps its work closely connected to university and state leadership. Anna McEntire, who has helped guide the institute since 2022, moved from managing director to executive director. Powell joins Stephanie Frohman, associate director since 2024, who leads external relations and supports strategy across the institute's work. In his role, Powell will oversee the institute’s research and programs, one of its strategic pillars, and expand the institute’s capacity to bring USU research to bear on natural resource challenges across the state. “Jake has been part of USU’s land, water, and air work since before the institute was formally launched, so in many ways he’s been a colleague in this effort from the start,” said Anna McEntire, executive director of the institute. “He understands the land-grant mission in a practical way. He starts with the problems communities are facing and then works out how research can help. That’s what the institute is here to do, and I’m glad to have him helping lead it.” Powell, a Utah native, has spent his career in land planning and conservation across the state. His work centers on collaborative planning and design, helping communities use those tools to address social, economic, and ecological challenges. As an Extension specialist, he has developed educational programs and interdisciplinary projects that use design and planning to drive positive change statewide. His research spans watershed planning, stormwater management, water conservation, and open-space design, and he has worked with gateway communities throughout the Intermountain West as a co-director of the Gateway and Natural Amenity Region (GNAR) Initiative. “I have long admired the mission, efforts, and impact of the institute and I am so honored to join the institute’s amazing team,” Powell said. “I have experienced the good that can come from connecting pressing issues with Utah State University’s research, teaching, and Extension faculty. I see so many exciting opportunities to build these kinds of connections on the horizon, and I am excited to be part of the growth of the institute moving forward.” Powell's honors include national and regional Innovation and Creativity awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals and the NACTA Faculty Teaching Award of Merit, which he has received twice. With Powell leading its research and programs, the institute expects to expand its capacity to deliver timely, high-quality data to the leaders and communities working to balance natural resource needs with the state's rapid growth. "The institute's work is reaching more of the state every year, and our project portfolio has grown to match," McEntire said. "Bringing Jake on means we can say yes to more of the research and projects Utah legislators, business, state agencies, and local communities are asking us to do." About the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air The Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air at Utah State University connects decision-makers with high-quality research to support informed land, water, and air policy in Utah. Through applied research, public convening, and cross-sector collaboration, the Institute helps the state address complex natural resource challenges. Learn more at usu.edu/ilwa .

title: Justen Smith Named Vice President for USU Extension After National Search
summary: Utah State University President Brad Mortensen has named Justen Smith as the next vice president for USU Extension after a national search. Smith has served as interim vice president since March. Before that temporary appointment, he served as director of the USU Extension Agriculture and Natural Resources Department and as the director of the Northern Region Extension. “Justen understands both the history and the potential of USU Extension,” Mortensen said. “He has worked at the county, regional and statewide levels, and he knows that our responsibility is not simply to preserve what Extension has been, but to continually ask what Utah needs from its land-grant university today and into the future and how we can work together to meet those needs.” During his nearly three decades with USU Extension, Smith has secured more than $11 million in grants and external funding to support Extension initiatives and agricultural development, oversaw operations in counties throughout the state, and led the effort to secure $1.2 million for the construction of the USU Extension building in Davis County, creating a dedicated space for agricultural education and outreach. "USU Extension is an essential part of Utah State University’s land-grant mission, and I am honored that President Mortensen and the board of trustees have entrusted me to lead this incredible 112-year-old organization,” Smith said. “USU Extension provides research-based, factual, technical information to Utahns across the state. Extension literally extends the tremendous resources of USU to the people and exhibits measurable statewide impact, economic return on investment, and solutions to Utah’s biggest challenges. I am excited to be part of such rewarding work and know that positive impacts are ahead in partnership with our elected officials, industry leaders, and academic partners." Smith’s contributions extend well beyond Utah and the U.S. He has worked in 24 countries across Africa, the Middle East, and Latin America, providing technical assistance to farmers and agricultural organizations. His work with USDA, USAID, and multiple international organizations has helped improve livestock production, enhance food security, and develop sustainable agricultural practices in diverse regions throughout the world. About USU Extension Utah State University Extension provides research-based programs and resources with the goal of improving the lives of individuals, families and communities in all 29 Utah counties. USU Extension plays a primary role in helping Utah State University fulfill its land-grant mission, operatingthrough a cooperative agreement between the United States Department of Agriculture, Utah State University, and county governments. For more information about individual county offices and Extension programs, visit extension.usu.edu .

title: Keeping Current: USU Experts Track Colorado River as Regional Water Crisis Deepens
summary: Water levels in Lake Powell and Lake Mead fell to historic lows this summer, with managers across seven Western states and Mexico anxiously watching winter forecasts for a chance to reverse a looming water-supply crisis. Lake Powell is at 21% capacity and Lake Mead at 26% as of late August. It is the lowest combined storage for the reservoirs since the late 1950s, when Glen Canyon Dam was still under construction. See a time-lapse of the reservoirs through the megadrough t compiled by geographer Doug Ramsey, from the Department of Wildland Resources. Last year’s record-breaking low-snowpack certainly played a part in the decline, but this crisis has been lurking in the eddies for decades, according to Gina Gilson, new interim director of the Center for Colorado River Studies . The problem is not one bad winter, or even a growing demand from urban populations — there is simply less water to go around, she said. The region is in the midst of a 26-year megadrought. The average flow of the Colorado River during the last two decades has been 16% less than it was between 1930 and 2000, according to Jack Schmidt, senior research scientist with the Center for Colorado River Studies. A warming atmosphere is also pulling more water from the system through evapotranspiration — a combined loss of water through evaporation and plant transpiration — before it ever reaches the river. Though cities do make large demands on the river, this crisis isn’t really about urban growth, Schmidt said. Since the onset of long-term drought in the early 2000s, the cities of Los Angeles, San Diego, Phoenix, Denver, and Las Vegas focused on water conservation, reducing water use even as their populations have grown. Still, states have not been able to agree how to share the burden of the water shortage, and the federal government is now rationing the supply and negotiating plans for short-term management. Meanwhile the river itself faces ecological upheaval as plummeting reservoir levels alter water temperatures, block sediment transport, and threaten native fish and bird species. In Utah, the stakes of the crisis are particularly broad, with the Colorado River system supporting communities, agriculture and ecosystems across the state. A major tributary to the Colorado, the Green River, flows through eastern Utah, with Flaming Gorge the largest of the upstream reservoirs to shore up declining levels in Lake Powell. The Central Utah Project transfers water from the Colorado River to the Wasatch Front, while agriculture in the Uinta Basin and southwestern Utah depends on the river’s water. As Lake Powell shrinks, Utah has also lost recreational resources. At the same time, submerged natural and archaeological sites in Glen Canyon have begun to re-emerge. It’s a complex, high stakes situation with no simple solutions. Experts at USU are keeping track of the latest developments and collaborating across disciplines to discern possible next steps. “The human angle is one of the most fraught,” Gilson said. “We know that we need to live with less water, but decision-making about how to accomplish that involves a complex web of laws, policies, and competing values tied to the river.” Gilson is a social scientist working to understand how decisions are made for what happens to the water supply from the Colorado River — who benefits, who loses, and how those tradeoffs come together. As water managers confront a system that can no longer reliably meet expectations, she is watching how the negotiations unfold. Her research looks at how science, law, politics, and competing interests come together at different scales. “We’ve assumed, up to now, that we would be buffered by the massive amount of water stored in the reservoirs, so coming to grips with these limits is a trial on all levels,” Gilson said. With a 40-year career in river restoration, ecosystem health, and the impact of dams under his belt, Schmidt can offer big-picture context for a public anxious to understand the problem. He’s been tapped by NPR , The Wall Street Journal, , Newsweek, CNN, and other major media outlets as the world grapples with the slow-moving catastrophe. Fish ecologist Phaedra Budy studies what happens when rivers change and what managers can do to keep native Colorado River fish alive in a river that has been heavily altered by dams, water use, drought, and invasive species. Though the ecology of the river has been almost a secondary consideration, every change has major impacts on the survival of native fish, and the downstream consequences of that shift, according to her research. Experts at the Utah Water Research Laboratory use water data and computer models to help people understand what the Colorado River can realistically provide, and how different ways of managing it might work as the watershed gets drier. “It’s a natural system with a lot of uncertainty, and we need to understand the range of future conditions we could be facing,” said Director Bethany Neilson. “Our job is to give water managers the best science and tools we can so they can make informed decisions about how to use and manage a shrinking water supply.” As the Colorado River enters this uncertain era, USU experts continue tracking changes, modeling possible futures, and studying the consequences for communities and ecosystems that depend on a river in change.

title: Keith Smith Named USU Head Volleyball Coach
summary: LOGAN, Utah – Utah State University Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker announced Keith Smith as the next head volleyball coach at Utah State on Saturday. Smith brings extensive experience working within the USA Volleyball pipeline and most recently served as an assistant coach at TCU in 2025, helping guide the Horned Frogs to a 21-11 record and a win in the opening round of the NCAA Tournament. TCU appeared in every AVCA poll during the season and finished the 2025 campaign ranked No. 9, marking the first top-10 ranking in program history. The Horned Frogs also recorded a program-best six victories over top-25 opponents. "I'm excited to welcome Keith to Utah State as our new head volleyball coach," said Walker. "He's a proven recruiter with a strong track record of developing players. From the start of the hiring process, his professionalism and expertise were evident, and his attributes and vision aligned with those of our volleyball student-athletes, making him the ideal choice to advance Utah State volleyball. His background with USA Volleyball will be invaluable as the program works to reach the next level." Before the 2025 season, Smith served as an assistant coach for the women's U21 national team at the 2025 NORCECA Pan American Cup, helping Team USA capture a gold medal in Costa Rica. The team swept all five matches en route to the championship. "I am grateful to USU Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker and the search committee for trusting me with the opportunity to continue Utah State volleyball's rich history," said Smith. "My goal is not to rebuild the program, but to retool it for long-term, sustainable success that keeps it on an upward trajectory." At Auburn, Smith spent three seasons (2022–24) as an assistant coach. The Tigers posted back-to-back 20-win seasons, including a modern program-record 22 victories in 2022, and earned back-to-back NCAA Tournament appearances in 2022 and 2023 for the first time in school history. Auburn recorded six top-25 wins during his tenure, matching the program's combined total from the previous 15 seasons. In 2023, the Tigers also made their first-ever appearance in the AVCA Poll. Working primarily with the setters, Smith helped elevate Auburn's offensive production. Jackie Barrett became the sixth setter in program history to reach 1,000 assists in a season, achieving the milestone in 2022 while earning SEC Setter of the Week honors twice. Barrett again surpassed 1,000 assists in 2023 and guided the Tigers to a .241 hitting percentage, the third-best in program history. Smith also played a key role in planning and conducting daily practices, including skill development, game strategy, and preparing scouting reports. "My philosophy and core values focus on putting people and connections first while maintaining the standards and discipline that lead to excellence," Smith added. "Success begins with the daily decisions we make to build winning habits. I'm excited to bring a highly competitive staff to Logan and develop a roster that will chase championships in the new Pac-12 and wins in the NCAA Tournament." Before Auburn, Smith served as an assistant coach at his alma mater, Grand Canyon, helping the men's program emerge as a national contender. The Lopes recorded 19 wins over top-15 opponents, including a straight-set upset of No. 1 BYU in 2021, climbed as high as No. 6 in the AVCA Poll and produced five All-Americans. An accomplished recruiter, Smith helped GCU secure the nation's No. 8-ranked signing class in 2021, highlighted by 10 of the top 50 recruits nationally. His work earned national recognition as a 2021 AVCA 30 Under 30 award winner, honoring the top coaches in the country under the age of 30. As an assistant coach at Providence in 2017, he helped the team earn its first winning season in 10 years and its most conference wins since it rejoined the Big East. In seven years with USA Volleyball, Smith has worked with the National Team Development Program, including the women's U21 national team in 2025 and as an assistant coach for the men's national team at the 2021 NORCECA Championships, where Team USA finished fifth. During his collegiate career, Smith was a setter at Grand Canyon, finishing with a school record 4,484 career assists. He totaled 1,294 assists in 2013, ranking 10th all-time in NCAA history during the 25-point scoring era. After college, Smith played professionally with Orion TopVolley in the Netherlands, helping the team finish in the top four in the regular season, playoffs and national club tournament. He earned a bachelor's degree in sports management and a master's degree in business administration from Grand Canyon University. Smith and his wife, Kierstin, have one son, Theodore.

title: Know the Signs, Find the Words: USU's Suicide Prevention Efforts
