summary: During Suicide Prevention Awareness Month, Utah State University Counseling and Prevention Services (CAPS) is encouraging Aggies to learn how to recognize when someone may be struggling and connect them with support. Through USU HELPS, a 60-minute training, CAPS teaches students how to spot suicide warning signs and support someone in distress. Students and employees can request a training on the CAPS website. "Hope and healing are important parts of suicide prevention," said Kaitlin Oliver, wellness promotion and suicide prevention coordinator at CAPS. "We want students to know that support is available even when things feel overwhelming." Warning signs can include talking about wanting to die or about feeling hopeless, trapped, or like a burden to others. Other signs include increased alcohol or drug use, agitation, mood swings, changes in sleep, and withdrawing from others. A sudden drop in grades or repeated absences may also signal distress. CAPS recommends starting with a private conversation: express concern, listen without judgment, and ask directly, for example, "Have you been thinking about ending your life?" "Students don't have to be mental health professionals to support someone who is struggling," Oliver said. "Checking in, listening and helping someone find support can be an important first step." CAPS has partnered with USU Dining Services to offer Logan campus students a free soup and salad bar meal at the Skyroom after they complete Live On Utah's Suicide Prevention Playbook . Students can show their certificate of completion at the CAPS office in the Taggart Student Center Room 306, to receive a coupon while supplies last. CAPS offers counseling, crisis services, wellness resources, and referrals for students at the Logan campus and statewide locations, in person or by telehealth. Students can call 435-797-1012 or visit during business hours. For immediate crisis support, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org/chat. Students can also reach trained crisis therapists 24/7 by calling the CAPS phone number 435-797-1012, option 0.

title: Lifelong Aggies Invest $4.5 Million in Future of Utah State Athletics
summary: Duane Shaw likes to say he was “born an Aggie.” Growing up just below the Utah State University campus in Logan, Duane could stand outside and see the A on the hillside. His father was a devoted Aggie fan, and Duane started attending football games when he was 5 years old. All six children in his family would eventually attend and graduate from Utah State. That lifelong connection to Utah State — and especially Aggie Athletics — is now at the heart of a $4.5 million commitment from Duane and Marci Shaw and their nephew and niece, Brian and Natalie Broadbent. The joint gift will support student-athlete scholarships , as well as the areas of greatest need within Utah State Athletics, with an emphasis on helping football and men’s basketball remain competitive. The Shaws are adding to an existing Athletics endowment, while the Broadbents are establishing a new endowment to support student-athletes. The families see the combined gift as an investment not only in Athletics, but in students and in the future of Utah State as the university begins a new chapter in the Pac-12. “We want to help the students, and we want Utah State to be competitive,” Duane said. “We’ve given the Athletics Department flexibility to use the gift where it’s needed and where it can make a difference.” Family of Aggies For the Shaws and Broadbents, the gift is the latest chapter in a family connection to Cache Valley and Utah State that stretches across generations, with family ties to the valley dating back to the 1800s. Duane earned a bachelor’s degree in finance from Utah State in 1973 and has supported the university for decades through scholarships, Athletics and the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business, including helping finance the construction of Huntsman Hall. Brian earned a bachelor’s degree in finance from USU in 1993, while Natalie earned a bachelor’s degree in elementary education that same year. In addition to the Broadbents’ established scholarships at the university, Brian has served on the USU Foundation Investment Committee and the Huntsman School’s National Advisory Board. The relationship between uncle and nephew extends well beyond their shared alma mater. Duane remembers teaching Brian how to ride a bike, swim, water ski, and snow ski, and, as adults, the two served together for 10 years on the Huntsman School advisory board. Still, neither knew the other was thinking about making a significant gift to Athletics until a pivotal conversation at the Mountain West basketball tournament in Las Vegas last spring. “I told him I thought it was a great time to invest in Aggie Athletics as they move into the new conference, and he laughed and said he had been thinking about the same thing,” Duane said. “We had basically the same idea. So, we said, ‘Why don’t we do this together?’” Investing in a New Era Utah State’s move to the Pac-12 represents a new era for Aggie Athletics, bringing new opportunities, new competition, and new expectations. For the Shaws and Broadbents, it is a moment when private support can help Utah State build momentum and position its programs for long-term success. Brian said he is encouraged by the direction of the university and Athletics and believes Utah State has an opportunity to build something special. “I think we’re in a really good spot at this point,” Duane said. “We’ve always focused our giving on students, and we wanted to continue that. We hope this helps Utah State become more competitive in all of the sports that USU participates in and gives student-athletes opportunities to compete, get an education, and have the best possible outcome.” For the families, that student focus is central to the gift. The Shaws have long favored investments that directly benefit students, including scholarships, and wanted this commitment to continue that tradition. At the same time, providing unrestricted support gives Athletics leaders the ability to respond to the rapidly changing landscape of college sports and invest where resources can have the greatest impact. “Duane and Marci and Brian and Natalie understand both where Utah State Athletics has been and where we have the opportunity to go,” said USU Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker. “Their investment gives us the flexibility to be responsive while keeping student-athletes at the center of what we do. As we compete in the Pac-12, this kind of commitment sends a powerful message about what our Aggies believe is possible.” More Than Wins and Losses Both the Shaws and Broadbents believe successful athletics programs can have an impact far beyond the field or court. Brian saw that firsthand while living and working in New York. In 2011, Utah State traveled to Auburn to face the defending national champions. The Aggies led 38-28 with less than four minutes remaining before Auburn rallied for a 42-38 victory. When Brian returned to work in New York the following Monday, people kept approaching him for days afterward about Utah State. “You would not believe how many people in New York approached me,” Brian said. “That was the first time it truly hit me what a successful athletics program could do. I don’t think there was anything we could have done that would have gotten our name out there like being on national television on a Saturday and showing that we could compete with a team like Auburn. We didn’t win, but we went toe-to-toe with the defending national champions, and people noticed.” The experience showed him the power Athletics can have in building awareness of a university far beyond its traditional geographic reach. “A successful program can build a national name and reputation,” Brian said. “I would love to see Utah State competitive in the national spotlight.” Duane sees another benefit: connection. Even though he no longer lives in Logan and cannot attend very many games, he remains closely connected to Aggie Athletics. He watches games on television, follows the teams, and keeps up with programs across the department. “I think a successful athletics program encourages alumni to be Aggies all their lives,” Duane said. “It keeps you connected to the school.” That connection can ripple across the entire university, strengthening alumni engagement, increasing visibility, and introducing new audiences to Utah State. “Athletics has an extraordinary ability to bring people together around Utah State,” said USU Vice President for Advancement Matt White. “Duane and Marci and Brian and Natalie are investing in that connection, but, more importantly, they are investing in students. Their generosity will create opportunities for student-athletes today while helping position Utah State for success for generations to come.” Every Gift Can Make an Impact For the Broadbents, the focus on scholarships is personal. Brian and Natalie married between their junior and senior years at Utah State. Both worked 20 to 30 hours a week while attending school, and both benefited from scholarships. “At that point, literally $20 would have made a difference,” Brian said. “The scholarships took some of the pressure off and helped us. So, when we were in a position to give back, that was something we wanted to do.” That experience also shapes the message he hopes others take from this gift: making an impact at Utah State is not limited to those who can make a multimillion-dollar commitment. “All gifts are helpful,” Brian said. “Every bit helps.” This is the first time the Broadbents have publicly announced a gift. They have generally preferred to keep their philanthropy private, but after conversations with Athletics leadership, they saw an opportunity for their story to encourage others to get involved. That is also one reason the Shaws and Broadbents chose to make their commitments together. They hope their combined investment creates momentum as Utah State enters the Pac-12 and inspires other Aggies to consider how they, too, can support the university and its student-athletes. For Duane, the invitation is simple. “Get on board and help us out,” Duane said. “Help us build a program we can all be proud of.” Support for Utah State Athletics to the Big Blue Club creates opportunities for student-athletes to pursue their education, compete at the highest level, and represent USU on a national stage. Whether through scholarships or support for Athletics’ greatest needs , every gift can help strengthen the Aggie experience and build momentum for the future.

title: Meet USU Eastern's New and Transitioning Technical Education Faculty
summary: As a new academic year begins at Utah State University Eastern, students are learning from faculty who bring professional experience, industry knowledge, and strong connections to the communities they serve. USU Eastern is introducing new and transitioning faculty, highlighting five members in Technology, Design, and Technical Education: Katie Horsley, engineering, drafting, and design. Jaime Cowdell, business. Mark Aldred, aviation maintenance technology. Leona Bowden, cosmetology. Krikit Butcher, medical assisting, and phlebotomy. While their fields are very different, each brings an emphasis on connecting classroom learning with the skills students will use in the workforce. Katie Horsley , engineering, drafting, and design lecturer, brings both local roots and professional industry experience to the classroom. A Price native, Horsley began her education at Utah State University before serving a mission in Poland and later returning to USU Eastern to complete her education. Her professional background includes civil, structural, and architectural drafting and design, along with experience using a variety of drafting software. Horsley said she enjoys the combination of creativity and structure the field provides and wants students to develop skills that go beyond learning software commands. Through hands-on creating, modeling and real-world design problems, students develop accuracy, communication, troubleshooting and problem-solving skills that prepare them to enter the workforce and continue learning. “If you enjoy creating things, solving problems, or working with technology, give it a try,” Horsley said. “Drafting can lead to a lot of different careers, and you may discover something you really enjoy.” Jaime Cowdell is no stranger to USU Eastern . After six years as part of the Eastern community, Cowdell is moving into the classroom as a professional practice assistant professor in the business department. Cowdell holds an MBA from the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business and has spent much of her career working with businesses, community partners, and university colleagues. She hopes to bring those relationships and experiences directly into her teaching. “What excites me most is helping students see how business concepts connect to the real world,” Cowdell said. “I want students to leave my classes with more than just knowledge from a textbook.” Her goal is to incorporate real-world projects, technology, problem-solving, communication, teamwork, and connections with local businesses and community leaders into students’ education. Cowdell also sees business as a strong option for students who may not know exactly where their careers will take them. “You don’t have to know exactly what career you want when you start,” she said. “A business education can give you a strong foundation while you figure out where your interests and strengths fit.” For Aviation Maintenance Technology students, Lecturer Mark Aldred brings more than 30 years of aerospace experience into the classroom. His career has included work on aircraft ranging from small two-seat Cessnas to Boeing 747s, with experience in aircraft maintenance and manufacturing in both civilian and Department of War environments. He has also been in quality engineering and management positions with companies including Lockheed and Bell Helicopter and spent time working with NASA. That experience now helps Aldred prepare students for careers in an industry with opportunities extending far beyond traditional aircraft maintenance. “I love teaching in this field for the amazing opportunities it can offer my students,” Aldred said. Hands-on learning is central to his classroom. Aldred strives to have students working with their hands during every class period, whether completing a lab project or performing maintenance on the program’s twin-engine Piper Navajo. He records many lectures for students to complete outside of class, creating additional time for practical work. While graduates may begin their careers “turning wrenches,” Aldred points out that aviation maintenance experience can also lead to careers in quality, reliability, engineering support, training, and other areas of the aerospace industry. In cosmetology, Leona Bowden is helping students build their skills progressively throughout USU Eastern’s 1,250-hour program. During the first two semesters, students focus on foundational theory and hands-on education. As they progress, instruction expands beyond technical cosmetology skills to include the business side of the profession. Students learn about the many directions a cosmetology career can take, including the possibility of owning their own business. They are introduced to basic steps involved in starting a business and the resources and organizations they may work with along the way. “It is always our goal to give students as much information as we can in order to begin a successful career, whatever direction they wish to take in the future,” Bowden said. Rather than overwhelming students with everything at once, Bowden said the program is structured so students build their knowledge and confidence as they progress through their required hours. Krikit Butcher , medical assisting and phlebotomy instructor, brings nearly 30 years of experience as a medical assistant to her students. Her career has included direct patient care, phlebotomy, assisting with office procedures, surgery scheduling, authorizations, coding, and other clinical and administrative responsibilities. Along the way, she worked with numerous healthcare providers who helped shape her approach to patient care. After nearly three decades in the field, Butcher chose to bring that experience into education. “I absolutely love my job and have had so many experiences and have so many skills I can bring and share with the students at USUE,” Butcher said. Butcher wants students to graduate with more than technical ability. She emphasizes empathy, compassion, teamwork, putting patients first, and being willing to continue learning. “I can teach the skills, the knowledge and confidence to perform the tasks at hand,” she said, “but if I do not teach the things I have mentioned above, I have not performed my job as an educator.” Students in the medical assisting program receive classroom and lab instruction before completing an externship that includes both administrative and clinical experience. The two-semester program prepares students to enter the workforce after completing the program and certification requirements, while also providing a foundation for those who want to continue their education in healthcare. From an engineering and design classroom to an aircraft hangar, cosmetology lab, healthcare setting, or local business, these five faculty members bring students something that cannot come from a textbook alone: experience. Their backgrounds allow students to learn not only the technical knowledge required in their fields, but also the communication, problem-solving, professionalism, and adaptability needed to build successful careers. Together, Horsley, Cowdell, Aldred, Bowden, and Butcher represent the hands-on, career-focused education at the heart of USU Eastern’s Technology, Design and Technical Education programs. To learn more about USU Eastern’s School of Professional & Technical Education, visit: qanr.usu.edu/spte .

title: Meet USU Eastern's New Arts and Sciences Faculty
summary: Editor’s note: In the first of a two-part series introducing new and transitioning faculty at USU Eastern, this feature highlights Jared Arnell, physics lecturer, and David Baca, professional practice assistant professor in criminal justice. Both bring unique professional and academic experiences to the classroom and a shared enthusiasm for helping students discover where their education can take them. As Utah State University Eastern begins a new academic year, the campus is welcoming faculty members whose experiences extend from exploring the mysteries of the universe to nearly three decades in law enforcement. For Jared Arnell, a love of teaching began in an unexpected place: high school debate. Growing up, Arnell was interested in theater and debate while also developing a fascination with science, mathematics and nature. After high school, he volunteered as an assistant debate coach for his former team and discovered how much he enjoyed teaching and mentoring others. That experience eventually led him toward higher education. Arnell earned a bachelor's degree in physics from Utah Valley University and a master's degree in physics from Utah State University. He is also nearing completion of a Ph.D. in learning sciences. When a physics teaching position became available at USU Eastern, Arnell saw an opportunity to combine his interests in science and education at the university where he had already continued his own academic journey. “It was a marvelous stroke of luck that a physics teaching position opened up at my own institution, so I was eager to jump at the opportunity,” Arnell said. This fall, Arnell is particularly excited to teach Introduction to Astronomy for the first time. “Who wouldn't love to spend an entire semester talking about the wonders of the cosmos?” he said. For Arnell, physics offers students more than equations and formulas. It provides a different way of looking at the world. “At its core, physics is about understanding patterns; how does the material world behave, and why does it behave in that way?” Arnell said. He hopes students learn to look beyond what they initially see and recognize the connections between everything from atoms to planets. Outside the classroom, Arnell enjoys cooking and has spent years building his own personal recipe book. He particularly enjoys experimenting with unexpected combinations of flavors. He is also looking forward to exploring southeastern Utah's state and national parks and finding others in the community who share his enthusiasm for the outdoors. David Baca comes to USU Eastern with nearly 27 years of law enforcement experience and a desire to help students turn their interest in criminal justice into meaningful careers. Baca joined Utah State University in 2024 as a Lecturer in the Criminal Justice Program at the Blanding campus. After building connections with students, staff and faculty there, he applied for a Professional Practice Assistant Professor position at USU Eastern in 2026. Eastern's history within USU's criminal justice program was a significant part of that decision. “USU Eastern is the founding site for the criminal justice degree program,” Baca said. “A desire to train and learn from the program's creators was one of the key factors in my desire to apply for this position.” Baca's path into law enforcement began after graduating from Brigham Young University in 1991. His original goal was to become an FBI agent, but with the agency not hiring at the time, he applied to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department after seeing a recruitment advertisement. He was hired as a deputy sheriff in 1992 and went on to spend nearly 27 years working with the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and the Murrieta Police Department. After retiring, Baca wanted to bring those experiences into higher education and help prepare the next generation of criminal justice professionals. “I believe the greatest joy is when a student reaches the threshold of acting on their desires,” Baca said. For Baca, that might mean seeing a student gain the confidence to apply to law school, pursue a position with a police department or seek a career with a federal agency. This year, he is especially looking forward to teaching Introduction to Forensic Science — USU Eastern has a dedicated room to simulate indoor and outdoor crime scenes for students. Baca also hopes to become involved throughout campus. After serving as a faculty and student mentor at USU Blanding, he will chair the mentoring program at Eastern and hopes to encourage participation from both faculty and students. He is also looking forward to attending athletic events and other campus activities. Baca's connection to eastern Utah also has a family tie. His mother's side, the Howell and Cordell families, were West Virginia coal miners during the 1930s and 1940s — a history that provides a meaningful connection to a region shaped by its own generations of mining families. Together, Arnell and Baca bring distinctly different backgrounds to USU Eastern, but both share an emphasis on experiential learning, mentorship and helping students recognize new possibilities for their futures. Whether students are examining the patterns that connect atoms and planets or processing evidence from a mock crime scene, Eastern's newest Arts and Sciences faculty members are ready to help students turn curiosity into knowledge and knowledge into opportunity. To learn more about USU Eastern Arts and Science programs, visit: artsci.usu.edu .

title: Middle School Students Conduct Summer Science Experiments at USU STARS GEAR UP Biotechnology Camp
summary: Utah middle school students from Sanpete County gained hands-on STEM experience during a two-day Biotech camp in June. USU STARS GEAR UP has a strong history of working with faculty in the College of Arts & Sciences to offer STEM summer camps to students from GEAR UP partner schools across Utah. “At the end of the day, it’s our goal to give these students a variety of exposure to new experiences,” said René Hernandez, GEAR UP grant five director. The camp brought together students from under-resourced schools where they will likely be the first in their families to attend college. For these students, opportunities to explore advanced science topics and have face-to-face time with world-renowned scientists are a rare but critical aspect to shaping their educational and career aspirations. At the camp, the students learned about galvanization in a new experiment in which they turned copper pennies to shades of silver and gold using zinc sulfate and sodium hydroxide. “They were comparing whose penny turned the brightest shade of gold,” said Amanda Martin, a biology undergraduate researcher. Other STEM highlights included a variety of neurobiology lessons from Sara Freeman’s lab, where students held a human brain with eyes still attached. “Some students were grossed out, and some thought it was so cool,” Hernandez said. They also learned that the body generates electrical signals and explored how modern technology can be used to better understand those signals. Using an electrocardiogram, students observed how the heart's electrical activity could be measured and even used those signals in experiments to influence each other’s arm movements. “The experiments were so interesting,” said Aubree Whitman, USU STARS GEAR UP college adviser. “It was so cool to see how engaged the students were.” The camp was led by Ryan Jackson, an associate professor of biochemistry, with support from biology and biochemistry students. Jackson worked to ensure success for each participant. USU student volunteers worked alongside the middle schoolers, walking them through each step of the experiment, answering questions and encouraging them to think critically about the results. By building their confidence early on, camp organizers hope the young students will be more likely to envision themselves pursuing a variety of STEM careers. “There were a lot of girls at this camp, which was exciting because the middle school age is where girls start turning away from science and math,” Hernadez said. “I loved to see them so excited about it.” One of the highlights of the camp was a laboratory experiment that introduced jellyfish genes into bacteria. The genetic transfer caused the bacteria to glow fluorescent green, blue or orange, which created an exciting visible result that helped the students better understand to what they were learning. The experiment exposed students to key concepts in modern biology, including gene transfer, gene expression, bacterial immune systems and CRISPR gene editing technology. “The students were all really involved this year by asking lots of questions and providing ideas about the experiments,” Martin said. For these middle school students, the experience was the first time they had worked in a university lab using professional-grade equipment and wearing personal protective equipment. “It’s fun to see the kids realize they can complete an experiment,” Martin said. “It’s cool to see them take our directions and have them get excited by the results.” USU STARS GEAR UP is a federally funded grant program at USU that serves students in under-resourced schools throughout urban and rural Utah from seventh grade through their first year of post-secondary education. GEAR UP site coordinators and college advisers help students navigate challenges such as finding programs and applying for federal aid and scholarships, often without a parent or guardian at home who has experience in higher education. Site coordinators and college advisers also organize college visits, tutoring, financial aid nights and college and career-related tours to benefit the students. USU STARS GEAR UP plans to offer more STEM enrichment opportunities to under-resourced Utah students.

title: More Than a Livestock Sale: Utah 4-H Communities Rally Around Youth
summary: Editor's note: This story has been corrected to reflect that Brandon Barela has already received a heart transplant. At a 4-H livestock show, youth spend months learning to care for an animal, develop responsibility, and prepare for the moment they step into the show ring. But at livestock auctions across Utah this year, communities demonstrated that these projects can mean far more than raising and selling an animal. In both Weber and Salt Lake counties, 4-H communities rallied around young exhibitors facing significant challenges, transforming livestock sales into powerful demonstrations of compassion, generosity, and support. In Weber County, nine-year-old Brandon “Chomp” Barela was preparing for his first year in 4-H and his first livestock show. A member of the West Weber Wether’s Club, he received a goat from club leader Brian Opheikens and named him Santa. Barela has faced significant health challenges throughout his young life. Born with Down syndrome and a congenital heart defect, he experienced heart failure in March and underwent surgery to receive a pacemaker and a new heart valve. Just one week before the Weber County Fair, he experienced heart failure again and was unable to show Santa. But his 4-H community stepped in. Barela’s best friend and fellow 4-H member, Tyttan Sappington, led Santa into the show ring on his behalf. When Santa entered the Junior Livestock Auction, the crowd rallied around Barela and his family. Bidding climbed until Santa sold for more than $41,000. The generosity did not stop there. The buyers returned Santa to Barela’s family, allowing them to take him home and care for him. His younger sister has also been able to spend time with Santa, and the family hopes Barela will be able to see his goat again soon. While his family faced an uncertain road ahead, the Weber County community’s support provided encouragement and financial assistance during a difficult time. Since then, the young boy has received a heart transplant, and his family looks toward the future with hope. A similar show of support took place in Salt Lake County, where a young 4-H member battling a rare form of cancer participated in the county livestock show. Despite the circumstances, he continued to find joy in his 4-H livestock projects. When asked whether he preferred showing pigs or lambs, his answer was simple – he loves it all. At the Salt Lake County livestock auction, buyers and community members rallied around the young exhibitor, ultimately raising approximately $15,000 through the sale of his animal. The two stories are different, but they share a common thread: When young people need support, their 4-H communities show up. “Sometimes a livestock sale becomes a whole lot more than selling an animal,” said Dave Francis, Utah 4-H director. “These moments remind us that 4-H is about so much more than what happens in the show ring. It is about the relationships young people build, the lessons they learn, and the communities that stand behind them.” For 4-H members, livestock projects teach responsibility, animal care, record-keeping, work ethic, and perseverance. But the experiences also create friendships and connections that can last far beyond the fair. The generosity displayed in Weber and Salt Lake counties is a reminder of what can happen when those connections come together. A goat can become a symbol of hope. An auction can become an opportunity to lift a family. And a livestock project can bring an entire community together around a young person. About Utah 4-H Utah 4-H is a youth development program of Utah State University Extension that empowers young people to develop leadership, confidence, responsibility, and life skills through hands-on learning experiences. Through clubs, projects, camps, competitions, and community experiences, Utah 4-H helps young people discover their passions and prepare for the future.

title: Mountain West Center for Regional Studies Announces 2026 Evans Biography Award Winners
summary: LOGAN – T he Mountain West Center for Regional Studies at Utah State University awarded the Evans Awards to authors whose selected works focused on the importance of documenting individual lives and their impact – the first examining the complex biography of Joseph Smith and the other telling the story of an important poet, May Swenson. The 2026 Evans Biography Award went to John G. Turner, and Margaret A. Brucia won the 2026 Evans Handcart Award. A national jury selected John G. Turner’s volume, “ Joseph Smith: The Rise and Fall of an American Prophet ” as the winner of the Evans Biography Award. “Joseph Smith” focuses on Joseph Smith Jr. (1805-1944), a religious leader who published the Book of Mormon and started what became the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints . Turner’s biography draws insights from newly accessible diaries, church records, and transcripts of sermons to illuminate Smith’s journey from impoverished farmhand to religious leader, crafting a balanced and extensively researched account of the Mormon prophet’s life. “ The Key to Everything: May Swenson, A Writer’s Life ” is an intimate and detailed biography of the American poet with a focus on the period between 1936-1959 when Swenson was living in New York City. Swenson (1913-1989) was born in Logan, Utah to Swedish immigrant parents and came of age as a writer during the Great Depression, the Federal Writers’ Project, and the emergence of gay culture. Margaret A. Brucia examines this period through Swenson’s own words through unpublished diaries and letters to friends, family, and colleagues. The Evans Awards recognize the best of research and writing in biographies, autobiographies and memoirs that focus on the stories of people who have shaped the character of the Interior West. The Evans Biography Award comes with a cash prize of $10,000, and the Evans Handcart Award winner is presented with $2,500. The prizes are made possible through an endowment created in 1983 by the family of David Woolley Evans and Beatrice Cannon Evans. Center Director, Molly Cannon, remarked, “The Evans Awards offer an incredible opportunity for Utah State University to showcase pinnacle works of the American West. We are grateful for the Evans Family and their continued support of writers and scholars in our communities.” The regional jury named one additional work as Evans Handcart Award Finalist from the over thirty submissions received. Laurie Lee Hall’s memoir “ Dictates of Conscience: From Mormon High Priest to My New Life as a Woman ” offers an articulate, forthright, and, at times, heartbreaking narrative of what it meant to transition from holding a patriarchal role in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints to being a woman. Awardees were chosen from works published in 2024 and 2025 and submitted to the national and regional juries for consideration. Winners will be honored at an awards ceremony occurring in tandem with the Arrington Mormon History Lecture on the Logan campus on September 25th . The Mountain West Center for Regional Studies is an outreach center in the College of Arts & Sciences that works to provide public programs, student scholarships, research and program funding, visiting scholars, and other projects directed at enhancing the work of Utah State University.

title: National 4-H Week Shows Utah Youth Are 'Beyond Ready'
summary: From fairgrounds to classrooms, and community gardens to robotics labs, Utah 4-H youth are proving they’re not just ready for the future — they’re Beyond Ready. During National 4-H Week, Oct. 4-10, the Beyond Ready initiative will come to life as local clubs share how 4-H equips them with the skills, confidence, and resilience to lead in a world of opportunity and change. The initiative aims to help prepare 10 million youth for work and life by 2030. The goal builds on 4-H's long-standing role as America's largest youth development organization, which empowers 6 million young people nationwide through hands-on learning experiences in clubs, camps, school programs, and community events. “The 4-H program helps young people turn their interests into experience, and that experience into a pathway for their future,” said Dave Francis, Utah State University Extension 4-H director. “Whether they’re raising an animal, building a robot, or leading a service project, youth learn to solve problems, work with others, and keep going when things get hard. That’s what Beyond Ready means: having the skills and confidence to take the next step in education, careers, and life.” Throughout National 4-H Week, Utah youth and communities will celebrate those skills through activities and service projects across the state. Kaitlyn Lunt, program coordinator for USU Extension 4-H, said each county in Utah will host its own 4-H Week events, and there will also be several statewide events. “Monday is ‘Go Green Day,’ so we’re asking people to light their homes green with decorations or programmable lights,” she said. “UDAF will light their building green to show their support, and we’re hoping other organizations will do the same. We’re also encouraging everyone to wear green that day.” Lunt said Thursday is “Thankful Thursday,” and each county will encourage its 4-H groups to find ways to thank and give back to those in their community who support them, whether it’s volunteers, teachers, government officials, or the local fire department. The activities planned across Utah reflect a larger national effort to highlight how 4-H prepares youth for success. “National 4-H Week is a powerful reminder that young people are already leading in extraordinary ways,” said Jill Bramble, president and CEO of National 4-H Council. “Through 4-H, youth discover their strengths, build lifelong career and life skills, and create opportunities for real change in their communities. They aren’t waiting for tomorrow — they are stepping up today and are Beyond Ready.” Learn more about Utah 4-H at USU Extension 4-H .

title: NEHMA Presents 'Pixelated: Mike Whiting' Across Utah State University
summary: LOGAN, Utah — What happens when the pixelated visual language of video games jumps from the screen and enters the landscape? The Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art at Utah State University presents Pixelated: Mike Whiting , a university-wide exhibition of monumental sculptures by one of Utah's best-known contemporary sculptors. On view Sept. 3 through June 5, 2027, the outdoor exhibition brings Whiting's colorful, pixelated animals and everyday objects across USU's Logan and Price campuses. Constructed from welded steel and finished with automotive paint, Whiting's sculptures transform the ephemeral pixels of a computer screen into physical objects with weight, scale, and permanence. Deer, birds, sailboats, and pretzels emerge from a vocabulary of squares and geometric surfaces. Intentionally scuffed paint and steel emphasize their physicality. These are not virtual images, but substantial objects anchored to the landscape. Their material presence reminds us that the seemingly invisible digital world also has tangible consequences. But Pixelated is about more than digital gaming. In an era where much of modern life is experienced through screens, the exhibition invites viewers to step outside and consider how our increasing dependance on technology shapes the way we experience the physical world around us. Born in Provo, Utah, Whiting has had work exhibited around the world. His art draws from two distinct visual styles — the 8-bit graphics of early video games and the geometric forms of minimalist art. He has long been fascinated by how the opposite intents of these two artistic approaches arrived at similar visual outcomes by entirely different means. Early video games like Pac-Man and Space Invaders relied on simplified graphics because the limited processing power of the day’s technology meant designers were required to communicate as much information as possible using a small number of pixels. Minimalist artists of the 1960s intentionally stripped away detail in pursuit of what they viewed as the essential qualities of art. Whiting’s sculptures are thoughtful and introspective, asking questions about artificial intelligence, the implications of data centers, and our reliance on screens. But they are also playful and whimsical. Dramatically increasing scale and using bright colors make the sculptures impossible to miss. By installing these pixelated figures outside directly on grass and dirt, the artist invites us to slow down, notice the small things around us, and see our familiar surroundings in new ways. "Gardens are in their own way virtual spaces — carefully created environments," Whiting says. "The contrast of the sculptures' geometric and manmade materials can seem at odds with the gardens, but they are connected in the dialogue about the re-presentation of nature." As Whiting gives these pixels weight and the permanence of steel, he asks us to consider how artificial intelligence and screens are increasingly shaping the way we experience the world and connect with each other. Sculptures and labels in Logan will be installed by Sept. 3. Join Whiting will host a sculpture walk starting at 12:15 p.m. Oct. 21 across the Logan campus. Meet at the Pretzel and end at NEHMA for a light lunch and desserts. About Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art The Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art at Utah State University fosters engagement with modern and contemporary art to facilitate learning and promote dialogue about ideas important to the people of Utah and the mission of Utah State University. Admission is free and open to all. Parking is available in the free museum parking stalls and at the Gateway Terrace. For more information, visit usu.edu/artmuseum or contact Chiara Sorensen at chiara.sorensen@usu.edu .

title: New Art Exhibition Celebrates Beauty of Utah's Native Plants at Swaner EcoCenter
summary: PARK CITY, Utah — Swaner EcoCenter and Utah Native Plant Society are inviting visitors to discover the beauty and importance of Utah’s native plants at Ephemeral, a new free exhibition. Ephemeral will run Sept. 12 through Nov. 29. Exhibit hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Wednesday through Sunday. An opening celebration will Featuring artwork inspired by Utah's native wildflowers, shrubs, grasses, and trees, Ephemeralis a juried art exhibition celebrating the talent of local artists and the beauty, resilience, and ecological importance of Utah’s native plants. Through a variety of artistic mediums, visitors will have the opportunity to explore the fleeting yet essential nature of native plant communities and reflect on the importance of conservation in a changing world. "Ephemeral invites visitors to see Utah's native plants through the eyes of local artists," said Hunter Klingensmith, director of visitor experience at Swaner. "By blending art and ecology, this exhibition creates a meaningful opportunity for our community to connect with the landscapes that make Utah unique. We’re excited to be partnering with the Utah Native Plant Society to creatively highlight the critical role these plants play in the health of our ecosystems." The exhibition’s free Opening Celebration will be from 5-7 p.m. Sept. 12. Community members are invited to meet artists, explore the exhibition, and celebrate the intersection of art, conservation, and place. “We hope that the beauty of these pieces representing Utah’s native plants will foster a connection between viewers and the place we all call home,” said Rose Torres with the Utah Native Plant Society. “Come and be inspired by these incredible native plants.” Many works in the exhibition will be available for purchase, with a portion of proceeds supporting both Swaner Preserve & EcoCenter and the Utah Native Plant Society. Ephemeral was made possible through the generous support of the John C. Kish Foundation, Summit County RAP Tax, and the Summit County Restaurant Tax Grant.

title: New Era: Utah State Announces Jim Laub Family Stadium
summary: LOGAN, Utah — A new era is coming to Utah State University, as the home of Aggie football will become Jim Laub Family Stadium on Jan. 1, 2027, honoring Jim and Carol Laub and their decades of extraordinary commitment to Utah State and Aggie Athletics. The naming recognizes the Laubs' longstanding support of Utah State Athletics and their continued investment in the university's future. Their support has helped advance Aggie Athletics through multiple conference affiliations and major periods of growth, including Utah State's move to the Pac-12 on July 1. "Jim and Carol have been instrumental in supporting Utah State throughout the years and have a clear vision for where Aggie Athletics can go, while helping our university make an impact on the national stage," said Utah State Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker. "Their unwavering loyalty, leadership and investment have been critical to the success and growth of the athletics department. This is a fitting tribute to all they have done, continue to do and will do for the future of Aggie Athletics." The Laubs' impact on Utah State can be seen throughout campus and across Aggie Athletics. Jim and Carol have made significant investments in facility projects, including the Stan Laub Indoor Facility, Jim & Carol Laub Athletics-Academics Complex and Wayne Estes Center. Jim was also instrumental in the construction of the Chuck & Gloria Bell Soccer Field and has supported renovations to the football stadium and Dee Glen Smith Spectrum. "Jim and Carol Laub represent what it means to be Aggies. Their generosity, leadership and commitment have made a lasting difference at Utah State and throughout Cache Valley," said President Brad Mortensen. "Their impact extends far beyond athletics, and having their name on this stadium is a meaningful recognition of the many ways they have invested in people, strengthened this university and made our community a better place." Their dedication to Utah State extends beyond athletics. Jim has been a member of USU's Old Main Society since 1987 and is a member of the athletics department's Blue A Society. A 1974 graduate of Utah State University, Jim was selected to the Utah State Athletics Hall of Fame in 2013. He received USU's Distinguished Alumnus Award in 2004, the Spirit of Old Main Award in 2006 and an honorary doctorate in business and entrepreneurship from Utah State in 2007. Jim was also presented the Contribution to Amateur Football Award by the National Football Foundation & College Hall of Fame Utah Chapter in 2013. The naming of Jim Laub Family Stadium represents a lasting recognition of the Laub family's commitment to Utah State and their belief in the university, its student-athletes and the future of Aggie Athletics. The Laub family extends beyond Jim and Carol to include Eric and Tatum Laub, and Mark, Renee and Lawson Laub.

title: New Location, Same Mission: Aggie Math Learning Center Reduces Barriers to Success
summary: While many of us would shy away from biting into a whole, raw onion, the savory veggie is often one of the first ingredients we reach for when preparing our favorite culinary creations. And so it is with mathematics and statistics. Not all of us will dive directly into advanced mathematical and statistical theory, and yet all of us need foundational quantitative literacy to pursue aspirations ranging from careers in science, health, education, and agriculture, to engineering, business, arts, and so much more. “Utah State University’s Aggie Math Learning Center exists to help with each student establish firm, foundational knowledge on which they can progress,” said Brent Thomas, AMLC director and assistant professor of professional practice in the Department of Mathematics and Statistics . “We’re here to ensure learning math and completing quantitative literacy requirements aren’t barriers standing in the way of any student’s dreams.” The AMLC, available to all USU students on the Logan campus and remotely at statewide campuses, has settled into its new, temporary location on the fourth floor of the Merrill-Cazier Library , during renovation of the department’s permanent location in the historic Animal Sciences Building on the USU Quad. “We’re in LIB 411 and online at amlc.usu.edu ,” Thomas said. “We’re open Monday through Saturday. Our phone number is 435-797-0970 and our email address is aggiemath@usu.edu . We are eager to provide free help to Aggie scholars throughout the university system.” Thomas notes many students seeking assistance from the AMLC are not STEM majors, and may be facing challenges with math learning. “For many Aggies, a serious barrier to staying in school and successfully completing their degree, is mastery of foundational mathematics or statistics,” he said. “Maybe they’ve had a bad experience with math in the past and have lost confidence. We provide a non-threatening, non-judgmental environment with the resources they need to overcome this obstacle.” AMLC tutors are primarily math and statistics majors who are committed to providing meaningful, effective help. “Our tutors are peers or near-peers to Aggies seeking help and we’ve found this enables tutors to connect well with students,” said Randall Haws, learning specialist with the AMLC. “Each tutor has not only achieved mastery of their area of tutoring expertise, they have also completed a teaching training program we’ve developed that is certified by the College Reading and Learning Association .” This curriculum, Thomas said, teaches tutors how to work with students and help them feel comfortable in the tutoring center environment. USU’s 2025 Science Valedictorian and first-generation college graduate Makenna Roberts said her experience as a tutor was a highlight of her undergraduate career and helped her get into a competitive graduate program. “I got to know all of the math and statistics department faculty and staff,” said Roberts, who was accepted into five graduate programs and is currently pursuing a rigorous degree in statistical science at Duke University. “The whole tutoring experience helped me build confidence and really learn math and statistics as I helped others.” Thomas says tutors are trained to welcome each student to the center and discuss their specific learning needs. “After receiving assistance, the student can remain and work on their homework and simply drop a question in the computer queue, if they need additional help,” he said. “It’s a convenient, non-intimidating environment.” In addition to being equipped with teaching and communications skills, AMLC tutors have guidance from faculty. “Our tutoring center doesn’t exist in a vacuum,” Thomas said. “We work closely with USU mathematics and statistics faculty, along with teaching assistants, to ensure our tutors are ready to help with the curriculum being taught at Utah State. Faculty share their teaching materials, Canvas notes and exam study guides, so we have the resources that will benefit students using the AMLC the most.” He added that math and statistics recitation leaders have their office hours at the AMLC, so students can discuss returned assignments and exams, and get feedback on their progress. “We also encourage students, even if they don’t have specific questions, to bring their homework and study at the center,” Thomas said. “That way, if they hit a snag while working on homework, they have immediate access to someone who can help them.” He said the center also encourages students to visit the center with their classmates, where they can study together. “Often, these groups are able to work through obstacles on their own, without consulting a tutor,” Thomas said. “Study groups can be a very effective way to master concepts and motivate students.” A recent development at the center is a collaboration with USU’s Center for Civic Excellence . “The Center for Civic Excellence has asked the AMLC for support for the quantitative literacy courses CIVC 1000, 1020, and 1010,” Haws said. “These are quantitative literacy courses designed to frame, model, and interpret real-world problems using mathematical reasoning, computational tools, and data analysis. We’re excited to partner with the CIVC to enhance these class experiences for students.” Thomas thanks USU Libraries for welcoming the AMLC into its new space and providing help in getting the word of the resource out to students. “Jennifer Duncan, dean of libraries, and Associate Dean Britt Fagerheim have gone out of their way to help us get settled and integrate us into their efforts to serve Aggies,” he said. “We’re very grateful for their support and assistance.”

title: New Publication Co-Authored by USU Professor Explores Lifelong Learning in Thailand
summary: For three decades, an educational movement in Thailand has reimagined how people learn, empowering them to solve local problems and improve their quality of life. Their successes are the focus of The Society That Learns , a new book published by MIT Press and co-authored by Deborah Fields, research professor in the Department of Instructional Technology and Learning Sciences in the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education and Human Services at Utah State. “Every time I talk with Debbie about this research, she shares stories of learning. Stories that connect people with each other, with Thai culture and communities, and stories that connect to Papert’s reshaping of learning theory into constructionism,” said Andy Walker, former department head of ITLS. “I’m excited to see these stories in a much longer book format.” The lifelong learning movement in Thailand was inspired by the constructionism philosophy developed by MIT professor Seymour Papert in the 1980s. Constructionism prioritizes learning by making. It is the belief that people learn best when they create tangible things they can share that then help them build new ideas and understanding. Drawing on Papert’s teachings, in 1996, a group of MIT alumni from Thailand began searching for new ways to address the challenges facing their country. They applied constructionism to their communities, schools and workplaces, recognizing that they would need to adapt Papert’s philosophy to the context of Thailand. Thirty years later, the efforts of the Thai Constructionist community — through the Suksapattana Foundation — have led to learning initiatives that are now among the longest-running community development projects in the world. When discussing the release of the new book, Fields explained that the Thai people have kept the entire effort about one concept: learning. “This book is about learning,” she said. “It tells the stories of how all the transformations came to be. The Thai people have learned about agriculture, finances, social organization, entrepreneurship, mathematics, science, computation, business administration — and most importantly, about learning itself and what they are capable of as learners.” The book combines 25 years of history through research that includes personal stories about the ways learning has transformed Thailand. The stories detail how a village restored its water supply through collective inquiry, how a farmer solved agricultural challenges through experimentation, and how a factory technician improved productivity by problem-solving. “Because the project was not about implementing ready-made models but about learning itself, the people developed creative ways to work through these challenges and learned in the process,” Fields said. “They became intentional learners.” Fields co-authored The Society That Learns with Paulo Blikstein, a ssociate professor at Teachers College, Columbia University’s graduate school of education. Blikstein is an internationally recognized scholar in the learning sciences, educational innovation and constructionist education. Fields’ complementary contributions to the project draw on her interest in community-based learning, mentorship and holistic approaches to education. Her research explores how learning communities can support personal growth and participation in society. In addition to documenting Thailand’s constructionist movement in The Society That Learns , the authors provide a vision for how other societies can cultivate lifelong learning and community growth. The Society That Learns can be purchased at MIT Press . All proceeds from the book will support the ongoing educational initiatives of the Suksapattana Foundation for the communities of Thailand.

title: New Research Explores the Riskiest Factor in Rising Wildfire Rates: People
summary: Three things are needed to start a fire: heat, fuel, and oxygen. But for the majority of destructive wildfires in the U.S., there is an overlooked fourth — humans. Through either accident, negligence, or intentional act, 84% of all wildfires are started by people, according to research. That percentage has increased steadily over the last three decades. Uncontrolled wildfires create staggering suppression costs, risks to lives and property, and smoke wafting across the continent. With stakes sky high, land managers are looking for strategies to reduce the number of human-ignited wildfires, said Catrin Edgeley, a wildfire social scientist in the Department of Environment and Society. Edgeley and a team of researchers published a series of studies to help managers better understand and work to reduce the number of these incidents. Human-caused fires tend to be more expensive and more destructive than others. While lightning-ignited fires tend to occur along with precipitation to slow the spread, people tend to start fires under extreme conditions — hotter temperatures, lower humidity, and stronger winds. Human-caused fires occur in predictable patterns, often near roads and structures. Understanding the patterns can help land managers target prevention efforts where and when they are most needed, particularly because human-caused fires can have greater potential for damage — to structures, from post-fire flooding, in danger to nearby communities, and long-term economic losses from declines in tourism. In the Southwest, where Edgeley’s recent work was completed, abandoned campfires account for 44% of human-caused wildfires, and 80% of those ignitions occur within a quarter-mile of a road. Human ignitions consistently clustered within 1.6 miles of campsites, trails, and primary roads. Fires started by people spiked dramatically during major holiday weekends — specifically Memorial Day, July 4th, and Labor Day when visitation surged. Ignition causes varied significantly by region. Arson was the leading human cause around Phoenix, whereas debris burning leads in central New Mexico. “To make the absolute most of our funding and staff in fire prevention, we need a game plan that addresses things locally,” Edgeley said. “That means documenting what actually works based on real data for specific regions so we have a clear guide on how to step in and connect with people using public lands.” Investing in wildfire prevention yields extraordinary return on investment. One study found that every dollar spent on wildfire prevention, education, and messaging prevented $35 in costs for damage and suppression. But prevention strategies still remain overlooked in annual budgets. “Prevention is one of the smartest investments public land agencies can make, but suppression work has been default for so long that pivoting where money gets spent is challenging,” Edgeley said. “Understanding what is most effective and what really makes a difference in reducing human-caused fires will make that easier.” How can land managers encourage people to take fire risks seriously? There are significant hurdles to overcome to get the right messages to the right audience in ways they can actually act on. Organizations like the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management use strategies like community outreach, school visits, road signs, and enforcement, but there has been almost no systematic evaluation to determine if these activities work. Edgeley is working to change that . Her research has already uncovered some important factors that could determine future efforts. Red Flag Warnings Agencies routinely issue public warnings when conditions become dangerously hot and dry, encouraging recreationists to keep out of forests. In a survey of recreationists using national forests, many visitors said that they understood Red Flag Warnings — at the same time they were recreating in forests on the very days warnings were in effect. Visitors knew the term but were often unaware how it applied to their visit, Edgeley said. Managers are working to provide clear, plain-language guidance explaining exactly what warnings mean for specific recreational activities and visitor safety. A Wider Net Interviews with business owners in Flagstaff, Arizona, showed that local gear shops, bike rentals, and outdoor outfitters act as trusted sources for visitors trying to understand fire rules. Visitors often asked store employees for information about fire bans and forest closures. Edgeley recommends that agencies build official partnerships with local businesses, supplying employees with easy-to-access information on current fire restrictions so they can share the information directly with customers. Know Your Audience The research also discovered that outdoor recreationists have distinct preferences for how wildfire prevention is practiced. Campers and backcountry recreationists wanted an engineering focus, such as metal campfire rings and access to water. Out-of-town visitors favored education, including posted safety information before they reached the forest. Local community residents showed strong support for enforcement tools such as campfire bans, permits for access, and forest stage restrictions during periods of high wildfire danger. This study complements efforts to advance wildfire science at USU, to develop and deliver research and tools to land managers, policymakers, and communities on forest health, wildfire risk reduction, and climate-adapted forests and woodlands through the Utah Forest Restoration Institute . The organization serves as a bridge between scientific research and actual land management implementation to help restore fire-resilient ecosystems in Utah. The lesson from focused, local data is that national, one-size-fits-all messaging alone cannot motivate changes in behavior, Edgeley said. Edgeley will continue her work to cut the number of human-caused fires with new funding from the Joint Fire Science Program to address national wildfire prevention and investigation training needs among land management staff in federal and state agencies. “Investing in and supporting fire prevention staff and the work they do lies at the heart of reduced wildfire risk to communities,” Edgeley said.

title: New Student Housing Project Represents Investment in USU Eastern's Future
summary: A new student housing project at Utah State University Eastern is about much more than adding rooms to campus. For university and community partners, the project represents an investment in Eastern’s future, one that can support enrollment, strengthen the student experience and give more students an opportunity to call Price home. USU Eastern currently offers several styles of on-campus housing, including traditional residence halls, suites, and apartments. The university’s approach to student housing focuses on creating safe and comfortable living environments that support academic success, leadership, and social connections. For Carla Saccomano, project manager for the new student housing project, that connection between housing and the future of the campus is what makes the project particularly meaningful. “What excites me most is seeing an investment being made in the future of USU Eastern and our community,” Saccomano said. “This project is about much more than constructing a new building. It is about creating opportunities for students to come to Price, attend USU Eastern, and have a quality place to call home while they are here.” The additional housing comes at an important time for Eastern. The university encourages students to secure housing early because housing reservations can fill quickly. The new three-story student housing facility will provide modern, apartment style living for approximately 95 residents. Plans include both private and shared bedroom spaces paired with shared kitchens, living areas, bathrooms, and laundry amenities. Accessibility, safety, privacy, and student comfort have also been incorporated throughout the design. Saccomano believes having additional options on campus can help remove a potential barrier as Eastern works to welcome students from throughout Utah and beyond. “Additional housing gives USU Eastern more opportunity to welcome students from outside our immediate area and provide them with a comfortable, convenient place to live close to campus,” Saccomano said. “We want housing to support enrollment and growth rather than be something that limits those opportunities.” For Mark Morley, the project also has a personal connection. Morley first attended USU Eastern in 1997 and his own experience as a student helped shape his enthusiasm for what the new housing can provide future generations. “I love USU Eastern and the opportunities it provides for students,” Morley said. “My own life was positively influenced by my experience as a student here and by living in Price. I’m excited that this project will allow more students to come to Price, attend USU Eastern and have the opportunity to build the same kinds of friendships, memories, and experiences that have meant so much to me.” There is even a unique connection between Morley’s time as a student and the location of the new project. “When I first attended USU Eastern in 1997, on-campus housing was limited even then,” Morley said. “I ended up living in a small house that actually stood where the parking lot for this new dorm is located today, so there is something pretty special about seeing new student housing being built on this site.” Morley said existing on campus housing is full and believes adding modern student housing will provide additional capacity while also becoming an important recruiting tool for prospective students. Both Morley and Saccomano see the project’s significance extending well beyond enrollment numbers. College housing is often where some of the most important parts of the student experience happen, including late night study sessions, roommates who become lifelong friends and the first real feeling of belonging to a campus community. “Some of my fondest memories from USU Eastern are of my roommates and the friendships we formed,” Morley said. “Many of those friendships have lasted throughout my life.” Saccomano echoed that sentiment. “A dorm isn't simply a place where students sleep,” she said. “It's where friendships are made, where students study together, support one another and really begin to feel like they are part of the university community.” That focus aligns closely with Eastern’s existing approach to residence life, which emphasizes engagement, academic success and social connection as central parts of the on-campus living experience. Kristian Olsen, associate vice president of USU Eastern, said the project represents another important step in the campus’s continued growth. “This project is an investment in our students and in the future of USU Eastern,” Olsen said. “As we create more opportunities for students to choose Eastern, we also need to make sure they have a place where they can feel at home, build relationships and truly become part of this campus and community. We’re excited about what this new housing will make possible for the next generation of students.” For Saccomano, the ultimate measure of the project’s success will be what happens inside the building long after construction is complete. “Ultimately, I hope we're creating more than student housing,” she said. “I hope we're helping create a place where students can build relationships and memories that stay with them long after they leave USU Eastern.” As the project moves forward, the new residence hall represents more than additional space on campus. For Saccomano, Morley and the many partners involved, it represents confidence in the future of USU Eastern and in the students who will call Price home. The building will eventually be measured in square feet, rooms and beds, but its greater impact may be measured in the friendships formed, memories made and students who discover a place where they belong.

title: New UWLP Report Shows Mixed Progress for Women Leaders in Utah's K-12 Education System
summary: The Utah Women & Leadership Project at Utah State University has released a new research and policy brief, The Status of Women Leaders in Public Education (K-12): A 2026 Update , providing the most comprehensive look to date at women’s leadership across Utah’s public and charter schools. Susan Madsen, founding director of the UWLP and sole author of the report, said it reveals modest gains in some leadership roles, declines in others and persistent gaps that continue to shape the state’s educational landscape. “The report updates earlier UWLP reports published in 2014, 2017 and 2022 and examines whether Utah has made measurable progress in advancing women into key leadership positions,” she said. “It also compares Utah’s progress with national trends.” Key Findings Women Now Have a Slight Majority of Leadership Roles Statewide. Across all state and district leadership categories, women comprise 51.3% of leaders—up from 50% in 2022. Yet the distribution varies significantly by role. State-Level Leadership Remains Strong Women hold 66.7% of seats on the Utah State Board of Education, an increase from 2022. Women also occupy 60.9% of leadership positions within the Utah State Board of Education’s organizational structure. District Superintendent Roles Show Slow Improvement But Remain Inequitable Women make up 18.2% of Utah’s district superintendents, a 6 percentage-point increase since 2022, but far below the national rate of 35.8%. Principal and Assistant Principal Roles Continue to Rise Women now hold 53.3% of principal and assistant principal positions statewide, up from 50.8% in 2022 and 43.2% in 2017. Growth is strongest in elementary schools, where 66.4% of principals and 75.4% of assistant principals are women. Charter School Leadership is a Bright Spot Women comprise 72.1% of charter school directors and more than half of charter principals and vice principals. “Progress has improved in some areas and slowed in others, but persistent barriers remain — including bias among school boards and self-perceptions among women regarding leadership readiness,” Madsen said. “And while women make up three quarters of K-12 teachers nationwide, only 30% of superintendents are women, up from 13.1% in 2000, but still far from equal representation.” Strengthening Utah’s Leadership Pipeline Helpful leadership development programs are available to Utah educators, including the Utah Principal Supervisors’ Academy, Principal Partnership Networks and statewide associations. There is also a broader shift in Utah’s policy environment following the passage of HB 261 (“Equal Opportunity Initiatives”), which restricts diversity, equity and inclusion programs across public institutions. “Whether this shift has affected women’s advancement in state government remains to be seen,” Madsen said. “Gender-diverse leadership teams make institutions more effective, innovative and responsive. Research continues to show that diverse and inclusive leadership teams produce more creative, innovative, productive and effective results.” From educator burnout to rising youth mental health concerns, Madsen said Utah faces extraordinary challenges that require strong leadership. “Finding, preparing and supporting future educational leaders is imperative for Utah’s future,” she said.

title: Northern Utah Home Visiting Program Adopts New Name, Keeps Same Services
summary: The Cache County Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting Program now has a new name: Northern Utah Home Visiting. “Our new name reflects our vision for the future,” said Tressa Johnston, associate director of the Services Division at the Institute for Disability Research, Policy, & Practice, where NUHV is housed. “It's an exciting step forward that allows us to continue investing in the families and communities we serve.” The name change will not affect services, she said. “Families will continue receiving compassionate, family-centered home visits from the same dedicated team. Our commitment to supporting parents, children, and healthy family relationships remains as strong as ever.” The Northern Utah Home Visiting program empowers families from pregnancy through kindergarten with no-cost, evidence-based support through the Parents as Teachers curriculum. NUHV partners with parents and caregivers through personalized home visits that focus on strengthening parent-child interactions, promoting healthy child development, and supporting overall family wellness. The family-centered approach recognizes and builds on the unique strengths of each family, empowering parents with the knowledge, skills and confidence to achieve their family goals. It creates a strong foundation for their children's growth and success. NUHV and IDRPP are both part of the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences at Utah State University.

title: Oye Cómo Va: USU Undergrad Scholars Curate Communitywide Latinx Art Exhibition
summary: Two Utah State University undergraduate scholars led the curation and installation of a communitywide Latinx art exhibit. The Latinx Art Exhibition/Exposición de Arte Latínx 2026 opened Sept. 9 and runs through Oct. 3 at the ReadyMade Gallery, 28 W. Center St. in downtown Logan. Gallery hours are noon to 7 p.m., Wednesday through Saturday. A free public reception will be 5-7 p.m. Sept. 12 during Cache Valley’s 6th annual Gran Latino Festival in the Historic Center Street District. Caine Scholars Kjrstine Landaverde and Ella White selected pieces by local and regional artists, drawing on varied media and styles that express a wide range of Latin American experiences in the United States. Neither student had previous experience with full curation and installation of an entire gallery. “The exhibition doesn’t have a specific theme, so we were free to select a range of works reflecting very different experiences,” said White, an art history major who is minoring in religious studies and earning a certificate in museum studies. “Our focus has been on how these pieces work together and how the installation tells a story.” Landaverde says she hopes the exhibition will create a space where people feel safe, connected and free to express themselves. She adds the “behind-the-scenes” setup to achieve meaningful, eye-catching displays involved careful thought and planning. “There’s a lot more math involved with the installation than you would assume,” said Landaverde, a photography major with a film studies minor. “Every installation venue is different. You have to map out the space, which requires patience. As you create the arrangement, you have to think about placement order and what you’re experiencing as you walk through it.” White, who gained skills with art installation and object handling during a previous internship with USU’s Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art, says the process was very methodical. “You have to consider what should be at the beginning to welcome guests to the exhibition and what should be at the end,” she said. “But we had a lot of freedom with the placement.” An inviting feature of the exhibition are the ofrendas — traditional Latino altars comprised of sentimental objects, photos, and food offerings framed by bright orange marigolds — that frame the gallery’s entrance and an interior table. “This custom is rooted in Latin American culture and we felt it would be a welcoming display that invites people to think of their own experiences and connections to the exhibition,” said Landaverde, who, along with White, added some of her own family photos and artifacts to the altars. Álvaro Ibarra, assistant professor of art history in USU’s Department of Art + Design and the students’ faculty mentor, recruited Landaverde and White to take on the project, which helped the undergrads develop career-ready skills. “Gaining experience is important, but my goal is to go beyond teaching career skills,” Ibarra said. “I offer intrepid students experiences they can put on their résumé. Experiences that will get them jobs. Experiences that will get them into graduate programs. Experiences that set them apart.” Both Landaverde and White, who will graduate from USU in spring 2027, plan to pursue graduate studies. “I’m grateful for the hands-on, experiential learning that will help me with my senior thesis and with future employment,” Landaverde said. “Ultimately, I’d like to pursue graduate studies in film production.” White, who plans to work toward a graduate degree in art history and a possible MBA, hopes to work in museum spaces and is grateful for the opportunity to work on a start-to-finish project. “Much of my undergrad career has been spent in the ‘basement,’ surrounded by artifacts and works of art,” she said. “It’s exciting to collaborate on a big project, to be involved in the curation and installation of an exhibition, and to experience the public’s reaction.”

title: Playing With Fire: USU Author Explores Hilarious-Turned-Tragic Consequences
summary: Childish pranks are part of being a kid. Calling a random number and asking if the caller’s refrigerator is running and, if so, to catch it; switching the plastic bags inside cereal boxes so Lucky Charms become shredded wheat; short-sheeting the bed; birthday candles that cannot be extinguished; the perennial whoopie cushion. But what happens if the prank isn’t quite so childish and the results are far from laughter? Utah State University author Jennifer Sinor explores this question in her new book, “ The Beautiful Plain ,” released Oct. 1 by the University of Nebraska Press. The novel opens on an August afternoon with three teenage girls hauling a cardbox box filled with another girl up to the loft of a barn. They tell the girl inside she is about to be pushed from the second-floor window as part of her initiation into their club. “I’m interested in what happens when something that appears ordinary ends up causing grief for decades,” said Sinor, professor and associate department head in USU’s Department of English . While this is her first novel, this is not the first time Sinor, author of other works, has considered ordinary trauma. Ten years ago, she published “Ordinary Trauma: A Memoir,” in which she explored a military childhood set amid explosive-filled speed bumps and men humping machine guns along the side of the road. Even longer ago, she wrote about the very ordinary diary of her great, great, great aunt, Annie Ray , who homesteaded the Dakotas in the late 1800s.
