In much of her work, the ordinary is not the backdrop to the subject, but the very thing to be considered. “The ordinary is where we spend our lives,” Sinor said. “We tend to tell stories of the extraordinary, but the ordinary tells the story of who we are.” Sinor’s novel follows Laura Runnell, one of the girls who carries the box up the barn stairs in 1982, and alternates between Laura’s childhood and her current life as a new professor at a Nebraska state school, where she struggles as a young teacher and a single mother. Failure is a story Laura knows well. As someone who has chased the shiny her entire life, she finds herself back in Nebraska, licking her wounds in a state she wanted to escape. “Nebraska reminds me a lot of Hawaii,” Sinor said of her setting. A military child, Sinor moved eight times in the first 18 years of her life and ended up at the University of Nebraska for college, even though she had never lived in the state. “My father kept his residency in Nebraska, so I was oddly an in-state student,” she said. Sinor was fairly certain she was the only student attending UNL with a family living 2,000 miles away on an island. “The first year was hard,” she said, “but I saw the ocean in the grasses of the plains, and it reminded me of home.” The landscape is a character in “The Beautiful Plain,” and one Laura often struggles against. Place matters to Sinor. “I set out to write a Nebraska novel,” she said. “I wanted the land to be part of what made the characters who they were, even though I readily acknowledge that I, myself, have never felt at home in a place.” Sinor said she also set out to write the kind of novel she enjoys reading. She began writing it the summer after the pandemic ended, during a time in which she turned to fiction with strong plots and vibrant characters who were facing the regular challenges of being human. “Things were so bleak then,” Sinor said. “I wanted something that pulled up rather than down.” Her students recognize Sinor in her fiction as readily as her nonfiction. One her former students, Millie Tullis, author of “These Saints are Stones,” wrote to Sinor: “The opening chapter really hooked me – such well-handled tension. So much heart and guts. Reading your work always feels a lot like spending time talking with you, generous and smart and big-hearted.” Another former student, Cami Pack, wrote Sinor, “Thank you for sharing your warmth and devotion to naming the full range of our experiences, while we make sense of how it's all come to be,” Pack wrote. “And for what you said about trauma being totalizing. So many layers. It was captivating, and I'm grateful. Grateful for Laura's character, for her innocent desire to belong, and for the experience of swimming with her toward that belonging, clothes on.” In response to the generous words of her former students, Sinor said she was thankful for her time at Utah State. “I have been teaching in the Department of English for twenty-six years, and have sat with thousands of students and their words,” she said. “Of my role as a teacher, I could not be more grateful for my job and the way I spend my days. It is a gift.” Sinor will be a guest on the “Access Utah” program on Utah Public Radio at 9 a.m. Oct. 6. “The Beautiful Plain” can be ordered wherever books are sold.

title: Pres. Mortensen Announces Strategic Plan Launch Event
summary: Editor's note: This message from Utah State University President Brad L. Mortensen was sent to all students, faculty, and staff Wednesday morning. Dear Students, Faculty, and Staff, Shortly after coming back to Utah State and following our first university-wide survey, I shared our four strategic pillars: statewide impact, student success, discovery with purpose, and civic-mindedness in all we do. In the months since, many of you shared your perspectives through additional surveys and conversations across the state, and over the last few weeks, teams from across the university have built upon that feedback to further develop our plan. On Friday, Oct. 16, I'm excited to show you the detailed efforts of those design teams and provide you with an opportunity for feedback. Strategic Plan Launch Event Friday, Oct. 16 | 9:30-11:30 a.m. | Quad on the Logan campus 9:30-10:15 a.m.: I'll provide an overview of the plan, and the executive sponsors of each pillar will share what their teams have been working on. Join us in person or register in advance to join by Zoom 10:15-11:30 a.m.: Visit booths around the quad related to each pillar to ask questions, learn more, and share ideas. Snacks will be provided. I hope you'll stop by, whether you can stay for the full event or stop by for just a few minutes between classes and meetings. I look forward to hearing your thoughts. Statewide Campus Visits If you're at one of our statewide campuses, our university leadership team will visit Oct. 27-30, and I look forward to seeing you there. You can also learn more about the plan and share feedback anytime on the strategic planning website . Go Aggies! brad

title: Pres. Mortensen Shares New Mission Statement, Higher Ed Updates, Feedback Survey
summary: Editor’s note: This message from USU President Brad L. Mortensen was sent to all employees Monday afternoon. Dear Utah State Family, With so much happening across Utah State this fall, I want to take a few minutes to update you on several important efforts. Last Friday, the Utah Board of Higher Education (UBHE) meeting included several actions that support our pillars. We are also making progress on our strategic plan, compensation study, leadership searches, and other work across the university. UBHE Updates for Legislative Session In preparation for the 2027 legislative session, UBHE approved the Utah System of Higher Education's (USHE’s) FY 2027-28 budget request, including systemwide requests for compensation, performance funding, technical college capacity, cybersecurity, and campus safety. In addition, UBHE prioritized two USU requests which align with our institutional areas of distinction (land and water, food, energy, space and national security, the student experience, and strengthening every community): Utah Land & Water Stewardship Initiative ($3,600,000 ongoing): A collaborative investment across multiple colleges; USU Extension; the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air; statewide campuses; and external partners to address increasingly complex challenges and support opportunities related to water resources, forests, and land. Space Research Lab and Quantum Systems ($2,000,000 one-time): Working with the Space Dynamics Laboratory and partners across the university, this effort would better connect our research, educational programs, workforce development, and industry partnerships to accelerate innovation in space and quantum technologies and create more hands-on opportunities for students within Utah’s growing aerospace and defense workforce. New USU Mission Statement Approved The UBHE also approved our new mission statement: As Utah's student-centered, land-grant research university, we expand opportunity and strengthen communities across the state through learning, discovery, extension, and engagement. As I shared in an email last week, our revised mission and four strategic pillars (Statewide Impact, Student Success, Discovery with Purpose, and Civic-Mindedness in All We Do) will guide our priorities and the work ahead. We’ll share more about how this work is taking shape at our Strategic Plan Town Hall on Oct. 16. Campus Safety Planning Another important area of focus at UBHE's meeting was campus safety. The board approved recommendations from the USHE Campus Safety Task Force that address behavioral threat assessment, emergency preparedness and response, campus events, facilities, training, and communication. Several of these recommendations align with steps we implemented earlier this year, including the centralized scheduling of campus events. This process provides greater visibility into university events and allows for appropriate safety and operational reviews. We will now evaluate the full set of recommendations and share more in the coming months. Compensation Study UBHE also gave approval to direct potential enrollment growth funding and performance funding toward priorities yet to be identified through our university compensation study. As we have learned more through the process, we have expanded the scope to include finalizing our job architecture and making sure every employee has an accurate job description. This is important work if we want to make thoughtful decisions about compensation and career opportunities. We anticipate the compensation study to be completed in early March. We will also begin implementing Avature, a new talent management system, this fall and into the spring. It will bring several processes together in one place, including job descriptions, searches and hiring, and performance reviews. We will share more information as implementation moves forward. Leadership Searches I also want to update you on several leadership searches. After considering the needs of the university, we have decided not to move forward with hiring the chief of strategic workforce partnerships position. As we bring other leaders on board, we want to have a better sense of their strengths and then consider where we might have gaps. Our search for the vice president for Statewide and Online Education is moving into its next stage. We are working with WittKieffer to screen candidates and anticipate bringing finalists to campus in mid-October. We are also working with AGB Search to develop the position profile for our vice president for Research and Innovation search. That position will be an important part of advancing the discovery with purpose strategic pillar. Our search for our executive director of Civil Rights and Title IX is also underway, with the goal of completing the search by the end of the semester. Looking Ahead We're also pursuing opportunities that build on Utah State's distinctive strengths, including our work with state, federal, industry, and higher education partners around the proposed United States Space Academy. There is much more work ahead, but we believe Utah State has an important role to play as Utah considers how best to support this national effort. Share Your Feedback Finally, please take a moment to complete our fall check-in survey . Your feedback over the past year has directly informed our strategic planning and many of the decisions we are making. I hope you'll take a few minutes to tell us what you think is working, where we still have work to do, and what you're seeing and experiencing across the university. Beyond these updates, I know much more is happening across our university to build systems, align resources, recruit great people, and make sure our structures support our future direction. I'm grateful for the work you do every day for our students and for Utah, whether that’s front and center or a little more behind the scenes. We're doing amazing things, and I am so proud to be part of it. I look forward to sharing more with you throughout the semester and seeing you across our campuses, extension locations, and the numerous events we’re hosting. Go Aggies! brad

title: Quinney College Week Celebrates With Camp, Food, New Traditions
summary: From and overnight field camp in Logan Canyon and BBQ on campus to the annual tractor parade through the heart of campus, the S.J. & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture & Natural Resources will showcase many facets of one of USU’s largest colleges during Quinney College Week, Sept. 26 through Oct. 2. The weeklong celebration brings students together for hands-on activities, college traditions, service projects and opportunities to connect with clubs, campus resources and industry professionals. “Quinney College Week is one of my favorite celebrations of the year,” said Sarah McBride, QANR college senator. “I love that we get to highlight the different parts of our large and diverse college through all of our events. It’s a great opportunity to celebrate everything that makes the Quinney College special.” The festivities officially kick off with Quinney Field Camp. Taking place Sept. 26-27 at the Grizzly Outdoor Learning Center in Logan Canyon, the weekend event takes Quinney College Week beyond campus for two days of hands-on learning, including birding, learning about Utah forests, and (weather permitting) an evening of stargazing with telescopes and learning some astronomy. The 30th Annual Utah Agricultural Products BBQ brings together great food and building scholarship support for students in the college on Sept. 26. Utah farm and food industry sponsors provide the BBQ with financial support, food, and volunteers to prepare and serve delicious Utah products. Over its 30-year run, the BBQ has funded more than $369,000 of scholarships. The event is from 2-5 p.m. at Craig Aston Park, 1390 N. 800 E. Other Quinney College Week events include: Sept. 28 — Quinney Fair : From 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Sept. 28 on the Quad, students can meet representatives from clubs, businesses, internship programs, and campus resources and participate in interactive activities. Free walking tacos will be available while supplies last, and an Aggie Ice Cream eating contest begins at 1:30 p.m. “The Quinney Fair is my favorite event,” McBride said. “It’s a great opportunity for students to find experiences and resources that can enhance their time at USU, support them throughout their educational journey and help prepare them for life after graduation as they enter the workforce.” Sept. 29 — Cow Milking Contest: From 6-8 p.m. at the USU Caine Dairy Teaching and Research Center in Wellsville. Students can try milking a dairy cow, riding motor ponies and roping. Prizes will go to the top three milkers, including a one-of-a-kind belt buckle for the winner. Free Aggie Ice Cream will be available while supplies last. Admission is one food item donated to the Student Nutrition Access Center. Sept. 30 — Snow Cones on the Patio : Students can stop by the Agricultural Sciences patio from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. for a free snow cone. Quinney College Week T-shirts will also be available for purchase. Sept. 30 — Dam Aggies : From 5-7 p.m. at First Dam in Logan, students can participate in a service project to clean up the area, followed by free hot dogs. The first 50 participants can also get a free flowerpot to paint. Parking is limited, so participants are encouraged to carpool. Oct. 1 — Meet and Eat: From 10 a.m. to noon at the Natural Resources Building atrium and patio, students can enjoy free pancakes and meet the Quinney College’s new dean, Derek McLean, along with academic and peer advisors and department heads. Oct. 2 — Tractor Parade : The annual Tractor Parade begins at 10 a.m. at the Agricultural Systems Technology and Education Building before making its way through campus. The parade began in 2006 to honor eight USU students and instructor Evan Parker who were killed in a van crash the previous year. Since then, it has grown into a beloved college tradition that remembers those who were lost and celebrating the college’s clubs, departments and students. Tractors provided by local businesses and the ASTE Department will pull floats representing departments and clubs, with candy tossed to spectators along the route. Together, these events let students see the breadth of QANR while finding new ways to connect with the college and each other. More information about Quinney College Week can be found at https://qanr.usu.edu/week .

title: Registration Open for USU's 16th Annual Hansen Life Sciences Retreat Oct. 23-24
summary: Registration is open for Utah State University’s 2026 Hansen Life Sciences Retreat , slated for Oct. 23-24 on the Logan campus. Celebrating its 16th year, the annual gathering is open to all USU undergraduates, graduate students, postdocs, faculty, and staff from varied disciplines involved in the study of biological processes at the molecular level. “Each fall, we invite scholars from all departments throughout the university who are pursuing study and research in the molecular life sciences to pause their experiments, throw off their lab coats, and join us to share ideas and approaches with one another,” said Sean Johnson, associate dean in the College of Arts and Sciences and associate professor in USU’s Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry , who is a member of the retreat’s organizing committee. “This is a gathering to encourage collaborative efforts and celebrate each individual’s contributions in the larger research community.” The keynote speaker for the gathering is neuroscientist Colin Saldanha , professor in the Department of Neuroscience at American University in Washington D.C. Saldanha’s research interests include neuroendocrinology, neuroplasticity, and neuroscience. He will speak at 5 p.m. Oct. 23 in ESLC 046. All are welcome to his talk. The Hansen Retreat continues with research presentations, poster sessions and career networking from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Oct. 24 at the Larry W. and Lindi Miller Champion’s Club at West Stadium Center of Maverik Stadium, 1000 N. Lars Hansen Drive (800 East), on USU’s Logan Campus. Registration for the full retreat is $30 per person, which includes meals each day, along with a retreat shirt for participants who register by Oct. 12. Scholars who wish to present a poster during the retreat should also register by Oct. 12,. Justin Jones, director of USU’s synthetic spider silk and biomaterials laboratory, encourages his students to attend the retreat each year. “This is a cutting-edge yet low-pressure, friendly environment for students to share their ideas,” said Jones, associate professor in USU’s Department of Biology. “It’s a great place for students to gain experience and confidence with their presentations.” He adds the retreat is also an ideal place to foster partnerships. “The retreat offers an easy way to build collaborations, which is a tremendous boost,” Jones said. “Every single time I’ve attended the retreat, I’ve become acquainted with other researchers from whom our lab has benefited. They’re just a stone’s throw away, yet we don’t always get to know each other without gatherings like the Hansen retreat.” The Hansen Life Sciences Retreat honors the memory of renowned biochemist R. Gaurth Hansen (1920-2002), a gifted scientist, teacher, and administrator who spent much of his career enriching Utah State University. A native of Cache Valley, Utah, Hansen began his undergraduate studies at Utah State, before transferring to the University of Wisconsin, where he completed bachelor's, master's, and doctoral degrees. Hansen joined USU's faculty as an academic vice president in 1968 and was soon promoted to provost. His efforts contributed to a 20-fold increase in the university's research budget. In addition to his administrative and teaching endeavors, Hansen published more than 100 peer-reviewed articles in professional journals, and he received many prestigious national accolades. He was named USU Distinguished Professor Emeritus in 1985 and retired from Utah State in 1994. The Hansen Retreat is supported by USU alum Lars Peter Hansen and Grace Tsiang, along with their son, Peter Hansen. For more information, contact the USU Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at 435-797-0544.

title: Scaling Up, Out, Across: USU Physicist Explores Light as Pathway to Quantum Computing
summary: Quantum computing promises computational advantages that would smoke classical computing, but the rapidly advancing technology still faces formidable barriers. Among these obstacles are limitations in hardware, software, and error correction, which stand in the way of developing commercially viable applications. “Quantum bits, or qubits — the basic units of information in quantum computing — are incredibly fragile,” said USU physicist Feng Pan . “Tiny fluctuations in temperature can disturb them and cause computing errors.” Pan, who studies nanophotonics, believes light may hold the key to solving these challenges. The assistant professor in USU’s Department of Physics was the recipient of the top research paper award at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s 2026 Molecular Foundry Annual User Meeting on Aug. 20-21 in Berkeley, California. Pan delivered an invited talk during the plenary session about his research on how sculpted light interacts with materials at the nanoscale. “Light is relatively inexpensive and operates at room temperature,” Pan said. “By learning how to use light to interconnect quantum processor units via optoelectronic materials, we aim to make a quantum supercomputer reachable.” Among his research interests are creating bright, controllable sources of quantum light, and using this light to study quantum materials. “Our computational design could enable the creation of a variety of nanophotonic platforms for these applications,” said Pan, who is currently teaching Physics Lab 3870 — Intermediate Physics Laboratory. “We have to invent some of our own tools,” he said. “And I’m recruiting undergraduates and graduate students in physics, chemistry, engineering, and other disciplines to join my team as we build our lab from the ground up.” Through his association with Molecular Foundry, Pan has garnered contacts with researchers at multiple national labs and plans to help students pursue internships and fellowships funded by the U.S. Department of Energy, NASA, the National Science Foundation, and other entities. “Nanophotonics, quantum computing, and computational design are fascinating research fields with exciting career opportunities,” he said. “I’m excited to work with USU students and introduce them to top-level, national learning opportunities.”

title: Scholarships Gave USU Alum Milo Maughan Freedom to Find Calling
summary: When Milo Maughan arrived at Utah State University, he thought he already knew exactly where life was headed: He planned to become an electrical engineer. But college has a way of introducing new possibilities, and as Maughan immersed himself in campus life, he discovered that his greatest passion wasn’t designing technology — it was helping people understand it. Looking back, he says donor-funded scholarships gave him the freedom to make that discovery. “Those scholarships gave me the freedom to focus on school and figure out what I was really passionate about,” Maughan said. “Without them, I would have needed a much more demanding job just to pay for college, and I don’t think I would have had the same opportunities.” A recipient of both a Presidential Academic Scholarship and the Farrell and Ann Edwards Teaching Scholarship, Maughan earned his bachelor’s degree in physics in 2011 before completing a Master of Education in secondary science education in 2013. Established in 2009, the Farrell and Ann Edwards Scholarship Endowment recognizes undergraduate and graduate students pursuing physics teaching who demonstrate a commitment to education and research. Like all endowed scholarships , it was created to provide lasting support for future generations of students — ensuring that the same opportunities Maughan received will continue to open doors for aspiring educators for years to come. For Maughan, that investment came at exactly the right time. “The scholarships helped fill the gap after my Presidential Scholarship ended,” Maughan said. “I was able to graduate with both my bachelor’s and master's degrees completely debt-free.” More importantly, the scholarships gave him something money can’t buy: time. Rather than working long hours to cover college expenses, Maughan immersed himself in opportunities that transformed both his college experience and his future career. He served as a supplemental instructor, conducted undergraduate research , participated in Utah State’s Get Away Special team , became a College of Science ambassador, joined the Society of Physics Students, and remained active in the Institute of Religion’s show choir. Milo also found one of his greatest passions through Utah State’s annual Physics Day at Lagoon . What began as volunteering eventually grew into leading one of the university’s largest STEM outreach events, coordinating thousands of middle and high school students as they explored physics through hands-on learning. “Those experiences taught me leadership, communication and how to teach in ways that really connect with students,” Maughan said. “The scholarships gave me the time and space to develop those skills instead of worrying about how I was going to pay my bills.” It was while working as a supplemental instructor that Maughan realized his future was shifting. “I found that I really enjoyed teaching,” Maughan said. “Helping students work through difficult concepts and seeing that moment when everything clicks — that was incredibly rewarding.” As he explored his options, Utah State launched a graduate route to teacher licensure in science education. The opportunity to earn both a teaching license and a master’s degree confirmed Maughan had found his calling. “I realized education was where I belonged,” Maughan said. “The scholarships gave me the freedom to choose my passion instead of feeling pressured to choose a different path simply because of finances.” After graduation, Maughan spent more than a decade teaching physics and astronomy in Utah public schools, inspiring students to see science not as a collection of formulas but as a way to better understand the world around them. Throughout those years, he also continued to give back to Utah State by volunteering at Physics Day, helping create the same experience for future students as the one that once inspired him. Today, Maughan’s influence extends even farther. As the secondary science specialist for the Utah State Board of Education, he supports science educators across Utah, helping strengthen instruction for thousands of students statewide. “The leadership experiences I had at Utah State are things I still use every day,” Maughan said. “I don’t think I would be where I am today without those opportunities.” For Maughan, the impact of donor generosity reaches well beyond a single scholarship recipient. “It’s hard to measure because so much of the impact happens behind the scenes,” Maughan said. “Scholarships provided financial stability, but they also gave me time to grow as a leader, participate in experiences that changed my life, and ultimately discover the career I was meant to pursue.” He believes that is the lasting power of endowed scholarships. “I can't thank them enough,” Maughan said about the donors who supported his scholarship. “Without that help, my life would have looked very different. Donors gave me the opportunity to pursue what I loved instead of simply pursuing what would help me make ends meet. That investment continues to impact every educator and student I have the opportunity to serve.” The Farrell and Ann Edwards Scholarship Endowment continues to support future physics educators just as it supported Maughan more than a decade ago. Its impact stretches far beyond the students who receive it, reaching the classrooms, schools and communities they will serve throughout their careers. For Maughan, that ripple effect is the true legacy of philanthropy. One scholarship gave Maughan the freedom to discover his purpose. Today, that investment continues creating opportunities for thousands of students across Utah through the educators and leaders he helps support. Create Your Aggie Impact Scholarships do more than make college affordable; they give students the freedom to discover their passions, develop leadership skills, and pursue careers that change lives. Endowed scholarships ensure those opportunities continue for generations of Aggies to come.

title: Seven Central Utah Communities Build Water Action Plans at Utah Growing Water Smart Workshop
summary: LOGAN, Utah — The Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air at Utah State University recently brought together teams from seven Central Utah communities to develop locally driven water action plans. The effort was part of Utah Growing Water Smart , a program the institute helps facilitate under the guidance of the Utah Division of Water Resources . This workshop was offered in partnership with the Center for Water Efficient Landscaping at USU , the Central Utah Water Conservancy District , the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy , and the Utah League of Cities and Towns . The participating communities — Alpine, Eagle Mountain, Highland, Lehi, Provo, Saratoga Springs, and Spanish Fork — each sent teams of planners, engineers, elected officials, utility managers, city managers, and other local leaders. Rather than attending presentations or leaving with a one-size-fits-all plan, each community spent three days working side by side with water experts to build its own roadmap for integrated land use and water planning. The workshop spaces quickly filled with sticky notes, papers, and markers as each community worked through its priorities together. By the end of the workshop, each team left with an action plan that looks five years into the future for water use and availability in the context of increased population growth and demand. “Every Utah community is different, so we don't hand communities a plan. We help them write their own,” said Anna McEntire, executive director of the institute. “The communities drive the process, and we give them sustained access to the expertise they need to get where they're going. They leave with an actionable plan that fits the needs of their community.” Utah Growing Water Smart is designed as a cohort-based experience rather than a one-time workshop. The program begins with guided onboarding and a community self-assessment, centers on a multi-day retreat, and extends into the implementation phase with continued technical assistance, peer networking, reunions, and shared case studies. “Our aim is for Utah Growing Water Smart to become a long-term feature of how Utah plans for its water future,” McEntire said, “so that every community, no matter its size or capacity, can plan for a secure, sustainable, and resilient water supply.” Through the Utah Growing Water Smart program, the institute convenes the facilitators, experts, and agency partners to support each cohort and bring the program to various regions throughout the state. This past cohort marks the latest in the program's third phase, and more than two dozen communities have now gone through the program. Three additional cohorts are planned through 2028. About the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air The Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, and Air at Utah State University connects decision-makers with high-quality research to support informed land, water, and air policy in Utah. Through applied research, public convening, and cross-sector collaboration, ILWA helps the state address complex natural resource challenges. Learn more at usu.edu/ilwa .

title: Seven Former Aggies Joining NFL Teams
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Following the conclusion of the NFL Draft on Saturday, Utah State had two of its former football players sign free agent contracts, while five more have been invited to rookie mini camps. Noah Avinger and Brady Boyd both signed free agent contracts with NFL teams as Avinger will join the Los Angeles Chargers and Boyd will join the Jacksonville Jaguars. Bryson Barnes, Miles Davis, Broc Lane, John Miller and Bryson Taylor have all been invited to rookie mini camps. Barnes will work out for the Cleveland Browns, Davis will work out for the Seattle Seahawks, Miller will work out for the Denver Broncos, Taylor will work out for the Atlanta Falcons, and Lane has been invited to work out for the Tennessee Titans and Indianapolis Colts. Avinger , a 6-foot, 190-pound defensive back from Cerritos, California (Servite HS/New Mexico), was named a HERO Sports Group of Five Second Team All-American and earned first-team All-Mountain West honors following his senior season. In his one year with the Aggies during the 2025 campaign, he started all 12 games he played in and finished the season with 84 tackles (40 solo), including 1.0 sacks and 3.5 tackles for loss. He led the team with 10 pass breakups and three interceptions, while adding one forced fumble, one fumble recovery and one quarterback hurry. He posted three double-digit tackle outings during the year including a season-best 12 stops at No. 18 Vanderbilt. Boyd , a 6-1, 195-pound wide receiver from Southlake, Texas (Southlake Carroll HS/Texas Tech), earned honorable mention All-Mountain West honors following the 2025 season. He started 12 of the 13 games he played in during his one year with USU and led the team with eight touchdown receptions, while ranking second on the team with 46 catches for 743 yards. His best game of the year was against Nevada as he had five receptions for a career-high 117 yards and a career-high-tying two touchdowns. Barnes , a 6-2, 210-pound quarterback from Milford, Utah (Milford HS/Utah) earned second-team All-Mountain West honors during the 2025 campaign as he started all 13 games and accounted for 3,543 yards of total offense, which ranks fifth all-time in school history. He completed 211-of-356 (.593) passes for 2,803 yards with 18 touchdowns and five interceptions and threw multiple touchdowns in five games, including three touchdowns three times. He rushed for 740 yards on 189 carries (3.9 ypc) and 10 touchdowns, which is a single season school record for rushing touchdowns by a quarterback. During his two-year Aggie career, Barnes set the school record for 100-yard rushing games by a quarterback with five as he rushed for 1,270 yards to rank 24th all-time in program history. He was 288-of-482 (.598) passing for 3,659 yards with 30 touchdowns and 11 interceptions and ranks ninth all-time in school history in completion percentage. Davis , a 5-11, 215-pound running back from Las Vegas, Nevada (Las Vegas HS/BYU), earned second-team All-Mountain West honors in his only season with USU. During the 2025 campaign, he recorded 1,000 all-purpose yards and scored 11 touchdowns. He started 11 of the 13 games he played in and finished the season rushing for 731 yards on 131 carries (5.6 ypr) and eight touchdowns, to go along with 28 receptions for 201 yards (7.2 ypr) and three touchdowns. He also returned four kickoffs for 68 yards (17.0 ypr). Overall, he had three 100-yard rushing games and four games with 100-plus all-purpose yards. His best outing of the season was against UTEP as he produced a career-high 184 all-purpose yards as he rushed for 88 yards on seven carries and one touchdown, caught a career-high six passes for a career-best 61 yards, and returned two kickoffs for 35 yards. He rushed for a season-high 118 yards on 13 carries and one touchdown against McNeese. Lane , a 6-4, 240-pound tight end from Chandler, Arizona (Perry HS), started seven of the 11 games he played in during the 2025 campaign and finished the season with 19 receptions for 218 yards and two touchdowns. His best game of the year was at No. 18 Vanderbilt as he caught a career-high seven passes for a career-best 98 yards. Lane played in 44 career games with 23 starts during his six seasons at Utah State (2020-25) and had 67 receptions for 662 yards (9.9 ypr) and six touchdowns. He earned honorable mention All-Mountain West honors following the 2023 campaign. Miller , a 6-1, 225-pound linebacker from Tualatin, Oregon (Tualatin HS/Oregon State) earned first-team All-Mountain West honors during the 2025 campaign. He started all 13 games during the season and led the team with 118 tackles (39 solo), including a team-best 8.0 sacks and a team-high 10.0 tackles for loss, while adding eight quarterback hurries, three pass breakups and one forced fumble. He recorded six double-digit tackle outings on the year, including a career-high 16 stops against Air Force. During his two-year Utah State career, Miller posted 170 tackles, including 10.0 sacks and 15.5 tackles for loss, to go along with five pass breakups, and one forced fumble. Taylor , a 6-1, 190-pound cornerback from Hoschton, Georgia (Mill Creek HS/New Mexico), appeared in 11 games and made five starts during the 2025 campaign. He finished his only season at USU with 32 tackles (15 solo), including 2.0 tackles for loss, to go along with five pass breakups. His best game of the year was at No. 19 Texas A&M as he posted a season-high seven tackles.

title: Shannon Karels, Kathy Miller Receive Shingo Publication Award for 'Steel Toes and Stilettos'
summary: The Shingo Institute, part of the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business at Utah State University, has announced that Shannon Karels and Kathy Miller have been awarded the Shingo Publication Award for their book Steel Toes and Stilettos: A True Story of Women Manufacturing Leaders and Lean Transformation Success . This award recognizes publications that make a significant contribution to the advancement and practical application of organizational excellence. Steel Toes and Stilettos chronicles the transformation of a traditional manufacturing operation into a lean enterprise through the shared experiences of Kathy Miller, an executive leader responsible for business performance, and Shannon Karels, a transformation leader charged with driving sustainable change. Through their unique perspectives, the authors provide an engaging account of the challenges, successes, and human dimensions of leading organizational transformation. Drawing on firsthand experience, they explore the complexities of culture change, the realities of implementing lean principles, and the leadership practices required to achieve lasting results. More than a lean transformation story, the book highlights the power of authentic leadership, collaboration, and inclusivity in creating high-performing organizations. Karels and Miller demonstrate how leaders can build trust, navigate change, and foster environments where people thrive while improving operational performance. Their story also offers a compelling example of women supporting one another in leadership roles and balancing demanding careers with the complexities of everyday life. “ Steel Toes and Stilettos reflects many of the principles that underpin organizational excellence,” said Ken Snyder, executive director of the Shingo Institute. “Through a powerful combination of practical experience, leadership insight, and personal storytelling, Shannon Karels and Kathy Miller show how authentic leadership and principle-based transformation can create meaningful and sustainable results. Their work serves as both an inspiration and a guide for leaders seeking to build cultures of excellence.” Across industries, readers have embraced Steel Toes and Stilettos as an engaging and relatable account of leadership, transformation, and the pursuit of operational excellence. Kathy and Shannon are systems-based thinkers, which makes their lean enterprise implementation successful and sustainable. Understanding their journey and challenges makes this book a must read for both new lean thinkers and seasoned lean professionals. — Rick Harris, President of Harris Lean Systems, Inc. Kathy and Shannon offer a glimpse of the struggles and barriers they have faced on their road to a successful lean transformation. It would behoove all leaders to truly understand these obstacles and perspectives through their eyes so that the unique traits of both genders meld into synergistic, winning organizations. This breakthrough publication is required reading if one is serious about building a diverse, world-class organization. — Mark DeLuzio, President & CEO Lean Horizons Consulting Not only a technically sound lean transformation, but a story of leadership, friendship, and camaraderie. These ladies demonstrate strength through vulnerability, perseverance through compassion, and remind us all of what true leadership looks like. — Diane Larkin, Executive Vice President Global Operations Valmont Industries This is an inspiring and important story, and one that is deeply relevant today, with timeless principles for both women and men, seasoned professionals, and those just starting their careers. It is a story of courageous women, working side by side with the masters of lean manufacturing to transform a business. It is the story of how they build an inclusive culture where teams felt connected, engaged and trusted. Through their rigorous and fulfilling work, they delivered for their employees, employer, and stakeholders alike. — Roger Lehman, Managing Partner, Oliver Wyman The Shingo Publication Award, one of the most respected honors in the field of organizational excellence, recognizes authors whose work meaningfully advances leadership and cultural transformation worldwide. Steel Toes and Stilettos exemplifies this standard. By sharing a compelling real-world story of lean transformation, Shannon Karels and Kathy Miller illustrate the power of principle-based leadership, authentic relationships, and a culture that empowers people to contribute their best. Their work makes an important contribution to the ongoing pursuit of organizational excellence by demonstrating how sustainable results emerge when leaders intentionally develop both people and systems. The authors will be formally recognized at the Awards Gala at Shingo Connect USA in Atlanta, Georgia, March 15-17, 2027. Shingo Connect includes workshops, site tours, keynotes, and sessions focused on achieving organizational excellence. Learn more at shingo.org/events . To purchase a copy of Steel Toes and Stilettos or other Shingo publications, visit https://shingo.org/books . About the Authors Kathy Miller is a senior operations executive who has held multiple global vice president and director roles in manufacturing and lean enterprise leadership. A Shingo Prize recipient for a large business as a plant manager, she began her career as a co-op student at a vehicle assembly plant and advanced through engineering, marketing, lean, and operations leadership roles within major publicly traded corporations. Kathy is recognized for driving transformational results through team development, process discipline, continuous improvement, and the creation of inclusive cultures grounded in trust, respect, and accountability. Shannon Karels is a senior operations leader who has led multiple lean transformations and managed operations across diverse industries for major publicly traded corporations. Beginning her career in supply chain management, she advanced through lean and operations leadership roles, helping organizations strengthen employee engagement, empower teams, and improve business performance. Shannon is known for fostering accountable, high-performing organizations built on trust, collaboration, and a relentless focus on customer and business results. About the Shingo Institute The Shingo Institute is home to the Shingo Prize, an award recognizing organizations that demonstrate an exceptional culture fostering continuous improvement. Part of the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business at Utah State University, the Shingo Institute is named after Japanese industrial engineer and Toyota adviser Shigeo Shingo, one of the world's thought leaders in the Toyota Production System. Drawing from Shingo’s teachings and years of experience working with organizations worldwide, the Shingo Institute developed the Shingo Model, the basis for its various educational offerings, including workshops, study tours, and conferences. Workshops are available in multiple languages through the Institute's Licensed Affiliates. For more information on workshops and affiliates or to register to attend an event, please visit https://shingo.org .

title: Show Me: Utah State Athletics Unveils Initiative to Unite Aggie Nation
summary: LOGAN, Utah — From fans to local businesses, Utah State Athletics calls on everyone to "Show Me" their support and get involved as the department gears up for its historic move to the Pac-12. Loyal Aggie supporters have long been pivotal members of Utah State Athletics' rich history, displaying unmatched pride at athletic events. With the Pac-12 era on the horizon, the department is inviting the community to play an important role in shaping the next phase of growth. The initiative is designed to strengthen the department's foundation and create lasting opportunities for student-athletes and the community. It also connects Utah State Athletics, the Cache Valley community and Utah State University's integration into the new Pac-12, building momentum around the athletics department and the university. That shared momentum comes at a critical time for Utah State Athletics as the competitive landscape continues to evolve. "From my opening press conference, I have been clear: everyone from Cache Valley is an Aggie," said Utah State Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker. "The passion and pride displayed by our outstanding fans are unmatched, and that is why we need everyone to join our pursuit of becoming one of the premier athletic departments in the West and the new Pac-12." Working in tandem with the previously announced Reach & Rise campaign, the Show Me initiative is an all-encompassing modernization effort that highlights the multiple ways investors, fans and community members can make an impact on Utah State Athletics. More than ever, in this new era of intercollegiate athletics, investments from Aggie Nation will be pivotal to the success of Utah State University and its athletics department. The current landscape has shifted what is required to remain competitive, driven by the transfer portal, internal name, image and likeness (NIL) and other factors that affect both the immediate needs and long-term future of the department. Increased investment directly impacts the Cache Valley community, giving USU the opportunity to attract and retain championship-level talent that leads to wins and the pursuit of titles. When the athletics department succeeds, the Cache Valley community benefits through greater visibility, supporting university enrollment and helping establish lasting generations of Aggie alumni who call Cache Valley home. "Everyone has the opportunity to make an impact, whether that's through buying tickets, making a donation to the Big Blue Club, purchasing Aggie merchandise or showing your USU pride," Walker said. "For our local business partners, join us on this journey and see how a partnership with Utah State Athletics benefits you in our community." Those opportunities reflect a broader effort to engage supporters at every level. The athletics department is calling on supporters to play an active role and make a meaningful impact through tickets, philanthropic giving and sponsorships. Fans are asked to "Show Me" they are Pac-12 ready by purchasing tickets and investing in the Big Blue Club or Blue A Society. Building on these core values, the athletics department is planning unique opportunities to engage with the community. These efforts will be showcased through upcoming events at USU athletic venues and community service initiatives, demonstrating to Aggie Nation the department's commitment to fostering a shared sense of community. Third consecutive men's basketball season-ticket sellout (first-time in program history). $42 million in cash and pledges (includes $20 million from 6-month goal). title: Sixth Annual Blanding Golf Tournament Raises Money for Student Scholarships
summary: MONTICELLO, Utah — Earlier this summer, Utah State University Blanding hosted its 6th annual Scholarship Golf Tournament. The tournament brought together 18 different teams that helped raise money toward nontraditional scholarships. Seventy-two golfers and 12 volunteers gathered on the Hideout Golf Course in Monticello on June 6. The event was sponsored by Redd’s Ace Hardware and Hideout Golf Course. The teams were made up of individuals from across the Four Corners region, with participants coming from Utah, Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona. “The tournament was full of amazing people who traveled from all over the Four Corners region to come and support the campus and what we are trying to do for all of our students,” said Megan Mower-Harris, campus events and community engagement coordinator at USU Blanding. In addition to the corporate sponsors of the event, several other local businesses showed their support, including Blue Mountain Hospital, San Juan Hospital and Redd’s Ace Hardware. According to Mower-Harris, a record number of volunteers came together to make the event a success. In past years, the event had as few as four volunteers come forward. This year, the event had 12. “They gave up some of their Saturday to come and help, and I appreciate them,” Mower-Harris said. “What makes the tournament a success is having a great team to work with. From the employees at the Hideout Golf Course to my events team and the volunteers who come and help. Offering residential campus housing and dining, Utah State University Blanding gives students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university, all while providing award-winning education. With degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees, plus technical education offerings in Business, Technical Trades and Health Professions, USU Blanding offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at blanding.usu.edu .

title: Space Dynamics Lab Names Lance Fife Vice President & Chief Operating Officer
summary: NORTH LOGAN — Utah State University’s Space Dynamics Laboratory announced Tuesday that it has named Lance Fife as vice president and chief operating officer, a newly created executive leadership position established to strengthen coordination and operational execution across the organization. In the new role, Fife will lead operations across SDL and facilitate program execution with oversight of engineering, information systems, facilities and property, and quality and mission assurance. “SDL continues to grow in the scope and complexity of the missions we support, and our leadership structure must evolve with that growth,” said Jed Hancock, SDL president. “Lance brings decades of technical, program, and organizational leadership experience to this role. His understanding of our government partners, our people, and our mission will help ensure that we continue to execute with excellence across the laboratory.” Fife brings more than 30 years of aerospace and defense industry experience spanning organizational leadership, program management, systems engineering, software development, and business development. Throughout his career, he has supported U.S. Department of War and national security missions. Prior to his appointment, Fife served as director of SDL’s Strategic and Military Space Division, where he led approximately 450 employees and oversaw the division’s strategy, workforce, stakeholder engagement, and program execution. The division’s technology portfolio includes missile defense and hypersonics, military space sensors, ground and spacecraft software systems, full life-cycle space missions, and advanced capabilities for sensitive and time-critical missions. Fife holds a Master of Business Administration and a Bachelor of Science in electrical engineering from USU. As part of the leadership transition, SDL has also named Tim McKenzie as director of its Strategic and Military Space Division, succeeding Fife. McKenzie has served as SMS deputy director since joining SDL in 2019 and has played an important role in the division’s growth and evolution. During that time, he has helped lead strategic initiatives, major programs, infrastructure investment, and partnerships across SDL and USU and with government sponsors. He brings more than 30 years of experience in the national security space, with expertise in program execution, strategy, technology development, and organizational management. Headquartered at USU’s Innovation Campus in North Logan, Utah, SDL is an independent nonprofit corporation owned by USU that solves technical challenges faced by the military, science community, and industry and supports NASA’s vision to explore the secrets of the universe for the benefit of all. SDL has field offices in Albuquerque, New Mexico; Chantilly, Virginia; Colorado Springs, Colorado; Huntsville, Alabama; Ogden, Utah; and Stafford, Virginia. For more information, visit sdl.usu.edu .

title: Space Dynamics Lab to Provide Deep Space Communications for NASA Moon Mission
summary: NORTH LOGAN — Utah State University’s Space Dynamics Laboratory announced at the 40th Annual Small Satellite Conference that it has been selected by Advanced Space LLC to provide deep space communications and time-keeping technology for NASA’s CAPSTONE 02 mission. This technology demonstration will further develop autonomous navigation, spacecraft-to-spacecraft communications, and proximity operations around the Moon in support of NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base programs. Building on the success of the original CAPSTONE mission, launched in 2022, SDL will design, manufacture, and test two flight-qualified Iris Radios and associated communication, navigation, and precise timekeeping hardware for CAPSTONE 02’s twin 400-kilogram small satellites. SDL’s radios will provide direct-to-Earth connectivity as well as an additional spacecraft-to-spacecraft link, enabling the spacecraft to communicate directly with one another. This will enable new capabilities for autonomous operations in a lunar orbit. CAPSTONE 02 expands on technologies first demonstrated during the original CAPSTONE mission, which successfully validated a near-rectilinear halo orbit, a fuel-efficient path around the Moon that repeatedly brings a spacecraft close to the lunar surface before carrying it thousands of kilometers away, making it ideal for future lunar exploration missions. It also demonstrated Advanced Space’s Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System, or CAPS, navigation software. CAPSTONE 02 will use two spacecraft operating in cislunar space, the region between Earth and the Moon, to demonstrate autonomous rendezvous and proximity operation, spacecraft-to-spacecraft communications, and advanced navigation techniques that reduce reliance on continuous tracking from Earth. “CAPSTONE was a true pathfinding mission that proved small satellites can accomplish big objectives beyond Earth’s orbit in lunar space. The Iris Radio on CAPSTONE continues to provide the reliable communications link and precision navigation and time-keeping capabilities that enabled mission controllers to reliably command and control the spacecraft and relay critical data throughout the mission. CAPSTONE successfully validated capabilities and built critical infrastructure that are helping shape humanity’s return to the Moon,” said Tim Neilsen, branch head of Spacecraft Missions and Technologies for Civil and Commercial Space at SDL. “SDL will help CAPSTONE 02 take the next step by advancing how spacecraft can communicate and coordinate with one another, navigate more autonomously, and perform complex proximity operations around the Moon.” SDL’s Iris Radio is a software-defined telecommunications spacecraft subsystem designed specifically for missions operating beyond low-Earth orbit. Developed from technology created at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and transitioned to SDL for continued development and production, the radio is engineered to withstand the radiation and thermal extremes of deep space while providing continuous contact with NASA’s Deep Space Network. The mission continues SDL’s long history of supporting NASA exploration beyond Earth’s orbit. In addition to supporting the original CAPSTONE mission, Iris Radios have flown on missions including MarCO, Lunar Flashlight, LICIACube, BioSentinel, LunaH-Map, NEA Scout, CuSP and ArgoMoon. CAPSTONE 02 is targeted for launch in late 2027. Headquartered at USU’s Innovation Campus in North Logan, Utah, SDL is an independent nonprofit corporation owned by USU that solves technical challenges faced by the military, science community, and industry and supports NASA’s vision to explore the secrets of the universe for the benefit of all. SDL has field offices in Albuquerque, New Mexico; Chantilly, Virginia; Colorado Springs, Colorado; Huntsville, Alabama; Ogden, Utah; and Stafford, Virginia. For more information, visit sdl.usu.edu .

title: Space Dynamics Laboratory's Pat Patterson Selected as AIAA Associate Fellow
summary: NORTH LOGAN, Utah — The American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics has selected Utah State University’s Space Dynamics Laboratory Director of Advanced Concepts Pat Patterson as a member of the Class of 2027 AIAA Associate Fellows, recognizing a nearly four-decade career advancing space systems for national and scientific missions. The grade of AIAA Associate Fellow is reserved for individuals who have accomplished important engineering or scientific work, performed original work of outstanding merit, or made significant contributions to aeronautics or astronautics. According to AIAA, only 17% of its members are ever selected for the distinction. Patterson’s AIAA citation reads: “For his distinctive and broad history in space systems engineering for upper atmospheric research, small satellite research and development, and mission operations planning.” “Pat’s selection as an AIAA Associate Fellow is a well-deserved acknowledgment of the expertise and perspective he has brought to the aerospace community throughout his career,” said Niel Holt, SDL’s executive director for strategic development. “It also speaks to the depth of knowledge across SDL. Our ability to solve difficult problems for our partners depends on people like Pat who have spent their careers advancing their fields while working alongside and developing the next generation of experts.” Patterson joined SDL in 1988 as a student employee and was subsequently hired as a full-time electrical engineer in 1991. He has since served in engineering, program management, and executive roles. His work has spanned sounding rocket missions, spacecraft development, and space operations. Today, as director of advanced concepts, he helps identify technologies that can address emerging national security and science exploration needs and guides promising concepts toward mission applications. Beyond his work at SDL, Patterson has contributed to the broader aerospace community through technical and advisory roles. He served multiple terms on the Department of the Air Force Scientific Advisory Board, the Science Committee of the NASA Advisory Council, and currently serves on the AIAA Small Satellite Technical Committee and USU’s Electrical and Computer Engineering Board. Patterson has also played a prominent role in the growth of the small satellite community. He has chaired the Small Satellite Conference for 27 years, a period during which attendance has grown tenfold. The conference now brings together more than 1,300 organizations from 48 countries. “I’ve had the privilege of spending my career working with exceptionally talented people to advance space systems and capabilities,” Patterson said. “To be named an AIAA Associate Fellow by peers in the aerospace community is a tremendous honor, and I’m grateful to everyone I’ve had the opportunity to work with and learn from along the way.” Patterson earned bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees in electrical engineering from USU. His doctoral research used NASA sounding rocket missions launched from Poker Flat Research Range, Alaska, to study atomic oxygen in the upper atmosphere. He also served as an adjunct assistant professor in USU’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in 2008. The Class of 2027 AIAA Associate Fellows will be formally inducted Jan. 13, 2027, during the AIAA SciTech Forum in Orlando, Florida. Headquartered at USU’s Innovation Campus in North Logan, Utah, SDL solves technical challenges faced by the military, science community, and industry and supports NASA’s vision to explore the secrets of the universe for the benefit of all. SDL has field offices in Albuquerque, New Mexico; Chantilly, Virginia; Colorado Springs, Colorado; Huntsville, Alabama; Ogden, Utah; and Stafford, Virginia. For more information, visit sdl.usu.edu.

title: Special Education Alumna Shares Love of Photography at Lyndsley Wilkerson Gallery
summary: A new photography exhibition by an Aggie alum will open to the public on Utah State University’s Logan campus on Oct. 19. “Through the Lens” features the works of Judy Silker, alumna from the Department of Special Education and Rehabilitation Counseling, and will be on exhibit in the Lyndsley Wilkerson Gallery. The gallery is located on the first floor in the Sorenson Center for Clinical Excellence, which is housed within the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences on the Logan campus. Silker’s love of photography has been lifelong, and her photos have been shared internationally with women’s organizations as well as displayed in local galleries and juried art shows. The exhibition celebrates the beauty of everyday surroundings and the joy that comes from simple things including high desert landscapes, frozen fog on tree branches, treasured family moments, and more. Silker, a California native and current Nevada resident, is a founding member of the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences Dean’s Advancement Board, a member of the Old Main Society, and a lifetime member of the USU Alumni Association. Part of Silker’s role as a member of the Dean’s Advancement Board was to provide her vision and feedback on the creation of the Sorenson Legacy Foundation Center for Clinical Excellence, which formally opened in 2018. Having her treasured photography now featured on the walls of its gallery is something she doesn’t take lightly. “Sharing my love of photography with fellow Aggies and friends is an honor that I will always cherish,” Silker said. “It is icing on the cake to see it hanging on the walls of the Sorenson Center’s art gallery.” Silker graduated from Utah State with a bachelor’s degree in special education in 1974. Her training in teaching and advocating for disabled children and adults took her to Idaho, California, and Nevada for a 32-year career in rural schools. She has volunteered for several cultural, youth, and community service organizations during her career and in retirement. Judy is a 47-year member of The Delta Kappa Gamma Society International, a women’s honorary society for teachers, and she served as Nevada State President for the organization from 2009-2011. “Through the Lens” will be open to the public from Oct. 19-30. The gallery is open from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday and is free of charge. For more information, visit the Sorenson Center website.

title: Standing Room Only: New Platform Uses Machine Learning to Tackle Recreation Crowding
summary: It can be discouraging lacing up boots, packing trail mix, and driving hours to a favorite trailhead only to find that a hundred other people had the same idea. Overcrowding is an ongoing issue at recreation sites across the West, with packed parking lots, overloaded boat ramps, and crowded trailheads. To make tough decisions about well-loved places, land managers have to understand the problem. How often does parking spill out of crowded lots? How long do boaters have to wait to launch? How many people are using a given trail? Answering these questions faces a major challenge — the daunting task of tracking recreation trends across dispersed access points and scattered destinations, says Jordan Smith, director of the Institute of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism. Various tools are used — surveys, mechanical counters, and in-person observations. But traditional tracking methods have a big tradeoff between cost and accuracy, said Chase Lamborn, assistant director of the institute. “Collecting that kind of high-quality data requires a substantial amount of staff time, especially when you are trying to understand trends across a lot of sites over an entire season,” Lamborn said. Artificial intelligence offers a new way to help. Smith and Lamborn decided to ask if AI could help managers better understand recreation patterns without dramatically increasing the cost of monitoring. In partnership with the U.S. Forest Service, the researchers tested the approach along the heavily used Payette River recreation corridor in Idaho. They used high-resolution aerial imagery to map where parking was available across the corridor. They installed cameras at recreation sites along the river to photograph activity over time (without collecting personal information). Computer vision tools — algorithms that identify and count objects in images and video — were trained and processed nearly a half-million images to identify the presence of vehicles in parking areas and watercraft on the river. The data they gathered provided a surprisingly detailed picture of recreation capacity in the corridor and how much of that capacity was being used. It showed where people concentrated, when demand peaked, and where physical bottlenecks occurred. The new approach demonstrates how AI could let land managers monitor large recreation areas more consistently and efficiently than would be practical through traditional methods, Lamborn said. The researchers turned photographs into continuously updated metrics — identifying crowding hotspots, estimating parking demand, and providing a more complete picture of recreation use. Managers could use this information for planning, to prioritize projects and build infrastructure to improve the recreation experience and safety, Smith said. Details about the methodology were recently published in the journal Machine Learning with Applications , and results were used by the Institute of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism for developing the Payette River Recreation Management Plan. The value of the approach is not just that AI can automate part of the monitoring process, Lamborn said — it’s that it offers substantially better information without substantially bigger budgets. Traditional monitoring is limited by budgets, creating tradeoffs between the number of sites monitored, the amount of data collected, and the level of detail managers receive. “Doing it well requires massive data sets,” Lamborn said. “If we were doing it by hand, it would take literally thousands of employee-hours to work through.” Another benefit of the new approach is that it improves the product without replacing people. “We hire the same number of staff, often students, to provide the same hands-on training and professional experience within roughly the same budget. The difference is that we can now collect and process far more information than was previously possible. It gives our funding partners better information, while still providing valuable work experience,” Lamborn said. By allowing field crews to collect large volumes of data that is efficiently processed, the approach preserves the workforce benefits of traditional recreation monitoring while increasing the amount, consistency, and usefulness of the information produced, the team said. “In practical terms, the same investment can support a better picture of how recreation sites are being used and where management attention may be needed most,” Lamborn said. The researchers were highly cognizant of privacy concerns. They used fixed cameras to compile counts without identifying individuals or license plates. Technicians positioned cameras to avoid human faces and used the lowest practical resolution for object detection. They applied automatic digital masks to sensitive areas and deleted raw photos once automated counts were complete. With proof of concept, the team has launched a Recreation Capacity Platform to share the approach more broadly. The platform combines aerial maps, camera counts, and environmental conditions into easy-to-use digital dashboards. “The goal is to continue to advance real-time and privacy-first monitoring systems needed in a variety of outdoor recreation contexts,” Smith said. “As outdoor recreation participation continues to grow, the public needs smarter systems to know when and where to have the kind of recreation experiences that they want.” By letting AI process the reams of complex visual monitoring into useful information, the team hopes to help land management agencies pinpoint problems more efficiently while keeping recreation destinations as accessible as possible to everyone heading outdoors, Smith said.

title: Take Harder Classes, Earn Bigger Scholarships at Utah State University Southeast Campuses
summary: Beginning with the 2027-28 academic year, Utah State University Southeast students will have more ways to earn scholarships and make a Utah State education more affordable. The updated scholarship approach aligns USU Southeast more closely with scholarship opportunities across the Utah State University system while continuing to reflect the lower tuition scale available at USU Eastern, USU Blanding and USU Moab. For students and families in Price, Blanding, Moab and surrounding communities, the message is simple: Your effort can pay off at Utah State, and a college degree can remain within reach close to home. New first-year students who apply to USU by the scholarship deadline will automatically be considered for eligible awards. The streamlined approach is designed to make scholarship planning easier to understand, with clearer criteria based on GPA, academic preparation and the number of challenging courses students complete in high school. “USU wants students across the state to have clear, consistent scholarship opportunities, no matter which campus they choose,” said USU President Brad Mortensen. “By aligning scholarships across the USU system and expanding access to stackable awards, we are helping more students in rural areas see that college is possible, affordable and within reach.” Scholarships Designed for Southeast Students The updated scholarship structure creates a more consistent review process for incoming students while recognizing that tuition and award amounts differ by campus. Beginning in 2027-28, incoming resident first-year students attending USU Southeast may qualify for the following awards: Premier Awards: These scholarships are based upon index score, which reflects the highest academic achievement with strong HS GPA and ACT or SAT test scores. High School GPA Awards: These academic awards are based upon HS GPA only. New Advanced Coursework Scholarships Beginning Fall 2027 New resident-first year Southeast students will also be eligible for the new Advanced Coursework Scholarships, a two-year scholarship that rewards students for taking challenging high school courses. Students may receive this scholarship in addition to high school GPA awards, giving them another way to increase their total scholarship support. Qualifying coursework includes AP, honors, International Baccalaureate, concurrent enrollment and technical education classes. The more rigorous coursework a student completes by Feb. 1, 2027, including completion of a first credential in high school, the more scholarship money they may unlock. This scholarship recognizes that college readiness is reflected not only in a student’s grades, but also in their willingness to challenge themselves academically. For students deciding whether to take a more challenging class, the scholarship helps make the value clearer: those courses can help students prepare for college, build confidence and earn additional scholarship money at USU. 1-5 rigorous courses: $500 per year, 2 years total. 6-10 rigorous courses: $1,000 per year, 2 years total. 11 or more rigorous courses: $1,500 per year, 2 years total. A Clearer Path for Students and Families Together, the updated Southeast scholarship model gives students and families clearer information earlier in the college planning process. Instead of navigating different scholarship rules from campus to campus, students can better understand what they may qualify for and how their grades, course choices and academic preparation can help them earn more support. For USU Southeast, affordability remains one of the strongest reasons for students to choose a local Utah State campus. Between lower tuition, first-year scholarships, the Affordability Grant and stackable scholarship opportunities, students at USU Eastern, USU Blanding and USU Moab have multiple ways to reduce the cost of earning a Utah State degree while staying connected to their communities. “This update is about opening doors for students,” Mortensen said. “When students can stay closer to home, pay less in tuition and still access meaningful scholarship opportunities, it changes what feels possible for them and their families.” The scholarship update reflects Utah State University’s mission as the state’s land-grant university: to expand access to higher education, support student success and serve communities across Utah. Students and families can learn more at usu.edu/scholarships .

title: Ten Scholars Join CEHHS Faculty for 2026-27 Academic Year
summary: The Emma Eccles Jones College of Education and Human, Health, and Human Sciences at Utah State University is welcoming new faculty members for the 2026-27 academic year. “We deeply value the fresh perspectives, cutting-edge expertise, and energy that our new colleagues bring to our college,” said Al Smith, Emma Eccles Jones endowed dean. “Their contributions to our student experience, scholarship, and community engagement will meaningfully advance our college mission and USU’s statewide impact.” Kaytlin Clegg, Professional Practice Instructor, Department of Nursing Kaytlin Clegg is a professional practice assistant professor in the Department of Nursing, teaching second-year nursing students. She began her formal teaching career in 2025 after spending two years in hospital education, where she discovered a passion for teaching and mentoring future nurses. Clegg has been a registered nurse for 10 years, with clinical experience in medical/surgical nursing and infusion services. She earned her Bachelor of Science in Nursing from Weber State University and is currently pursuing her Master of Science in nursing through Western Governors University. She is passionate about helping students develop the knowledge, skills, and confidence needed to succeed in nursing practice. Outside of work, Clegg enjoys spending time outdoors with her two young sons. Evin Daines, Professional Practice Assistant Professor, Department of Psychology Evin Daines joined the Department of Psychology as a professional practice assistant professor. She earned her Ph.D. in counselor education and supervision from Utah State University in 2026 and her M.Ed. in school counseling from USU in 2020. Before joining the faculty, Daines worked as an elementary and middle school counselor, facilitated groups for Juvenile Justice Services, and served youth in a residential treatment center for mental health and behavioral disorders. Daines is passionate about preparing future school counselors to support the academic, social-emotional, and career development of K-12 students across Utah. Her research focuses on school counselors’ roles in mental health and behavior as well as professional advocacy within the school counseling profession. Outside of work, she enjoys spending time with her family. Aaron Fischer, Associate Professor, Department of Psychology Aaron Fischer was hired as part of the college’s initiative focused on technology and healthcare delivery. Before joining USU, he was a full professor at the University of Utah. A licensed psychologist and board-certified behavior analyst, Fischer’s work focuses on using technology to improve behavioral health, professional training, and school-based services. His research spans telehealth and consultation, artificial intelligence, virtual and immersive learning environments, and integrated models of behavioral healthcare. Fischer is the author of Teleconsultation in Schools and founder of the Utah School Mental Health Collaborative, which brings together schools, healthcare systems, universities, and communities to build better systems of support for children and families. Outside of work, he enjoys spending time with his family, playing music, practicing yoga, rock climbing, and getting outside. David Fukuda, Department Head, Kinesiology and Health Science David Fukuda is a professor and the Department Head for Kinesiology and Health Science at Utah State University. Prior to joining USU, he spent 13 years at the University of Central Florida, most recently serving as professor and division chair of kinesiology. His research focuses broadly on human performance and exercise physiology, with interests spanning sport science, body composition, exercise testing, lifespan development, and ergogenic aids. Fukuda earned a Bachelor of Business Administration in Production/Operations Management from Boise State University and a master’s and Ph.D. in exercise physiology from the University of Oklahoma. He is a fellow of both the American College of Sports Medicine and the National Strength and Conditioning Association. In his free time, Fukuda enjoys hanging out with family, exercising (preferably outdoors), and practicing the Olympic sport and martial art of judo which he’s been involved with for over three decades. Lora Israelsen, Clinical Assistant Professor, Department of Psychology Lora Israelsen isa licensed psychologist who specializes in diagnostic assessments related to neurodevelopmental disorders and cognitive differences. She has a doctorate in clinical psychology from University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center and a master’s degree from Harvard University. Following her doctorate,Israelsencompleted a postdoctoral fellowship at ChildServe, a large medical clinic in Iowa that provides care to children with complex medical needs and/or developmental disorders. She has also received specialized training in the treatment of sleep disorders and perinatal/postpartum mood disorders. Outside of work, Israelsen prioritizes spending time with her family and friends. She also loves long walks and hikes, learning about fiber arts and crafts, and reading. Charles Jenks, Professional Practice Assistant Professor, School of Teacher Education and Leadership Charles Jenks is a professional practice assistant professor in the School of Teacher Education and Leadership. He recently joined USU after 18 years in K-12 public education, serving in a variety of roles including special education teacher, principal, and superintendent. Jenks earned his doctorate in educational leadership from the University of Wyoming. His research interests focus on educational leadership and organizational improvement, particularly what helps educational leaders thrive, how organizational conditions affect leader well-being, and how healthy leaders contribute to healthy, improving organizations. Jenks is passionate about preparing and supporting educational leaders and bringing his experiences as a practitioner into his teaching and scholarship. Outside of work, he enjoys spending time with his wife and five children and being outdoors, particularly backpacking, hiking, and fly-fishing.
