Dorie Noll, Clinical Assistant Professor, Department of Speech and Hearing Sciences Dorie Noll is a clinical assistant professor in the Listening and Spoken Language Deaf Education Graduate Program at Utah State University, where she also serves as the director of Sound Beginnings. With nearly two decades of experience as a teacher, certified Auditory-Verbal Educator, researcher, and university instructor, Noll specializes in family-centered early intervention, caregiver coaching, and listening and spoken language development for children who are deaf or hard of hearing. She has a Ph.D. in rehabilitation sciences from the University of Ottawa and serves on national and international leadership boards, including the Board of Directors for the AG Bell Academy for Listening and Spoken Language and the National Language Acquisition Workgroup through the National Beacon Center. Before coming to USU, Noll was an assistant professor at Fontbonne University in St. Louis. Her work is deeply informed by both her academic research and her personal experience as the parent of a highly successful adult son who uses a cochlear implant. She enjoys reading, hiking, camping, walking her dogs, and playing with her grandson. Kellsie Prather, Assistant Professor, Human Development and Family Studies Kellsie Prather is an assistant professor in the Department of Human Development and Family Studies at Utah State University’s Vernal campus in the Uintah Basin. She completed her Ph.D. in human development and family science at the University of Georgia. Her work focuses on parenting and family relationships, particularly in rural communities and among families navigating economic and community challenges. Her research emphasizes parents’ lived experiences, parent-child relationships, emotion socialization, and how families draw on personal and community resources. She is especially interested in community-engaged research that can translate into meaningful support for families. Originally from rural Appalachian southeastern Ohio, Prather is excited to make a home in eastern Utah and learn from the communities she serves. Outside of work, she enjoys exploring new places with her partner and dog and staying connected with friends and family across the country. Lauren Ralston Ruesch, Assistant Professor, Department of Speech and Hearing Sciences A native of La Porte, Texas, Ralston Ruesch came to Utah State University from The University of Texas at Austin, where she completed her Doctor of Audiology and Ph.D. in speech, language, and hearing sciences with a supplemental focus in neuroscience. During her Ph.D. training, Ralston Ruesch also practiced clinically as a licensed audiologist. At USU, she is an assistant professor and directs the Clinical Auditory Neuroscience Laboratory, where her work uses cortical electrophysiological methods, such as electroencephalography, to better detect and understand auditory pathologies like hearing loss and tinnitus. Ralston Ruesch lives with her husband and their dog, Wynnie. They have already taken to hiking in Logan Canyon and exploring Bear Lake and are looking forward to discovering more of Utah's natural beauty and outdoor adventures. In her free time, she also enjoys camping, boxing, sewing, and baking. Amanda Stark, Assistant Professor, Department of Speech and Hearing Sciences Amanda Stark is a voice scientist and speech-language pathologist specializing in clinical and performance voice, laryngeal physiology, respiratory science, and translational voice technologies. She is an assistant professor at Utah State University and adjunct professor in the Department of Otolaryngology and Utah Center for Vocology (previously the National Center for Voice and Speech) at the University of Utah. She is also part of the college’s initiative focused on technology and healthcare delivery. Stark earned her bachelor’s from the University of Colorado Boulder, her master’s from the University of Utah, and her Ph.D. in speech, language, and hearing sciences from the University of Arizona. A licensed speech-language pathologist and ASHA-certified clinician, Stark has more than 15 years of clinical experience in voice, swallowing, and upper-airway disorders. A central focus of Stark’s current research is the physiologic, acoustic, aerodynamic, and respiratory basis of elite and extreme vocal production, with special emphasis on professional metal vocalists, harsh vocalizations, and the high-performance demands of stage singing.

title: The Other Kind of Flock: How Animal Camera Traps are Supporting Wildlife Research
summary: Melany McEntee uses camera traps to tackle a significant threat to hikers in and around Park City, Utah: aggressive moose. When trail users reported several risky encounters with these unpredictable, 1000-pound animals, local trail groups asked her to help them understand the issue. She is using a network of motion-activated cameras posted near popular trails to document what might be causing the moose to become confrontational . These aren’t Flock cameras — though they might appear similar at first glance — they are motion-activated cameras set to capture pictures of wildlife. Wildlife ecologists at USU want the public to understand the difference between the two kinds of devices. Animal camera traps differ from Flock traffic-monitoring cameras in fundamental ways, said Julie Young, a wildlife ecologist in USU’s Department of Wildland Resources . They are mounted by researchers in specific locations to collect images of wildlife, and sometimes recreationists, for science and wildlife-management purposes. Camera traps provide valuable science information, so USU researchers who rely on them work to be transparent to avoid misunderstanding and mistrust, Young said. Animal camera traps use motion and infrared sensors to detect passing animals with photographs or video. Infrared illumination lets them capture images at night without disturbing wildlife. They are used by ecologists and land managers to count animals, track their movement, and observe their behavior. If people are captured incidentally, or as part of the outdoor recreation research, researchers follow strict protocols to protect their privacy — the presence of humans is noted, but only as it applies to recreation, without personal information. Camera traps are essential to ecological science, Young said, because when researchers get too close to animals, they may change the animal’s behavior, defeating the purpose of the observation. Efforts toward transparency start on ground level. Many camera traps are labeled with contact information so that curious passersby can find out why they are there, who is collecting the data and how the information is used. “We always have a sticker on our cameras with our contact information, so anyone who encounters a camera trap can find out why it’s there,” Young said. McEntee uses the cameras to capture images of wildlife, and recreationists using the trails to understand how they are interacting with wildlife. The images are sent through a blurring protocol before she accesses them, and the original is deleted. The system used to analyze them is a “closed program,” so the blurred photos exist only on a local computer. She uses software to help code the images — if a dog is present, for example, to note hiking group size, or to track other kinds of animals — and compares these factors with moose encounters. Because McEntee's research involves images of recreationists, her study follows protocols established with USU's Institutional Review Board, which oversees research involving human participants for privacy, safety, and ethical considerations. The standard she uses to blur and delete any personal information is part of that protocol. Another USU researcher, Richard Evans tracks where mule deer gather, when they move, and how many are in a given square mile of Utah’s backcountry. He is gathering information to slow the spread of a fatal illness specific to deer, elk, and moose — chronic wasting disease. When deer populations reach higher densities, the disease seems to spread more quickly, though it’s not yet clear how or why. Wildlife managers want to understand these factors and thresholds to protect Utah’s herds. Other researchers at USU use camera traps to monitor large carnivores like bears and wolves. Rae Nickerson measures how stress levels of cattle change with different carnivore activity across grazing allotments in places like Montana, Washington, and Arizona. The cameras allow her to monitor predator and cattle behavior without disturbing the animals or constantly moving through the hundreds of miles grazing areas. “Camera trap technology has revolutionized wildlife science,” said David Stoner, USU Extension wildlife specialist. Researchers are able to observe even rare, shy, or nocturnal animals that humans rarely have the chance to see, to accurately count wildlife populations. In some cases they can even rediscover species thought to be extinct. “The modern digital camera is helping us to understand and avoid conflicts, protect animals, and respond to management concerns faster and more efficiently than ever before,” he said. If you see a wildlife camera trap in the backcountry, please don’t disturb it, Stoner said. These units are key to understanding how animals respond to each other and the world, though if you reach out for information, most wildlife ecologists are eager to share with the public the ways they use camera traps to benefit wildlife, information about specific research projects — and what they’ve learned about wildlife they're watching.

title: Third Annual STEAM Expo to Bring Hundreds of Students to USU Uintah Basin
summary: ROOSEVELT, Utah — Utah State University Uintah Basin will host the third annual STEAM Expo on Oct. 1-2. The event– which aims to foster excitement for math, science, and the arts– will bring students in grades 5th-8th from Duchesne and Uintah counties to campus for two days of exhibitions. “The annual USU Uintah Basin STEAM Expo is one of the great events that USU sponsors for the community,” said Don Busenbark, senior lecturer of mathematics and statistics at USU Uintah Basin and one of the leaders of the expo. “Students are able to learn about drones, dinosaurs, engineering, water, safety, fire, police, animals, robotics, mathematics, building, art, music, and more. The goal is always to connect students to a college campus, teach them, and help them see potential careers in STEAM fields.” The two-day event will bring together USU faculty, community partners, and business leaders to share fun-filled workshops, booths, interactive demonstrations, and campus tours with students. “What began as an exciting opportunity to inspire young learners has become one of the region's premier educational events, connecting students with hands-on experiences in science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics,” said David Law, associate vice president for USU Uintah Basin. Last year, more than 1,300 students participated in the STEAM Expo, as well as more than 30 different USU department and community organizations. “The Expo's reputation now extends well beyond the Uintah Basin, attracting exhibitors, educators, and industry partners from across Utah who are eager to share their expertise and inspire the next generation of innovators, problem-solvers, and community leaders,” Law said. “This growing statewide participation reflects the quality of the event and the important role it plays in preparing young people for tomorrow's opportunities. According to Busenbark, the students who participate regularly leave with an excitement that was not necessarily present when they first step in the doors. “It is amazing to hear students when they come and say "why do we have to come?" and "this looks boring" and then when they are ready to leave the same students say "that was so cool" and "do we have to leave?",” he said. “The STEAM Expo gives us an opportunity in the basin to have the same experiences as students in the larger cities in the state.” Organizers view this STEAM Expo as an important way of fulfilling and reinforcing USU’s land-grant mission. “The STEAM Expo represents Utah State University Uintah Basin at its very best,” Law said. “It is a powerful example of the university's land-grant mission in action—serving communities by expanding educational opportunities, fostering curiosity, and investing in the future of our region. While Utah State University proudly provides exceptional academic degrees, its commitment extends far beyond the classroom. Through initiatives like the STEAM Expo, the university creates meaningful experiences that enrich lives, strengthen communities, and elevate opportunities for all residents of the Uintah Basin.” The STEAM Expo will take place on USU’s Roosevelt campus. Both days will begin at 8:30 a.m. and conclude at 1 p.m. Operating campuses in Vernal and Roosevelt for more than 50 years, Utah State University Uintah Basin gives students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university, all in the backdrop of the outdoor oasis that is the Uinta Mountains and Ashley National Forest. With degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees and more than 125 programs available, as well as access to the renowned Bingham Research Center, USU Uintah Basin offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at uintahbasin.usu.edu .

title: Trading a Helmet for a Headset: USU's Chuckie Keeton on the Super Bowl Sidelines
summary: A former Utah State quarterback is headed to Super Bowl LX — he’ll just be donning a headset instead of a helmet. Currently an offensive assistant for the New England Patriots, Chuckie Keeton spent time at USU as both a player and coach and was instrumental to the USU football program’s turnaround in the 2010s. Prior to joining the Patriots this season, Keeton spent 2024 as an offensive assistant with the Patriots’ Super Bowl opponent — Seattle. While with the Seahawks, the Houston, Texas native primarily worked with then-Seattle QB Geno Smith who set single-season franchise records in passing yards, pass attempts, completions, and completion percentage. Since joining Mike Vrabel’s staff, Keeton has been part of one of the most surprising turnarounds in the NFL as New England went just 4-13 in 2024. This year’s Patriots team, which went 14-3 in the regular season, became the first team to reach the Super Bowl with a first-year head coach after winning four or fewer games the previous year. Keeton’s arrival also coincides with the emergence of second-year quarterback Drake Maye, who built off a solid rookie campaign to throw for 31 touchdowns, nearly 4,400 yards, and insert himself squarely in the MVP mix. An unheralded 2-star recruit out of Cypress Creek High School, Keeton burst into the national spotlight in 2011 as a true freshman when he nearly led the Aggies to an upset over defending national champion Auburn. The following year was even better as Keeton led USU to its first outright conference championship since 1936 and first Top 25 finish (No. 16 AP) since 1961. He set then single-season school records for touchdown passes (27), passing yards (3,373), total offensive yards (3,992), completions (275) and completion percentage (67.6%). In 2013, Keeton got off to a blistering start, throwing 17 touchdown passes through USU’s first five games (second in the nation) to just two interceptions and even generated some Heisman buzz. Unfortunately, a season-ending knee injury derailed that campaign. Keeton, who graduated from Utah State in 2015 with a degree in business administration, finished his playing career as the holder of more than 10 school records, including the top spot in total touchdowns with 74 and passing touchdowns with 62. In 2016 he jumped into the coaching ranks at Oregon State where he joined former USU head coach Gary Andersen as an offensive quality control assistant and offensive graduate assistant. Keeton returned to Utah State in 2018 for his first coaching stint with the Aggies as an offensive quality control coach for a team that finished with an 11-2 record and Top 25 ranking. After two seasons at Texas Tech, Keeton returned to USU once again in 2021, this time as the running backs coach. That season, USU’s offense set six school records, while the Aggies tied the program record with 11 victories, won the school's first-ever Mountain West Championship, and defeated Oregon State in the Jimmy Kimmel LA Bowl. Keeton spent one more season in the college ranks as an offensive analyst at Marshall before making the jump to the NFL, and and finding success with both Super Bowl teams. So, whether you’re cheering for the Patriots, Seahawks, or your team didn’t make the big game this year, you can still cheer for an Aggie on Sunday.

title: Two Debates Demonstrate Democracy in Action
summary: Utah State University will host two evenings of debate Oct. 12-13, bringing the top leaders of both parties in the Utah House of Representatives and candidates for Utah's 2nd Congressional District to its Logan campus. Across the Aisle: A Civil Debate With Utah House Leaders | Oct. 12 Utah House Majority Leader Casey Snider and House Minority Leader Angela Romero will debate Utah's challenges and opportunities at 6 p.m. Oct. 12 in the Eccles Conference Center. “We are not going to agree on every issue,” Snider said. “That is the point of debate. Civility means we can have those disagreements and still work together where we agree.” Romero added: "The best policies are made when people with different perspectives come together. We need those voices at the table to make sure all of Utah is represented. At the same time, working across differences does not require us to abandon the values that matter most. We can find common ground without losing sight of who we are or the communities we serve.” Snider, a USU alumnus who represents Cache County's District 5, and Romero, who represents Salt Lake City's District 25, will model civil debate and discuss how leaders in Utah work together to serve the state. Brian Steed, USU vice president for government and external affairs, will moderate. “Utahns hear a lot about what divides us. This is a chance to watch two leaders from different political parties, who are also good friends, disagree on real issues, make their case, listen to each other and still find ways to get work done for the state,” Steed said. “They show us that disagreement doesn’t have to come at the expense of friendship or respect. That’s a skill our students, and all of us, can learn from.” The event is free and open to the public. Anyone interested in attending must register online . Bags will not be permitted. 2nd Congressional District Debate | Oct. 13 The Utah Debate Commission's debate for candidates in Utah's 2nd Congressional District will begin at 6 p.m. Oct. 13 in the Morgan Theatre in the Chase Fine Arts Center. The debate is presented in partnership with PBS Utah and will stream live on the Utah Debate Commission YouTube channel and air on PBS Utah. The Utah Debate Commission is a nonpartisan consortium of higher education institutions, media organizations and elected officials that organizes debates among qualified candidates for statewide and federal offices in Utah. Registration is required to attend in person, and bags will not be permitted. For more information visit the Utah Debate Commission website.

title: Two USU Faculty Are Shaping the Future of Artificial Intelligence in Utah
summary: As artificial intelligence reshapes industry and society, two Utah State University professors are being recognized for leading decades of groundbreaking AI research. Heng-Da Cheng, a professor of computer science, and Kevin Moon, associate professor of math and statistics and director of USU’s Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Center (DSAI), were both selected to be featured in the AI Utah 100 2026 Yearbook. The award highlights AI experts leading meaningful work in product development, research, and infrastructure. For over 40 years, Cheng has researched AI and its applications and has produced more than 140 journal papers, 200 conference papers, and 15 books and book chapters. “I am honored and grateful,” Cheng said. “I can exchange ideas with people from different fields, explore the theory and practice aspects of AI, and I can further help the students.” As his work continues, his team is integrating classical AI and deep learning to improve system performance, develop new directions in AI, and apply it to various fields. Moon said the award honors the contributions he and his group have made in AI and his leadership at DSAI. “I'm grateful for the recognition this brings to the research I've been doing with USU students and the broader work in AI that's happening at USU through the DSAI Center,” Moon said. The pair were honored Thursday at an event in Sandy celebrating AI innovators, community partners, and supporters of Utah’s AI ecosystem.

title: Unpacking Ultra-Processed: What USU Experts Have Learned About Food on U.S. Plates
summary: Ultra-processed foods now make up an estimated 73% of the U.S. food supply . This includes the hotdogs, ice cream and fries from our freezers and fast-food restaurants — as well as the strawberry-flavored yogurt you had for breakfast, the ham-on-whole-wheat you ate at lunch, and the pasta ragú for dinner. Ultra-processed foods are ubiquitous, inexpensive, convenient, and inevitably good-tasting. They are formulated to be shelf-stable and widely appealing with refined ingredients, flavors, colors, emulsifiers, and other additives that aren't used in home kitchens — plus extra sugar and fat. The average adult in the U.S. now gets 53% of their daily calories from ultra-processed foods , while children and teens consume even more. Recent research from Oluyemisi Akinsola, working with Abiodun Atoloye in the Department of Nutrition, Dietetics and Food Science at Utah State University, found that ultra-processed foods make up a staggering 68% of teens' total daily calorie intake. Akinsola is working to determine the connection between snacking habits and ultra-processed food intake for teens. The relative health and safety of ultra-processed foods have been the subject of fierce national debate. It’s not necessarily an easy topic to digest, according to Lacie Peterson, clinical professor at USU and a registered dietician — partly because many of the food processes and additives are so new that research hasn’t yet fully determined their impact on human health. The consequences for such a shift away from traditional eating are only just emerging, Peterson said, and food experts at USU are working to understand how ultra-processed foods impact everything from food choices to long-term chronic disease, and they’re are finding ways to push the food system to a healthier standard. Are Ultra-Processed Foods Really That Bad for You? “It’s a fair question,” Peterson said. “Since these kinds of products are literally everywhere, it’s easy to wonder how bad they might actually be. The answer is — they aren’t ‘poison,’ but they really aren’t at all good for your health in any quantity.” Many consequences for consuming UPFs occur in the long term, she said. People eating diets high in processed foods put on weight, miss out on key nutrients, have elevated cholesterol levels, and have increased chances of long-term heart disease and diabetes — but not necessarily immediately. You can’t necessarily point the finger at any one ingredient, she said. It’s a combination of the stress to your body from eating a cocktail of industrial products and missing out on the foods and nutrients you would otherwise be eating. There are a few other factors that make ultra-processed foods especially problematic, according to USU food and nutrition experts. Hyperpalatability . UPFs taste too good. They are packed with ingredients like hydrogenated oils, high-fructose corn syrup, artificial flavors, and chemical emulsifiers that may be “safe” to eat but trick the brain’s reward system so that it’s hard to stop when you are full (think of movie theater popcorn). Bite-for-bite, there are typically also more calories in ultra-processed foods than in whole or minimally processed ingredients (things like frozen fruits, pre-chopped vegetables, or rolled oats), said Stephan Van Vliet, director for the Center for Human Nutrition Studies at USU. People consume 500 more calories per day when eating UPFs than eating whole foods, research from the National Institutes of Health shows. When Van Vliet and his team compared ultra-processed and minimally-processed diets, those eating ultra-processed foods were unhealthier — even when the total calorie count was the same. This suggests that the health issues related to diets rich in ultra-processed foods are not due to the calories alone. Foods That are Pre-Digested. Processing breaks down the physical and chemical structure of natural foods so they become soft and stripped of fiber. When it’s so easy to chew and swallow, your gut doesn't have time to signal to the brain that you’ve had enough, Peterson said. Ultra-processed foods are typically high in saturated fat, sodium, and sugar, and low in water and fiber. You can consume a huge number of calories in a few bites without ever stretching your stomach enough to feel full, she said. Missing Nutrition. Whole and minimally-processed foods like vegetables, fruits, grains, meat, milk, and eggs are a carnival of nutrients that bodies need, Van Vliet said. Even when UPFs are artificially fortified, they can’t mimic the broad array of natural phytonutrients, minerals and antioxidants found in whole foods. Processing adds back in a few things that people like to see on the label — protein and vitamin C for example — but does not give people the other thousands of compounds in foods, he said. Recent research from Van Vliet evaluated official systems for food rating and found that they tend to oversimplify what is labeled “healthy” and potentially underestimate the metabolic risks of highly processed foods. So What Should We Eat? The question is not simply how to stop people from eating ultra-processed foods, according to Atoloye, whose research focuses on food insecurity and community food systems. It’s how to make healthy foods easier to choose, more affordable, more appealing, and a normal part of everyday life. “We need to look beyond individual choices and improve the food environments where children, adolescents, and adults make food decisions. This includes at schools, in retail food environments, on social media, and in advertising,” she said. “It’s easy enough to say to just eat more whole and minimally processed foods,” Peterson said. “But there are complex questions attached to that advice — who has access to good foods? Can everyone afford them? Do we know how to prepare them and store them? Can we retrain our palates to appreciate the taste of natural foods?” One answer, Van Vliet thinks, is to source whole foods with better taste. “People choose UPFs because they are engineered for flavor and palatability,” he said. “Some produce doesn’t have a lot of flavor when it’s grown strictly for high yield — it tastes bland.” Van Vliet is researching the way regenerative farming practices can be used to produce foods with better flavor. (Think of a home-grown tomato versus one from the grocery store in winter). Without high levels of pesticides and synthetic fertilizers, plants get a little more stressed out but in a good way, he said, and produce more complex defense compounds that can translate to richer flavors and higher antioxidant levels. Another area that needs more attention is food education, Atoloye said. “Young people need opportunities to build the knowledge and skills that help them make healthy food choices on their own,” she said. While some health effects of ultra-processed foods are well-established, other areas require ongoing research, according to Van Vliet. Future studies could focus on the cocktail effects of food additives on human health — the complex mixtures of synthetic additives we are exposed to interact within the body in ways we still need to understand, he said. Researchers are also working to establish exactly how strongly these cumulative exposures are linked to long-term diseases. For more information about UPFs and balanced eating, visit USU’s Create Better Health website, or resources here and here .

title: USU Bastian Agricultural Center Opens New Youth Livestock Barn
summary: Utah State University Extension recently celebrated the opening of the Youth Livestock Barn at the Bastian Agricultural Center in South Jordan. It expands opportunities for young people to experience agriculture, develop life skills, and serve their communities. Josh Dallin, the center's executive director, said the project began in 2022 when three young people approached the center because local animal ordinances prevented them from raising livestock in their backyards. The center initially accommodated the three youth and six animals in abandoned horse stalls, but by 2026, the program had grown to serve nearly 80 youth. As participation continued to grow, the program quickly outgrew the limited space available in the center’s existing horse stalls. Temporary pens and other available areas were used to accommodate additional animals, but it became clear that a permanent facility was needed to safely support the growing number of youth and livestock. The new Youth Livestock Barn was created specifically to meet that need, providing dedicated space where 4-H and FFA members can raise and care for project animals while receiving hands-on agricultural education and mentorship. "This barn was built for you," Dallin told the participating youth in the audience. "We're not just cutting a ribbon on another building. We're opening a place where young people are going to learn how to work." A central component of the program is its partnership with the Bastian Family Foundation, which purchases the animals raised by participating youth, pays for processing, and donates the resulting meat to help feed families throughout Salt Lake County. The arrangement allows participants to earn money while learning responsibility, animal husbandry, and community service. "These kids aren't just raising an animal for a ribbon," Dallin said. "They're raising an animal that will eventually help feed a family." USU Extension Vice President Justen Smith emphasized the importance of 4-H programs in helping young people develop confidence, responsibility, and a sense of belonging. Smith said the program also provides agricultural education for urban families who may have limited connections to farming and ranching. He expressed hope that similar opportunities could eventually expand throughout the Wasatch Front. USU President Brad Mortenson highlighted the project as an example of the university's land-grant mission to serve communities through education and outreach. Mortenson, who grew up on a small farm, said raising animals teaches more than a strong work ethic. It also develops an ethic of care and responsibility that benefits young people throughout their lives. Jake Anderson, representing the Bastian Family Foundation, described the facility as an extension of the Foundation's commitment to preserving agriculture and creating meaningful educational experiences. He emphasized that raising livestock teaches young people valuable lessons about patience, perseverance, and responsibility. “Animals don’t take a day off from needing to be fed and cared for,” he said. Also highlighted was the center’s partnership with the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food through a pollinator program. Hundreds of donated plants are ready to be planted in the coming weeks. “This is the cleanest this barn is ever going to be,” Anderson said, joking. “So, enjoy it now. Come back in a year. It's going to be even better, even though it's going to be full of manure.” To learn more about the center, visit the Bastian Agricultural Center website .

title: USU, Brigham City, and Hi Tech Solutions Partner to Establish New Nuclear Energy Tech and R&D Campus
summary: Editor's note: Brigham City is awaiting official approval from city council before signing this MOU. LOGAN — Utah State University, Brigham City Corporation, and Hi Tech Solutions, LLC, have officially agreed to a memorandum of understanding to evaluate, plan, and advance a collaborative Technical Training, Certification, and Research & Development Campus. The proposed campus will serve as a premier regional hub dedicated to world-class education, workforce training, and innovation in the advanced nuclear energy, national defense, and nuclear technology sectors. By aligning academic rigor with industry demand, the initiative aims to boost the local economy, strengthen national energy resilience, and secure high-quality career pathways for students and skilled tradespeople. "This partnership reflects Utah State’s land-grant mission and our responsibility to help meet the evolving needs of our state,” said USU President Brad Mortensen. “Working alongside Brigham City and Hi Tech Solutions, we have an opportunity to explore new approaches to technical training and research that prepare students for high-demand careers, support economic growth, and strengthen Utah’s leadership in energy and national defense." A Regional Hub for Innovation and Economic Growth The nuclear energy and defense supply chains are rapidly expanding, driving an urgent regional and national demand for specialized talent. The envisioned campus will address this gap by offering a centralized environment for: Professional certification and technical trades: Equipping workers with advanced skills tailored to nuclear operations, quality assurance, and advanced manufacturing. Applied research and testing: Providing industry-sponsored simulation laboratories, equipment testing, and validation opportunities. Public-private synergy: Utilizing underutilized university-owned property through a strategic public-private partnership structure to foster long-term infrastructure sustainability. Dedicated Pathways for Military Veterans A core pillar of the newly signed agreement is a dedicated focus on support for military veterans and transitioning service members. The campus will actively design credentialing, apprenticeship, and workforce transition programs that leverage veterans' technical military experience. This targeted pathway will rapidly prepare them for high-stakes careers in nuclear engineering support, plant operations, maintenance, and safety critical to national security. Shared Roles and Next Steps Under the framework of the MOU, the three entities will divide operational and planning responsibilities to ensure the project's long-term viability. USU will provide academic leadership, curriculum development, faculty expertise, research capabilities, and administration of credentialing and degree programs, while also providing a long-term ground lease of the designated property. Brigham City Corporation will support site master planning, infrastructure coordination, regional economic development initiatives, and local permitting processes. Hi Tech Solutions will serve as the master developer responsible for financing, developing, and coordinating sub-development, alongside providing industry expertise, equipment, technology resources, and internship or employment pathways. Utah State University is Utah’s land-grant and space-grant university with a mission of learning, discovery, and engagement. With 30 education locations and 38 Extension sites throughout the state, USU provides access to higher education for Utahns wherever they live, research and expertise on critical issues affecting the state, and outreach to improve Utah communities and families in all 29 counties. As a Carnegie R1 research institution, USU is home to over 50 world-class research facilities and boasts the second-oldest undergraduate research program in the nation.

title: USU Brigham City to Host Restored Art Exhibition from Intermountain Indian School
summary: BRIGHAM CITY, Utah — A collection of artwork created by students of the former Intermountain Indian School will return to Brigham City during a ribbon cutting event celebrating the history, art, and stories connected to the school. “Coming Home to Remember the Past” will take place Sept. 11 at the Utah State University Brigham City campus. All community members are invited to attend, with a special invitation to all Intermountain Indian School alumni. The artwork, which was salvaged and restored after years of preparation, fundraising and patience, was originally re-displayed at the Nora Eccles Harrison Museum of Art in Logan from Jan. 25, 2025, through Jan. 17, 2026. The murals will now return to the site where they were created. “We always planned to exhibit the restored murals where they were created to be enjoyed by the Intermountain alumni and community,” said Katie Lee-Koven, executive director and chief curator for NEHMA. “The former Intermountain Intertribal Indian School was located where the USU Brigham City campus is now. Alumni from Intermountain travel from all over to meet annually at the campus for their reunion.” The exhibition will begin at 5:30 p.m. with a lecture, “Creating, Saving, & Preserving Art,” describing the Intermountain art experience, the art salvage efforts, and its restoration. Following the lecture, Dan Black, associate vice president of the Brigham City Region, will invite members of the Intermountain alumni reunion planning committee to participate in a ribbon cutting to officially open the “Coming Home” exhibit. The exhibit includes six pieces of artwork, including large Intermountain murals, Sheila Nadimi photographs and individual student artwork that tells the story of Intermountain. Students in art classes at Intermountain were encouraged by their teachers, including nationally renowned Chiricahua Apache artist Allan Houser, to create artwork depicting their native homes and cultures. Some students created large murals directly on the walls of the school. When buildings associated with the school were demolished, individuals worked to preserve some of the murals, carefully removing them from the walls. Koven led efforts to determine whether the artwork could be restored, identify restoration experts, and secure funding from donors. Expert Scott Haskins and his lab restored the murals. “It’s amazing to have the art come to the USU Brigham City campus,” Black said. “These were created in Brigham City, and we are happy to be able to showcase the art here. We hope that the alumni and descendants of the Intermountain School will find the opportunity to come and embrace the past by experiencing the restored art.” Following the exhibit opening, guests can tour the exhibit at 7 p.m., explore art and craft activities in a restored historic building, and gather for a campfire and storytelling at 8 p.m. USU also saved one of the buildings to preserve the history of both Bushnell Hospital and the Intermountain Indian School. The building remodel is now complete and is ready to become part of a traditional skills preservation program. Returning the artwork to the campus where it was originally created provides a symbolic homecoming for the pieces and a connection to the history of Intermountain Indian School. Schedule of Events (USU Brigham City - 989 South Main Street) 5:30 p.m.: Lecture— Creating, Saving, & Preserving Art 6:30 p.m.: Ribbon Cutting & Opening of Exhibit 7:00 p.m.: Exhibit Tour and Exploring Art & Craft Activities in the Historic Building 8:00 p.m.: Campfire & Story Telling at the Historic Building With two locations in Box Elder County, Utah State University Brigham City and Tremonton offer students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university. With more than 100 degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees, plus technical education offerings, USU offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at brighamcity.usu.edu .

title: USU Celebrates Independence Day With Flag on the Quad
summary: LOGAN – The American flag is back on the Quad at Utah State University's Logan campus, as part of the annual celebration of Independence Day. Crew members from the university's Landscape Operations and Maintenance department cut the grass on the Quad to showcase the flag early Tuesday morning. The grass on the Quad is watered using canal-fed irrigation water periodically throughout the day to keep the highly used area healthy and green. USU follows a Landscape Resiliency and Drought Plan which makes protecting State Champion Trees, mature trees, athletic fields, the Quad and other heavily used campus areas a priority. The Quad is not only a heavily used campus area, but a landmark for USU's main campus. This year's flag on the Quad is just a small part of the university's celebration of the country's 250th anniversary. To kick off the celebration, the American Festival Chorus & Orchestra is performing at 7:30 p.m. July 1 at the Logan Tabernacle. This event is free and open to all — no ticket required. More information on USU's water conservation plan is available online .

title: USU Cuts Ribbon on Thomas and Patricia Willis Veterinary Medical Education Building
summary: Utah State University and the College of Veterinary Medicine celebrated the grand opening Friday of the Thomas and Patricia Willis Veterinary Medical Education building. “If you are involved in animal agriculture in any way, today is your day,” said John Ferry, one of a cast of speakers at the event and a key figure in the creation of the veterinary college as a former USU Board of Trustees vice chair. The festivities included a ribbon cutting and the debut of a limited-edition Aggie Ice Cream flavor: Neigh-apolitan. The event marked the culmination of years of planning and preparation in service of expanding the field of veterinary care throughout all corners of Utah and the Intermountain West. Manning the pair of giant scissors, Thomas and Patricia Willis, donors for whom the building is named, cut the ribbon. It fell away on the first snip. The Willises donated $5 million toward the facility and an endowment to support the college on the path ahead. The pair have deep roots in agricultural life and aim to see veterinary medical education thrive at Utah State. “We saw this as an opportunity to invest in future generations,” Tom said. The three-story, 113,000 square-foot building took two years and three months to complete. It was designed by Salt Lake City-based VCBO Architects and built by Jacobsen Construction. Thirty of the 41 subcontractors involved in the project are headquartered in Utah. Guests at the ceremony toured the building, which features a tiered lecture hall, research labs, wet labs, cold rooms, veterinary exam rooms, classrooms, sub-zero freezers, faculty and staff offices, student gathering spaces and outdoor animal enrichment areas. Hidden from view, a complex labyrinth of sophisticated mechanical, electrical and water systems support the capabilities typical of a state-of-the-art animal hospital. Dirk Vanderwall, the dean of the veterinary college, said facilities like this didn’t exist when he was in vet school. The design, he said, was intentional and tailored with veterinary students top of mind. “For example, the new building includes a suite of 10 mock exam rooms, each with an adjacent observation area, so that students can interact with an actor playing a client as part of clinical communication training,” Vanderwall said. USU President Brad Mortensen expressed thanks for the collaborators statewide who came together to make the plans a reality. “We are especially grateful to the Utah Legislature and key partners for their commitment to our land-grant mission and for recognizing and investing in our vision to establish Utah’s only veterinary school in a state facing a critical shortage of veterinarians,” he said. A week prior to the ribbon-cutting, the college welcomed 77 new students as the Class of 2030 donned white coats symbolizing their transition into the veterinary profession and the responsibilities therein. In four years, when they graduate as day-one-ready doctors of veterinary medicine, they will be armed with the clinical skills, practical knowledge, communication tools and personal resilience necessary to contribute to the communities they serve. Other speakers at the ribbon cutting ceremony included Kelby Anderson, the veterinary college’s president of the Class of 2029; Utah State Rep. Casey Snider, Utah State Sen. Chris Wilson, former state senator Scott Sandall, Geoffrey Landward of the Utah Commission of Higher Education, and Michael Bowen of USU’s Advancement office. Another addition to the veterinary medical building made its public debut Friday: A bronze sculpture featuring a seated veterinarian with a foal at her side, a dog at her feet and a cat looking on from a neighboring bench. Titled “A Long Tale,” it takes its name and inspiration from James Herriot’s 1972 book All Creatures Great and Small , which describes the life of a veterinarian as “a long tale of little triumphs and disasters.” “A Long Tale” was commissioned by a committee of USU representatives, architects, state project managers and local visual arts specialists, through the Percent-For-Art Act, which uses 1 percent of legislative appropriations for capital development projects to commission, install, and maintain public art across the state of Utah.

title: USU Eastern Applauds Major Investment in Helper City Ballfields
summary: Helper, Utah — Utah State University Eastern is celebrating a $1.16 million investment in the Gardner and Heritage fields. The City of Helper has secured a $580,000 grant through the Land and Water Conservation Fund, paired with a matching contribution from the Houston family for the project, which will transform the historic ballfields into a modern collegiate-level sports complex while preserving the deep baseball heritage that has long been part of Helper’s identity. For USU Eastern Athletics, the investment represents more than facility upgrades; it strengthens a long-standing partnership between the university and the community. Jess Brinkerhoff, athletic director for USU Eastern, said the project reflects the power of community vision and collaboration. “First and foremost, this is a huge credit to Helper City, Mayor Lenise Peterman, and the Houston family,” Brinkerhoff said. “Their vision and generosity are what made this possible. We’re incredibly grateful that USU Eastern is able to continue using Gardner and Heritage Fields and be part of something that means so much to this community.” Brinkerhoff noted that the improvements will help USU Eastern baseball continue building its program in a location that holds significant historical value. “For our baseball program, this investment allows us to keep building in a place with deep history,” he said. “We’ve invested a great deal over the last two seasons to help maintain and improve the fields, and we look forward to continuing to care for them and use them the right way for many years to come.” The upgraded facilities will enhance the experience not only for collegiate athletes but also for local youth and families who use the fields. “These upgrades benefit not just our student-athletes, but everyone in the community who uses these fields,” Brinkerhoff said. “Our players get to train and compete in a better environment, but just as importantly, youth programs and local families benefit as well.” He added that improved facilities can play an important role in recruiting future student-athletes. “In recruiting, it helps when prospects see a community that takes pride in its facilities,” Brinkerhoff said. “Newer and improved facilities allow players to feel more valued and have a better experience. But we always want it to be clear — this is about Helper investing in Helper. We’re just grateful to be part of it as members of the community.” Helper Mayor Lenise Peterman said the investment is part of a larger vision to strengthen recreation and economic development while honoring the community’s historic connection to baseball. “This funding will allow us to upgrade playing fields and create a state-of-the-art collegiate sports complex,” Peterman said. “We believe these upgrades will serve as yet another recreational draw to the area, activating economic streams via new guests and visitors. It also plays into our rich baseball heritage, which is something we want to honor and respect as we move into a new phase of activating these fields.” Community enthusiasm for the project has already been evident. “Anytime you can upgrade an existing asset, it’s a notch of community pride,” Peterman said. “People are excited about baseball and softball returning in full force. They contributed en masse when we cleaned and painted bleachers, and the feedback about the upgrades has been amazing. The citizens are all-in.” The success of the project reflects a strong partnership between the City of Helper, community supporters and the state. Peterman explained that the Houston family played a critical role by providing the matching funds needed to secure the federal grant. “We approached the Houston family to request a cash donation as the matching funds for the Land and Water Conservation Fund opportunity,” Peterman said. “John Houston graciously agreed to match up to $580,000 so we could possibly double that.” She also credited the Utah Division of Outdoor Recreation for helping guide the application process and USU Eastern coaches for assisting in identifying the most impactful improvements. “Both Coach Haney and Groves were integral in determining the most necessary field upgrades,” Peterman said. “They did the legwork collecting estimates and evaluating potential vendors for the project.” Major Upgrades Planned for Both Fields The funding will bring significant improvements to both Gardner Field and Heritage Field. At Heritage Field, upgrades will include: A new press box. Restroom facilities. Expanded dugouts. Turf outfield for water conservation and reduced maintenance. Wind screens. ADA-accessible gravel areas. Batting cages. At Gardner Field, improvements will include: Restroom upgrades. Expanded dugouts. Turf infield. Relocated fencing inside existing light poles. Fence slats replacing wind screens. Batting cages. Peterman said the larger outfield space at Gardner Field may also allow for the addition of two future T-ball fields to support youth programs. Brinkerhoff said the upgraded facilities will create new opportunities for tournaments, camps and regional events that bring visitors into the community. “Improved facilities create opportunities for more games, camps and tournaments, which ultimately benefits the entire community,” Brinkerhoff said. “More visitors, more families in town, more business and pride in Helper and for Utah State Eastern baseball and softball.” Mayor Peterman echoed that sentiment, noting that visiting teams often bring dozens of families who stay overnight and spend locally. “Visiting teams bring an average of 40 or more people who spend the night, eat locally and hopefully shop on our historic Main Street,” she said. For USU Eastern, the partnership with Helper represents a shared commitment to preserving the legacy of these historic fields while investing in the future. “Community partnerships are everything for a place like USU Eastern,” Brinkerhoff said. “We don’t exist in isolation, we’re part of Helper, Price and the communities of Carbon and Emery counties.” He added that the university remains committed to honoring the fields’ history and ensuring they continue serving the community for generations. “Our role is simple,” Brinkerhoff said. “We want to be good stewards. We want to continue investing time, effort and resources into maintaining and improving the fields while respecting the history of everyone who has played there before us — and those who will play there in the future.”

title: USU Eastern Athletic Camps Welcome More Than 1,600 Participants to Campus
summary: USU Eastern welcomed more than 1,600 athletes to campus this summer through a series of team and individual athletic camps, letting participants improve their skills while experiencing life as an Eagle. Throughout the summer, the university hosted high school team camps in women’s basketball, women’s soccer, men’s soccer, men’s and women’s volleyball, football and cross country, along with individual camps in cheer, women’s basketball, baseball and volleyball. In total, approximately 1,400 athletes representing 50 different teams participated in team camps, while more than 200 additional athletes attended individual skills camps. Beyond competition and instruction, the camps gave visiting athletes an opportunity to experience the USU Eastern campus, interact with coaching staff and explore the Price community. “The impact summer camps have on our athletic department is vast,” said Morgan Warburton-Nelson, USU Eastern athletic camps director and assistant women’s basketball coach. “Not only do they help support our teams on and off the floor, but they allow for us to have a front row seat to recruiting future student-athletes. The participants are given an inside look on what it means to be a USU Eastern Eagle through our coaching staff, campus and community.” Warburton-Nelson said the success of the camps extends well beyond athletics and reflects the collaborative effort of the entire campus. “What stands out the most is the hospitality and culture,” she said. “Every campus department involved goes above and beyond to ensure the experience is one to remember. The goal is for each participant to take a little bit of Eastern with them and potentially return to our campus as future students and/or athletes.” Each camp let athletes develop their skills, compete against quality competition and build relationships with USU Eastern coaches and current student-athletes. At the same time, the events brought hundreds of visitors to campus, highlighting the college’s facilities and strengthening connections with schools and communities throughout the region. By combining athletic development with a welcoming campus experience, USU Eastern’s summer camps continue to serve as an important part of the college’s recruiting efforts while creating lasting memories for the next generation of Eagles. As the fall semester approaches, USU Eastern Athletics is gearing up for another year of competition. Fans can find team schedules, rosters, news, ticket information and updates throughout the season by visiting USUEasternAthletics.com .

title: USU Eastern Prehistoric Museum Celebrates 4th Annual Don Burge Day
summary: PRICE, Utah — The community gathered at the USU Eastern Prehistoric Museum on June 26 to celebrate the life and legacy of Don Burge during the museum's fourth annual Don Burge Day. Observed on Burge's birthday, the celebration honors the man whose vision and leadership helped shape one of Eastern Utah's most treasured cultural institutions. Burge played a pivotal role in founding the museum in 1961 and served as its director for more than 40 years, leaving an impact that continues to inspire generations of visitors, students, researchers and museum staff. Visitors enjoyed free admission throughout the day, exploring the museum's exhibits while learning more about Burge's remarkable contributions. The first 100 guests also received a limited-edition Utah mammoth commemorative pin created especially for this year's celebration. Throughout the day guests visited the Don L. Burge Room in the Hall of Archaeology, where memorabilia from Burge's life and career remain on display. Many also stopped to see Gastonia burgei, the armored dinosaur species named in honor of Don Burge and Rob Gaston. The dinosaur displayed in the Hall of Paleontology recently gained national attention after being featured in the PBS series Walking with Dinosaurs during the episode "Band of Brothers." One of the afternoon's highlights was the annual folk music jam from 2-4 p.m. Local musicians filled the Hall of Archaeology with the sounds of acoustic instruments honoring Burge's lifelong love of folk music and his favorite instrument, the banjo. Whether performing or simply listening, attendees shared an afternoon that reflected the warmth, curiosity and sense of community that Burge fostered throughout his life. New to this year's celebration was a Museum Members Cookout celebrating Burge's enduring influence while strengthening the museum community he helped build.

title: USU Eastern Receives $25,000 Donation to Establish Health Scholarship Endowment
summary: PRICE, Utah — Utah State University Eastern has announced a $25,000 donation from Daniel and Jane Madsen to create a new scholarship endowment. The donation will establish the Spencer-Madsen Health Scholarship that will exist in perpetuity, impacting generations of students. This fund will support students in pre-med, pre-dental and the registered nurse program. The scholarship prioritizes high-achieving students and is intended to help cover tuition and fees, reducing financial barriers for those entering critical health care fields. “This endowment represents more than a single scholarship,” said Bayley Hedglin, associate director of development at USU. “It signals long-term confidence in the future of health care education at USU Eastern. As a permanent funding source, it creates stability for the nursing pipeline and helps the program continue attracting strong, committed students.” The Spencer Madsen Health Scholarship is named for Orson and Olga Spencer and Daniel and Jane Spencer Madsen. Both Orson and Daniel were physicians who graduated from Utah State University Eastern (then the College of Eastern Utah) prior to attending medical school. Both practiced medicine in Price. “This endowment was inspired by a multi-generational legacy of physicians who served the Price and Carbon/Emery communities and were deeply connected to USU Eastern,” Hedglin said. “Their commitment to both health care and education reflects a long-standing belief in building local talent to serve local needs. At a time when rural communities are facing growing health care workforce shortages, this investment comes at a critical moment to strengthen the pipeline of future providers.” Orson Spencer started his medical practice in Price in 1949 before retiring in 1983. Orson and Olga Spencer were ardent supporters of the College of Eastern Utah, with Orson having served on the college’s Board of Regents. Daniel Madsen attended CEU in the 1960s and later practiced as an internist in Price from 1977 to 1990. His father also practiced medicine in Price from 1944-1966 and dedicated his life to serving the medical needs of patients in the Carbon/Emery area. This scholarship is intended to help those who attend USU Eastern in the pursuit of careers in medicine or nursing. It is also a tribute to dedicated educators at USU Eastern for enriching the lives of many students. It is intended to invest in students from rural communities who are historically more likely to stay and serve those same communities. This investment will help address provider shortages, improve access to health care and support long-term community health outcomes in the Carbon and Emery regions. To be eligible for the scholarship, applicants must be enrolled at USU Eastern as either an undergraduate or graduate student, be enrolled at least as a three-quarters-time student, and have a 3.5 GPA or higher. A preference will be given to students who are enrolled full-time. Eligible students must be enrolled as a pre-med, pre-dental or registered nurse student. To learn more about the Spencer-Madsen Health Scholarship requirements and for help applying, visit eastern.usu.edu/advising or call (435) 613-5034 to schedule an appointment with the appropriate academic adviser. Located in picturesque Price, Utah State University Eastern provides the best of both worlds for students­ — the personalized attention and small student-to-faculty ratio of a small-town college, with the educational opportunities and resources of a large university. USU Eastern boasts student government opportunities, clubs and programs like theater, choir and the award-winning student newspaper “The Eagle,” as well as its own athletic program. USU Eastern provides personal or professional development training, technical education in health professions, technical careers and business, as well as associate, bachelor’s, master’s and doctorate degrees and certificates of proficiency. Learn more at eastern.usu.edu .

title: USU Elementary Education Program Earns A+ in Science of Reading Instruction
summary: USU’s elementary education program has received a national A+ ranking for teacher preparation using the core tenets of the science of reading. The National Council on Teacher Quality gave the A+ ranking to USU's School of Teacher Education and Leadership (TEAL), which is part of the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences, after comparing nearly 700 teacher preparation programs across the nation to targets set by literacy experts. “ The science of reading is the foundation of our students’ literacy coursework, which prepares them to become effective reading teachers in the early childhood and elementary grades ,” said Steven Camicia, department head of TEAL. “ This grade from the NCTQ reflects our commitment to providing evidence-based methods that students put into practice during their practicum experiences and student teaching, which in turn equips them to create highly impactful learning environments in Utah schools .” The science of reading uses evidence-based literacy practices, particularly in elementary settings, that are based on more than a half-century of research. It includes five core components of effective reading instruction: phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension. Instruction focusing on these areas has been shown to vastly increase the success of students who are learning to read. Future teachers who are educated in the science of reading learn how to recognize and analyze trends in their own classrooms so they can apply evidence-based interventions to help their students excel. Because the science of reading is focused on individual student needs, it leads to improved outcomes for students who may not respond well to less effective teaching methods. A comprehensive bill passed by the Utah legislature in 2022 incorporated the science of reading into Utah’s education curriculum. The legislation requires state-funded universities to hire a dedicated science of reading professional to help train future educators. Jake Downs, an assistant professor in TEAL, is USU’s designated science of reading professor. Downs designs coursework to help students see what science of reading instruction looks like in real classrooms by incorporating state-approved science of reading curricula so students can analyze how lessons are structured and how well they align with research. To complement their classroom instruction, the program also includes valuable practicum experiences in which pre-service teachers can practice their skills with real students and under supervision as they implement science of reading instruction. “It’s hard to learn in a vacuum,” Downs said. “When students can see firsthand how classrooms work to employ the science of reading, it’s a big deal for them.” USU students receive more than 250 hours in practicum experiences before they begin full-time student teaching prior to graduation. “We’re helping support our undergraduates and preparing them to become effective reading instructors right out of the gate,” Downs said. “I feel our students are very, very well prepared for classroom instruction.” Just prior to graduation each year, elementary education majors take an intensive written exam on science of reading skills and knowledge that is required for teacher licensure in Utah. In the 2024-25 academic year, USU students achieved an 88 percent pass rate on the Utah Foundations of Reading Assessment.

title: USU Expert Examines Growing Evidence for Climate Benefits of Lawns
summary: In your backyard is a giant, underground carbon vault — a dense tangle of roots pulling carbon out of the atmosphere to store it deep underground. It’s your lawn. There is growing research evidence that turfgrass plays an important ecological role in urban environments, according to Kelly Kopp from Utah State University’s Department of Plants, Soils, and Climate. As communities look for ways to conserve limited water supplies, some homeowners are choosing to replace lawns with gravel, xeriscaping, or artificial turf, in some cases prompted by city incentives. But research suggests that there are environmental tradeoffs for removing turfgrass, because lawns offer underappreciated benefits for cooling, water infiltration, and even carbon storage, Kopp said. Kopp and collaborator Alec Kowalewski from Oregon State University compiled and presented findings from peer-reviewed research that show when it comes to turf removal, the greener choice isn't always so clear-cut. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere traps heat from the sun and changes climate patterns. Plants and trees offer a partial remedy to that, pulling carbon out of the atmosphere through photosynthesis and storing it in their roots, stems, leaves, and surrounding soils — in a process called carbon sequestration. Some of that carbon will eventually cycle back into the atmosphere as materials break down, but some remains trapped, especially when it is underground. Systems that store more total carbon than they release over time are called “carbon sinks.” “Well-managed turfgrass systems are pretty effective as carbon sinks,” Kopp said. “They can collect and hold organic carbon in the soil over the span of decades.” It had been thought that intensively managed turfgrass soils were inherently neutral or even producers of carbon, but research is increasingly challenging that assumption, she said. Turfgrass systems move carbon into the soil three ways: as fine roots die and are replaced, as living roots leak carbon-rich fluids into the soil, and as soil microbes consume those fluids and convert them into stable organic matter. Once incorporated into soil, carbon can remain stored for years or decades, accumulating for up to 50 years before a lawn reaches a state of carbon equilibrium, according to the research. If lawns are eliminated, not only do they stop collecting carbon, but the carbon already stored in the soil begins to break down and returns to the atmosphere. “There is an unfortunate perception that lawns are an environmental villain," Kopp said, “But if you look at the evidence, the tradeoffs are more complicated than that.” There are additional ways lawns benefit urban environments, Kopp said. They act like giant swamp coolers, helping to moderate urban air temperatures locally. The dense, fibrous root networks also increase the ground's capacity to absorb rainfall and anchor the soil, which reduces runoff and protects against erosion. But even if turfgrass isn't the nemesis it's made out to be, it isn't by default an environmental hero, Kopp said. Potential ecological benefits of lawns could be offset by how they are managed, losing the carbon-equation advantage with emissions from lawn care equipment, improper fertilization, and overirrigation. There are ways to find balance . You can increase underground carbon storage in lawns by leaving grass clippings on the ground to enrich the soil, raising the height on mowers to encourage deeper rooting, and switching to electric mowers, Kopp said. Using organic or controlled-release fertilizers reduces nutrient loss and the carbon cost of fertilizer production. Installing smart irrigation systems that measure soil moisture levels helps to keep soil carbon high while reducing unnecessary water use, she said. “The goal shouldn’t be to eliminate lawns simply because they use water. It should be to use science to plant and maintain turfgrass in the right places — and manage it so that every gallon of water delivers as much environmental benefit as possible,” Kopp said.

title: USU Extension Launches New Course to Help Young Workers Build Durable Skills
summary: Communication, teamwork, and problem-solving are becoming some of the most valuable skills a young worker can bring to the job. The USU Extension Center for Rural Economic Development & Emerging Technologies (CREDET) recently launched Durable Skills for Workplace Excellence , a new online course that helps teenagers and young adults build the people skills employers look for most. Created by USU Extension professors Paul Hill and Jared Hawkins, Durable Skills for Workplace Excellence is self-paced, takes about two hours to complete, and costs $25. The course includes five modules covering professionalism, communication, emotional intelligence, teamwork, and productivity, with exercises learners can apply immediately in their jobs. Participants earn a certificate of completion. "Durable skills hold their value in any job, in any industry, through every wave of new technology," Hawkins said. "When young people learn to communicate clearly, manage their time, and contribute to a team, supervisors notice quickly. Every module includes exercises they can apply on their very next shift." The course directly addresses the needs identified in the study “A Discrepancy Evaluation of Workforce Capacity and Emerging Skills: A Utah Case Study,” published in Administrative Sciences. In that study, employers identified communication, teamwork, and analytical problem-solving as the most critical skills for the next 5 to 10 years, and over half (58%) said demonstrated skills matter more than degrees in hiring decisions. The need is especially pressing for young people. Only 53% of Utah teens worked at any point during 2024, down from 67% in 1990. "Fewer teens are working today than a generation ago, which means they have fewer chances to practice the skills that careers are built on," Hill said. "Employers told us these durable skills are exactly what they struggle to find. This course gives youth and young adults a practical start and pathway to develop those skills and apply them at work right away, whether they are starting their first job or working toward a promotion." A facilitated, in-person version of the course will be released in March 2027. USU Extension experts will offer the 6-hour program over four weeks in select counties throughout the state. Visit the USU Extension Durable Skills for Workplace Excellence page to learn more and sign up.

title: USU Extension Researchers Identify Ways to Recognize Youth Trauma, Stress
summary: Jill's sixth-grade teacher noticed that she had been missing assignments and acting out in class more than usual since returning from summer vacation. After speaking with her, the teacher learned that Jill's parents had divorced in July, which was likely the cause of her behavioral change. This is one example of an adverse childhood experience (ACE) that can create stress and challenges for young people. Utah State University Extension faculty Cara Murray, Anna Gilliam, Jared Hawkins, and Christina Pay recently released Understanding and Supporting Youth Affected by Trauma and Stress . The fact sheet explains that ACEs may include family instability, loss, bullying, and exposure to violence. These can affect brain development, emotional regulation, behavior, attention, relationships, and the ability to manage further stress. Adults who work with young people can play an important role in helping youth cope with trauma, adversity, and stress. Signs of ACEs may include trouble concentrating, withdrawing from others, strong reactions to seemingly small problems, or testing boundaries. Adults can learn to recognize these behaviors as stress responses rather than intentional misbehavior. The authors emphasize that adults do not need to be mental health professionals to make a difference. Simply providing safe, predictable, and supportive environments can help young people build trust and resilience. They recommend several strategies: Create predictable routines. Knowing what to expect can help young people feel safer and provide stability when other areas of their lives may be unpredictable. Simplify choices. Even small decisions, such as choosing an activity or deciding where to sit, can give youth a greater sense of control. Remain calm and consistent. A steady adult response can help de-escalate difficult situations and model healthy ways to manage strong emotions. Listen before correcting. Youth are more receptive to guidance when they feel heard and understood, not judged. Recognize strengths and effort. Acknowledging progress and positive choices helps young people see themselves as capable and resilient. Encourage healthy relationships. Connections with peers and trusted adults can strengthen self-worth, trust, and the ability to navigate challenges. Adults should also know how to respond when a young person discusses self-harm, suicide, abuse, or other safety concerns. The fact sheet recommends staying calm, taking the concern seriously, and following appropriate reporting procedures. Adults should not promise confidentiality when safety is at stake and should contact emergency services if there is immediate danger. Supporting young people can also take an emotional toll on adults. Caregivers, educators, and adult volunteers should protect their own well-being by maintaining healthy work-life boundaries and seeking support from colleagues or supervisors. The authors emphasize that caring adults are not expected to be a substitute for therapists. Their role is to provide consistency, empathy, and connection while helping youth access professional assistance when necessary. For help in Utah, download the SafeUT app and call or text the Utah Crisis Line at 988. National resources include the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741.

title: USU Extension Youth Honor 9/11 Through Service Across Utah
summary: Utah State University Extension youth in eight sites across Utah recently participated in community service projects as part of the 9/11 Day of Service, honoring the anniversary by supporting veterans, first responders, and community members in need. USU Extension organized the effort through its Teens Lifting Teens program after receiving funding through a 9/11 Day of Service grant. “We really want youth to feel empowered that they are capable of making a difference in their communities,” said Megan Hall, USU Extension youth director of Teens Lifting Teens. “One thing we often say in our program is, ‘We’re not here to teach the leaders of tomorrow. We’re here to empower the leaders of today.’” Participating groups identified needs in their communities and developed projects to address them. In Utah County, youth organized a dinner honoring veterans and assembled kits for first responders. Another group addressed food insecurity by preparing kits for children to take home over the weekend. Other youth wrote letters of appreciation to first responders, contacted local EMTs to identify needed supplies, and assembled kits that EMTs could distribute to people in distress. In Weber County, participants created appreciation letters and kits for correctional officers. Each project also included an educational component about the events of Sept. 11 and their lasting impact. Because today's youth were born years after the attacks, organizers wanted participants to understand not only what happened but also the sense of unity and service that followed. “It doesn’t take a tragedy to help us come together and be united in our communities and be able to make a positive impact,” Hall said. “We don’t need to wait for a crisis. We can find ways to connect with others and serve each other now.” The projects gave youth an opportunity to take the lead themselves. In Utah County, 15-year-old 4-H member Darcie Thurgood took on the challenge of organizing a free banquet honoring veterans and first responders. She spent months arranging the venue, coordinating catering, contacting businesses for donations, and recruiting volunteers. The event brought together approximately 120 people, including about 35 volunteers and 90 veterans, first responders, and guests. Thurgood said the experience pushed her outside her comfort zone, particularly when it came to approaching businesses for support. As she gained confidence, she learned to delegate responsibilities, speak in front of unfamiliar audiences, and recognize what she could accomplish. “I learned a lot more about being a leader and about pushing myself for the benefit of myself and others,” she said. That emphasis on youth leadership is central to Teens Lifting Teens, a statewide program with approximately 25 participating sites. The program focuses on helping youth develop positive relationships, build competence and confidence through peer teaching, and strengthen resiliency. Service projects provide another way for young people to develop those skills while seeing the impact they can have in their own communities. “Young people just need to know that they can do hard things,” Thurgood said. “People love coming together to help each other out. They love being able to be a part of something bigger than themselves.” This was the first year the program participated in the 9/11 Day of Service grant, but organizers hope it becomes an annual event. To learn more about Utah 4-H, click here .

title: USU Faculty Author Commentary Outlining Research Priorities for Robust Climate Assessments
summary: LOGAN — Jessica Schad and Stacia Ryder, faculty in Utah State University’s School of Social Sciences, are co-authors of the commentary “Research priorities for robust climate assessments in the United States” published in Earth’s Future and Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society . The paper brings together 175 authors to outline research priorities that can inform future national, regional, local, sectoral, and topical climate assessments. The commentary is the first paper in the U.S. Climate Collection: Informing Assessment of Risks and Solutions — a joint special collection of the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society that will publish U.S.-focused climate assessment science and research synthesis papers to inform future national and sub-national assessments. Schad contributed expertise on rural communities, focusing on how demographic and economic change can shape their exposure and response to climate risks.
