She emphasized the need for future assessments to examine the distinct challenges rural places face, the resources they can draw on, and the local factors that affect their ability to prepare and adapt. “Rural communities face very different climate risks, and they don’t all have the same resources to respond,” Schad said. “Understanding those local differences can help communities and decision-makers identify solutions that fit the places and people they serve.” Ryder contributed expertise on the U.S. Southwest region, focusing on managing uneven water supply extremes, increasing aridity, heat and temperature-related risks, the uneven impacts of compounding and cascading disasters, and how differences in communities’ vulnerability and adaptive capacity affect their resilience to the impacts of these risks. “Over half of the world’s largest lakes and reservoirs are shrinking, and about 2 billion people live in these drying lake basins. Recent climate models suggest that up to 850 million people could face water shortages due to river drying. Yet this global problem is perhaps more acutely felt in arid regions like the U.S. Southwest, which continues to experience prolonged drought and declines in surface and groundwater availability,” Ryder said. “Given this, managing uneven water supply extremes in the U.S. Southwest is essential for sustaining our communities in the region.” The commentary identifies assessment opportunities and research needs across planetary-scale systems, environmental settings, economic sectors, U.S. regions, and U.S. international interests. Across these areas, the authors identify several cross-cutting priorities for research synthesis, including How greenhouse gas emissions continue to alter and amplify climate hazards; How compounding extremes and cascading risks are straining legacy policies, infrastructure, and institutions; How social systems shape both climate impacts and responses; How future assessments should evaluate mitigation, adaptation, disaster management, climate interventions, and resilience planning and implementation decisions as a climate action portfolio. Scientific assessments synthesize complex bodies of evidence so households, communities, businesses, institutions, and governments can make informed decisions as climate hazards intensify. The most recent U.S. National Climate Assessment was published in 2023; scientific understanding has advanced since then, and climate assessments are continuing by states, localities, and businesses. The commentary argues that the pace of assessment and the integration of science with decision-making must accelerate as climate impacts continue to grow.

title: USU Flutist to Help Premiere Utah Composer's 'Bouquet for Flute and Piano'
summary: At her upcoming faculty recital, flutist and Assistant Professor Jeiran Hasan, in collaboration with pianist Amy Glenn, will premiere Andrew Maxfield’s “Bouquet for Flute and Piano.” A Utah composer, Maxfield just received a 2026 Barlow Endowment commission from the Barlow Endowment for Music Composition to work with the Utah Symphony and Sound of Ages. As part of his visit to Utah State University, Maxfield will give a short talk about his work. The performance features internationally acclaimed musicians and composers, including Chen Yi of China, Ian Clarke of England, and Lala Jafarova of Azerbaijan. The event will begin at 7:30 p.m. Sept. 18 in the Russell/Wanlass Performance Hall on USU’s Logan campus. The recital is free and open to the public and will also be streamed live on the Caine School of the Arts’ YouTube page .

title: USU Geophysicist Chosen for AGU Jason Morgan Early Career Award
summary: A Utah State University researcher has been selected for one of the top honors for early career geophysicists. Srisharan Shreedharan, an earthquake geophysicist from USU’s Department of Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences has been selected for the 2026 Jason Morgan Early Career Award in Tectonophysics from the American Geophysical Union (AGU). The award recognizes an individual each year for outstanding and significant contributions through research, education, and outreach activities. “It’s a well-earned milestone and major achievement,” said Dennis Newell, Water, Earth, and Environmental Sciences department head. “It represents the tremendous impact that Dr. Shreedharan has already made at USU as a researcher, teacher, and mentor.” Shreedharan will be presented with the honor at the American Geophysical Union’s annual meeting, which draws more than 25,000 scientists in the field from around the world. “I'm grateful for this recognition and understand that it belongs to more people than just me. I've been fortunate to have mentors, collaborators, and students who invested in me and my vision, and I hope to give back to my students at USU the same opportunities and mentorship I've been given,” Shreedharan said. The award highlights the growing impact of Shreedharan’s work in earthquake mechanics, building on his experience at the University of Texas at Austin’s Institute for Geophysics , where he was a postdoctoral researcher. Shreedharan’s current work focuses on deciphering fundamental earthquake mechanics and translating fault-zone data into improved hazard assessments. He sailed as a scientist aboard an international deep-sea expedition on the research vessel D/V Chikyu, co-authoring a landmark study published in the journal Science that revealed how a hidden layer of clay acted as a lubricant to amplify Japan's devastating 2011 Tohoku megathrust earthquake and tsunami. His research into rock mechanics and fault re-strengthening processes provides key insights applicable to fault systems worldwide, including earthquake-prone regions like Utah’s Wasatch Fault. Shreedharan directs the Rock Deformation and Earthquake Mechanics Laboratory at USU, a one-of-a-kind geomechanics facility in the Intermountain region and one of only a handful of facilities worldwide that can create realistic earthquakes on faults up to a meter long. Research in the lab focuses on the mechanics of faulting, friction, and rock deformation to decipher how earthquakes trigger and unfold. Another of Shreedharan’s major pursuits is integrating machine learning with lab data to analyze acoustic emissions and investigate the timing and shear stress associated with laboratory-generated earthquakes.

title: USU Geotechnical Engineer Studies Earthquake Aftermath in Search of Answers for Utah
summary: Data generated from earthquakes can quickly start to disappear as cleanup begins. Facing environmental volatility, a Utah State University professor is employing new tactics to preserve data and develop more robust infrastructure in Utah and around the world. Brady Cox, a geotechnical engineering professor, has been selected to join the executive committee for the Geotechnical Extreme Events Reconnaissance Association, known as GEER. The appointment, spanning from Oct. 1, 2026, to Sept. 30, 2031, is part of a collaborative research proposal to collect and archive AI-ready perishable data with funding from the National Science Foundation. Established in 1999, GEER captures critical observations to advance post-event reconnaissance, the collection of data in the aftermath of earthquakes, and share these findings with U.S. and international organizations. Returning to his home state in 2020, Cox came to USU with the ambition to use his global geotechnical experience to address the looming threat of earthquakes in Utah. “About 80 percent of Utah's population lives within 15 miles of the Wasatch fault, which has the potential to produce earthquakes at least as large as a magnitude seven,” he said. The state also has around 140,000 unreinforced masonry buildings prone to damage and collapsing. Many of these structures exist on K-12 school campuses. Considering Utah’s seismic hazards, Cox founded and now directs the Utah Earthquake Engineering Research Center, or UEEC. Here, researchers conduct studies to encourage the retrofitting and replacement of the state’s infrastructure. This includes the robust design of nuclear energy power plants. Cox has advised on these facilities around the world, from Poland to South Africa and all over the U.S. He hopes the UEEC will be involved in Utah’s design for nuclear power plants and contribute to other projects that benefit citizens. “Utah has legitimate seismic hazards and we have to address those when we're designing anything,” Cox said. “It's important that these reconnaissance teams are out there looking for important lessons that we can bring back to the U.S. and incorporate into our building codes and construction practices.” In his new role, Cox will conduct reconnaissance using laser scanners to collect millions of data points that will be archived in a format that AI can interpret. These AI algorithms can be trained by researchers to recognize patterns and understand how extreme events affect soil and infrastructure. “Every new earthquake reveals different lessons,” Cox said. “We don't want earthquakes to happen, but when they do, we need to take advantage of what we can learn from them.”

title: USU Honors Presents 51st Annual Honors Last Lecture With Benjamin Burger
summary: LOGAN, Utah — The Utah State University Honors Program presents the 51st Annual Honors Last Lecture featuring Associate Professor Benjamin Burger, the 2026 Honors Outstanding Professor. Burger will deliver a lecture titled “Beyond Extinction: The Prehistoric Past and Surviving the Future” in the Russell/Wanlass Performance Hall on USU’s Logan campus from 3:30-4:30 p.m. Oct. 21. The talk will explore how we can use the fossil and rock record to understand the fragility of life in times of dramatic change, the remarkable resilience of ecosystems throughout Earth’s history, and the meaning of this record for our shared future. Burger is an associate professor in the Department of Water, Earth, & Environmental Sciences at Utah State University, with an interest in paleontology. He received his Ph.D. (2009) and BA (1997) in Geology from the University of Colorado and his MS (1999) from Stony Brook University in Anatomical Sciences. He worked at the American Museum of Natural History from 1999-2004 and enjoys researching the extensive history of life on Earth through his extensive study of fossils in the American West. He is experienced in conducting fieldwork in Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming, and he has published research on all three eras of the Phanerozoic. He is also heavily involved in science outreach, with numerous educational videos about paleontology and geology available on YouTube. Each year, Honors students nominate tenured faculty whose teaching and mentoring have made a difference in their lives to deliver this high-profile lecture to the USU community. A committee of Honors students interviews nominees and selects one exceptional professor to imagine and deliver what might be a “last lecture” at USU, if they had only one more to give. Burger, from USU’s Uintah Basin Campus in Vernal, is the first statewide faculty member to receive this award. “This event engages the entire community — students, faculty, alumni, friends, and other stakeholders — in celebrating the teachers and mentors who have transformed the experience of our students here at USU,” said Kristine Miller, professor of English and executive director of the Utah State University Honors Program. The lecture is free and open to the public and will be followed immediately by a reception in the Russell/Wanlass Performance Hall lobby. The livestream for a statewide audience and the recording of the event after its completion can be accessed from the University Honors Program website .

title: USU Invites Students, Faculty, Staff to Participate in Statewide Read-a-Thon on Oct. 2
summary: Utah State University President Brad Mortensen is supporting the Governor and First Lady’s Read-a-Thon on Oct. 2 anytime between 9:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. All students, faculty, and staff are encouraged to participate in the event at each of the Statewide Campuses and Extension locations. “There’s something special about reading a book with a child. It sparks their imagination and reminds us as adults what it feels like to believe anything is possible,” Mortensen said. “I invite everyone across Utah to join us on Oct. 2 to enjoy a good book, whether on your own or with a child in your life.” There will be designated reading areas across the Logan Campus to promote reading and the joy of finding a great book. In the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences, the School for Teacher Education and Leadership will celebrate reading in the Education Building at the Young Educational Learning Center (YETC) with events from 9-11 a.m. including the Educators Rising Student Club and The Literacy Clinic. The Merrill-Cazier Library will also host specific areas for reading. Gov. Spencer Cox is encouraging all Utahns to set aside an hour to read: “On Oct. 2, mark your calendars — we are having a statewide Read-a-Thon,” Cox said. “We want businesspeople in their pajamas and bringing their pillows and their books to work. Let’s get reading again.” Elementary students at Edith Bowen Laboratory School, a K-6 charter school located on the Logan Campus, are excited to lead the effort to get everyone involved in the statewide event. EBLS students will be reading with groups across campus, including the Sound Beginnings kindergarten class, ASSERT Autism preschool, Natural Resources library, Heravi Peace Institute, the English department, ASPIRE, College of Veterinary Medicine and student athletes from USU Athletics programs. “At USU, we are bringing our faculty and students together with our young readers here on campus to share this reading experience together,” said Shannon Rhodes, first-grade teacher at Edith Bowen Laboratory School. “Edith Bowen teachers and students have requested guests on campus to join them at this read-a-thon or where they want their students to go and read — we have paired student-athletes with some classes, and some sixth-grade students are reading with our young friends who cannot read themselves.”

title: USU Kicks-Off New Tradition with Welcome Home, Aggies Event
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Utah State University will kick off a new campus tradition this month with its first Welcome Home, Aggies move-in event as new students and their families arrive on campus. The event will be held Saturday, Aug. 22, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., as new students move into their residence halls. Throughout the day, faculty and staff volunteers stationed across campus will help unload belongings, distribute and collect move-in carts, provide directions and answer questions. USU is inviting faculty and staff from across the university to volunteer. Shifts are available in one-hour increments throughout the day, and hourly employees are asked to check with their supervisor before signing up. As a thank-you, all volunteers will receive a T-shirt, along with water and snacks during their shift. "There's nothing quite like the excitement of move-in day, and together we can help every new Aggie feel at home from the moment they arrive," said Kris Winter, vice president for Student Success. "We hope you'll join us in welcoming new members of our Aggie family to campus and making the first Welcome Home, Aggies event a tradition to remember." Volunteers may talk with students about their role on campus if asked, but recruitment, solicitation and advertising are not permitted during the event. Other opportunities to promote clubs, jobs and activities to students will be available during Day on the Quad. To sign up, complete the short sign-up survey. For questions, or to make changes to a shift after signing up, please contact Student Success at (435) 797-1712.

title: USU Launches Building Together Series to Strengthen Faculty Industry Collaboration
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Utah State University's Office of Research will launch its Building Together series with an Industry Relations Workshop from noon to 4 p.m. Oct. 15 in room 205/207 of the Eccles Conference Center. The Building Together series is designed to help USU faculty develop the strategies, skills, and connections needed to work effectively with industry. The kickoff workshop focuses on skills and strategies for academic-industry relations, with examples from USU of how academic expertise and industry needs can lead to collaborative research, commercialization, and broader impact. "With the changing federal funding landscape putting an increased emphasis on industry involvement in research projects, understanding how to develop effective collaborative relationships is vital to remaining competitive,” said Jeri Hansen, executive director of research innovation and impact at USU. The Industry Relations Workshop will introduce faculty to the different ways universities and companies can work together, including sponsored research, consulting, licensing, and collaborative research. Workshop speakers and panelists from USU will offer guidance on identifying industry needs, communicating the value of academic research, and developing productive, long-term partnerships. Sessions will address why industry engagement matters; pathways for working with industry; identifying and defining industry problems through market research; intellectual property considerations when working with industry; and case studies of successful academic-industry collaborations. "Faculty do not need previous industry collaboration experience to attend the workshop," Hansen said. "The information provided during the workshop will benefit faculty new to industry relationships as well as those with previous industry collaboration experience." Hannah Feinsilber, a doctoral candidate in biochemistry at USU and previous business development and marketing specialist with Technology Transfer Services, developed and organized the workshop. Feinsilber created the program to help faculty better understand how to identify, initiate, and sustain relationships with industry partners. The Building Together: Industry Relations Workshop will provide the foundation for topic-specific Building Together events throughout the 2026-27 academic year. These follow-on events will give faculty and companies opportunities to have direct conversations about research capabilities, technologies, facilities, services, and innovation needs. "The goal of the Building Together workshop and event series is to help faculty develop new research relationships that will enable them to increase the impact of their work and remain competitive in today’s external funding landscape," Hansen said. The Oct. 15 workshop is free, but space is limited. Faculty can learn more and register at research.usu.edu/rii/external-research-partnerships/building-together . The USU Research Innovation & Impact (RII) division, housed within the Office of Research, helps grow ideas into real-world impact through a holistic, hands-on approach to supporting research through every stage of its journey. The three core teams — Research Development, External Research Partnerships, and Technology Transfer Services — work together to help faculty find funding, craft competitive proposals, build meaningful collaborations with external partners, and bring innovations to society. RII works to strengthen USU’s research capacity, connect expertise with opportunity, and help research make a difference that reaches far beyond campus.

title: USU Launches New Learner Portal and Application to Streamline the Prospective Student Experience
summary: Utah State University has launched a new learner portal and application designed to simplify how prospective students apply, track their application, receive decisions and respond to offers. The new experience went live on Thursday, serving students applying for Spring 2027 and beyond. Prospective students now apply through a single, modern entry point at applynow.usu.edu . The portal reduces confusion, streamlines steps and creates a clearer, more intuitive path from interest to enrollment. “For prospective students, the primary improvements are simplicity and clarity,” said Ian Anderson, executive director of Enrollment Strategy & Innovation. “Students apply through one modern entry point, and behind the scenes Salesforce allows us to reduce friction, limit duplicate steps and respond more quickly. The goal is that students don’t have to think about the system itself. They can focus on applying and learning about USU rather than navigating processes.” This launch represents the first production release supporting the full undergraduate and graduate application experience in Salesforce and marks a major milestone in the OneUSU CRM initiative. “It reflects our shift from fragmented, system-centered workflows to a unified platform that improves how we engage students and support staff,” Anderson said. “It lays the foundation for more personalized, data-informed recruitment at scale.” Behind the scenes, the launch establishes Salesforce as the system of record for recruitment and admission activity, replacing multiple disconnected tools and creating a more consistent and connected experience for recruitment and admissions teams. Enrollment support staff will see immediate benefits through more streamlined processes, reduced application processing time, improved system integration and better visibility into applicant data. “The clearest change will be in how prospect data is created, managed and shared,” said Lindi Brown, USU Salesforce admin. “Recruiters will see more standardized records, clearer ownership and improved visibility into student interactions. This work sets a strong foundation for everything student-related that we can build on.” Brown said that success is not defined by perfection on day one, but by trust and usability over time. “It’s less about perfection on day one and more about creating a solid, usable foundation that we can continue to improve,” she said. “This launch enables us to better understand where a student is in their journey and respond accordingly, rather than treating each interaction as a one-off. It’s the first step toward a more personalized and supportive recruitment experience.” The launch also supports USU’s broader vision for connected, student-centered engagement across the institution. “For OneUSU CRM, this proves that a shared CRM is no longer just a concept, it’s a functional platform that will someday support recruitment at scale,” Brown said. “For the university, it’s a critical step toward breaking down data silos and creating a more coordinated, student-centered approach. This launch isn’t just about technology; it’s about building trust, shared ownership and a better way of working together at Utah State University.” These improvements mark an important shift in how USU approaches student engagement. By moving to a shared, scalable CRM platform, the university is creating the infrastructure needed to connect people, processes and data across the student journey, while setting the stage for continued growth and collaboration beyond recruitment and admissions. “This go-live represents a major milestone in the OneUSU CRM journey by establishing Salesforce as the long-term platform that will support student engagement across the full student lifecycle,” Lindsay Farnworth, director of Enrollment Systems & Data, said. “While this release focuses on Recruitment and Admissions, it lays the foundation for more integrated engagement over time across enrollment, student success and advancement.” Work on the advancement phase of OneUSU CRM is already underway, with foundational sprints complete and marketing beginning development of advancement email templates and a preference center. “This launch signals that OneUSU CRM is becoming a real, extensible platform,” Farnworth said. “For stakeholders beyond recruitment and admissions, it creates cleaner data, clearer processes and a shared system that supports collaboration. It lays the groundwork for future enhancements that will benefit alumni, advising, retention and student success efforts.” To learn more about OneUSU CRM, explore project phases, or follow progress updates, visit crm.usu.edu . Questions or feedback may be shared by emailing oneusucrm@usu.edu or submitting the OneUSU CRM feedback form .

title: USU Libraries Hosts Book Talk on Playful Philosopher Bernard Suits
summary: LOGAN — Utah State University Libraries and USU faculty member Javi López Frías will host a book talk on Bernard Suits: A Playful Philosopher from 3:30-4:30 p.m. Oct. 7 in Library Room 101. Co-authors López Frías and Alex Asay will share how they teamed up to write a book about the philosopher who most shaped their careers and lives. Their book offers a clear introduction to Suits’ ideas and why they matter in philosophy, game, and leisure studies, and the philosophy of sport. The talk will explore how gameplay illuminates enduring philosophical questions — such as those concerning definitions and the good life — and ultimately explain the unity of Suits' philosophical project: providing individuals who live in societies that glorify work and productivity with other more meaningful ways to live. López Frías is an assistant professor in USU’s Department of Kinesiology and Health Science. He earned a doctorate in philosophy from the University of Valencia in Spain and spent nine years at Penn State before joining USU. He serves as president of the Spanish Association for the Philosophy of Sport and editor-in-chief of the journal Sport, Ethics, and Philosophy. Asay is a philosophy graduate student in his final year at the University of Georgia. He has extensive publishing and teaching experience and has earned prestigious accolades, including the R. Scott Kretchmar Student Essay Award, in his relatively short career. He is also a father of five wonderful children and has a brother who studies at USU. There will be an opportunity for those interested in meeting with him to learn more about his graduate school experiences and insights into the current job market. For more information, visit library.usu.edu/news/2026/bernard-suits-faculty-book-talk .

title: USU Libraries Spotlights 'Home' for Utah Archives Month
summary: LOGAN — Utah State University Libraries’ Special Collections & Archives is marking Utah Archives Month this October by spotlighting digital collections tied to this year’s theme, “Home in the Archives.” Utah Archives Month is part of American Archives Month. For this year’s theme, the Utah State Historical Records Advisory Board invited cultural heritage organizations and individuals across the state to share photographs, letters, postcards, scrapbooks, and other documents that show what “home” means to them. USU Libraries is answering that call with two collections. The Cache County Tax Assessment Collection holds approximately 3,400 photographs of residences and businesses in Cache County, Utah, taken between the 1930s and the 1960s. The photographs were taken by the county for record-keeping purposes and were stapled or taped to tax assessment cards. The A-Board Historical Photograph Collection includes about 8,800 images mounted on archival boards. Many show Logan and Cache Valley, along with Idaho and Wyoming. The collection also documents railroads, the Western cattle industry, wagon freighting and Mormon historical sites. Both collections are available online through USU Libraries Special Collections & Archives at libraryusu.access.preservica.com. For more information, contact Sarah Berry, digital archivist, at sarah.berry@usu.edu.

title: USU Libraries to Present Arrington Mormon History Lecture Featuring Benjamin E. Park
summary: LOGAN — Historian Benjamin E. Park will present his lecture “Declarations of Independence: Why the Latter-day Saints Just Can’t Quit the United States” at this year’s Arrington Mormon History Lecture on Sept. 24. Park’s presentation will trace the long and evolving relationships between The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and the United States, focusing on key moments when patriotism, allegiance and citizenship took on heightened significance within the Mormon tradition. Park is an award-winning historian. He has a master’s degree in theology from the University of Edinburgh’s School of Divinity and a doctorate in history from the University of Cambridge. He currently teaches history at Sam Houston State University and serves as president of the Mormon History Association. He is the author or editor of five books and winner of the American Society of Church History’s Philip Schaff Prize for the Best Book in the History of Christianity. His YouTube and social media channels have over 30,000 subscribers and several million views. The Arrington Mormon History Lecture will be 7 p.m. Sept. 24 at the Logan Tabernacle, 50 N. Main St., Logan, Utah. The event is free and open to the public.

title: USU Moab Creates Nursing Lunch & Learn Professional Development Series
summary: MOAB, Utah — Utah State University Moab hosted several Lunch and Learn sessions aimed at connecting nursing students, faculty and medical professionals throughout the region during the spring 2026 semester. The Lunch and Learn series, developed in partnership with USU Moab administration and facilitated by Connie Wilson and Jessica Elkon, expands professional development opportunities for students by offering career mentoring and strengthening healthcare networking across Grand County. “I developed this idea to create meaningful connections between community healthcare providers and nursing and pre-nursing students at USU Moab,” Wilson said. “I modeled this education series after other series that I have experienced working in large hospitals.” Wilson, who also works at the Moab Regional Hospital, used her connections to recruit local nurses to attend the lunches. These lunches were open to the community and included local nurses and nurse leaders, social workers, nursing and pre-nursing students, biology faculty and students, hospital administrators, and USU staff. Wilson said she was beyond pleased by the presentations that were part of the lunches, saying that they surpassed her dreams for the project. The topics spread far and wide on parts of the profession. “The topics have been diverse and engaging — ranging from pathways to becoming a flight nurse to compassionate care for patients with substance use disorder, presented by USARA-Utah Recovery Peer Support,” she said. Wilson and Elkon hope to expand participation even further in future years among physicians, physician assistants and nurse practitioners, with a focus on strengthening nurse-to-provider collaboration. They feel that the series can bring people together to learn and connect in person. “In a time when much education and training is delivered virtually, these sessions provide valuable space forauthentic human interaction and relationship-building within our healthcare community,” Wilson said. Located in the outdoor recreation paradise of Moab and boasting one of the greenest buildings on any USU campus, Utah State University Moab offers students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university. With programs such as Nursing, Elementary Education, Recreation Resource Management and Social Work, technical education in Health Professions, Automotive and Business, and degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees, USU Moab offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at moab.usu.edu .

title: USU Moab Graduates Nine Students in Inaugural EMT Program Cohort
summary: MOAB, Utah — There are now nine more emergency medical technicians in Grand County, as the Utah State University Moab campus celebrated the inaugural group of graduates of its emergency medical technician certificate program in July. The program, which is offered in collaboration with Grand County Emergency Medical Services and meets at the GCEMS Station in Moab, looks to strengthen the local healthcare workforce, improve emergency response capacity in Grand County, and encourage students to build lasting careers within the community. The new certificate program has secured ongoing funding and will run several times each year. During the three-month intensive course that began in February, students received specialized training from active EMTs and paramedics at GCEMS, as well as from a variety of guest lecturers, including doctors from Moab Regional Hospital, first responders in Grand County Search and Rescue, flight crews from the local Intermountain Health Care base, and first responders from the Moab Valley Fire Department. “It really enriched the learning experience for the students to have the course so integrated with local community resources,” said Anna Knight, USU EMT instructor and the education captain for Grand County Emergency Medical Services. “This has been a great start to the partnership between USU and Grand County EMS, and we're excited to continue working together to bring high-quality EMS courses to Moab.” With the course being taught at the Grand County EMS, students also participated in ride-alongs to gain real-world experience. These clinical shifts allowed students to join responders during real events in the local community. “My ride-alongs with the Grand County EMS crew helped me understand how what we were learning was applied on the job,” said Keltain Reece-Sullivan, one of the nine graduates. “I got to see the providers demonstrate both the hard skills and soft skills of the job.” Students also appreciated the course being taught by active EMTs and paramedics. They felt that all the information and scenarios they were given were as up-to-date as possible. “All of the knowledge provided is current and accurate and as real-world as it gets,” said Andrew Kalinyak, another participant in the certificate course. “Clinical shifts are with GCEMS personnel and responding to real events in the local community. It was an incredibly rewarding program, and I am happy I was able to attend.” As part of the course, students worked closely together in scenarios to simulate working as a team. Reece-Sullivan said that people taking the course should quickly connect with other students and study together. This helped them work better in scenarios and learn from each other. “The sessions with other students were very valuable to me,” Reece-Sullivan said. “You also need to really engage in the class. There will be times during scenarios when you'll feel embarrassed or shy, but I encourage you to embrace that feeling and lean into it. Those scenarios are where so much of the practical learning takes place.” Several of the graduates are now working as EMTs for Grand County EMS, while others have their eyes set on different goals. “Several EMT class grads were recently hired to work as EMT s for Grand County EMS, and we're excited to have them on board,” Knight said. “Some students now have their eyes on paramedic or nursing programs as a next step in their healthcare careers. Others are using their new medical training to improve their skills as outdoor recreation guides. “Guides are often the first people on scene for outdoor recreation medical emergencies, so having guides in the community with strong medical training who can stabilize a patient and report key information to 911 dispatchers can really help incoming EMS and SAR responders provide great patient care and evacuation.” The class is capped at 12 students. To be able to take the course, students must be enrolled at USU. For more information, visit usu.edu/degrees-majors/emergency-medical-technician_tc . Specific questions about the program can be directed to Anna Knight (anna.knight@usu.edu).

title: USU Moab Nursing Instructor Dianne Wright to Retire
summary: MOAB, Utah — After 25 years in the nursing teaching industry, including nine years at Utah State University Moab, Dianne Wright has announced her retirement. Wright spent three years teaching part time and six years teaching full time as a professional practice assistant professor in the S.J. & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture & Natural Resources at USU Moab. During her time at USU Moab, she also spent time as the CNA program coordinator. Wright said the best part of her time at USU Moab was seeing her students. “I am proud of the accomplishments of the students and being a part of helping them meet their goals,” she said. “I love teaching and have enjoyed watching the students grow in knowledge and seeing their confidence increase.” Samantha Campbell, associate vice president of USU Moab, described Wright as someone who believed in her students, celebrated their accomplishments, and who helped launch the careers of countless healthcare professionals that now serve in Grand County. “Dianne has had an incredible impact on USU Moab through her unwavering commitment to her students and to the CNA program,” Campbell said. “She was deeply invested in every student's success, going out of her way to help them feel prepared and confident as they entered the healthcare profession. Each semester, she eagerly waited to hear how her students performed on their licensure exams because their success truly mattered to her.” Campbell hopes that Wright is remembered for her genuine kindness, generosity and the sense of community she created at USU Moab. She said that Wright’s caring presence will be missed. “Diane wasn't just an outstanding instructor — she made a point of checking in with faculty and staff, sharing produce from her garden during the growing season, and encouraging all of us to collect bottle caps to support a charitable cause that was important to her,” Campbell said. “Whether she was teaching, caring for patients as a nurse, serving her faith community or volunteering through her sorority, Dianne consistently looked for ways to serve others.” Prior to joining USU Moab as a full-time instructor, Wright spent five years as a registered nurse at Canyonland Care Center in Moab. She also worked in the nursing profession at healthcare facilities in Texas as well as a two-year stint as the school nurse at the American School of Kuwait. In total, Wright spent more than 25 years in the nursing teaching profession and more than 30 years as a nurse. A native of Monticello, Utah, Wright began her college studies at USU, taking first-year classes. She would later earn an associate degree in applied science in nursing at Victoria College in Texas, then a bachelor’s degree in nursing and a master’s degree in occupational training and development from Texas A&M University-Corpus Christ before serving as a captain in the US Army Nurse Corps Reserves. Now entering retirement, Wright plans to spend time doing things she has put off. “I'm looking forward to getting back to my oil painting, sewing, reading, gardening and just spending time with my family,” she said. Located in the outdoor recreation paradise of Moab and boasting one of the greenest buildings on any USU campus, Utah State University Moab offers students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university. With programs such as Nursing, Elementary Education, Recreation Resource Management and Social Work, technical education in Health Professions, Automotive and Business, and degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees, USU Moab offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at moab.usu.edu .

title: USU Moab Provides Hub for Community Engagement, Events
summary: As the hometown university for Grand County, Utah State University Moab prioritizes community engagement. Since the beginning of the year, the campus has hosted more than 160 events, bringing people of all ages and backgrounds together to learn, connect, and experience what USU Moab has to offer. Community events are an important part of USU Moab’s role. The campus aims to be more than a place where people take classes; instead, it serves as a resource for the entire community. These events allow the university faculty and staff to build relationships, better understand community needs, and help people see the many ways USU Moab can serve them. “Community events are important to USU Moab because we want to be more than a place people come to take classes — we want to be an active and accessible part of the community,” said Samantha Campbell, associate vice president for USU Moab. “Our goal is for the campus to be a resource for everyone, whether they are pursuing a degree, earning a certificate, participating in non-degree programming, or simply engaging with us through a community event.” Through these events, USU Moab has connected with community members ranging from young children to older adults. “We've welcomed participants ranging from kindergarten-aged children to adults in their 80s, bringing together people from all walks of life and a wide variety of socioeconomic backgrounds,” said Crystal Fletcher, technical coordinator. “One of the most rewarding aspects of these events has been seeing community members connect, learn, and engage with one another regardless of age, experience, or circumstance.” School field trips have been one example of how USU Moab brings young people onto campus to explore different opportunities. During one fourth-grade field trip, students received an interactive introduction to the plumbing trade from a local professional. “From learning about the profession to trying their hand at plunging toilets, the students were fully engaged and having a blast,” Fletcher said. For Campbell, welcoming grade school students to campus is particularly meaningful. “I love the energy the students bring and having the opportunity to welcome them to campus and let them experience some of the different things we have to offer,” she said. “It’s especially rewarding to help kids see USU Moab as a place that is part of their community and somewhere they can picture themselves in the future.” Located in the outdoor recreation paradise of Moab and boasting one of the greenest buildings on any USU campus, Utah State University Moab offers students the personalized attention and small class sizes of a small-town college with the resources of a large university. With programs such as Nursing, Elementary Education, Recreation Resource Management and Social Work, technical education in Health Professions, Automotive and Business, and degree options ranging from associate to doctorate degrees, USU Moab offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. Learn more at moab.usu.edu .

title: USU Moab Provides Local Bilingual Residents With Free Medical Interpreter Training
summary: MOAB, Utah — Utah State University Moab successfully completed an intensive 40-hour Community Medical Interpreter Training program over the summer, equipping 18 local bilingual residents with critical skills to expand healthcare access and clear communication across Grand County. The training was developed through a collaboration between Utah State University Extension and the Department of World Languages and Cultures at Utah State University. The initiative is part of a broader effort led by the Translation & Interpretation Studies program to expand access to qualified language professionals in rural and underserved communities across Utah while creating pathways for bilingual residents to enter high-demand careers in healthcare interpreting. The program addresses a gap in rural health infrastructure by offering local, high-level instruction at no cost to participants. The course eliminated travel and financial barriers for rural residents. Graduates represented four languages — Navajo, Spanish, Vietnamese, and Korean — and spanned professionals working in education, community services, and healthcare and pharmacy, alongside individuals looking to advance their careers. The curriculum was designed and overseen by Elsa Perez, assistant professor and co-director of translation & interpretation studies at USU, and delivered by Maria Jose Velasco, assistant professor with USU Extension. Perez created specialized training for each language. "Medical interpreters play a critical role in reducing communication barriers and improving patient outcomes," Perez said. "By bringing professional interpreter training directly to rural communities, we are helping build a local workforce that can support equitable access to healthcare while creating meaningful professional opportunities for bilingual residents." For community member Irene Thompson, the course had value beyond interpreting alone. "This course was a great opportunity to learn specialized vocabulary and techniques to improve my interpretation for parents at school. It also equipped me to teach my ESL students the health terminology they need, making it a strong addition to my resume," she said. The training included five instructional days each week, culminating with a graduation ceremony on July 23 attended by city and county officials. These newly trained interpreters will be ready to support local institutions, including Moab Regional Hospital, the Moab Free Health Clinic, San Juan Health, pharmacies, and area schools. "The energy throughout the class was amazing, and participants remained highly motivated despite the demanding schedule,” said Beatriz Jarvis, Extension home and community program coordinator. The program also reflects ongoing efforts by Utah State University to strengthen Utah's language-access infrastructure. Through interpreter education, community partnerships, and multilingual workforce development initiatives, the Translation & Interpretation Studies program is working to increase the availability of trained interpreters throughout the state, particularly in rural areas where language services are often limited. Student Mariany Valero said she's not stopping here: “This course is just the first step in my journey. My goal is to earn the national certification so I can continue helping communities in critical need. Having the opportunity to take this course for free allows me to continue my education and move closer to that goal. This is a meaningful investment in us and our communities, and I am truly grateful for the opportunity.”

title: USU Moab Students Examine Healthcare Practices in Nepal Study Abroad Experience
summary: MOAB, Utah — A group of Utah State University students traveled to Nepal as part of a two-week study abroad immersive learning experience centered around the local healthcare practices. The trip of nine USU students included five from USU Moab. Students who participated in the program expanded their understanding of global health by navigating unfamiliar healthcare settings and embracing new ways of learning. The students traveled to three different communities, giving service and collaborating with local healthcare workers at hospitals, clinics and community organizations. The students also gifted 10 water filtration systems to families in need. The Moab campus partnered with the Utah nonprofit Youthlinc and Waves for Water, as well as the Nepal organization Insight Himalaya. “Hospitals and schools were selected to give students experiences in public, private, rural, urban and specialty healthcare settings,” said Shanda Thompson, USU Moab academic advisor. “Study abroad can be a grounding experience for students and the direction they want to go once they finish their program. Our program was focused on healthcare, and it allowed students to see similarities and differences between our healthcare system and Nepal’s.” Some of the local healthcare facilities the students saw included a maternity hospital. Nursing student Haley Rice, who is an aspiring NICU nurse, was amazed to see how the nurses at the hospital worked to meet the needs of patients while being equipped with scarce resources She said it reminded her that the heart of nursing is the people behind it. “As a nursing student, this experience reminded me why I chose this career,” she said. “It made me want to be the kind of nurse who is compassionate, open-minded and willing to learn from people with different backgrounds and experiences. I came home with a new appreciation for the healthcare system we have, but also with a better understanding that there's always something we can learn from others.” The trip also included a visit to a hospital that treated people with leprosy. The students were inspired by the resilience of patients and doctors and nurses alike in a setting that did not include basic amenities that the students took for granted, including air conditioning and clean drinking water. “This experience made me realize how different healthcare can be in other parts of the world,” said nursing student Jeferlita Zul. “To actually see with your own eyes makes a huge difference. Seeing it firsthand made me appreciate what I have and gave me a new perspective on how lucky I am.” In addition to their work, students saw remote regions of the mountains and hiked one of the most famous mountainous regions of the world. “The trekking was definitely challenging, and at times it felt like we might have overdone it, but it was still an amazing experience,” Zul said. “I loved seeing the mountains and getting to visit places that felt very different from home. I still shed tears when people ask me about Nepal.” Students described their experience as eye-opening. “More than anything, Nepal taught me gratitude,” Rice said. “I came home with a greater appreciation for the opportunities I've had, the education I'm receiving, and the healthcare resources we often take for granted. The people we met were so welcoming, resilient and kind, and I know those are lessons I'll carry with me for the rest of my life, both as a person and someday as a nurse.” More information is available at studyabroad.usu.edu or by contacting a USU Study Abroad advisor at studyabroad@usu.edu

title: USU Names News Police Chief Ahead of Fall 2026 Semester
summary: Erik Christensen has been named Utah State University’s new chief of police. Christensen has been serving as a member of USU Police Department since March 2015. He was serving as interim chief since September 2025 and named acting chief this past May. He will officially begin this role on Sept. 1. "Erik is a respected leader who brings extensive law enforcement experience, a strong commitment to community engagement, and a deep understanding of higher education public safety," said Ellis Bruch, executive director of the USU Department of Public Safety. Over the years, Christensen has played a key role in advancing the mission of the police department by building trust and strengthening safety initiatives across the campus community. As chief, he will lead the police division in close partnership with students, faculty, staff, and local stakeholders to ensure USU remains a safe and welcoming environment. "I am confident that his experience, vision, and commitment to our university will continue to strengthen the outstanding work of the USU Police Department, Department of Public Safety, and further support the mission of Utah State University," Bruch added.

title: USU Names Valentina Salotti Next Dean of Huntsman School
summary: After a nationwide search, Utah State University has named Valentina Salotti as the next dean of the Jon M. Huntsman School of Business, effective Jan. 1, 2027. “Valentina brings strong academic and leadership experience from a fellow land-grant research university, along with a deep commitment to students, collaborative leadership, and connecting higher education with industry and the communities we serve,” USU President Brad L. Mortensen said. Valentina joins USU from Iowa State University, where she began her academic career and currently serves as the senior associate dean for academic affairs at the Ivy College of Business. She also previously served as an associate dean for undergraduate programs. Salotti received a bachelor’s in economics, a master’s in banking and finance, and a Ph.D. in finance from the University of Bologna, Italy. “What drew me to the Huntsman School and Utah State University was not only their record of excellence and dedication to the land-grant mission, but also their people,” Salotti said. “I felt their warmth, their pride in this community, and their genuine commitment to helping students thrive. I look forward to making Logan our home and am excited to work alongside this community to build on the Huntsman School’s remarkable momentum.” Salotti will be the second dean of the Huntsman School since its naming nearly 20 years ago. In his announcement to faculty and staff about Salotti’s appointment, USU Provost Chris Corcoran reflected on the significance of the moment and this transition. “Throughout the search, we were looking for a leader who could build on the school's strengths while bringing new perspectives and ideas, strengthening collaboration and culture, and positioning the Huntsman School for its next chapter,” Corcoran said. “Valentina stood out as the right leader for this moment. She is thoughtful, collaborative, and student-centered, and she understands the opportunities and responsibilities that come with being part of a land-grant, research university.” Mortensen also thanked Frank Caliendo for his leadership and service as the interim dean of the Huntsman School of Business, a role he will continue through the end of the year. The president will host a reception welcoming Salotti and celebrating David Huntsman’s service on the board of trustees at 4 p.m. Sept. 18 at the Perry Pavilion.

title: USU Offers Free Student Tickets to 2026 Zero Gravity Summit
summary: Utah State University is offering a limited number of free tickets for USU students of any major to attend the Zero Gravity Summit at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City, Oct. 28-29. This is a unique opportunity to experience the forefront of aerospace and defense technology, connect with trailblazing companies, and learn about cutting-edge innovations. The event will include sessions with industry leaders and a keynote address by Olympian Shaun White. A total of 100 tickets are available on a first-come, first-served basis. Each ticket grants access to both days of the event, though attendance on both days is not required. For those interested, a free shuttle will depart from the Logan campus and return from the Salt Palace Convention Center on both days. Students will also receive a complimentary event shirt to wear during the summit. The Zero Gravity Summit is the nation’s premier dual-use technology and national security summit, hosted by 47G, an organization dedicated to making Utah the leading hub for aerospace and defense innovation. The summit brings together universities, industry, government, and community partners to foster talent, fund entrepreneurship and fuel innovation across Utah’s deep tech frontier. Students can secure their free tickets here. Add the code USUSTUDENT2026, select one ticket and press “Continue.” Please use your USU student email to register. If all available tickets are claimed, there is an option to join the waitlist. Students should only request a ticket if they plan to attend.

title: USU Offers Virtual Campus Experience Through Roblox
summary: For a new generation of future students, exploring Utah State University begins long before stepping foot on campus — it starts on Roblox. Recognizing the power of interactive digital spaces, University Marketing and Communications teamed up with Professor Ramy Shaaban and students in the Human Experience Design and Interaction (HEDI) program. Together, they built the first full, interactive university experience in the metaverse. Launched in Fall 2026, the USU Experience — known as Aggie Campus Life — challenges users to "earn" their degree across three colleges through daily interactive activities. Players can explore inside campus buildings, snap a photo with Big Blue, and dive into Aggie traditions, preparing the next generation of students through hands-on design and immersive play. Aggies and future Aggies interested in checking out the Aggie Campus Life can play the Roblox Beta right now.

title: USU Prepares for Animal Science Building Renovation
summary: LOGAN — Beginning next week, visitors to Utah State University’s main campus will notice something new near the Quad: temporary fencing signaling the start of a construction project expected to last through November 2028. The fencing, scheduled to be erected on or after Oct. 14, is in preparation for the full renovation of the Animal Science building, which includes an addition on the historic structure’s north side. The project, designed by Method Studio, will not only prioritize modernization, including updates to HVAC systems alongside the building’s elevator and restrooms, but will also marry historic preservation and improved seismic safety with significant upgrades to benefit the broader USU community. Originally intended to house animal husbandry and veterinary science programs, the Animal Science building is the birthplace of Aggie Ice Cream, but it has served many uses over its near 110-year history. According to university records, it was constructed between 1917-18 with government funds appropriated to USU for military trainee barracks and was temporarily used as a convalescent hospital during the Spanish Flu pandemic. The Animal Industry Department was allowed to reclaim the space in 1920. Since 2012, the building has been home to USU’s Mathematics and Statistics Department. Professor John Stevens, department head, said the renovation would create “expanded space for the Aggie Math Learning Center (AMLC) that provides highly utilized drop-in tutoring for students in Logan and statewide in math & stat courses taken by essentially every major, a research lab for the Data Science and AI Center — a joint venture among multiple campus units — and modernized research collaboration spaces for faculty and students.” The first stage of the construction project is to relocate underground utilities. Crews will place fencing on the west and north sides of Animal Science from the Eccles Science Learning Center to the Geology building. Pedestrians will be able to pass by the site on the west side of the building by traveling on existing walkways adjacent to the ESLC. Pedestrian access between Animal Science and Geology to the Quad will be blocked. While the utility work is likely to be concluded before the end of the year, additional fencing to the east and south of the building will be placed in January and extend onto the pavement on the north side of the Quad. “We understand that this is a major disruption to central campus but feel that this plan will preserve the safety of faculty, staff, students, and construction personnel during this period,” said Tom Graham, project architect/manager for USU Facilities Planning, Design, and Construction. The College of Arts & Sciences’ Math & Stats Department main office was relocated to the third floor of Old Main over the summer. Students needing help with math and statistics are advised to visit the AMLC in its temporary location on the fourth floor of Merrill-Cazier Library. Additional information about department programs and locations during construction can be found on the Math & Stats moving page .

title: USU President Invites All Employees to Campus Picnic
summary: Utah State University President Brad L. Mortensen has invited all faculty and staff across the university system for a campus picnic on the Quad in Logan to kick off the new academic year. Employees are encouraged to drop by for lunch when they can between 12:30 and 2 p.m. Aug. 18. “I’m so excited to connect with our university community and hear about the remarkable work our faculty and staff are doing in the areas of research, teaching and outreach,” Mortensen said. “I hope to make this an annual gathering where we can hang out and get to know each other more.” For those unable to attend the campus picnic in Logan, Mortensen and his leadership team will also again tour USU campuses across the state Oct. 27-30 to connect with faculty, staff, students and local community members. Statewide campuses will hear more about the tour in the coming months.

title: USU Psychology to Launch Behavioral Neuroscience Major
summary: Utah State University will launch a new behavioral neuroscience program for undergraduate students in October. Students can begin coursework in January for the new major, part of the Department of Psychology within the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences in January. Behavioral neuroscience examines the relationship between the brain and behavior and includes training in chemistry, biology, and psychology. Behavioral neuroscience gives students specialized knowledge and practical skills that prepare them for a variety of educational paths and careers in research, health, technology, and other rapidly developing areas. Scott Bates, head of the Department of Psychology at USU, said that student interest was the primary motivator in the creation of the new major. Currently, psychology is one of the most popular majors at USU, with an average of 200 students graduating with a bachelor’s degree each spring. Many of those have expressed a desire to dive deeper into connections between the brain and behavior during their time as undergraduates at USU. “Our behavioral neuroscience degree came directly out of conversations with our students,” Bates said. “We were hearing from students who were deeply interested in the connections between the brain and behavior and wanted a degree that would let them pursue those interests in a focused way. Our students will graduate with a distinctive combination of knowledge and skills that will prepare them for graduate and professional education as well as a wide range of careers.” Students in the program will build a strong foundation in neuroscience, brain and behavior, biology, chemistry, research methods, and quantitative reasoning. They will also have opportunities to explore areas such as cognition, learning, genetics, neurodevelopment, mental health and psychological disorders, and behavior analysis. “One of the things that distinguishes our program is its strength in behavior analysis,” said Christopher Warren, associate professor of psychology and director of the behavioral neuroscience program. “USU has nationally recognized expertise in the experimental analysis of behavior, giving students an opportunity to study behavior using rigorous experimental and quantitative approaches.” Students who earn their bachelor’s degree in behavioral neuroscience from USU can step directly into the workforce and pursue careers in research, public health, laboratory sciences, and other related fields. Students can also choose to continue their education through graduate school or professional training. The USU behavioral neuroscience program is designed to align well with many common medical-school prerequisites . “One of the great strengths of our program is that it prepares students for a wide range of options after graduation,” Warren said. “Utah’s growing technology industry is one example of where this training can be especially valuable, because employers increasingly need people who understand human behavior and have experience with experimental design and data analysis.” Undergraduate students can apply to the USU behavioral neuroscience program next month by reaching out to their academic advisor. The Department of Psychology will also host a launch party from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Oct. 22 in the International Lounge at the Taggart Student Center. Students may meet with faculty, ask questions about the program, and apply to the program if they are interested. For more information, visit the USU behavioral neuroscience program website or email psychology@usu.edu . To learn more about the Department of Psychology, visit cehhs.usu.edu/psychology .

title: USU Public Safety Distributes Annual Security & Fire Safety Report
summary: As part of its commitment to transparency, Utah State University has distributed its 2026 Annual Security and Fire Safety Report, which outlines campus crime statistics, fire safety data, and university policies related to campus safety. “At USU Public Safety, our mission is to foster a safe, secure, and welcoming environment for every member of the USU community, including students, faculty, staff, and their families,” said Ellis Bruch, executive director of public safety. “As an open and accessible university, we are equally committed to the safety and well-being of all visitors across our campuses.” The 2026 report includes: Campus crime, arrest, and referral statistics provided by USU Police, Campus Security Authorities, and local law enforcement Fire safety data for residence halls University policies and procedures addressing alcohol and drug use, sexual assault, relationship violence, stalking, hazing, and other safety practices “Campus safety is a shared responsibility,” Bruch said. “We encourage everyone in the USU community to review the report and share feedback, concerns, or suggestions as we continue to strengthen our efforts.” USU’s annual security report also includes recent campus safety improvements: Increased outreach on safety measures to the campus community, including 205 events to 12,667 individuals, an 80% increase. A new position to coordinate statewide emergency management and better serve statewide campuses. A new position to coordinate security cameras across USU’s statewide campus system. USU Public Safety has three branches: a police department, emergency management, and the fire marshal’s office. These units work together to ensure USU remains a safe place to learn, live, and work. The report is published each year in accordance with Utah Code Section 53B-28-401, the Campus Safety Plan, and the federal Jeanne Clery Act. It is designed to provide students, faculty, staff, their families, alumni, and the public with important information about safety at USU. The 2026 Annual Security and Fire Safety Report is available on the Department of Safety website. A copy of the report is available upon request or may be accessed online through the institution's website. Please contact the USU Department of Public Safety or the USU Police Department for additional information.

title: USU Research Challenges the Accepted Paradigm for Pregnancy Recognition in Ruminants
summary: New research from Utah State University has transformed biologists’ understanding of pregnancy recognition in ruminants, invalidating a key theory that had gone unchallenged for over 40 years. A paper describing this research, Pregnancy in type I interferon receptor (IFNAR2) knockout sheep challenges the accepted paradigm for pregnancy recognition in ruminants , was published in the August 2026 issue of the Biology of Reproduction, by Christopher J. Davies. Evan K. Peterson. Aaron J. Thomas. Andrea L. Giles. Young-Min Lee. Irina A. Polejaeva. Heloisa M. Rutigliano. The research team was comprised of individuals affiliated with The Department of Veterinary Clinical and Life Sciences in the College of Veterinary Medicine. The Department Animal, Dairy, and Veterinary Sciences in the Quinney College of Agriculture and Natural Resources. The Center for Integrated Biosystems. In an editorial commentary, Alan D. Ealy from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, wrote: “Davies and colleagues have unequivocally answered an important question and, in doing so, have opened the door to new questions, challenged prevailing assumptions, and stimulated the rigorous debate that drives scientific progress.” The “prevailing theory” Ealy referred to had been the basis for more than 1,900 peer-reviewed publications examining the biology of ruminant reproduction. The emergence of this theory in the 1960s and 1970s suggested that, in sheep, the conceptus (the fetus and surrounding placenta) must produce a signal during a critical window of early pregnancy to maintain progesterone levels necessary to sustain gestation. Research pointed to a protein called interferon tau, produced by the outer cells of the placenta. Scientists believed interferon tau was the signal that “tells” the female sheep that she is pregnant, kicking off biological processes necessary to maintain a growing fetus. Decades of research established that interferon tau has important biological effects during early pregnancy; however, researchers had not been able to directly test whether interferon tau’s signaling through the classical type I interferon receptor was essential for pregnancy to be established. Although it was clear that interferon tau is released by the conceptus and has biological effects associated with early pregnancy, the question remained: is interferon tau signaling essential for maternal recognition of pregnancy? USU researchers had previously created, through gene-editing and animal cloning technologies, a sheep model that was ideal for testing this theory. This model in which the type I interferon receptor is inactivated was originally created to study Zika virus infection. These sheep lack a subunit of the type I interferon receptor, rendering this receptor non-functional. This receptor, when functional, binds to interferons alpha and beta, two type I interferons central to the immune response in sheep. It also binds to interferon tau. The original goal was to study how Zika virus infection progresses without a functional type I interferon receptor. After the viral study concluded, these knockout sheep remained in USU’s herd and were used to study the receptor's impact on early pregnancy. The researchers initially hypothesized that female interferon receptor knockout sheep would be infertile. For this study, two 9-month-old knockout ewes (female sheep) were placed in a pen with a ram (a male sheep) to be bred. Davies then monitored the ewes’ levels of progesterone. Of the experiment’s outset, Davies said: “We expected to get some interesting information about how the signaling works in early pregnancy. However, the results forced us to reject our initial hypothesis that interferon receptor knockout ewes would be infertile.” In a non-pregnant or cycling sheep, after 17 days, or the length of a sheep's reproductive cycle, the progesterone level should drop, but in the two interferon receptor knockout ewes, the level remained elevated. “When after 25 days the progesterone level was still elevated, I thought, Gee, it looks like these sheep could be pregnant,” Davies said. The two sheep were pregnant, as subsequently confirmed by ultrasonography. In May 2023, the pregnant ewes gave birth to healthy, normal lambs. The experiment demonstrated that sheep lacking functional receptors for type I interferons, including interferon tau, could still establish and maintain pregnancy. “That was shocking because it challenges the accepted paradigm of how reproduction works in ruminants,” Davies said. In presenting these findings at international conferences, the researchers faced a barrage of questions. After all, other experts in the field had relied on the previously accepted notion of pregnancy recognition in ruminants for decades. Ealy, who holds the position of Board of Reviewing Editors for Biology of Reproduction, noted in his editorial that the strong reaction to the findings was to be expected, and an essential part of the scientific process when a long-standing paradigm is challenged. He pointed out that Davies embraced the questions and used the feedback to strengthen the experiments and their interpretation. The findings open new avenues for study, and more questions. The research does not rule out other biological roles for interferon tau or the possibility that it acts through alternative mechanisms. “Interferon tau might help protect the conceptus against infections, which is a more normal function of a Type I interferon,” Davies said. And are there other candidates for doing the job interferon tau was previously thought to do? That will require more research, too. Revelations like these have been made possible by advances in genome sequencing and gene editing, which allow scientists to directly test biological assumptions that earlier generations could investigate only indirectly, Davies said. “I think it’s important to point out that the people who did the original work weren’t trying to mislead anybody, they were very smart people,” he said. “It’s just that they didn’t have the tools back then to directly test the hypothesis the way we were able to do in this study.” Dr. Heloisa Rutigliano, Davies’ co-author and colleague, says the unknowns raised by the USU team’s findings are an example of what makes science so exciting. She is currently developing further testing methods to attempt to answer some of these emerging questions. “New technologies allow us to go back and directly test ideas that have been accepted for decades, sometimes because the evidence supporting them was very strong. When new evidence challenges those ideas, it doesn’t diminish the science that came before it, it’s just how science advances,” Rutigliano said. “That constant process of questioning, testing, and revising our understanding is what makes scientific discovery so dynamic.” This research was supported by Agriculture and Food Research Initiative Competitive Grants no. 2021-67016-33504 and 2024-67016-42366 from the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

title: USU Researchers Modeling Burn Scars to Predict Potential Flood Severity
summary: A wildfire is a dazzling spectacle of dread and destruction. As it dances through a landscape, it moves and bends with the wind, sometimes created from the depths of its own consumption. Its yellow-orange light has tantalized and traumatized generations of humans and animals alike — stretching back eons to Earth's creation. The smoke and ash produced from the flames darkens and reddens the sun, sometimes for hundreds of miles, signaling that somewhere the world is alight. Left in the wake of this brightness and heat is a place darkened and muted. And like its creator, it is itself now a manufacturer of mayhem. Burn scars, as the name suggests, are the semi-permanent remains of a landscape torched by wildfires — charred trees, burned-over bushes, and soil that's been baked by temperatures reaching thousands of degrees Fahrenheit. As a result, "the soil becomes very hydrophobic," says Belize Lane, a watershed hydrologist with the Utah Water Research Laboratory. --- The remainder of this article will be featured in the fall issue of the Utah State Magazine coming in October .

title: USU Statewide Campuses to Host Paying for College Events
summary: Utah State University Statewide Campuses will be hosting several Paying for College Events at various USU campuses around the state beginning Oct. 19. All prospective students and their families are welcome to attend at the campus that best fits their schedule and location. Paying for College Events are designed to help students and their families better understand the financial side of attending college and connect them directly with people who can help. The goal is to make paying for college feel more understandable and manageable by bringing admissions and financial support resources together in one place. These events provide an opportunity to ask questions, learn about available resources, and get hands-on assistance early in the college planning process. “I’ve worked with students and families for many years, and I know that figuring out how to pay for college can feel overwhelming,” said Vanessa Liesik, director of Statewide Recruitment and Engagement. “Often, the hardest part is simply knowing where to start. That’s what I love about these Paying for College events. We’re bringing people and resources together in our local communities so families can ask questions, understand their options, and leave feeling like they have a plan. Students and families don’t have to figure this out on their own.” During the events, prospective students and families can meet with officials to explore local scholarships and federal aid. They can also get help with the application process and learn about the resources USU Statewide Campuses have to offer to support student success. Representatives from Student Financial Support and Admissions will be available to answer questions and help students understand their next steps. These representatives can also help with completing FAFSA and explore budgeting and financial planning resources. “Understanding how to pay for college can feel overwhelming, but students and families do not have to navigate it alone,” said Craig Whyte, executive director of Student Financial Support. “Our goal is to help students understand the resources available to them, how to access those resources, and what steps they can take to make college more affordable. These events are an opportunity to ask questions, get personalized guidance, and build confidence in the path ahead. We encourage students and families to come visit with us and take advantage of the support available. While these events are especially helpful for high school students and their families, anyone considering attending USU who has questions about paying for college is encouraged to participate. Students who would like FAFSA assistance are encouraged to create their FSA ID in advance and bring the information they need to work on the FAFSA. USU Paying for College Event Dates and Times Oct. 19 – USU Tooele , 5-7 p.m. Oct. 20 – USU Brigham City , 6-8 p.m. Oct. 21 – USU Wasatch (Salt Lake) , 5:30-7:30 p.m. Oct. 22 – USU Kaysville , 6-8 p.m. Oct. 27 – USU Blanding , 11 a.m.-1 p.m. Oct. 28 – USU Moab , 11:45 a.m.-2:30 p.m. Oct. 29 – USU Uintah Basin (Roosevelt), 5-7 p.m. Nov. 2 – USU Southwest (Virtual), 5-7 p.m. Utah State University’s Statewide Campuses create impact by bettering the lives of the people and places they serve. From career and technical certificates to doctorate degrees, USU offers programs that help fuel local economies and empower individuals and their communities. With multiple locations across 85,000 square miles, USU can be the hometown university to anyone, no matter where they live. Learn more at statewide.usu.edu .

title: USU Study Finds Why Some Companies Face Greater Stock Market Penalties for Missing Earnings Forecasts
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Missing Wall Street's earnings expectations can come at a steep cost for publicly traded companies, but new research from Utah State University's Jon M. Huntsman School of Business reveals that not all companies face the same consequences. Lynn Rees, the Bonnie B. and James H. Quigley/Deloitte Foundation Professor of Accountancy, and Grant Bischoff, a USU accounting alumnus currently pursuing his doctorate at the University of Georgia, recently published their findings in the Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting. Their study, "Factors that attenuate the negative stock price response to missing analyst forecasts," analyzed more than 207,000 quarterly earnings announcements from 1990 to 2019 to examine how investors respond when companies fail to meet earnings expectations.
