The researchers found that companies missing analyst forecasts experience an average stock price decline of approximately 3% to 4% surrounding the announcement. However, the severity of that penalty varies significantly depending on company characteristics. Larger companies, those already reporting losses, and those with widely differing analyst forecasts generally face smaller penalties. Meanwhile, companies with substantial intangible assets or rising stock prices leading up to an announcement experience more severe reactions. The findings provide new insight into the pressures executives face to meet earnings targets, which can influence financial reporting practices and business decisions. Understanding these differences could help investors, regulators, and researchers better identify where incentives for earnings management are strongest. The publication also highlights the lasting impact of faculty mentorship at the Huntsman School, with Rees and Bischoff continuing their academic collaboration beyond Bischoff's graduation from Utah State. The study is available open access at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11156-026-01511-y .

title: USU Survivor Support, Advocacy, and Violence Intervention (SSAVI) Office Expands Scope, Updates Name
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Utah State University’s sexual assault and anti-violence office is expanding its focus to support students who have experienced a broader range of harm and has updated its name to the Survivor Support, Advocacy, and Violence Intervention (SSAVI) Office. The updated name reflects the office’s expanded scope of services while maintaining its commitment to providing confidential advocacy, resources, and support to students navigating experiences of harm. The SSAVI office will continue providing the same confidential services, and advocates will work with students to help them understand what happened to them, learn about their rights, explore available resources and determine what type of support they want. Support is available based on each student’s needs and preferences, with students able to receive as little or as much advocacy as they would like. The office also provides limited legal support related to protective orders and stalking injunctions. As part of its expanded services, SSAVI is collaborating with Reach Peers through USU’s Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS). Reach Peers provide students with ongoing, peer-based support and opportunities to develop skills for managing mental health and life challenges. Students can meet with a Reach Peer for 30-45 minutes, up to once a week. Peer support can include active listening, basic emotional support, and practicing skills selected from a range of available options. SSAVI is also providing an office space for Space Makers. Space Makers is a USU program that gives students a confidential setting to talk through life’s challenges. The Space Makers are USU students trained in conflict management and facilitation through coursework, observation, ongoing training, and practice in holding safe, exploratory conversations. Lastly, SSAVI is also expanding its ability to serve students at USU’s Statewide Campuses through the addition of BreAnna Taylor, who is based at the USU Price campus. Taylor has been involved with SSAVI team for several years, first serving as a volunteer and intern before formally joining the team last spring. She will be working 25 hours per week providing virtual advocacy services to USU students throughout the state. Through virtual services, confidential advocacy can be provided to help students understand their options, connect with resources, and determine what type of support may be most helpful. For more information about the Survivor Support, Advocacy and Violence Intervention Office and its services, visit usu.edu/ssavi or email ssavi@usu.edu More information about the Reach Peer program is available here . More information about the USU Space Makers program is available here .

title: USU Teams Up With Utah Startup Company to Advance Retinal Disease Research
summary: A local biotechnology startup built on research from Utah State University has received federal funding for a new biomaterial that could help scientists better study age-related macular degeneration and other eye diseases. MyxTek Bio, a Cache Valley biotechnology company, received a $305,000 award from the National Science Foundation to further develop the material, which is made from engineered hagfish proteins. Researchers hope the material can be used to create improved laboratory models of tissues in the back of the eye, helping scientists learn more about retinal diseases and test potential treatments. The one-year grant brings together MyxTek Bio and Utah State University researchers. Specifically, the team will refine how the engineered proteins are produced and evaluate whether the resulting material can serve as a synthetic version of Bruch's membrane, a thin layer of tissue that plays an important role in maintaining eye health. The project builds on nearly eight years of research at Utah State University and represents a step toward turning a university discovery into a product that could support scientists now and commercial development in life science, biotechnology, and more down the road. "This award is an important validation of both the technology and the commercial opportunity," said Christian Iverson, co-founder and CEO of MyxTek Bio. "We're building a company around a unique material that could improve biomedical research today while opening the door to entirely new applications in healthcare, advanced materials, and sustainable manufacturing in the future." The engineered hagfish protein technology was developed in the laboratory of Justin Jones, associate professor of biology at Utah State University and co-founder of the company. Hagfish are best known for producing large amounts of slime as a defense against predators. The slime contains strong protein fibers, and Jones and his research group at USU have developed ways to produce those proteins in the laboratory using microorganisms rather than harvesting them from hagfish directly. One goal of the project is to show that the proteins can be produced reliably and consistently, an important step in moving a laboratory discovery toward broader research and commercial use. "For a biomaterial to move beyond an academic laboratory, you have to be able to make the same material reliably and know exactly what you are producing," Jones said. "We have spent years learning how to produce and process these proteins. This project allows us to establish the manufacturing and quality-control framework needed to make the material available for broader research and, ultimately, commercial use." A second part of the project will focus on retinal disease research in the laboratory of Elizabeth Vargis, associate professor of biological engineering at Utah State. Vargis proposed using the engineered hagfish proteins to create a synthetic version of Bruch's membrane. The membrane supports retinal cells and plays an important role in maintaining healthy vision. Changes to the membrane are linked to age-related macular degeneration and other eye diseases. AMD is one of the leading causes of vision loss among older adults. Scientists rely on laboratory models to better understand how the disease develops and to evaluate possible treatments. However, existing models often do not accurately reflect the environment found in the human eye. Researchers on this project will create thin membranes from the hagfish-protein material and test how well retinal cells grow and function on them. The goal is to create a more realistic research tool that could improve studies of retinal disease and speed up the development of future therapies. "Bruch's membrane is remarkably thin, but it plays a critical role in supporting retinal cells," Vargis said. "I was searching for the right material to build better lab-based models of age-related macular degeneration. Through collaborations with Justin Jones and MyxTekBio, we've developed a hagfish protein-based biomaterial that more closely mimics the natural environment of the retina, giving us a more physiologically relevant platform to study this disease." The collaboration reflects the goal of the NSF's Small Business Technology Transfer program, which helps universities and small businesses work together to move promising research toward real-world applications. While MyxTek Bio focuses on producing and refining the material, researchers at Utah State University will continue developing and testing its use in retinal research. Although the current project focuses on eye disease research, the research teams believe the protein technology could eventually be used in other biomedical and advanced-material applications. Potential future uses include research tools, medical devices, sustainable materials, regenerative medicine, and other biomaterials. MyxTek Bio also received support from the Nucleus Institute during development of the proposal. Through commercialization training, proposal review, and connections to funding resources, Nucleus helped strengthen the funding application. “Every MarketEdge team gets the same eight weeks, and MyxTek Bio made full use of every one of them. They came in with strong science and emerged with a clear understanding of their customer and what it will take to reach the market, something that often takes founders years to determine,” said Angela Smith, COO of the Nucleus Institute and leader of MarketEdge Scale. The Utah State University Office of Research also supported development of the project. This project highlights Utah State University's commitment to helping researchers move discoveries beyond the laboratory and into the marketplace. For MyxTek Bio, the award represents a critical milestone in transforming a promising university discovery into a technology platform with wide-reaching applications. For USU, it demonstrates how federally funded research and collaborative industry partners can work together to create meaningful scientific, societal, and economic impact. In addition, the award provides an opportunity for MyxTek Bio to expand operations in Cache Valley, create skilled jobs and strengthen Utah's growing biotechnology industry. "This is just the beginning," Iverson said. "Our vision is to build a platform biomaterials company in Utah that creates value from university-developed innovations. This award gives us an opportunity to demonstrate the technology, strengthen the company, and position MyxTek for future growth." About MyxTek Bio MyxTek Bio is a Utah-based biotechnology company commercializing engineered hagfish protein technologies licensed from Utah State University. The company is developing a platform of tunable biomaterials for applications in cell culture, regenerative medicine, advanced materials, and sustainable manufacturing. About Utah State University Utah State University is a Carnegie R1 research institution committed to advancing discovery, innovation, and entrepreneurship through research, education, and industry partnerships. About Nucleus Institute The Nucleus Institute is a Utah-based innovation and entrepreneurship organization that helps researchers, inventors, and startup founders translate scientific discoveries into commercial ventures. Through customer discovery training, mentoring, proposal development support, and connections to industry and funding partners, Nucleus helps emerging companies accelerate commercialization and create economic impact. About the NSF STTR Program America's Seed Fund powered by NSF supports deep-technology startups and small businesses translating breakthrough scientific discoveries into products and services with societal and commercial impact.

title: USU Tech Startup Wins First Place at 2026 Utah Business Innovation Awards
summary: In 2016, Bedri A. Cetiner founded a company commercializing antenna designs from Utah State University engineering students. Ten years later, those efforts have led to a major award. Cetiner’s USU-backed startup, i5 Technologies, won first place in the Industrial Manufacturing, Materials & Construction Tech category at the 2026 Utah Business Innovation Awards. USU teams create the antennas of various wireless communication systems, enabling users to provide more service with less energy, power, or battery. i5 Technologies is currently commercializing these solutions. “I didn’t plan to be on the commercialization side of my academic work, but then I realized how fun and exciting it was,” said Cetiner, an electrical and computer engineering professor. “For us to take first place was a big accomplishment we weren’t expecting.” These antennae are developed by Cetiner’s research group at i5 Technologies, as well as graduate students, some of whom join the company after finishing their studies. “Seeing the reward for that hard work in the form of a real-life product is an amazing experience,” Cetiner said. "We’re developing next-gen technologies, like quantum communication, and I'm also trying to instill that innovation into my students through my teaching at USU.” While students are contributing to the success of the startup, Cetiner said the work also benefits their learning. “You need to keep updating teaching material in this very fast paced world,” Cetiner said. "This startup process helps, because it shows you need to be competitive in the commercial domain and keep pushing the pedal to develop technologies that can be incorporated into teaching." Cetiner hopes the collaboration between i5 Technologies and USU’s Technology Transfer Services and Integrity and Compliance Office serves as an example of jointly managing conflict of interest, academics, and commercial environments for faculty to pursue their innovative ideas. “This is a critical management skill to translate your university work into real-life applications,” Cetiner said. “If your hard work is combined with integrity, everyone benefits from the innovation.” Since winning the award, i5 Technologies has received growing attention, Cetiner said. With USU as a company stakeholder, he hopes to propel more student and faculty startups that will achieve commercial success and show what USU-born companies are capable of.

title: USU to Feature Connection, Education, Celebration at National Hispanic Heritage Month Events
summary: LOGAN — Utah State University’s Heritage & Culture team is celebrating National Hispanic Heritage Month with a series of free events. The celebrations, beginning Sept. 29, will honor the histories, cultures, and contributions of Hispanic and Latin American communities. A National Hispanic Heritage Month program will take place on from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Sept. 29 in the TSC International Lounge. Heritage & Culture has invited community members to present interactive exhibits and share personal perspectives. The event will feature a photography exhibit by J.P. Spicer-Escalante, Nuestros Vecinos (Our Neighbors), showcasing members of the local Hispanic community. Attendees will also connect with campus organizations engaged in activities centered around Hispanic language, culture, research, and education. The celebration will continue 6 p.m. Oct. 2 in the TSC Ballroom with Fiestas Américas, one of USU's longstanding cultural events originating in 2003 under the name “Salsabration.” This annual event celebrates Latino culture through a mix of dance performances, singers, art displays, traditional foods, and other cultural practices. Attendees are invited to join a high-energy community Zumba session and Latin dancing to finish off the festivities. National Hispanic Heritage Month, originally established in 1968 and now observed annually from Sept. 15 through Oct. 15, recognizes the generations of Hispanic Americans who have enriched the nation's history and society. This monthlong observance coincides with the independence anniversaries of several Latin American countries, making it a meaningful opportunity to recognize the histories, cultures, and contributions of Hispanic Americans. USU’s Heritage & Culture fosters community-building through the celebration of heritage and shared experiences. All events are free, and everyone is warmly bienvenido ( welcome) to join us para conectar, aprender, y celebrar (to connect, learn, and celebrate).

title: USU to Mark Sept. 11 With Day of Service, Memorial Stair Climb
summary: This year marks the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. To honor the spirit of sacrifice made that day and the sacrifices that continue to be made by members of the armed forces and their families, Utah State University is inviting its students, faculty, and staff across the state to participate in the National Day of Service and Remembrance. Memorial Commemoration & Moment of Silence As part of USU's commemorative events , wreaths and photos will be displayed outside Champ Hall on the first floor of Old Main and at the outdoor Sept. 11 Memorial north of Huntsman Hall. A moment of silence will be observed at 6:46 a.m. Sept. 11 at the outdoor memorial. Day of Service Those interested in giving back can find local or virtual service opportunities and log the university's collective impact through USU's GivePulse page . Departments with a service project to host can contact Nelda Ault-Dyslin, assistant director of community-engaged learning, to have it added to GivePulse. In support of this year's anniversary of the attacks, USU will permit employees to use regular work time for volunteer service projects on Sept. 11, subject to advanced supervisory approval. For those not scheduled to work on Sept. 11, employees are still encouraged to volunteer, but it will be on their own time because employees may not defer any paid service time for this event to another day. Memorial Stair Climb In the evening, the USU Department of Public Safety will host the 9/11 Memorial Stair Climb at Maverik Stadium in honor of the nearly 3,000 lives lost that day and the first responders who made the ultimate sacrifice. Participants will climb in remembrance of those who were lost and in tribute to the courage, service, and sacrifice of first responders who climbed to save others. The stair climb is presented in collaboration with the USU Veterans Resource Office and the Logan City Fire Department. Registration opens at 5 p.m., and the climb begins at 6 p.m. For more information on the stair climb, contact Rhett Hellstern at rhett.hellstern@usu.edu . For questions about hosting a service project, contact Nelda Ault-Dyslin at nelda.ault@usu.edu. More

title: USU UWLP Releases New Report on Educational Attainment of Utah Women
summary: The Utah State University Utah Women & Leadership Project has released a new research and policy brief, Educational Attainment of Utah Women: A 2026 Update . The report provides an in-depth analysis of how Utah women’s education levels have changed over time and how they compare to national trends. It draws on the most recent American Community Survey data and highlights persistent gender gaps, regional differences, and statewide challenges in degree completion. Susan R. Madsen, founding director of UWLP and coauthor of the report, said educational attainment is widely recognized as a driver of opportunity, health, and economic mobility. “Through our research, we learned that higher levels of educational attainment are consistently linked to improved health and fitness, greater marital satisfaction, enhanced child welfare, stronger mental health, and higher levels of civic engagement,” she said. “Yet these benefits are not evenly distributed — and Utah’s patterns reveal both progress and areas of concern.” Utah’s Educational Landscape Shows Mixed Progress The report analyzes current ACS data and historical trends to assess how Utah women and men are faring across key educational milestones. Utah continues to outperform national averages in high school completion, with only 7.3% of adults lacking a diploma compared to 10.3% nationally. Women in Utah have earned high school degrees at slightly higher rates than men for two decades. However, Utah remains among the states with the highest percentage of adults who start college but do not finish. In 2024, 22.2% of Utah adults aged 25 and older had completed some college but no degree. The report highlights that Utah still ranks among the worst states for its high percentage of men and women who start college and do not finish, underscoring the need for targeted retention strategies. At the bachelor’s level, Utah women and men earn degrees at similar rates, and Utah outperforms national averages. But gender gaps persist in graduate education. Utah men earn graduate and professional degrees at higher rates than women across all age groups, with the largest gaps appearing among older adults. Regional Differences Across Utah Counties The report includes detailed county-level data showing substantial variation in educational attainment across the state. Rural counties face specific challenges in high school completion, while some rural areas — such as Summit and Wasatch counties — lead the state in bachelor’s and graduate degree attainment. Gender gaps also vary widely by county, with some rural regions showing significant disparities in graduate degree completion. Policy Implications for Utah The report outlines several policy priorities to strengthen educational outcomes statewide: Expand access to high-quality secondary and postsecondary education, especially in rural regions. Invest in evidence-based strategies to improve college retention and completion. Address gender gaps in graduate education through targeted recruitment, support, and financial pathways. Strengthen partnerships among higher education institutions, policymakers, and community organizations to align educational goals with workforce needs. “As Utah continues to navigate rapid economic change, workforce demands, and persistent gender disparities, these findings highlight both progress and urgency,” Madsen said. “Utah needs to continue to aggressively focus efforts on increasing enrollment and completion rates for both women and men at all degree and certification levels.” Yvette Young, research manager, Utah Women & Leadership Project, is lead author of the report.

title: USU Welcomes Utah Symphony to Logan on Sept. 17
summary: The world-renowned Utah Symphony will bring world-class artistry to Utah State University’s Logan campus Sept. 17 with a one-night-only performance featuring internationally acclaimed cellist Zlatomir Fung . Tickets for the concert, hosted by the Caine School of the Arts in the College of Arts and Sciences , are free for USU students, faculty, and staff. Tickets for the general public are $20, with $10 tickets for patrons ages 8-18. The performance, which begins at 8 p.m., will be in the Daines Concert Hall of the Chase Fine Arts Center on campus. The age limit for the concert is 8 years and older. “This is an extraordinary opportunity to experience an unforgettable evening of breathtaking live music,” said Nicholas Morrison, director of the Caine School and professor of music. “We hope our community will join us for this exciting and enriching event.” Fung earned First Prize at the 2019 International Tchaikovsky Competition Cello Division, becoming the first U.S. musician, and the youngest artist ever, to receive the award. His recent career highlights include his Hollywood Bowl debut with the Los Angeles Philharmonic, opening the Utah Symphony’s 2026-2027 season, and performing with the London Philharmonic Orchestra. An increasingly active composer as well as musician, Fung serves as a faculty member at his alma mater, The Juilliard School. “Tickets are going quickly and we encourage our patrons to reserve their tickets right away,” Morrison said. “We are thrilled to offer this performance, which embodies the caliber of experiences we strive to provide for our students, to the local community.” He adds the Caine School is grateful to the College of Arts and Sciences and the Tanner Trust for Utah Universities, which provided support for the concert as well as master classes for USU music students conducted by Fung and Utah Symphony musicians. To reserve concert tickets, visit the Caine School of the Arts Box Office site .

title: USU's New College of Veterinary Medicine Comes to Life
summary: As summer wraps up, so does the construction at the newly completed Thomas and Patricia Willis Veterinary Medical Education Building — USU's cornerstone hub for its College of Veterinary Medicine . The state-of-the-art facility will provide modern classrooms, laboratories and clinical training spaces designed to support hands-on learning, research and collaboration. The building plays a critical role in addressing the growing demand for veterinarians — particularly in rural communities, where access to large-animal care remains a significant challenge. Utah's agricultural industry contributes an estimated $1.82 billion to the state's economy, underscoring the importance of expanding veterinary training within the state. With the addition of this facility and the continued growth of its four-year Doctor of Veterinary Medicine program, Utah State has expanded enrollment to 80 students per graduating class, helping build a sustainable veterinary workforce for Utah and beyond.

title: USU's Restoring the West Conference Is Restored
summary: The Restoring the West workshop, founded in 2006, brings together leading scientists and managers from across the West to bridge the gap between university research and on-the-ground experience. It will be Oct. 22-23 at the Utah State University Eccles Conference Center in Logan. USU Forestry Extension is teaming up with the Utah Forest Restoration Institute to present the two-day event. It features presenters from state and federal land-management agencies, private industry and nonprofits, as well as scientists, researchers, practitioners, and others representing forest restoration and natural resource management. “After a six-year hiatus brought on by the pandemic and staffing changes, Restoring the West returns this year with new partners, renewed energy, and the same commitment to bringing people together to advance forest and land restoration,” said Darren McAvoy, USU Extension forestry specialist and co-organizer. He said the conference is designed to create meaningful opportunities for communication and collaboration between managers and scientists. Beyond presentations and discussions, the format gives participants ample time to exchange ideas, build connections, and continue conversations over meals and refreshments. USU has also partnered with the University of Utah to host a bonus event on Friday afternoon. Charting a Roadmap of Wildfire Research and Policy in Utah will feature presentations from USU and U of U researchers, followed by small-group sessions. The half-day workshop the afternoon of Oct. 23 is free and aims to highlight potential research and policy collaborations between USU and U of U faculty and map directions for wildfire research in Utah. Walk-up and online registration is $125 and includes lunch on both days and heavy hors d’oeuvres during the evening poster session. Although the Charting a Roadmap of Wildfire Research and Policy in Utah workshop is free, attendees are encouraged to register. For more about Restoring the West and a detailed program, click here . title: USU's Science Unwrapped Explores Hidden Physics Behind Artistic Expression on Sept. 18
summary: The world is filled with moments that make us stop and wonder: A beautiful piece of music, the colors of a rainbow, the shimmering surface of a soap bubble, or the rich sound of a musical instrument. “Although these experiences seem completely different, they are connected in remarkable ways,” says Utah State University physicist David Smith. “At Science Unwrapped , we’re going to explore the surprising physics behind wondrous sights and sounds we encounter every day.” Smith, senior lecturer in USU’s Department of Physics , will present “The Hidden Science Behind Artistic Expression,” at 7 p.m. Sept. 18 in the Eccles Science Learning Center Emert Auditorium, Room ESLC 130, on the Logan campus. All ages are invited to the free gathering, hosted by USU’s College of Arts and Sciences (ArtSci) . Hands-on learning activities led by USU student groups and community volunteers, along with refreshments, will follow the half-hour presentation. “Our Sept. 18 event is the kick-off of our new Fall 2026-Spring 2027 ‘InterPLAY of Art & Science’ series,” says Brynja Kohler, Science Unwrapped chair, associate dean in the College of Arts and Sciences, and professor in the Department of Mathematics and Statistics. “I won’t give away all the talk’s surprises, but get ready to make music together.” Smith’s presentation will be video-recorded and posted on the Science Unwrapped website following the in-person event. The InterPLAY of Art & Science series schedule is as follows: Sept. 18: “The Hidden Science Behind Artistic Expression,” USU physicist David Smith . Oct. 16: “The Physics of Ballet,” USU physicist Tonya Triplett and ballet dancer Becky Erickson . Nov. 13: “Uncreated: Being Human in the Age of AI,” Jordan Leary, visual artist and video game designer . Jan. 22: “Serious Sport as Serious Play,” USU kinesiologist Al Smith, Endowed Dean of the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences . Feb. 26: “Science in Stage Effects,” USU video artist and set designer Joshua Legate . March 19: “Human Possibilities in Interplanetary Exploration,” planetary scientist Amanda Hendrix, Planetary Science Institute . April 2: “Sustainability in the Arctic,” science communicator Cana Itchuaqiyaq, Center for Sustainable Engagement in the Arctic, Virginia Tech University . Parking for the event is free in the Aggie Parking Terrace at 700 E. 600 North, and in the Big Blue Parking Terrace at 850 E. 700 North. summary: What do physics and ballet have in common? A lot!
