title: USU's Utah Women & Leadership Project Releases New Research on Suicide in Utah
summary: The Utah State University Utah Women & Leadership Project has released a new research snapshot, Suicide Among Utah Girls and Women: A 2026 Update . The report provides an overview of suicide trends in the state and how they vary by gender, age, race, ethnicity, and geography. Drawing on the most recent data from a variety of sources, it highlights persistent challenges, demographic disparities, and areas where targeted prevention efforts are urgently needed. Cindy Jenkins, co-author of the report, said suicide remains one of Utah’s most pressing public health issues. “Suicide is a complex, multifaceted problem that affects individuals, families, and communities across Utah, and its impacts extend far beyond mortality rates,” she said. “Utah continues to experience higher suicide rates than the national average, with notable differences across gender and age groups.” The snapshot reports that Utah’s age-adjusted suicide rate is 20.6 deaths per 100,000 people, significantly higher than the national rate of 14.9. Although Utah’s rate has fluctuated over the past decade, it remains consistently elevated. Key findings include: Men die by suicide at much higher rates than women, accounting for nearly three-quarters of suicide deaths in Utah. Women attempt suicide more often, reflecting different patterns of risk and help-seeking behavior. Youth and young adults continue to experience high rates of suicidal ideation and attempts, with suicide remaining the leading cause of death for Utahns ages 10 to 24. Middle-aged adults (35-54) also show elevated suicide rates, aligning with national patterns. Native American and White Utahns experience the highest suicide rates among racial and ethnic groups. The research shows that suicide is influenced by multiple factors — including mental health conditions, substance use, economic stress, relationship challenges, and access to lethal means — requiring comprehensive, evidence-based prevention strategies. For girls and women, risk can be heightened by depression, anxiety, eating disorders, body image concerns, bullying, trauma, intimate partner violence, reproductive and hormonal changes, minority stress among LGBTQ+ populations, and limited access to supportive relationships or care. Regional Differences Across Utah Counties Suicide rates vary substantially across Utah’s counties. Rural counties — including Duchesne, Uintah, Carbon, and San Juan — show some of the highest suicide rates in the state. These regions face unique challenges, including limited access to mental health providers, longer travel distances for care, and higher rates of firearm ownership. Counties along the Wasatch Front generally report lower suicide rates, though youth suicide remains a concern statewide. Policy Implications for Utah Inspired by the work of the Utah Suicide Prevention Committee and Coalition and other key partners, the report outlines several policy priorities to strengthen suicide prevention efforts: Expand access to mental health services, particularly in rural and underserved regions. Increase evidence-based prevention programs in schools, workplaces, and community settings. Strengthen crisis response systems, including continued investment in 988 and SafeUT. Reduce access to lethal means, especially firearms, through safe storage education and community partnerships. Support families and communities affected by suicide through postvention resources and coordinated care. “As Utah continues to navigate rapid demographic change, mental health challenges, and persistent disparities, these findings highlight both progress and urgency,” said Susan R. Madsen, founding director of UWLP and coauthor of the report. “Utah must continue to aggressively focus efforts on prevention, early intervention, and access to high-quality mental health care for individuals and families across the state.”

title: USU's Utah Women & Leadership Project Releases Research on Utah Employers Championing Women
summary: The Utah State University Utah Women & Leadership Project has released a new research and policy brief, 2026 Companies Championing Women: Best Practices for Utah Employers , which summarizes the latest data from the statewide Companies Championing Women initiative. The report highlights how Utah employers are adopting flexible, family-friendly, and women-focused policies that strengthen recruitment, retention, and advancement for women across industries. The CCW initiative — originally launched as 100 Companies Championing Women in partnership with the Governor’s Office of Economic Opportunity — continues today under the stewardship of City Journals community newspapers, with the UWLP and Sego Leadership serving as partners. For the fourth consecutive year, the CCW initiative recognized companies that demonstrate meaningful commitment to supporting women in the workplace. In 2026, 145 companies were honored, representing sectors such as finance, education, healthcare, manufacturing, technology, nonprofit, retail, arts and culture, and human services. “Utah’s long-term economic success depends on workplaces that better support all Utahns,” said Susan R. Madsen, founding director of UWLP and lead author of the report. “This year’s CCW cohort shows that many employers are stepping forward with policies and practices that help women thrive at work, strengthen leadership pipelines, and improve overall workplace culture.” Key Findings Demographics The 145 recognized companies reflect broad statewide participation. Nearly 59% were based in Salt Lake County, 15.9% in Utah County, and the remainder were distributed across Summit, Davis, Weber, and other counties. The organizations ranged from small businesses to employers with more than 1,000 employees. Of these, 54.5% were for-profit, 37.9% were nonprofit, and 6.2% were government. These demographics illustrate the CCW initiative's growing reach and employers' commitment across Utah to advance women in the workplace. Family-Specific Policies and Benefits Family-friendly policies remained a cornerstone of CCW participation. The most common offerings included transition back-to-work support (64.8%), paid maternity leave (64.1%), paid paternity leave (53.8%), paid family leave (46.9%), and unpaid family leave (44.1%). Companies also reported childcare support (28.3%), adoption and fertility benefits (20.7%), and return-to-work or reentry opportunities (36.6%). Employers described flexible schedules, phased return-to-work programs, lactation accommodations, caregiver resources, and innovative offerings such as infant-at-work policies and transition coaching. These supports help retain women through major life transitions and reduce barriers to workforce participation. Flexible Work Policies and Benefit Flexible work arrangements were among the most widely adopted practices, such as flexible hours (87.6%), remote work (85.5%), and quality part-time positions (72.4%). Other offerings included compressed workweeks, part-time roles with benefits, and job-sharing programs. Employers emphasized that flexibility improves recruitment, retention, productivity, and employee well-being – particularly for women balancing caregiving responsibilities. Professional Development and Leadership Many companies were investing in leadership pathways and development opportunities for women, including gender diversity at mid- and senior-level leadership (67.4%), women serving on boards (54.2%), mentoring or sponsorship programs (45.1%), women-focused professional development (38.2%), unconscious bias training (36.1%), and women’s employee resource groups (ERGs) or networks (25.7%). Employers reported that diverse leadership teams strengthen decision-making, innovation, and organizational performance. Leadership academies, coaching, stretch assignments, and structured recruiting strategies help expand women’s representation across industries and roles. Other Workplace Practices Additional practices included pay equity efforts (73.6%), tuition reimbursement for employees (35.2%), unlimited PTO (17.9%), and tuition reimbursement for dependents (6.2%). These policies reflect growing recognition that equitable compensation, career development, and supportive benefits are essential to attracting and retaining women in the workforce. Implications for Utah Employers The findings highlight several opportunities for Utah employers to strengthen workplace culture and advance women’s careers. These include: expanding flexible and family-friendly policies, investing in leadership development and sponsorship for women, increasing women’s representation in executive and board roles, strengthening pay equity and transparent compensation practices, and building inclusive cultures through ERGs, allyship initiatives, and bias training. “As Utah continues to navigate workforce shortages in some industries, demographic shifts, and rising employee expectations, these findings underscore both progress and urgency,” Madsen said. “Employers that champion women strengthen their organizations, their communities, and Utah’s economic future.” Additional co-authors of the report are Brie Sparks, associate director, UWLP, and Deborah Lin local outreach and resource manager, UWLP.

title: Utah 4-H Youth Get World Perspective in Ireland, Peru
summary: This summer, two groups of Utah State University Extension 4-H youth experienced life way beyond the county fair. They built roads and friendships in Peru and explored agricultural innovation in Ireland. The Utah 4-H international travel program was established to provide youth with opportunities to broaden their understanding of agriculture, culture, leadership and personal growth through experiences abroad. Reflections from participants on trips to Ireland and Peru show that these programs create lasting impacts that extend far beyond sightseeing. During the trip to Ireland, youth discovered that while agriculture varies around the world, farmers everywhere share similar values. Sharon Bee, Weber County 4-H program coordinator, said her group observed that successful farming there is very un-Utah-like in its climate, geography and natural resources. “Irish agriculture is highly export-oriented and relies on technology to remain competitive,” she said. “Robotic dairy operations, apple processing facilities and modern crop production systems demonstrated how innovation is transforming agriculture there.” Entrepreneurship was another important lesson, Bee said. The 4-H youth saw how international businesses continually refine products and services to create greater value. The Peru experience, led by Vernon Parent, Extension professor, 4-H statewide youth leadership and civic engagement, emphasized personal relationships, cultural understanding, resilience and self-confidence. He said whether playing soccer with neighborhood youth after visiting Machu Picchu or living in a remote village while completing a road-building service project, they formed genuine friendships that left lasting impressions. “Many of the 4-Hers gained a deeper appreciation for their own lives after witnessing the living conditions in rural Peru,” Parent said. “Despite limited resources, local residents displayed remarkable optimism and resilience. Happiness often comes from perspective rather than possessions, leading to meaningful discussions about gratitude and perseverance.” The Peru trip was also physically and mentally challenging, he said. Hiking at elevations between 7,500 and 14,000 feet, hauling rocks and helping construct village roads tested the youths’ ability to accomplish difficult tasks. Their hard work earned the respect of local villagers, and the blending of cultures created new perspectives for everyone. “Students learned traditional dances, explored local customs and discussed family roles in Peru,” Parent said. “Visits to ancient historical sites and conversations with local guides also enriched their appreciation for Peru’s heritage and history. The youth also met families living on floating reed islands; a centuries-old way of life. They experienced the challenges of preserving culture while adapting to change.” Both the Ireland and Peru trips helped youth recognize the value of earning and saving money to pay for their trips. They gained a sense of independence, responsibility and pride. Although the journey included challenges, most agreed the experience was worthwhile, and they were going to start saving for the next international trip. For more information about 4-H programs, visit extension.usu.edu/utah4h .

title: Utah Agricultural Products BBQ to Celebrate 30 Years of Community, Agriculture, Student Scholarships
summary: Utah State University will celebrate the 30th anniversary of the Utah Agricultural Products BBQ on Sept. 26. This year’s event marks three decades of bringing together agricultural producers, community members, alumni, and students in support of scholarships in the S.J. & Jessie E. Quinney College of Agriculture & Natural Resources. What began as a grassroots idea to connect the agriculture industry with university students has grown into a beloved annual tradition and a powerful force for creating bright futures for students. Over the past 30 years, the Ag Products BBQ has raised more than $369,000 to build an endowment and funded more than 400 scholarships, helping students pursue careers across agriculture, food production, and natural resources. “This really started as a way for the industry to invest in its future,” said Randy Parker, chair of the Ag Products BBQ Board. “It’s become a labor of love, an event that brings together the university, the industry, and the community to do something meaningful for students.” This year, the BBQ is in conjunction with Utah State’s Homecoming football game and festivities. The food-fair-style BBQ attracts over a thousand attendees each year and highlights the best of Utah’s agricultural industry. Producers, including cattle ranchers, fruit and vegetable growers, dairy farmers, and wool growers, prepare and serve food directly to guests — assisted by current college students, faculty, and staff members — to create a unique farm-to-table experience and a rare opportunity for connection. That direct interaction makes the event so impactful as participants get opportunities to meet the people who grow and produce their food, strengthening understanding and appreciation for agriculture. “There’s tremendous value in that connection,” Parker said. “People can talk directly with producers and better understand where their food comes from. It’s a powerful way to bring everyone together.” For students, the event’s impact goes far beyond a single day. Scholarships funded through the BBQ help alleviate financial burdens, allowing students to focus on their education and career goals. Allie Crumley, a veterinary science student, scholarship recipient, and Quinney College Ambassador, said the experience has been life-changing. “This scholarship really allowed me to focus more on my classes and not worry as much about the financial side of my education,” she said. Crumley has also witnessed firsthand how the BBQ fosters lasting relationships. “It really brings together the students, donors, sponsors, and the community, and you can see how they all are working toward a common goal,” she said. “You can make lifelong friendships and be part of something bigger than yourself.” In addition to strengthening relationships, the BBQ plays a critical role in educating the public. By creating a space where consumers and producers interact directly, the event helps bridge the growing gap between people and their food sources, highlighting the importance of agriculture in a time when that connection may get lost. As the Ag Products BBQ enters its 30th year, its legacy is clear: a community-driven event that has grown into a lasting partnership dedicated to supporting students and advancing agriculture. “This is something people look forward to every year,” Parker said. “It’s a feel-good event that has done a tremendous amount of good.” The 30th anniversary celebration will be from 2-5 p.m. Sept. 26 at the Craig Aston Park on the USU Logan campus, 1390 N. 800 East. For more information and to purchase tickets, go to qanr.usu.edu/alumni/ag-bbq .

title: Utah Assistive Technology Program Awarded Grant to Boost Accessibility for Victim Services
summary: Nationwide, people with disabilities experience violence at nearly four times the rate of people without disabilities. The need for services is great, but sometimes inaccessibility stands between help and the people who need it. A three-year, $600,000 project funded earlier this fall by the U.S. Department of Justice and led by Utah Assistive Technology Program Director Bora Lee seeks to tear down accessibility barriers. It provides training and connects service providers to appropriate assistive technology devices that help people with disabilities live independently throughout the state of Utah. UATP’s partners on the grant are the National Federation for the Blind of Utah and the Sego Lily Center for the Abused Deaf. UATP is part of the Institute for Disability Research, Policy, and Practice, which is located on the USU Logan campus within the Emma Eccles Jones College of Education, Health, and Human Sciences. “What interested me most about this work is recognizing that survivors with disabilities can face additional barriers when trying to access victim services,” Lee said. “Those barriers can involve communication, technology, physical access, or simply not knowing what accommodations and resources are available. She added: “We are working with experts who support people who are blind or have low vision, as well as a victim service organization that specializes in serving people who are Deaf or hard of hearing. Their expertise helps ensure that the training is grounded in real experiences.” The Importance of Accessibility and Training Hildegard Koenig, an advocate who has served as a liaison between UATP, victim services, and underserved communities, explained why accessibility and training are so important. “A lot of times, we work in silos . That’s when the survivors will fall in the cracks of the system,” Koenig said. She stressed that disability takes many forms, and it isn’t always obvious. People who have experienced domestic violence may have sustained a traumatic brain injury as a result. These injuries can have lifelong effects, but they’re often hidden. Training can prepare service providers to serve victims of all abilities. They will have a better understanding of why a domestic violence victim may have trouble focusing or remembering, or why they are tired all the time. Training can help them know where to go for a portable ramp if a person with disabilities needs one. It can tell them where to find a device to facilitate communication or navigation within a shelter. NFB-Utah Director Everette Bacon said the technology that helps overcome accessibility barriers to the blind may be unavailable at a domestic violence shelter. For example, if the abuser has been using a mobile phone to track a partner’s movements, that phone may be left behind by the victim, or confiscated by the shelter. But the phone may also have an app on it that helps the victim read print. “ The centers themselves are not equipped with any type of technology to help,” Bacon said. “Most of the time, blind people who go to those types of facilities for help are treated like they're very dependent on the staff. And the staff is not really understanding how to best fit the need.” Bacon hopes the grant will help service providers connect individuals with the right equipment. A secure phone or iPad, equipped with a visual interpretation service, can do a lot to help a blind client navigate a shelter and access printed material. But more than that, Bacon hopes to improve staff expectations through training offered by the grant. Erin Kelly Watkins, executive director of the Sego Lily Center for the Abused Deaf said through an interpreter that the deaf community needs to have access for communication. Ninety percent of people who are deaf come from hearing families — sometimes with limited signing skills. Watkins said the result is often language deprivation. “Deaf people are manipulated easily because of that lack of communication,” Watkins said. “It leads to isolation, especially for women, especially in rural areas.” Those who are deaf may struggle to communicate that something is wrong at home. They may be left out of conversations at school about what constitutes abuse. And once they come to a shelter, they may encounter communication and daily living barriers all over again. Assistive technology like virtual interpreters can help, but Watkins also stressed the need for live interpreters who are not affected by computer glitches or firewalls. Other technology aids could include a flashing alarm to let a deaf mother know her baby is crying, or technology that alerts a hard of hearing individual to an incoming phone call. Training could also help staff understand the need for interpretation, and that deaf patrons may need longer to fill out forms or paperwork. “The lasting effect I hope to see is that accessibility becomes part of everyday practice, rather than something organizations think about only when a specific need comes up,” Lee said. “We want providers to feel more confident recognizing barriers, making appropriate accommodations, and knowing when and how to connect with disability-specific experts and resources. A major strength of this work is that we are not approaching accessibility in a general or one-size-fits-all way.”

title: Utah Conservation Corps Host Service Events to Celebrate 25 Years of Service
summary: LOGAN, Utah — The Utah Conservation Corps is hosting service events In Logan, Moab, and Salt Lake City in celebration of its 25-year anniversary. Members of the public are invited to serve alongside current Utah Conservation Corps AmeriCorps members at these events that highlight current projects with longstanding community partners. The first event will be from 2-4 p.m. Sept. 24 in Moab and will spotlight Utah Conservation Corps’ role in the ongoing multi-partner Pack Creek restoration project. Utah Conservation Corps AmeriCorps members have been removing invasives like Russian olive in the Pack and Mill Creek riparian corridors in Moab. The cut invasives will be used as firewood, and volunteers are invited to assist loading firewood into a dump trailer for the Warm Elders Program, which serves the Navajo Nation. An event from 2-4 p.m. Oct. 15 in Salt Lake City will focus on Utah Conservation Corps work with the city’s Department of Public Lands at the Cornell Wetlands along the Jordan River. Volunteers are invited to plant natives in wetland areas where Utah Conservation Corps crews have worked with Salt Lake City to remove invasive species. Interested volunteers can directly sign up at https://slc.volunteermatters.org/volunteer/sign-up/2957 . Finally, an event on Oct. 17 at the Flores Family Community Garden (357 ½ S. 100 West) in Logan will showcase Utah Conservation Corps’ support of local food security efforts. Volunteers will assist in preparing the garden for winter season. “We’re excited to show off some recent projects our AmeriCorps members have served at in support of our mission to develop the conservation leaders of tomorrow. Project sponsors like those at these three events have been critical giving our AmeriCorps members mentorship, high-impact skills, and experiences completing critical natural resource projects throughout the state,” said Sean Damitz, executive director for the USU Center for Community Engagement and co-founder of the Utah Conservation Corps. For more information about volunteer events, please contact Sean Damitz at 435-770-6104 sean.damitz@usu.edu . Utah Conservation Corps is an AmeriCorps program within the Utah State University Center for Community Engagement, Since 2001, more than 3,000 Utah Conservation Corps AmeriCorps members have served 2.3 million hours creating or maintaining over 5,000 miles of trail and nearly 700 miles of fence, restoring approximately 90,000 acres of public land and reaching nearly 600,000 students individuals with environmental education. For more information about the Utah Conservation Corps please visit www.usu.edu/ucc .

title: Utah State Athletics Announces Bobby Wagner Number Retirement Ceremony
summary: Utah State Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker announced Monday that Aggie football legend Bobby Wagner will have his No. 9 retired during a halftime ceremony in either the 2026 or 2027 season. The specific game date will be determined based on Wagner’s availability, with additional details to be announced at a later time. “Bobby exemplifies what it means to be an Aggie, and this honor is long overdue,” said Walker. “We are excited to recognize his achievements in a Utah State uniform and all he has accomplished in the NFL and in his community. Retiring his number and displaying it on the side of our press box for current and future Aggies to see is a well-deserved honor to celebrate an amazing football career and a remarkable person.” Wagner will become just the third player in program history to have his number retired , joining Merlin Olsen (No. 71) and Elmer “Bear” Ward (No. 35). “I’m truly honored to have my number retired,” said Wagner. “This is something I could have never imagined. Utah State took a chance on me. They were my only offer and the only school that truly believed in me. They gave me more than just an opportunity to play football. They helped me build a career and provided stability during a difficult time in my life. The coaches, professors, staff, and students all played a role in shaping who I am today. I’ll forever be grateful. Go Aggies!” Regarded as one of the greatest linebackers in NFL history, Wagner was selected in the second round (47th overall pick) of the 2012 NFL Draft by the Seattle Seahawks. During his 14-year professional career, Wagner has been named to the NFL’s All-Decade Team (2010–2020) and was a key member of Seattle’s Super Bowl XLVIII championship team. He is a six-time First-Team All-Pro selection, a five-time Second-Team All-Pro honoree, and a 10-time Pro Bowl selection. Wagner helped lead the Seahawks to back-to-back Super Bowl appearances, including a championship victory in 2014. During his illustrious NFL career, Wagner has recorded 2,000 tackles to rank third all-time and is just 60 tackles shy of becoming the career leader in tackles in NFL history. Off the field, Wagner was named the 2023 Art Rooney Award winner and the 2025 Walter Payton NFL Man of the Year. He is also a minority owner of the WNBA’s Seattle Storm. One of the most accomplished players in Utah State history, Wagner earned first-team All-Western Athletic Conference honors three times and led the Aggies in tackles in three seasons. He started 46 of 48 career games and finished with 446 tackles, tied for the most in school history. His career totals also include 29.5 tackles for loss, 4.5 sacks, four interceptions, three fumble recoveries and one forced fumble. He recorded 23 double-digit tackle performances during his career. As a senior in 2011, Wagner helped lead Utah State to its first bowl appearance in 14 years and its first winning season in 15 years, culminating in a berth in the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. He totaled 147 tackles that season, which still ranks seventh all-time in program history, after recording 133 tackles as a junior and 115 as a sophomore. Wagner concluded his collegiate career by earning Most Valuable Player and North Team Most Outstanding Player honors at the 2012 Senior Bowl. In 2021, Wagner was inducted into the Utah State Athletics Hall of Fame .

title: Utah State Athletics Receives $2.5 Million Pledge
summary: LOGAN, Utah — Utah State Vice President and Director of Athletics Cameron Walker announced a transformative gift to the athletics department Monday. An anonymous donor pledged $2.5 million over five years, motivated by their belief in the department's vision and its potential to make an immediate impact on coaches and student-athletes as Utah State Athletics begins its inaugural season in the Pac-12 Conference. "I am deeply grateful for the generosity and the significant impact this gift will have on the future of Utah State Athletics," Walker said. "Our goal is not only to compete in the Pac-12 but to excel. Gifts like this provide crucial support for our coaching staff and student-athletes as they strive for competitive excellence. Utah State needs more dedicated supporters to help us achieve these ambitions." Read more at UtahStateAggies.com .

title: Utah State Celebrates Record Fall Enrollment
summary: Utah State University enrolled a record 32,286 students this fall, an 8% increase driven in part by significant growth in concurrent enrollment and at campuses across the state. “USU’s growth is about more than enrollment numbers. It’s about creating opportunities for more students and communities across Utah,” President Brad L. Mortensen said. “As the state’s land-grant university, we have a responsibility to make higher education accessible whether that’s helping high school students get an early start on college, providing educational opportunities closer to home, or offering a vibrant residential college experience in Logan.” Statewide Enrollment Growth This fall, 15,563 undergraduate students enrolled at the Logan campus, while enrollment at USU’s statewide campuses increased 39%, reflecting growing demand for educational opportunities in communities throughout Utah. USU’s fall 2026 enrollment highlights also include: A 18% increase in male student enrollment of first-time undergraduate students who had delayed college for over a year after high school graduation. A 1% increase in graduate enrollment, with an 11% increase in new graduate students, largely driven by the new College of Veterinary Medicine. The new college saw the largest growth with 76 students welcomed on campus this fall. Twenty-two percent of new students are the first of their family to pursue a college education. As USU welcomes more students, the university remains focused not only on expanding access to higher education but also on helping students succeed and complete their degrees. That commitment is reflected in Utah State's new strategic plan , launched Oct. 16, which focuses on statewide impact, student success, discovery with purpose, and civic-mindedness in all the university does. The plan will guide the university's efforts to expand opportunities for students, advance research and discovery that expand knowledge, and create new possibilities and strengthen communities across Utah.

title: Utah State Football Hires Skyler Ridley as Wide Receiver Coach
summary: LOGAN, Utah – Skyler Ridley has been named Utah State's wide receivers coach it was announced Monday by second-year head coach Bronco Mendenhall. Ridley comes to Utah State after spending the last 10 years on staff at Weber State, including seven seasons as a full-time assistant. With the Wildcats, Ridley coached the tight ends and wide receivers and served as the special teams coordinator each of the last four seasons. "Skyler Ridley is an elite in-state recruiter with deep relationships throughout Utah, and that will be invaluable as we continue to build our program the right way," said Mendenhall. "He brings a strong special teams background, a clear vision for developing wide receivers, and most importantly outstanding character. Skyler aligns perfectly with our culture, our standards, and how we want to represent Utah State Football." In his time with the Wildcats, Ridley was part of nine-straight winning seasons, four Big Sky Championships, and six trips to the FCS Playoffs. With Ridley on staff, Weber State finished the season in the top 10 in the nation five times. "I'm extremely excited and grateful for the opportunity to join Utah State as the wide receivers coach," said Ridley. "Working alongside Coach Mendenhall and his staff is a tremendous opportunity, and I'm eager to get to work building strong relationships with our receivers, the entire team, and the Logan community. My family and I are truly excited to be part of what makes Utah State such a special place. I'm looking forward to getting to work, serving our players, and helping contribute to the success of Aggie football." During his time at Weber State, Ridley coached five all-conference players. In 2025, he coached Sloan Calder to All-Big Sky honors as a kicker. Ridley coached a pair of all-conference wide receivers in Jacob Sharp (2024) and Tyler MacPherson (2022). MacPherson was the first 1,000-yard receiver at WSU in 15 years. He also helped develop a pair of all-conference tight ends in Hayden Meacham and Justin Malone. After three seasons (2016-18) as a graduate assistant at Weber State, Ridley was named an assistant coach in 2019 and coached the Wildcat tight ends for three seasons. Prior to the 2021 season, he was elevated to special teams coordinator, in addition to coaching tight ends. In 2022, he began coaching the wide receivers. Under Ridley, the Wildcats had tremendous success on special teams, especially in kickoff returns. During the 2022 season, Ridley coached Abraham Williams to consensus All-America honors as he broke the Big Sky record with four 100-yard kickoff return touchdowns during the season. He was the only player in all of NCAA football (all Divisions) to have more than two kickoff return touchdowns and he set an NCAA record with all four returns being 100 yards. In 2022, Ridley helped lead Weber State to another 10-win season, including an FBS victory at Utah State. He also coached MacPherson to All-Big Sky second-team honors in 2022 and Meacham to third-team honors in 2021. In 2021, he coached Rashid Shaheed who earned All-America honors as a kick returner and finished his career as the FCS all-time leader with seven kickoff return touchdowns. During the spring 2021 season, Weber State finished 5-1 and captured its fourth straight conference title, including the first outright title in school history with a perfect 5-0 Big Sky record. The Wildcats were ranked as high as second in the nation during the season, the highest ranking in school history. A native of Murrieta, California, Ridley graduated from Murrieta Valley High School. He played four years of football at BYU from 2010-13 under Mendenhall. Ridley lettered in each of his last two seasons at BYU and served as a team captain as a senior in 2013. He appeared in 26 games in his career with the Cougars and had 60 catches for 659 yards and three touchdowns. He had a career-high eight catches for 106 yards and caught the game-winning touchdown in BYU's win at Houston in 2013. Ridley earned his bachelor's degree in psychology from BYU in 2014 and earned his master's degree in professional communication at Weber State in 2017. He started his coaching career at Bountiful (Utah) High School where he coached the wide receivers and defensive backs in 2014 and 2015. Ridley and his wife Jasmine were married in 2012. The couple has four children.

title: Utah State University Highlights LGBT+ History Month With Educational Community-Building Event
summary: LOGAN — Utah State University’s Heritage & Culture welcomes students, faculty, staff, and community members to join in commemorating LGBT+ History Month through a free event focused on learning and connection. This educational and celebratory event will be from 11:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m. Oct. 6 along the sidewalks south of University Inn. USU student organizations and departments will host interactive tables encouraging attendees to learn with, and from, each other. These campus partners will offer opportunities to participate in activities, connect with student leaders, learn about campus resources, and interact with academics involved in LGBTQ+ scholarship. Attendees can learn about LGBT+ History Month and learn how it differs from Pride Month. LGBT+ History Month is observed annually in October, highlighting the history, contributions, achievements, and experiences of LGBT+ individuals and communities while promoting understanding, education, and the preservation of LGBT+ history and culture. The month encourages reflection on historical milestones and provides opportunities to learn from a wide range of experiences and perspectives. USU's Heritage & Culture fosters community-building through the celebration of heritage and shared experiences. All events are free, and everyone is welcome to learn, connect, and celebrate.

title: Utah State University Libraries to Open 'Eating the Past: Cookbooks in the Archives' Exhibit Sept. 17
summary: LOGAN — Utah State University Libraries will open “Eating the Past: Cookbooks in the Archives” Sept. 17 in the Merrill-Cazier Library atrium, featuring rare and historic cookbooks from Special Collections & Archives. The exhibit celebrates five years of Eating the Past, a food history podcast on Utah Public Radio. An opening reception will be from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Sept. 17 in the atrium. Visitors can meet the podcast’s hosts, sample historic treats and explore the exhibit before it closes Nov. 23. The event is free and open to the public. The exhibit examines how cookbooks document culture, community, health, innovation, and everyday life. Historic cookbooks appear alongside photographs, menus, advertisements, and other archival materials that show how food traditions have changed over time. Selections range from early medicinal and home economics guides to community cookbooks and modern food trends. Eating the Past debuted in 2021 as a video series before becoming a weekly radio program on Utah Public Radio, hosted by USU faculty. Each episode explores the history behind the foods we eat through recipes, research, interviews, and personal stories. The program airs Sundays at noon before The Splendid Table.

title: Utah State University Surpasses Fundraising Goals With More Than $79 Million Raised Over Past Year
summary: Utah State University achieved a remarkable fundraising milestone, securing $79.2 million through nearly 40,000 contributions from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026 — a significant rise in donations since 2019. Gifts came from more than 10,000 donors, including a record 17 gifts of $1 million or more. At the same time, more than $13.5 million came from donations under $25,000, reflecting the breadth of support from across the USU community. “This year’s results reflect the extraordinary commitment of the Aggie community,” said Matt White, vice president for advancement and president of the USU Foundation. “More than 10,000 donors chose to invest in Utah State and the people and programs that move our university forward. That collective generosity creates opportunities for students today while building a stronger USU for generations to come.” Creating Aggie Impact Donors contributed more than $41.8 million toward “ Building a University of Distinction ,” supporting spaces and resources that strengthen the Utah State University experience. Among these investments is the Thomas and Patricia Willis Veterinary Medical Education Building, the central hub for USU’s College of Veterinary Medicine, featuring modern classrooms, laboratories, and clinical training spaces designed to support hands-on learning, research, and collaboration. The building was named in recognition of a $5 million gift from Thomas and Patricia Willis , whose shared agricultural roots inspired their investment in veterinary education and workforce development. Their generosity, which also includes an endowment supporting the long-term success of the College of Veterinary Medicine, will help USU educate more veterinarians and address workforce needs, particularly in rural and agricultural communities throughout Utah and the Intermountain West. Donors contributed $25 million to “ Accelerate Access and Opportunities ” for students. Among those donors is Daria Wightman, whose experiences at USU helped launch a career in wastewater treatment engineering and inspired her to establish the “daria” Clean Water Scholarship in the College of Engineering . The scholarship supports civil and environmental engineering students interested in water quality and environmental stewardship, helping future engineers pursue their education and prepare to address increasingly complex water challenges. “My giving back to USU was inspired in part by seeing scholarships established by people who shaped my own path,” Wightman said. “I realized I could help future students the same way others helped me.” Another $7.1 million supported “ Elevating the Educational Experience ” through faculty excellence. Alan and Jeanne Hall made a major gift through the Hall Foundation toward the Craig D. Jessop Chair for Choral Conducting and Community Engagement . When fully funded, the endowed position will help USU attract and retain distinguished faculty leadership in choral music while providing students with mentorship, performance, and professional development opportunities and strengthening connections between the university and broader community. Donors contributed an additional $5.4 million toward “ Developing Solutions to the World’s Challenges ” through research and innovation. Chevron’s longstanding partnership with USU includes support for the Janet Quinney Lawson Institute for Land, Water, & Air, where philanthropic funding helps faculty and student researchers investigate issues affecting Utah’s natural resources and provide science-based information to decision-makers. Chevron’s support of the institute has surpassed $130,000 over the past six years , helping advance research on issues including air quality, Great Salt Lake dust, and Utahns' concerns about natural resources. Scholarships Expand Student Opportunity Scholarships are one way donor support directly expands access and opportunity for USU students. This year, 64 new endowed scholarships were created, distributing more than $6.1 million to assist over 2,500 students, and USU welcomed 36 first-time endowment donors. Expendable scholarships also provided more than $5.8 million to students. For Justin and Leslie Haskell, seeing USU students work alongside entrepreneurs in the Dominican Republic demonstrated the transformative power of experiential learning. Inspired by that experience, they established the Justin & Leslie Haskell Family SEED Endowment to help future Aggies participate in the Small Enterprise Education and Development program . Through SEED, students apply classroom knowledge while mentoring entrepreneurs in developing communities. Students in the program gain professional skills and a broader understanding of how their education can improve lives. The Haskells’ endowment will help ensure those opportunities continue for generations of students. Donor support also provides critical financial relief when students need it most. Secondary education major Elizabeth Leishman received the Lonnie & Cheryl Smith Scholarship , an expendable scholarship that is helping her reduce work hours and focus on student teaching as she completes her final semester at Utah State. “This scholarship has helped a lot,” Leishman said. “Not having to worry as much about tuition and fees during this time has reduced a huge amount of stress. Knowing I can dedicate my time and energy to teaching rather than finances has been life-changing.” University-Wide Support Nearly 900 USU faculty and staff contributed almost $630,000, demonstrating their dedication to the university. Through Employee Giving , faculty and staff like Kirsten Barton, an accounting assistant in the Office of the Registrar, support students and programs across USU. Kirsten gives through payroll deduction to the SNAC food pantry, where she sees students benefiting firsthand. Her experience demonstrates how even modest, recurring gifts can collectively make a meaningful difference. “My contribution, combined with giving from other employees, is a simple way to make a collective difference,” Barton said. Alumni giving remains a cornerstone of support. Aggies contributed $34.7 million through more than 4,500 gifts. Scott ’97 and Mindy ’97, ’05 Pratt exemplify this support. Drawing on their shared connection to agriculture and natural resources, the Pratts established two scholarships to support students . They have also created internship opportunities through their company. Their giving helps students gain hands-on experience, explore career paths, and connect their education with the landscapes and communities they hope to serve. Through their philanthropy and mentorship, the Pratts demonstrate how alumni can help prepare the next generation of Aggies for meaningful careers. USU received donations from all 50 states and the District of Columbia, and 28 counties within Utah. The highest totals came from Cache County with $16 million from about 3,000 donors, Salt Lake County with $13.1 million from more than 1,000 donors, and Davis County with $5.4 million from over 600 donors. Out-of-state donations were led by Kansas ($6.6 million), Montana ($6 million), and California ($3.3 million). The Aggie License Plate Scholarship Program has also contributed nearly $3.5 million to student scholarships over its lifetime. "Philanthropy expands what is possible at Utah State University,” said USU President Brad L. Mortensen. “The generosity of our alumni, employees, friends, and partners creates opportunities for students, supports the work of our faculty and staff, and strengthens our ability to serve communities across Utah. We are grateful for their confidence in Utah State and for the difference their generosity makes for our students and our state." To learn more about how philanthropy creates Aggie impact — and the many ways to support Utah State University — visit usu.edu/advancement/ .

title: Utah State University to Host 11th Annual Connections Luminary
summary: Utah State University will celebrate the start of a new academic year with one of its longstanding traditions, the annual Connections Luminary, on Aug. 28. Events will take place at USU campuses in Logan, Price, Blanding and Tooele, bringing together students, faculty, staff, alumni and community members to welcome the incoming class. At the center of the celebration are students enrolled in USU 1010: Connections, Utah State's signature first-year experience course. Each student will carry a lantern inspired by the iconic Old Main tower and participate in a procession that marks the beginning of their journey as Aggies. “The Luminary gives students a chance to reflect on their goal of being part of the graduating class of 2030,” said Jennifer Grewe, the director of the Connections program and associate professor of psychology. “As the USU community members throughout the state participate in these celebrations, these students have a tangible reminder that they are not alone in this journey. They have a community behind them to support and challenge them through their college experience and beyond.” In Logan, students will walk from the Dee Glen Smith Spectrum to the Quad, following the reverse route they will take during commencement. The evening will conclude with a welcome from President Brad Mortensen, delivered in Logan and broadcast to the Eastern, Blanding and Tooele campuses. In a shared moment across the state, each campus will light the "A" blue as a symbol of students' official welcome into the Aggie community. Faculty, staff, alumni and members of the community are invited to attend and celebrate the incoming class. Events are free and open to the public. For more information about the Luminary, contact Student Orientation and Transition Services at (435) 797-0283. Logan Campus Community members should arrive on the east side of the Quad at 8 p.m. Lanterns will be distributed for attendees to hold as they welcome students along the processional route before Mortensen’s remarks and the lighting of the "A" on Old Main tower blue at approximately 9:35 p.m. Blanding Campus Community members should arrive at the Friendship Amphitheater at 7:30 p.m. Lanterns will be distributed before attendees walk to the Blanding Arts & Events Center for speakers and cultural performances. The evening will conclude with Mortensen’s remarks and the lighting of the Block "A" blue at approximately 9:35 p.m. Eastern Campus Community members should arrive at the Geary Events Center at 8:30 p.m. Following a brief program, lanterns will be distributed and participants will walk to Fountain Field. The event will conclude with President Mortensen’s remarks and the Eastern campus lighting of the "U-State” at approximately 9:35 p.m. Tooele Campus Community members should arrive at Veterans Memorial Park, located at 15 Vine St. in Tooele, at 8:30 p.m. Lanterns will be distributed before participants walk to the pergola for speakers and activities. The evening will conclude with Mortensen’s remarks and the lighting of the "A" blue at approximately 9:35 p.m.

title: Utah Survey Uncovers Why Residents Oppose New Data Centers
summary: LOGAN — A new Utah State University statewide survey examines Utah residents’ views on data centers. The results indicate that 75.8% of respondents oppose or strongly oppose building new or additional data centers in Utah. The survey offers insights about what drives this opposition. The findings appear in the first executive summary from a broader research project led by Gina Gilson, Stacia Ryder, and Jessica Schad of USU’s Community and Natural Resources Institute (CANRI). The project will examine data centers’ water and energy demands, Utah residents’ views on data centers, and generate information that could help state and local leaders evaluate proposed development. The August 2026 survey gathered responses from nearly 900 Utah residents and is representative of the state adult population. “We are excited to share some of the initial results from our statewide survey on data centers,” said Schad, CANRI director and administrator of the survey. “One of the most important findings in my view is that public participation in decision-making processes is nearly as important as the amount of energy and water projects consume, meaning that government and business leaders may want to consider how they can engage communities throughout the planning process.” The results show that water and energy use, location, and opportunities for public participation are important considerations for residents evaluating data center projects. The survey predominantly measured reported views of hypothetical project features; it only asked about whether residents support or oppose the Stratos data center in Box Elder, which 60.7% strongly opposed. More than half of respondents (57.2%) strongly oppose data center development, and opposition rises when proposed projects are closer to where respondents live. Residents’ responses also vary with the characteristics of a proposed project. Asked how specific features would affect their views of a data center within 3 miles of home, 54.1% said usage of recycled or other non-potable water would make them more likely to support it. Renewable energy infrastructure had a similar effect for 51.2%, while 43.4% said a project that built or paid for new energy infrastructure would increase their likelihood of support. By comparison, 61.3% said using nonrenewable energy would make them more likely to oppose a local project. The use of nuclear energy increased the likelihood of opposition for 41.4%. Responses to a proposal for public reporting of annual water and energy use were more mixed. “Similar to what we have seen in the context of other energy infrastructure project siting processes, like for shale gas, residents in our survey indicate the continued importance of processes creating avenues for meaningful community participation in these decision-making processes,” said Ryder, assistant professor of sociology. "Additionally, the type of energy and water used to support data centers matters to residents, as respondents were likely to respond more positively to the use of renewable energy and recycled or non-potable water. These are important considerations for shaping planning and public reception." Gilson, assistant professor of environment and society and interim director of USU’s Center for Colorado River Studies, said: “Our survey findings underscore the concern that Utahns feel about our water resources. I think it’s important for us to better understand where the water comes from, how much water is used on-site, and how much is used to generate the electricity that powers data centers. Our research will gather information to help answer these questions." The survey is one part of an ongoing project. CANRI researchers also want to examine public documents and media coverage to assess what information is available about data centers’ water and energy use, and to interview policymakers, developers, community leaders, and residents of select Utah communities affected by data center development. A follow-up survey in 2027 is planned to assess whether residents’ views change over time. To learn more, read the executive summary: https://artsci.usu.edu/canri/projects/data-center-development-in-utah .
